en: I have been idly dwelling on a leisurely day at the origin of the *Śūraṅgama* [Sūtra]. White clouds seal the door; the striking of bamboo against rock has become a tradition like that of Huangyan, and fragrant flowers fill the seat like those of Huìtáng.
Suddenly, the sound of footsteps is heard; a guest opens the door and enters. Sitting upright for a long while, he sighs and says: "Man..."
"Born into the gaps of existence, one is busy and bustling all day long; what is the ultimate reality?
I replied offhand, "To have purple ribbons at the waist and yellow gold on the elbows—this is sufficient. The guest did not respond. I spoke again, saying, "In life, simplicity and purity;
after death, the ink-stained robe—this is the end. The guest said, "Heh! What I call the ultimate is not merely a great matter of human life..."
"Is it nirvana? I did not understand, and the guest also withdrew with hesitation. Several days later, I took up the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and read it;

only then did I come to know that among all phenomena and dharmas, there is none that does not possess an ultimate consummation. What our Master Confucius spoke of—knowing by birth, knowing through learning, and knowing through hardship;
acting with ease, acting with benefit, and acting with diligence—all these ultimately converge in the single accomplishment of returning to the root and attaining knowledge. They are all one.

All dharmas are ultimately [one]. People suffer only from not studying them. If a student unifies their mind upon a single path, then whether sharp or dull, gradual or sudden, what distinction is there between those of the Mahāyāna (Superior Vehicle) and those of the Hīnayāna (Inferior Vehicle)?

The Elder of Wenling said: "It guides one toward the Chan vehicle and decisively discerns right view. The Master Who Observes the Mind said: "It broadly encompasses the Dharma-realm and minutely analyzes it down to the level of atoms. This is...
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* closes off heterodox paths and blocks byways, providing refuge in all ultimate dharmas and serving as the true commentary for clarifying the mind and realizing its nature.
However, its purport is profound and its meanings are manifold; moreover, many in this world possess dull faculties. Study must necessarily proceed through gradual entry.

To discard the commentaries and sub-commentaries while claiming to have realized the true commentary is like casting away a precious raft in the midst of a vast, boundless ocean—without it, who could reach the other shore? [To remain] in the dimness of both...
The Eye: Discarding the Golden Needle. Who can turn the twin pupils? Master Tǎng was truly a precious raft for crossing the river and a golden needle for pricking the eye.
I have personally taken up this work for perusal, extensively translating and searching through its depths, and have gathered the commentaries of Tiānrú.
It extracts the authentic pulse of True Light and gathers the guiding pointers from the Celestial Capital (Tianchu).

It repairs the target-post of Contemplating the Mind and further incorporates the "Elephant-Grasping" (moxiang) of the Patriarch Yunqi. It continues with the "Cutting the Stream" (jueliu) of the Master of Tiantai.

Furthermore, there are masters such as Changshui, Gushan, Wenling, Zuiji, Wuxing, and Hanshan—numbering no fewer than several dozen houses. Their writings fill entire volumes and accumulate across many scrolls; when one unfolds them...
The scrolls were brilliantly displayed, renewing the Dharma-eye of the world. Laborers were assembled and materials gathered; after passing through spring and summer, the work was completed.
Suddenly, the golden winds brought forth the chill, and the jade dew spread across the autumn. He closed the gates to rest, burned incense, and sat in the lotus posture.
He chanted the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* several times with solemnity. A guest again knocked on the gate and requested, saying, "Have you realized the ultimate Dharma? The Dharma is one; you—"

He practiced the supramundane Dharma, banishing delusive thoughts and transcending illusory appearances; from this point on, he clarified his mind and realized its true nature, and the lotus flower manifested before him day by day.
I, however, practiced the mundane Dharma, severing the two characters of "indolence" and "habituation. From this point on, I advanced even further beyond the tip of the fishing pole;

with my black pouch and white tablets, my merit shall be recorded in the annals of history, and attaining the purple robes will be as easy as picking up a blade of grass. At that moment, I was suddenly enlightened.
In conversation with a guest throughout the entire day.
Recorded on the waxing moon of the seventh month in the first year of the Tianqi era by Ling Hongxian, Shudu, the Layman of Tianchi in Wuxing.
Preface to the Annotated Guide to the Śūraṃgama Sūtra:
I have served as a disciple of Confucius and devoted my mind to ancient prose and rhetoric. I have observed that the Six Classics are profound and unadorned—truly the words of the Sage.
The writings of Zuo Qiuming are ornate yet patterned after those [classics], while the stratagems of the State Counsellors are eloquent yet their style is eccentric and expansive.

When Qu Ping was in obscurity, his writings were impassioned with resentment; when Zhuang Zhou was expansive, his writings were unrestrained and marvelous; when Han Fei was analytical, his writings were incisive and penetrating;
and when Sima Qian and Ban Gu were broad in their learning, their writings were grand and majestic. Such were the works of the various masters prior to the Han dynasty.

Although their words differ from one another, for the most part they are expansive and flowing, upright and marvelous. Taking the Six Classics as their standard, they raise the banners of their doctrine;
there is none who does not bow their heads and prostrate themselves in submission. These are regarded as the supreme excursions through the ages—ultimate, exhaustive, and beyond compare.
Yet these are all merely mundane truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not supramundane truths (*lokottara-satya*). [The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* emerges...]
This is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). There is existence, there is non-existence, there is both existence and non-existence, and there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Mysterious, wondrous, strange, and marvelous, it cannot be named. It is like the great void of space: its coming has no beginning, and its going has no end.

Sound becomes the myriad pipes; form becomes the hundred flourishing things. In the eyes, it fills the eyes; in the ears, it overflows the ears. That which departs becomes the old; that which comes becomes the new. As for the substance of that void—what is it?

What exists and what does not exist? What is their name and what are their characteristics? Thus, they are as high as Mount Sumeru, yet their height can be measured; they are as deep as the vast ocean, yet its depths can be fathomed;
their adornments are like floating banners, yet their beauty can be described; they are like the illusions of Master Yan, yet their artistry can be replicated;

their voices are like those of the kalaviṅka bird, yet their tones can be transcribed; their appearing and disappearing, their emerging and submerging, are like the towers of vapors or the illusory cities of merchants. They are but shadows.
It is something that can be anticipated. Yet, it is lofty without being manifest, deep without being measured, majestic without being ornate, and illusory without being artful.
It is seen not as a shadow, nor heard as a sound; neither existent nor non-existent—who could define its names and characteristics?

The Confucian scholars of the world cling to existence and base themselves on the lowly, adhering exclusively to the old and the fragmentary to block their ears and eyes. Next, they embroider them into sashes and handkerchiefs to seek worldly fame.
As for these resources, even the hundred schools have not yet roamed their borders; how could one find leisure to discuss that which lies beyond the Six Classics?
Now, what does carving jade into a writing tablet compare to the ingenuity of the Creator? What does fashioning a monkey from thorns compare to the mastery of form and nature?

What does roaming within the enclosures of the hills compare to the penetration of the four voids? Thus, there is the wandering within the realm of space, and there is the wandering beyond the realm of space. People today are constrained by...
In a dark chamber, the eyes see nothing and the ears hear nothing; one is somber and finds no joy. When a hole is pierced and a crack reveals falling rain, one sighs with relief.
How much more so when one leaves the chamber and sits in the hall, beholding the light of the sun and moon! Seeing the light of the sun and moon, one rejoices with unrestrained delight;
how much more so when ascending Mount Tai, treading upon the Stone Mound, and gazing at the celestial capital, where the rivers and seas appear like a canopy and a sash.
All things exist within it. To ascend Mount Tai, one already feels vast and joyful;

how much more so when one is beside the sun and moon, embracing the universe, taking lightning as a whip and thunder as wheels, letting the will roam and the spirit expand as one wanders through the Great Void—how could such joy not be immense?
The various schools and the Six Classics represent the realm within; the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* represents the realm beyond. To wander therein—
To wander beyond the world is the ultimate form of wandering; to wander within the world is not the ultimate wandering. Nevertheless, if one lacks a worldly mind, one’s practice will lack substance;
if one lacks the aspiration for transcendence, one’s destination will not be lofty. To be substantial, one must be lofty; to be lofty, one must be substantial.
This teaching likely originated from Confucianism. Those in the world who read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* all harbor aspirations for transcendence. Following [this path]...
The sutras possess profound phrasing, while following the commentaries results in a proliferation of meanings; neither approach, taken alone, is entirely adequate.

Therefore, I have divided them into chapters, sections, and phrases to directly expose the mind of the ancients. Having integrated the meaning of the *vibhaṅga* (sections) to divide the *śākhā* (branches), I have further integrated the meaning of the *śākhā* to divide the chapters.
Having integrated the meaning of the sections to divide the phrases, I have likewise integrated the meaning of the phrases [to divide the words].
I have set forth these meanings to clarify the principles. My aim is to ensure that the vital currents flow unimpeded, following the subtle and elusive channels of the *sūtras* without confusion;
and to ensure that the spirit and sentiment are focused and concentrated, stabilizing the profound and mysterious gates and wheels with constancy.

Thus, like the serpent of Mount Changshan, where a strike at the head is answered by a response from the tail, and like the mirror that reveals demons, wherein form appears and spirit is made manifest, I have swept away the weeds and filth of a thousand years and breathed new life into them.
The divine radiance of ten thousand ages—how could it be thought merely capable of wandering through this world?

It is simply that, beyond the hundred schools and the Six Classics, there exists further the Tathāgata’s precious treasury, shining brilliantly across heaven and earth; therefore, I wish to cast my gaze upon it, taking it as the "left-shoulder baring" of Confucius.
In the spring of the *wànlì* *bǐngwǔ* year, on the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth, Yú Wángyán Gāorú of Xīn'ān composed the *Léngyán Moxiàng Jì*.
It quotes from the sutra as follows:
"There were some blind men who, with their hands together, felt an elephant. Those who felt its trunk said that the elephant was like a winnowing basket."
Those who felt its thighs said they were like pillars; those who felt its tail said it was like a broom; those who felt its belly said it was like a stone.
Even when feeling its eyes, they said they were like bellows filled with wind; feeling its ears, they said they were like inverted hanging leaves;
feeling its hooves, they said they were like overturned cups resting on the ground. As each person clung to what they had felt and disputed one another, the onlookers—
I cover my face in laughter. How is today’s discourse on the scriptures any different from this? The Buddha has already entered *nirvāṇa*; there is no way to consult him directly.
We reach out with the hands of our own emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā-vijñāna*) to grope for an image. Each stands like a blind man criticizing another blind man; I am truly grieved by this.

Knowing that we are all blind, it is urgent to remedy this failing. Thus, I have joined the ranks of the blind to grope along with the multitude. Only the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*—among all [the scriptures]...
There are further points of doubt within the sutra. Consequently, these blind men clamored together, clasping arms and pressing their fingers, unable to determine who was right or wrong.
Thereupon, I have taken more than one hundred passages from this sutra and briefly analyzed them as examples for the entire volume.
Formerly, when the disciples of the Buddha each presented their own views, the Buddha said to the assembly: "What you all have said is not my intention. Yet each...

When principle is sufficient to benefit all things, then those various attempts at comprehension—provided they exclude what is contrary to principle and instead comprehend through principle—even if they do not capture the actual form, they have never failed to be forms.
Therefore, one need not worry about the act of comprehending; rather, it is only attachment that is the worry.

If one leaves the mind empty and does not prioritize what entered first, then when the phrasing accords with principle and the principle harmonizes with the phrasing, the underlying meaning will manifest of itself. Thus, the "form" as form will leap forth vividly.
It is as clear as day: one does not obtain a distinct image apart from what is being felt. It is like grasping at a solid wall and holding fast to it;

the more diligently one feels it, the further one strays from the truth. This merely increases frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and incurs the fault of slandering the Dharma—what benefit is there in this?
This is especially true of the matter of instruction, but those who discourse on Chan practice are even more extreme in their "feeling. Some feel a horse and claim it is an elephant; others...
Some feel in the air, claiming it is an elephant; some feel everywhere simultaneously, claiming that all places are the elephant;
others, feeling throughout everything and finding nothing, claim there is no elephant. Such diverse views would require more attendants than one could easily shift to enumerate.
I pray that you, virtuous sirs, turn back and feel for your own eyes. Once you have obtained the faculty of sight, there is no need to feel for the elephant.

In the *Kejing Lianchi* (Lotus Pond Commentary on the Sections), it is stated that there are three parts: the Introduction (*nidāna*), the Main Body (*samyag-mūla*), and the Dissemination (*parivarta*). This is largely the same as the divisions established by Wēnlíng and Chángshuǐ.

Within the Main Body, however, it further divides the text into five sections: Seeing, Cultivation, Realization, Conclusion, and Auxiliary; this too is highly reasonable. First is the Section on Seeing the Path (*darśana-mārga*), beginning from [the character] "Ā" (阿).

It is difficult to request [this teaching], yet it is for the purpose of proclaiming the true nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), so that practitioners may first clearly perceive their own eternally abiding true mind (*tathāgatagarbha*) as the standard for their cultivation. Second is the section on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*):
from the "Two Definitive Meanings" for the beginner, up to the proclamation of the divine mantra (*dhāraṇī*), it enables practitioners to give rise to true cultivation based upon true vision.

There is no separate activity apart from the mind. Third, the Section on the Stages of Realization (*sākṣātkriyā-bhūmi*). From the passage "How is it that the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) is named?
up until "finally exhausting the wondrous enlightenment to achieve the Unsurpassed Way," this causes the practitioner to know that the cause is true and the fruit is correct;

for if the causal ground is not true, the resulting fruit will be circuitous and indirect. Fourth, the Section on the Conclusion of the Sutra. From "What is the name of this sutra? up until "you... [the text continues].
One should uphold this so that practitioners may understand the meanings of the five categories, which are subsumed within the twenty characters of the present title.
These five divisions of the aids to the path range from the seven realms of existence beginning with the hells to the most subtle demonic activities.

By causing practitioners to employ both the primary and auxiliary practices in mutual support and to maintain urgency regarding both the vehicle and the precepts, one can swiftly reach the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). The intermediate detailed sub-sections are either minor or...
They are not the same, yet there is no great obstacle [to this]. Those who study later need only follow the ancients;
they need not establish new regulations or add superfluous details, for in doing so they will attain understanding. For this reason, I shall join with the assembly in following them.

Regarding the general principles for this ink-carved edition of the scripture: we have followed the *Zhengshu* (Commentary on Verification) by Master Tanying throughout. While consulting various editions, there were occasional discrepancies or omissions;
however, fearing that we might inadvertently alter the text, we have merely marked these points with black ink above them, while below, we have used either a circle (○) or...
This is clarified by pointing it out directly.

This scripture was printed in vermilion ink; its general purport elucidates the essential core of the Dharma King and compiles the discussions of various masters to supplement and verify what was omitted in the commentaries.
Where there were occasional words or phrases that were not fully explained, these have been further annotated in detail.
Appended here for the sake of profound examination:

this commentary on the sutra provides a dark-blue clarification (a detailed exposition), correcting the errors of those who, like the great masters [of old], were like men feeling their way with an elephant.

Where there were occasional passages of excessive wordiness and prolixity, I have slightly pruned the words and phrases to preserve the essential meaning. Furthermore, regarding certain insights not yet reached by other masters, I have further refined them.
A single character is provided for the purpose of reference.

When various masters in the sutras address [the Buddha] directly by name, it is out of reverence for the Buddha; this is similar to how names are commonly used in the annotated commentaries and expositions of Confucian texts.
In this scripture, the general outlines and essential questions are marked with ◎. The specific sections and essential answers are marked with ‧.
The major divisions of the scripture are marked with ﹄, while the minor subdivisions are marked with ﹂.

In the sutras, when expounding upon the points of profound realization and spiritual awakening, use [the term] *yong*. When the translated terminology is exquisite, clear, and manifest, use [the term] *yong*.
When there are detailed elaborations branching out from the main outlines and sections of the sutras, use [the term] *yong*.
Regarding the punctuation in the sūtra, the *danda* (。) and the double *danda* (。。) are employed.
In the commentary (*śāstra*), these are likewise used to clarify and elucidate the sūtra.
"Not having seen the Buddha, though one calls it praise, it is actually slander; having already seen the Buddha, to contemplate and offer such praise [is true praise]."
Truly there is nothing to praise. It cannot be praised; it cannot be spoken of; it is inconceivable. For this reason, it is called "Buddha.
After Ren Wenzzi had copied this image, he requested that the Layman (Jushi) copy it again and compose words of praise.
The Layman truly had nothing to praise, so he spoke these verses: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-dharma. No-dharma..."
The Dharma is also the Dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting the non-Dharma, how has the Dharma ever been the Dharma? Sāgara entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa;
Kāśyapa entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda. Thus it is, thus it is—this is what constitutes praise.

The Layman Bi’an Shi Yibin burned incense and transcribed the first fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary] The sūtra has five names; three are preserved in the title while two are omitted—namely, "Mahāvaipulya" and so forth—which are general titles for various sections of the canon. The present title is taken to distinguish it from those.
The title uses "From the Great Buddha-Crown" (*Buddhōṣṇīṣa*) to signify its supreme majesty and, concurrently, to clarify that the esoteric mantra is spoken from the crown. [Wenling says:

The King of Awakening reveals it through the Great Dharma so that one does not lose oneself on the narrow path, and he causes one to silently attain the essence that is beyond all bounds; he illustrates it by means of the Buddha’s crown so that one does not stagnate in the perception of forms, thereby reaching the wondrous pinnacle of the Unsurpassed. [Commentary:

Regarding the term "Tathāgata," according to the sutra, it refers to the "wondrous true suchness-nature of the original Tathāgata-garbha," which is what the *Prajñāpāramitā* refers to as "all... (the *dharmas*).

The Dharma is the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*). What is now called the "secret cause" refers to the fundamental awakening-mind of sentient beings; because all Buddhas attain Bodhi by means of this, it is termed the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata. Because this mind is inherently possessed yet remains hidden and unmanifest, it is called "secret";

when it is realized through cultivation and its manifestation is attained, it receives its name from the perspective of the fruit, thus being called "Tathāgata. Therefore, the name "Tathāgata" applies both to the cause and the fruit, and encompasses both the innate nature and cultivated practice.

When one proceeds from the cause toward the fruit, one is called a "Bodhisattva" of the myriad practices; when the fruit is made to encompass the cause, it is called the "Tathāgata-van" (the Forest of the Tathāgata).
Regarding the title *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-nirvāṇa*, it is translated as "The Ultimate Accomplishment of All Affairs," which is the name of the Great Samādhi.
Section One: The Exposition of the Origin (in four parts).
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom—

These are the great Arhats, free from outflows (anāsrava), who abide within the inner darkness as the Middle Way—neither falling into the two extremes of grasping at signs nor grasping at signlessness. They are the sons of the Buddha who maintain the Dharma; they have excellently transcended all realms of existence. They are able to perfect dignified deportment within the lands, turning the wheel of the Dharma following the Buddha.

Wondrously worthy of his final charge, they strictly purify the Vinaya and propagate the broad model for the three realms (the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm). Their response-bodies are infinite, delivering and liberating sentient beings, uprooting and rescuing those of the future, and transcending all worldly dust and burdens. Their names are as follows:

The great wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana (son of the Makuṣṭha clan), Mahākauṣṭhila (Great-Knee), Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (Son of Full Compassion), Subhūti, Upānanda, and others were the leaders. (This fifth section lists the seating order of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), together with those at the initial stage of their resolve, all of whom came to where the Buddha was. This occurred while the bhikṣus were observing the summer retreat.

During the period of *pravāraṇā* (from summer to autumn, when the Vinaya is relaxed for three days of wandering), bodhisattvas from the ten directions inquire to resolve their mental doubts and respectfully attend to his compassionate grace and majestic authority, seeking the profound meaning. At that moment, the Tathāgata spreads his seat and remains in peaceful repose; for the sake of the assembly, he proclaims the deep and abstruse teachings.

The pure multitude at the Dharma feast attains what they have never experienced before (hearing what they had never heard before). With the *kalaviṅka*’s celestial voice, his sound pervades the worlds of the ten directions, and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gather at the site of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī was the leader. [Initial Assembly and Praise of Virtues] [Commentary]:
Regarding the term "outflow-free" (anāsrava), this is a general praise of their virtues; because they have exhausted all outflows, they are called Arhats. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"By the power of the supreme teaching, that noble path arises, and thus they are named 'Sons of the Buddha' (*buddhaputra*). Abiding in the Dharma they have attained and maintaining it without loss, they are named 'Abiders as Sons of the Buddha. They sustain all realms of existence."

These are the three tainted (*āsrava*) phenomena—karma, afflictions, and their fruits—which, while being extolled for their distinct virtues in the lower realms, constitute a majestic and awe-inspiring model for practitioners; thus they are called "perfected in dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha-sampanna*).

Those who receive the Buddha’s final instructions and are able to establish the Great Purpose are called "wondrously worthy of the testament. Even down to the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they act as models and manifest in response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to deliver sentient beings.

Because they employ both wisdom and compassion and accumulate merit over long kalpas, they are able to rescue future beings and transcend all worldly entanglements. This refers to the *pratyekabuddha*.

Regarding the Pratyekabuddha, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the moment the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, one is termed "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), as they perform only deeds for the benefit of others.

The *Madhyama Āgama* refers to the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) as "liberation from [the precepts]," meaning that upon the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one is released from the restrictions and permitted to act as one pleases; thus, while Ānanda specifically requested leave to travel far and had not yet returned, the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions had already assembled at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

As for the kalaviṅka bird, it belongs to the class of "phoenix-crows"; according to the *Guihai yuheng zhi*, the phoenix-crow resembles a phoenix, and its call is as clear and resonant as a sheng or xiao flute.
Because the combination of the *gong* and *shang* notes can produce the sounds of a hundred insects, the sūtras frequently compare [the Buddha's voice] to the voice of the Buddha.

At that time, King Prasenajit, for the anniversary of his deceased father’s death (*śrāddha*), prepared a vegetarian feast and invited the Buddha to the inner palace (as for the location, it was within; as for the invitation, he went in person). He extensively provided rare delicacies (as for the offerings, they were distinct and precious) and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors (as for the taste, they were sublime).

Furthermore, he personally invited all the great Bodhisattvas (his companions being the same). Within the city, there was also an elder (whose age, virtue, and rank were all eminent), a lay devotee (who dwelt in purity), who at that same time was providing a meal for the Saṃgha and awaiting the Buddha’s arrival.

The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the Bodhisattvas and Arhats to respond to the various hosts of the feast. Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation; having traveled far and not yet returned, he was unable to join the ranks of the monks.

Since there was neither an Elder nor an Ācārya, he returned alone along the way. On that day, there was no offering for him. At that moment, Ānanda took up his alms-bowl and proceeded through the city where he was traveling, visiting house by house in order.

When begging, one should first seek out a final donor (dānapati) to serve as the host of the fast, regardless of whether they are pure or impure—be they of the noble Kṣatriya caste or even a Caṇḍāla. Only then does one practice impartial compassion.

Without discriminating between the lowly and the humble, he resolved to bring all to perfection. All sentient beings possess immeasurable merit. Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for their hearts being uneven as Arhats;

yet he revered the Tathāgata’s impartiality in opening the way for all without exception, thereby delivering them from doubt and slander. Passing through that parched city (a place without water), he walked slowly toward the city gate, his majestic demeanor solemn and composed, observing the rules of pure discipline with reverent gravity.

[The Causes for the Two Errors] [Commentary]: Regarding the "讳日" (huidì—anniversary of a name) in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), the *Bosiruo mingyi yueguang dexing shidi* (The Ten Stages of the Moonlight Virtuous Conduct of King Boshiruo), the *Jiu li* (Book of Rites) states:

"One begins to avoid the names of the deceased after the final wailing. This refers to the fact that after the burial of a feudal lord, seven months later a sacrifice is held in the courtyard of the ancestral temple, which is called the "final wailing.

Thereupon, an edict is issued within the palace to abandon the old names and begin avoiding the new ones; henceforth, no one dares to utter the name. Thus, King Boshiruo established a vegetarian feast on this day to respectfully invite the assembly of sages, thereby providing spiritual sustenance for the spirit of his late sovereign. As for "gongye" (palace quarters), according to the Tang...

According to the *Song Yuan Gong Dian Lu* (Records of the Palaces and Halls of the Song and Yuan Dynasties), the term *yè* (掖) refers to the side-walls (*yèyuán*) and side-gates (*yèmén*), rather than the inner courtyard; it refers to the palace city itself. [Wenling] states:

According to the Vinaya regulations of the Senior Preceptor (*upādhyāya*), when monks travel far, they must be accompanied by at least three companions—one senior preceptor and one instructor (*ācārya*)—so as to solemnize their conduct and prevent errors or omissions.

Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that when entering a village for alms, one should be accompanied by another bhikṣu; this also reflects the intent of guarding against transgressions of the precepts. Finally, regarding the donor (*dānapati*), it refers to one who has not yet fed the Sangha, embodying the compassion of equality.
One maintains an impartial mind toward oneself while transforming others to do the same, thereby perfecting the immeasurable merit of sentient beings.

As for Raṅga, she was filthy and lowly, yet Ānanda did not discriminate against her and thus mistakenly allowed her to fall [into his bowl]. The following passage explains the meaning of equality: Subhūti abandoned the poor to follow the wealthy, while Mahākāśyapa abandoned the wealthy to follow the poor.

One was because the poor plant the causes [of merit], and the other was because the wealthy find it easy to give; therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked them, desiring that their minds be free from attachment.
These restrictions are established to quell doubts and slanders regarding inequality. [Commentary] Regarding the method of the *zhāi* (fasting/observance):

the *Piṇḍapāta Sūtra* states that because all worthies and sages wish to relieve the suffering of the poor, when they enter a village to beg for food, they should maintain the perception of being in a non-city and the perception of seeing no people; thus Ānanda maintained his deportment with strict integrity and solemn reverence according to this dharma.

At that time, while Ānanda was on his almsround, he passed by a brothel (a house of prostitution) and encountered a great illusionist (the sorcery of a non-Buddhist heretic). The woman Mātaṅgī used the *Sāvikāra* mantra, the ancient Vedic incantation of Brahmā.

He was drawn into the seat of lust; his body was caressed by her, and he was on the verge of destroying his precept-body. The Tathāgata, knowing that the arts of lust were being employed against him, returned immediately after the meal.

The king, the great ministers, the elders, and the lay devotees all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essentials of the Dharma. At that moment—precisely when [the destruction] was about to occur but had not yet occurred—the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness (by which all heterodoxies were simultaneously subdued).

From within this light emerged a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), proclaiming a divine mantra. He commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go protect [him]; thus the evil spells were extinguished (as if awakening from a dream), and [the Buddha] led them forth.
Ānanda and Mātanga returned to the Buddha’s presence, their lustful minds suddenly stilled.

[The Buddha recited the mantra three times and went to rescue them. For the sake of the ultimate meaning of the *Sūtra on the Vidyā for Delivering One's Own Kinsmen*, he used Mātanga as the introductory narrative.

The *Mātangī-sūtra* speaks of the incident of the accidental fall: while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, Ānanda was walking for alms when he encountered a woman drawing water; her name was Mātanga. Ānanda asked the woman for water. The woman...
She then followed Ānanda to the place where he was staying, returned home, and informed her mother; weeping and prostrating herself, she desired to give Ānanda in marriage.
Her mother, having no other recourse, used sorcery (*gū-dhāra*) to bind Ānanda and led him into the room. Ānanda refused to go to bed, so his mother took him and attempted to cast him into fire.

The Buddha, knowing this, immediately dispatched a spirit to liberate Ānanda; such was the event. Furthermore, in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*, there is also a secret account of Māra’s realm concerning the past causes and conditions of Matangi.

Since no sūtra other than this one is capable of delivering them, it is taken as the condition for the profound emergence of the Great Teaching. It is said that when the Dharma was being preached within that sūtra, the Māra King intended to cause disturbance;

there was a bodhisattva named *Māragocarānupalipta* (Untainted by the Realm of Māra) who entered the palace of Māra. At that time, the various daughters of Māra each conceived lustful desires toward the bodhisattva.
Knowing that they possessed the karmic conditions to be delivered, he manifested the body of a deva and engaged with them, whereby they attained deliverance.

Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself (touching his head to the ground), and wept with grief. He lamented that from the beginningless start of his births, he had been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet had not fully perfected the power of the Way (failing to perceive the non-existent and thus giving rise to lustful desire; it was simply that his power could not overcome the evil). With earnest devotion, he requested:

"May the Tathāgatas of the ten directions explain the initial expedient means for attaining Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. At that time, there were also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as great Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and others from the ten directions, all of whom likewise wished to hear this.

They withdrew to sit silently, awaiting and receiving the Sage’s instructions. The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "You and I share the same vital breath (*qi*); our sentiments are equal to those of Heaven."

“Brothers, when you first resolved your minds [on enlightenment], what superior signs did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy bonds of worldly affection?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha: “I see that the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks, which are supremely wonderful and extraordinary; his physical form is translucent, like lapis lazuli. I have constantly reflected that these marks could not have been produced by sensual desire. Why is this?

The breath of desire is coarse and turbid, characterized by the mingling of stench and the chaotic mixture of pus and blood; it cannot give rise to such a supreme, pure, wondrously bright, and purple-golden mass of light. Therefore, I am thirsty for it.”

Ānanda bowed and requested to be ordained by the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Excellent! Ānanda, you and all others should know that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, undergone the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure and luminous nature. By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic wandering.

If you now wish to investigate the true, manifesting nature of unsurpassed Bodhi, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind. Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow the same path, they all escape birth and death and do not fall into cyclic wandering precisely by means of a straightforward mind."

Because their speech is straightforward, from the beginning to the end of the stages of realization, they are forever free from any trace of deviousness (all entering through the direct mind). Ānanda, I now ask you:

when you first resolved to attain enlightenment, taking the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks as your object, what did you see, and who was it that felt this longing? Ānanda replied to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, such longing arose by means of my mind and eyes.
Through the eyes I beheld the Tathāgata’s sublime marks, and in my heart I conceived this longing; thus I resolved to leave behind birth and death."

[The Essential Meaning of the *Catuḥpratyaya-sūtra*] Ānanda’s subsequent narration of the futility of mere erudition (*bahuśruta*) serves as the basis for the purpose of initiating diligent cultivation. The three contemplations, such as *śamatha*, constitute the method of practice in this sutra;
indeed, it is by cultivating this dharma that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi. For those with the initial resolve to enter [the path], there must necessarily be skillful means.

What is called "the beginning" refers to the initial resolve of one who has not yet attained right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). [Wuxing says: Since Ānanda had grown weary of mere erudition and delighted in wondrous concentration (*samādhi*), the Tathāgata...

Because one must first interrogate false conditions before discussing the true reality (*tathatā*), this inquiry into the origins of the arousal of the mind and the perception of signs serves as the foundation for ceasing distraction and entering stillness. [Commentary] The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" demonstrates the cause of delusion regarding the Truth:

because of delusion regarding the True Purity, there exists the false cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). This refers to Ānanda’s perception of signs and arousal of the mind, which is the nature of clinging to birth-and-death.

Its essential nature is firm and stable, not involving worldly dust or falsehood; it is called the "Ever-Abiding True Mind. It is wondrously perfect, free from defilement, and devoid of all obscurity; it is called the "Essence of Innate Pure Clarity. This is the teaching of this sutra.
Because this is the wondrous nature discussed therein, the Buddha established the ultimate principle through profound mystery at this point to seal and determine the core tenet of the sutra.

However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s "Pure Seal" (*Vimalaprabhā*) states that the arousal of the mind [for enlightenment] occurs by seeing the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* also takes loving joy as its condition.

One should know that while this sutra intends to reveal the true mind and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), thereby distinguishing it from the substance of dependent conditions, it is not the case that the arousal of bodhicitta does not occur by way of seeing these marks and signs; thus, the *Vimalaprabhā Sūtra* says: "One arouses the mind upon seeing the marks."

There are four kinds: first, bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds attain purity by seeing the adornment of marks; second, bodhisattvas at the stage of practice attain purity of mind by contemplating the merits of the Buddha;
third, bodhisattvas at the stage of non-retrogression attain purity by contemplating the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha;

and fourth, bodhisattvas at the stage of the final birth before Buddhahood attain purity because they resolve their minds by being free from the two extremes—neither having any phenomenon to contemplate, nor being without contemplation. Therefore, O Śuddhamudrā, you should answer my question with a straightforward mind.
The Sūtra says: "Those who resolve their minds are free from flattery and deception; their minds are upright. This is what is meant by transcending birth and death entirely through the true mind.
Thus, it continues until the final stages of the bodhisattva grounds, meaning that all are realized and entered into by means of this very mind.
Part Two: The Section on Expedient Means (Great Outline Six) I. The Initial Inquiry Regarding the Mind (Section Seven) The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"As you have said, that which you truly love and cherish depends upon the mind and the eyes. If you do not know the location of the mind and the eyes, you will be unable to subdue the afflictions of dust and toil (*rajas-kleśa*).

It is like a king who, having been invaded by bandits, dispatches an army to eliminate them; that army must first know the whereabouts of the bandits. So it is with that which causes you to wander through the cycle of existence: the mind and the eyes."

This constitutes a fault. I now question you: where, precisely, do the mind and the eyes reside? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, throughout all worlds, there are ten kinds of ordinary beings."

[Ānanda] likewise maintains that the consciousness-mind resides within the body. Even when he observes the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are seen to be upon the Buddha’s face; yet when he now observes these four types of sensory objects of the physical roots, they are seen to be only upon his own face.

Thus, he concludes that the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body. The Buddha said to Ānanda: “You are currently sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall, looking out at the Jeta Grove. Where is it located now? [Ānanda replied:

“World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is located in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (the name of the donor who built the monastery). The Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall. “Ānanda, you are currently in the hall...”

[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, what did you see first? (Ānanda replied: 'World-Honored One, while I was in the hall, I first saw the Tathāgata; next I observed the great assembly; looking out from there, only then did my gaze fall upon the grove and gardens. (The Buddha told Ānanda:)"

"You gaze upon the groves and gardens; for what reason do you see them? (Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to look far from within the hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden-hued arm and stroked Ānanda’s head, instructing Ānanda and the entire assembly:

"There is a samādhi (right concentration) named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama (the Unsurpassed, All-Pervading, Ultimate, and Firm Mind) King, which is fully endowed with the myriad practices (cultivated and realized through each gate). It is the single gate through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend [samsara] via the path of wondrous adornment. You should now listen attentively. Ānanda prostrated himself in worship.
He accepted the compassionate instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, one's body is in the lecture hall; with doors and windows wide open, one gazes afar at the gardens and groves.

Yet there are sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, while those outside the hall can see him. Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, it is impossible for one to be in the hall and not see the Tathāgata, yet be able to see the forests and springs.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "You are also like this. Your spiritual mind is all-pervasive and clearly manifest. If the mind that is clearly manifest before you were actually inside your body, then at that time—"
First, one must understand the internal body. Is there any sentient being who first perceives within their own body and only afterward observes external objects?

Even if they cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, they certainly should clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, and the shifting of tendons and throbbing of veins. How could they fail to know this? If they do not know what is within, how can they know what is without?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognition dwells within the body—is impossible.

[The first refutation is internal. Having already established the thesis, the meaning shall now be clarified. To clear away the obstructions on the path and to frustrate those who harbor resentment in their hearts, the Buddha uses the seven locations of objective clinging as a skillful means for entering contemplation.

When the Buddha asks where the "eye-mind" resides, he is refuting false attachments. [He says that] the physical organ and the four sense-objects constitute the substance of the eye, while the mind resides within the body and the eye sees what is outside;

this is the intent behind his answer based on worldly perception. When the Buddha says, "As for you now," and so forth, he addresses Ānanda’s claim that the mind resides within. Regarding this "residing within":
Because the mind must necessarily perceive the internal, he asks what was first seen within the hall. "The Samādhi named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King" is the designation of this samādhi.

[Wenling]: The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is that wherein a thousand sages have traveled together; thus it is called the "Single Gate. It is a sea of wondrous adornment, and because one reaches it by way of this, it is called a "path. [Shu]:
According to the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*, only Bodhisattvas dwelling in the tenth stage attain this samādhi. This samādhi is not [attained] by means of a single...

The fact that all phenomena share a single object and a single meaning can be understood through analogy: just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-rāja* is said to be fully endowed with the myriad practices (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, the *Vajrasamādhi-prakṛti-viśuddha-sūtra* states: "When Bodhisattvas at the stage of Dharma-cloud (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*) abide in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, their minds are serene and they dwell in immovability, like the full moon on the fifteenth day, whose bright features are perfectly complete. Thus, one knows that all that is discussed in this sutra is the dharma of this very samādhi. It further says: "Abiding..."
Having already cultivated these three samādhis and then entered the Vajra-samādhi—like the light of a *maṇi* jewel shining upon one another—he enters the ocean of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.
All his wisdom is like the sun in the sky, while the ocean of all afflictions is like a faint mist or haze. [Commentary: Regarding the passage "If your mind were within," it means:
if the mind were inside, then when it encounters the body, there would have to be sentient beings within it; would you first see those within the body and only afterwards observe external objects?
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have heard the Tathāgata’s Dharma-sound, and I have realized that my mind truly dwells outside the body.

Why is this? It is like a lamp burning within a room; that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only after passing through the door of the room does its light reach the courtyard (the exterior).

All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies, but only see outside their bodies, just as a lamp situated outside a room cannot illuminate the interior. This principle is certainly clear and free from confusion; it is as you, the Buddha, have understood."

[The Buddha asked: "Do you have confidence that this meaning is not false? The Buddha told Ānanda: "These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī with me, begging for alms-food, and have returned to the Jeta Grove."
"I have already prepared the midday meal; observe this one bhikṣu eating. Are all the people satiated? Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
Although these bhikṣus are arhats, their bodies and lives are distinct. How could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?

The Buddha told Ānanda, "If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were actually outside the body, such that the body and mind were external to one another and did not interact, then what the mind knows, the body would not perceive; and what the body perceives at its own boundaries, the mind would not know."
"I now show you my hand of tūla-cotton. When you see it with your eyes, does your mind not discern it? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "If they are mutually cognizant, how could [the mind] be outside? Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind which perceives and knows resides outside the body—is impossible."

[The second inference is that the mind is external: That food cannot satisfy this external mind, yet the mind cannot know the body; therefore, one knows that this mind does not reside outside the body.
"I have already finished my fast" means that the Buddha has already accepted the meal. "Observe the bhikṣu" refers to the fact that when one person receives food, it cannot satisfy the others;

this serves as a metaphor for how the external mind cannot know the body. Furthermore, he raises his hand as proof. Regarding *tūla* (cotton): the *Gegu lun* states that it grows from trees in places such as Western Tibet, yet we see with our own eyes that it comes from the hand.

Since mental discrimination does not occur outside the mind, the mind itself is not external. Because the eye belongs to the body, it is said that awareness resides at the boundaries of the body. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has stated, because one does not see within, the mind does not reside inside the body. Yet, because the body and mind are mutually cognizant and inseparable, it does not reside outside the body.

As I now reflect, I am uncertain whether it might reside in a single location. The Buddha asked: "Where, then, is this location? Ānanda replied: "This cognizing mind, which neither knows the interior nor..."

As I observe from the outside, it is as I have contemplated: the sense organ is hidden within, like a person holding a lapis lazuli bowl (a metaphor for the eye) over both eyes (a metaphor for the mind).

Although objects are placed against it, there is no obstruction; that organ perceives as soon as it sees, and immediately discriminates. Thus, my conscious mind that is capable of cognition does not see the interior because the mind resides within the eye;

yet it clearly gazes at the exterior without obstruction because the mind resides within the eye. Because it is hidden inside the organ, the Buddha told Ānanda: "As you say, that which is hidden inside the organ is like lapis lazuli. That person should take the lapis..."

"Ānanda, suppose a person has their eyes covered by a crystal cage. Would they see the mountains and rivers as being made of crystal? " "Yes, World-Honored One. If that person had their eyes covered by a crystal cage, they would indeed see the crystal.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If your mind were united with the crystal in this way, you should see the mountains and rivers; why do you not see your own eyes? If you could see your own eyes, then the eye would be identical to its object, and it could not function as a faculty of perception.

If you cannot see them, how can you claim that this 'cognizing mind' resides hidden within the faculties, like a crystal covering them? Therefore, you should know that your statement regarding 'awakened cognition' is incorrect."
The mind capable of cognition cannot be latent within the sense organs, like a crystal vessel; such a thing is impossible. [Threefold Refutation of Latency in the Organs] (Changshui):

The analogy of crystal represents the sense organs, while the eye represents the mental consciousness. Since the sense organ and its object are pure, they do not obstruct the mind, just as a crystal bowl does not obstruct external forms.

As one reflects upon a mirror, the mind accordingly knows it. [Commentary]: It is like seeing through a crystal with the eye; the mind does not see the eye. Even if it could see the eye, the eye would then become [an object].

Since the objective realm has already become the object of the eye, how could it be immediately subject to conceptual discrimination? Furthermore, because lapis lazuli is a substance characterized by physical obstruction, when one uses it as a lens for the eyes, one sees both the mountains and rivers outside as well as the lapis lazuli itself.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I have now further reflected upon the bodies of these sentient beings: the internal organs reside within, while the orifices are situated on the outside.

Where there are internal organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light. Now, when I am before the Buddha, opening my eyes and seeing light is called ‘seeing the external,’ and closing my eyes and seeing darkness is called ‘seeing the internal.
What is the meaning of this? The Buddha told Ānanda, “When you close your eyes and see darkness, does this realm of darkness face the eye, or does it not face the eye? If it faces the eye,”

Darkness is right before your eyes; how can it be established as "internal"? If it were established as internal, then when you are in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, that darkness within the room would all be your own entrails.

If it does not face outward, how can it be established as seeing? If it is established internally by facing inward, apart from external seeing, then when you close your eyes and see darkness, it is called being "within the body.

When you open your eyes and see light, why do you not see your own face? If you do not see your face, then internal facing is not established. If seeing your face were established, then this cognizing mind and the faculty of the eye would both reside in empty space; how then could they be said to reside within the body?

If it were internal, or if it were in empty space, it would not be your own body; in that case, when the Tathāgata now looks at your face, it would also have to be your body. Your eyes already know this; if it were truly your body, your physical form should not be able to perceive it.

If you insist that there must be two cognitions for the two perceptions of body and eye, then this single body of yours would have to become two Buddhas. Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal" is untenable.
[The Fourfold Examination and the Dual Presence] [Wuxing]: Within a single body there is concealment, and because it is dark, seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal.

Why must one necessarily see the objects within the body? Where there are apertures there is light; thus, seeing light is itself seeing the external. How could one further demand that these two not interfere with one another? [Commentary]:

This is because when the eyes are open one cannot see light, and when closed one does not see what is within the body. Thus, one cannot avoid the subsequent question: you must immediately distinguish "internal seeing. That is to say, when darkness confronts the eye, it is dark.
If it were not called "seeing" when it does not face the eye before one's eyes, that would be untenable in all cases.

If you claim that the eye only sees outwardly and cannot face inward, then even if we grant that it faces inward to form its own perception, since you name this "seeing darkness," why do you not see your own face when you open your eyes?

[Wenling] This successive clarification shows there is no principle of self-reflection. Since your eye already knows that it is conjoined with the body, yet it is not the conscious subject; for if the eye were in empty space, it would not be your own substance.

[Commentary: Regarding the "Jiao Fu" (Triple Burner), the *Suwen*, in the "Discourse on the Distinctions of the Five Viscera," states that those which can store the essence and qi without leaking them out are called "viscera" (*zang*); those which transmit and transform substances without storing them are called "burners" (*fu*).

As for the Triple Burner, it is that by which the five grains are digested and their moisture distributed throughout the channels; because there are distinctions between the upper and lower [sections] and between the clear and turbid [substances], it is called the "Triple Burner."
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;

and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now reflect, this very essence of reflection is truly my own mind-nature. Wherever it conjoins with something, the mind follows and exists there; yet it is not located within, without, or in between—these three places.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you now say that because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise, and that wherever they conjoin, the mind follows and exists there, then this mind has no substance. If it has no substance, then there is nothing for it to conjoin with."
If that which lacks substance could nevertheless combine, then the nineteen realms would combine with the seven objects; this principle is not so.

If it possesses substance, then as you touch your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within, or does it enter from without? If it emerges from within, it should still see the interior of the body. If it comes from without, it should first see your face. Ānanda said: "Seeing is the function of the eyes (only the eyes can see);

the mind’s cognition is not the function of the eyes (the mind merely cognizes, whereas the eyes do not). [To say it is] "seeing" is not correct. The Buddha said: (The following uses a metaphor to demonstrate that the ability to see is solely the mind. "If the eyes were able to see, then while you are inside a room, the door—"

If seeing were not dependent on the gates [the eyes], then even those who have already died still possess eyes; they should all be able to see objects (this is a metaphor for how the eye alone cannot see). If they could see objects, how could they be called dead? Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is conscious and capable of knowing:
if it must have a substance, does it have a single substance or many substances? Now that it resides within your body, does it pervade the entire body or does it not pervade it?

If it has a single substance, then when you prick one limb with your hand, your other four limbs should feel it. If all of them feel it, then the pricking would have no specific location. If the pricking has a specific location, then your [mind] is not one...

A single body cannot establish itself. If there were multiple bodies, then there would be many persons; which body, then, would be yours? If it were a pervasive body, it would be the same as the previous point regarding being pierced. If it were not pervasive, [the same fault would apply].

When you touch your head, you also touch your feet; while the head has sensation, the feet should be without cognition. But this is not the case for you. Therefore, you should know that wherever there is contact, the mind must be present accordingly;
it is impossible for it to be otherwise.

[Fivefold Inference and Conjunction] [Wenling]: When mental phenomena arise in succession, the contemplation that follows the objects is itself the substance of the mind; the point where the mind and its phenomena coincide is precisely where the mind resides.
