They realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At that very moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were struck silent and lost in self-reflection. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "All those people in the world who practice and study..."

Although you have now attained the nine successive meditative absorptions, you have not yet achieved the exhaustion of outflows to become an Arhat. This is entirely because you cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality.
Therefore, although you have now acquired much learning, you have not realized the fruit of sainthood.

[1. The Nature of Permanence Apart from Dust] Ānanda, the following section reveals the nature of permanence apart from dust. "Dust" refers to the seeing that discriminates according to conditions; "permanence" refers to the essence of the original, inherent self-nature.

Because the true mind is devoid of delusion, it is said to be "apart from dust. When the Tathāgata raised his arm, he was directly manifesting fundamental luminosity; yet Ānanda recognized the conditions and lost the truth, using his deluded mind to investigate and pursue them.

As soon as a single thought arose, he turned toward external objects and lost his original permanence—this is precisely what is meant by "that which is abandoned by conditions. If one were to clarify this point:

[Lower Section] [Wuxing]: Ānanda, taking the capacity for cognitive awareness in response to objects as being distinct from wood or stone, has designated this as his "self. This is precisely the mark of human attachment.

Suddenly hearing the rebuke, he takes the insentient as his point of contention, failing to realize that the True Self is non-self, that wondrous, pure, and luminous mind of spiritual knowing is beyond knowing, and that it is omnipresent. [Commentary]:

That all dharmas arise solely as manifestations of the mind clarifies the principle of the "upright fist"—all of which is the meaning of "pushing back" to the mind. All causes and effects are the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) and the *sabhāga-vipāka* (retributive body). This is the nature.

"All minds" means that even grasses, trees, and the like all have this mind as their nature. "If you" below reiterates the mind capable of inference; "this mind" below demonstrates the meaning of its being detached from objects.
It means that the nature understood through discrimination, reflection, and observation is a mind devoid of substance and detached from objects, and thus one should not grasp at it.

Furthermore, it is shown: "As you now listen to my Dharma," this is precisely the nature of discrimination conditioned by objects. "Even if you were to extinguish" below distinguishes the matter of shadows and reflections; it means that even if you were to extinguish seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing...

Externally detached from the discrimination of objective conditions, one internally maintains a profound stillness; yet this mind of profound stillness is still merely a reflection of the *dharmas* (mental objects).

One must simply achieve perfect quiescence both internally and externally so that all reflections vanish; only then is it the essence of the true mind. Therefore, when the Buddha replied to Ānanda, "I am not commanding you to hold this as being the non-mind, but I wish for you to recognize what is truly real.

What is meant by "truly real"? It means that if there is discrimination independent of external conditions, then the entirety of that nature is the true mind. For example, even when external conditions are dark, the seeing-nature remains aware and does not cease.
When sounds and echoes both vanish in darkness, the faculty of hearing does not perish; is this not the complete nature existing apart from objects?

Therefore, one should not take the discrimination of objects as the mind, for objects are not permanent and perish immediately. How can such a cause yield a permanent fruit? The mind that relies on objects has such faults.

Thus, although practitioners may achieve the nine stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); this is entirely due to grasping at these deluded thoughts as real. Hence, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Even up to [the stage of] having..."

Even those at the Peak [of Existence] may still fall back, all because they do not understand the faults of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi* states: "If a person attains the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) but cannot enter the various dhyānas, they are called 'liberated by wisdom' (*prajñāvimukta*).

The commentary explains: According to these two types of attainment, both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are able to cultivate them; however, when the Sūtra says such a person does not attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it refers specifically to ordinary persons in training (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet severed their attachments to sense objects (*viṣaya*).
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt upright with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha and resolved to leave the household life, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, constantly thinking to myself that there was no need for me to practice. I presumed that the Tathāgata would bestow upon me samādhi; I did not realize that body and mind can never substitute for one another (the Tathāgata’s body and mind cannot practice on my behalf).

I have lost my original resolve; though I have left the household life in body, my mind has not entered the Way. It is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees; only today do I realize that although I possess much learning, if I do not practice..."

"Practicing [the teachings] while remaining ignorant of them is like a person speaking of food who can never satisfy their hunger. World-Honored One, we are now entangled by the two obstacles precisely because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us, who are destitute and exposed; please manifest your wondrously luminous mind and open our eyes to the Way. Immediately, from the *svastika* mark on the Tathāgata’s chest, a precious light surged forth.

This light was brilliant and radiant, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors. It simultaneously pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, universally bathing all the precious lands in the ten directions.
The crowns of all the Tathāgatas turned toward Ānanda and the great assembly. Addressing Ānanda, they said:

"I now establish for you the Great Dharma Banner, so that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions may attain the wondrous, subtle, and secret (unfathomable) nature-pure (unstained by defilement) and luminous (undimmed by darkness) mind, and obtain the pure eye (seeing free from the disease of cataracts). Ānanda, when you previously answered me regarding the seeing of the light of my fist—the radiance of this fist—"

"By what cause does it exist? How is it formed into a fist? By whom do you perceive it? Ānanda replied, "Because the Buddha’s entire body is made of Jāmbūnada gold, blazing like a mountain of jewels and born of purity, it possesses radiance.

I truly see with my own eyes the tips of the five fingers; because they are bent and clenched to show others, there is the appearance of a fist. The Buddha told Ānanda, "Today, the Tathāgata speaks these true words to you.
All those who possess wisdom must rely upon parables to attain awakening. Ānanda, take for example my fist: if there were no hand, it would not be formed."

"My fist. If you did not have your eyes, your seeing would not be established. Applying the principle of my fist as an analogy for your faculty of sight, is the meaning not the same? Ānanda replied, "Indeed it is so, World-Honored One."

Since there is no eye of a self, the vision of a self cannot be established. To take the faculty of the eye as being like the Tathāgata’s fist is an analogy where the facts and the meaning are similar. The Buddha said to Ānanda: “Your statement that they are similar is not correct. Why is this?
For instance, if a person has no hands, the fist is ultimately non-existent; yet for one who has no eyes, it is not the case that seeing is entirely absent.
Why is this so? You should try asking a blind person on the road, ‘What do you see? Those blind people will surely answer you, ‘Before my eyes now I see only darkness; I perceive nothing else.’”

"Observe this principle: the external objects are themselves dark; what deficiency could there be in the faculty of seeing? Ānanda said, "If those who are blind see only darkness before their eyes, how can it be called 'seeing'?

The Buddha told Ānanda, "Those who are blind lack eyes and thus perceive only darkness. Is there any difference between this darkness and that of a person with sight who is situated in a dark room? Or is there no difference? [Ānanda replied,] "It is so, World-Honored One.

When one compares the darkness of the person in the dark room with that of the group of blind people, there is never any distinction. "Ānanda, if a person without eyes perceives the total darkness before them, and suddenly obtains..."

The visual faculty returns to the external objects before it and perceives various forms; this is what is called "seeing with the eyes. When that person in the darkness sees only the surrounding blackness, and suddenly obtains the light of a lamp, they likewise perceive various forms within those same external objects.

If this were called "seeing by the lamp," then since the lamp possesses the capacity for seeing, it would no longer be called a "lamp. Furthermore, if it is the lamp that observes, how does it concern you?

Therefore, you should know that it is the lamp that can reveal color; likewise, that which sees is the eye, not the lamp. That which can reveal color is the nature of seeing (fused into a single whole); this is the mind, not the eye.

[The Second: Seeing Apart from the Roots] The nature of the mind is quiescent and eternal; it is the nature that has been primordially abiding. This nature is originally my own possession, yet I have sought it externally.

Since it is neither attained through another's cultivation nor acquired by me, how could I rely upon the majestic power of the Buddha? Only today do I realize that if one does not practice, it is the same as not having heard the Dharma at all.

Therefore, I reproach myself and request instruction, hoping to clarify the Eye of the Path. Regarding the two obstacles: the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states, "The first is the obstacle that continues the cycle of birth and death; the second is the obstacle of principles that hinders correct knowledge and vision."

It is further said: "To eternally sever craving, one must first eliminate the obstacle of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), before eliminating the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*). The commentary explains: according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, craving and the like constitute the obstacle of phenomena, while the vision of the truths constitutes the obstacle of principle.

Thus, when Ānanda mistakenly entered a house of prostitution, this was because the obstacle of phenomena had not yet been severed; that he engaged in conceptual discrimination regarding sensory objects was because the obstacle of principle had not yet been severed.

Regarding the question of similarity in the passage where Ānanda stepped on the previous fist: the intent of the question is to clarify why they are dissimilar. They are dissimilar because without a hand there is no fist, whereas without eyes there is still seeing.

Therefore, they are not of the same category. Since the perception of fists involves arising and ceasing, it is neither existence nor non-existence; thus, even a group of blind people can perceive darkness—this is the reality of the permanent nature (*nitya-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, both the sūtras and the śāstras state that the eye does not see forms. Thus, the *Pòsèxīnlùn* (Treatise on the Refutation of Form and Mind) says: "Because in dreams, one sees forms where there are no forms, and does not see forms where there are forms.
The commentary explains: "Where there are no forms" refers to the objects of the dream state; "where there are forms" refers to the objects of the waking state. As for the forms in the dream...

Because it is not an object of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), it is said that "the eye does not see form. Nevertheless, in the world, the eye is regarded as seeing; yet when the eye is absent, one cannot see.
The meaning of the eye's lack of permanence lies in its being distinct from the sense faculty (*indriya*).

“Ānanda, although they had heard these words, the great assembly remained silent; their minds were not yet enlightened, and they still hoped for the Tathāgata’s compassionate voice to provide further instruction.

With palms joined and hearts purified, they waited expectantly for the Buddha’s merciful teaching. At that time, the World-Honored One extended his hand, which was marked with the webbed fingers like fine cotton-wool and radiated light, and opened his five fingers to instruct Ānanda and the great assembly:
‘When I first attained the Way in the Deer Park, for the sake of Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya, the five bhikṣus, and you fourfold assembly, I declared that all sentient beings do not [attain]...’”

"Bodhi and Arhatship are both attained by being freed from the delusions of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). At that time, by what means did you all achieve awakening and now realize the fruit of sainthood?

Then Kauṇḍinya (also known as Kauṇḍinya) rose and addressed the Buddha: "I am now the eldest among this great assembly, and I alone have earned the name 'The Liberated. It was through awakening to the two characters 'adventitious' (*āgantuka*) and 'dust' (*rajas*) that I achieved the fruit.

World-Honored One, it is like a traveler who stays at an inn, whether to sleep or to eat; once his stay or meal is finished, he packs his bags for the road ahead and has no leisure to remain. As for the actual host, they have no such need to go anywhere."

"Go. Thinking thus, that which does not abide is called a guest, and that which abides is called the host; for the meaning of "guest" is defined by its non-abiding. Furthermore, it is like when the sky has just cleared after rain and the blue sun rises in the heavens.

When light enters through a crack, it illuminates the space within, and all various appearances of dust become manifest. The substance of the dust moves, yet empty space remains tranquil. Reflecting thus, one understands that what is clear and still is called "space," while what is moving is called "dust.
For that which moves is defined by the meaning of "dust. The Buddha said, "It is so."

[The Nature of Being Free from Adventitious Defilements] When Kaundinya attained realization, he understood that "adventitious defilements" (āgantuka-rajas) are established by name based on their origin from the beginning. [Wuxing’s Commentary]: The metaphor of "adventitious dust" refers to the arising and ceasing of the afflictions of views and thought;

the "host" (the space) is a metaphor for the quiescence of the True Truth (paramārtha-satya). The meaning of "adventitious" (āgantuka) is coarse and refers to the delusions regarding phenomena; the meaning of "dust" (rajas) is subtle and refers to the delusions regarding principle. [The Sub-commentary]:

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the afflictions of views arise from delusion regarding the principles of the truths; they are easy to sever and do not regress—this is the meaning of "adventitious. The afflictions of cultivation arise based on coarse phenomena; they are difficult to sever.

The *Yì* (Book of Changes) explains this as the meaning of "dust" (*rajas*). The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states that there are nine types of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*): first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, active delusions; fifth, ignorance;

sixth, those abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*); seventh, those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); eighth, the delusions of the impure stages; and ninth, the delusions of the pure stages.

Regarding these two categories of delusions [the last two], the commentary explains that the sequence from greed up to the delusions of the pure stages provides a general explanation of the meaning of all adventitious afflictions belonging to both ordinary beings and sages. Furthermore, as for what is taught in the sutras and śāstras:

There are four interpretations regarding the meaning of "adventitious defilements" (*āgantuka-kleśa*): 1. **In terms of what is revealed:** The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states that the term "adventitious defilements" is used to reveal that the nature of the mind is eternal.

2. **In terms of what is cultivated:** Regarding the cultivation of *śamatha*, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) states: "For one who cultivates *śamatha*, awareness perceives the agitation of consciousness; when tranquil wisdom arises, adventitious defilements are forever extinguished. 3. **In terms of what is realized:** The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"In order to sever adventitious defilements, one realizes the pure Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). 4. **In terms of what is abandoned:** The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is perfectly pure and stainless, being free from adventitious [defilements]."

Because it is defiled by adventitious dust (*āgantuka-rajas*), its essence is such that it is characterized by discrimination (*vikalpa*). Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Just as space is pure, the mind is eternally luminous and without transformation;

yet it is defiled by the adventitious afflictions of false discrimination. However, the sutra designates that which does not abide as "adventitious" and that which abides as the "host. It takes the clarity and stillness as "space" and the agitation as "dust. Furthermore, it says:

"If the actual host has no place to go, then when discrimination is removed, the eternal mind abides of itself. One should know that within this context, it is precisely the discrimination of objects that constitutes the dust.
Regarding the meaning of the mind as a guest-dust (*āgantuka-rajas*):

at that time, the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, bent his five fingers; having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them once more (making the gesture of opening and closing). He said to Ānanda: "What do you see now? Ānanda replied:

"I see the Tathāgata’s palms, adorned with hundreds of jewels, opening and closing amidst the assembly. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "What you see is my hand opening and closing amidst the assembly; is this [the movement] mine..."

"The hands open and close. Is it your vision that opens and closes? Ānanda replied, "World-Honored One, when Your Honored One’s precious hands open and close amidst the assembly, I see the Tathāgata’s own hands opening and closing;

it is not my seeing-nature that opens and closes. The Buddha asked, "Which moves and which is still? Ānanda said, "The Buddha’s hand does not remain still (the Buddha’s hand is moving), yet my seeing-nature is not even still (the seeing-nature is without movement).

"What is it that is 'not remaining'? The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted a single precious light from the wheel-mark on his palm, which hovered to the right of Ānanda. Immediately—

Ānanda turned his head to look to the right, and another ray of light was emitted, appearing on Ānanda’s left. Ānanda then turned his head to look to the left. The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Why is your head shaking today?
Ānanda replied, “I saw the Tathāgata emit wondrous jewel-like rays of light coming from my left and right; therefore, as I looked to the left and right, my head shook of its own accord.

“Ānanda, as you looked at the Buddha’s light and moved your head to the left and right, did it move because of your head, or did it move because of what you see? “World-Honored One, it was my head that moved of its own accord; yet my nature of seeing remains still.”
"There is stillness; who is it that moves? The Buddha said, "It is so. Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: "If sentient beings take that which moves as real, they call it 'dust';

if they take that which does not abide as real, they call it a 'guest. Observe Ānanda: though your head moves of its own accord, you see nothing that truly moves. Furthermore, observe me: my hand opens and closes of its own accord."

Seeing has no expanding or contracting. Why is it that you now take movement as your body and movement as your environment? From beginning to end, thought after thought arises and perishes; you have lost the true nature and act in delusion.
Your fundamental mind has strayed from truth, mistaking external objects for yourself. You revolve within this cycle, bringing about your own continuous wandering.

[The Nature of the Fourfold Immovability] [Changshui]: "The hands have opening and closing, yet one sees no movement or stillness"—this is a discernment made in relation to external objects. Next, regarding the internal body, there is its own inherent movement and stillness; within movement, there is immovability. [Commentary]:

The Buddha inquires about seeing the nature (*dharmatā*) to reveal that which transcends ordinary emotion. He speaks of "immovability" to clarify that the wondrous seeing-nature is quiescent and detached from delusion.

Thus, the *Akṣayamati-sūtra* states: "Śamatha is tranquility, near-quietude, secrecy, immovability, and non-shaking. Furthermore, knowing contentment is the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
It is the essence (*tattva*). Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) takes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as its objective support;

because it continues uninterruptedly until the end of saṃsāra, it is called 'unwavering' (*aniñja*), which is the function of the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The commentary explains: Śamatha takes stillness as its essence and cessation as its characteristic. Yet Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "In the seeing of nature (*darśana-dhātu*), there is not even stillness.

This is because the wondrous nature of clarity transcends the emotions; it is stillness that is detached from stillness. Furthermore, when the Buddha asked, "What moves and what is still? he replied, "The seeing of nature."

Furthermore, there is no such thing as "stopping," for this clarifies that the wondrous nature is non-attachment; thus, it is stopping itself, yet detached from stopping. Therefore, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* says: "One should stop;
once stopped, there is no stopping, nor does one dwell in non-stopping, nor does one dwell in non-dwelling. It further says: "To know that the mind is no-mind is for there to be no mind to stop;

when the manifesting consciousness does not arise, there is no arising to stop. Why? Because stopping is non-stopping. If, moreover, [the text] below points to the dharmas to reprove and exhort, taking movement as the body, this refers to looking left and right.

Thus, to take movement as one's object—wherein the hand has opening and closing—is to be deluded; it is to reject the eternally abiding true essence and instead grasp at the body and its objects, which are characterized by agitation and birth-and-death.
Is this not to lose the true nature and act in a state of inversion? Therefore, know that the body is a source of weary toil, a false and illusory movement.

Thus, internally eliminate the notion of self and externally resist the notion of others, severing attachment to the delusions of the mundane world to dwell in the reality of the Dharma-realm. This is why the Tathāgata opened the way for *śamatha*.

Zheng Cheng praised him, saying: "Ānanda manifested his fall; the Tamer of Men (the Buddha) bestowed compassion. Through seven layers of interrogation, clinging was shattered; the mind and eyes shone upon the golden fist. Truth and falsehood were seen as simultaneous."
The determination lies in the present authority.

As transmitted by Cechu (Cher-lu), who said: "The Great Uṣṇīṣa is the miraculous manifestation of Śākyamuni’s Great Enlightenment. It uses symbols to convey the meaning; this is the consensus of the holy teachings.

Now, while Ānanda was immersed in a house of debauchery and the great assembly desired to hear the essential points of the Dharma, the World-Honored One, though possessing great majestic power, did not reach out his hand to rescue him; though possessing great eloquence, he did not speak.

The opening [of this scripture] describes how, from within the *uṣṇīṣa*, a hundred jewel-lights surge forth, and a transformation Buddha appears to proclaim the divine mantra (*dhāraṇī*). This signifies that both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are supreme, and demonstrates that both form and sound are wondrous.

It clears away the illusory cataracts of seeing and hearing; thus, the great purport of this single scripture is fully realized without remainder. Regarding "the supremacy of both Exoteric and Esoteric": the Sūtra represents the Exoteric, while the Mantra represents the Esoteric.

The essence of the Mantra and the essence of the *Tathāgatagarbha* (Heart-Store) are non-dual and without distinction. The *uṣṇīṣa* is the sign of the Unsurpassed, and the Sūtra is the discourse of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). By encompassing the Exoteric with the Esoteric, it fully manifests the *uṣṇīṣa*.

Therefore, it is said they are "both superior. As for that which is "mysterious in both form and sound": the transformation Buddhas in the light atop the head are forms beyond form; the incantations of the transformation Buddhas are sounds beyond sound.

Since both form and sound transcend the realm of conceptual thought, it is said they are "mysteriously combined. Those with the cataracts of seeing and hearing perceive only floating dust and illusory transformations—empty, false appearances—and fail to understand anything at all, giving rise to false grasping and attachment.
This obstructs the pure eye of wisdom, the fundamental root of penetration. Thus, the practitioner says: "I see the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks."

It is supremely wondrous and extraordinary; therefore, with thirsty longing, he followed the Buddha to shave his head and leave the household life. Furthermore, it is said: "I have awakened to the Buddha’s manifested voice of the Dharma, and now, with my conditioned mind, I truly look up to him.

Is this not like the seeker of goodness who pursues form and sound? Once one is attached to form and sound, the fundamental luminosity becomes obscured. As for Manoharā, how could she not have exploited that interval? Why is this so?

Because the Buddha-body and the female body are identical in their characteristics; the Buddha’s vision and the woman’s vision are identical in their sentiments. Ānanda alone regrets that his own body was touched by lust, which allowed Māra to enter.

This constitutes an obstruction. Failing to reach the supreme marks, one takes delight in them, which becomes a treacherous step. Truly, it is like a thief harbored within the house, remaining dimly unaware while one relies on the wisdom of extensive learning and what can be grasped through the ancient Brahmanic mantras;
such instances surely exist. Now, by showing the transformation Buddha of the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa*, one comes to know that the forms of the thirty-two marks are not forms;

and by the transformation Buddha’s preaching of mantras, one comes to know that the sounds of the four unhindered eloquences are not sounds. From this, one awakens to the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great dharmas are none other than within the Tathāgatagarbha.

They manifest according to karma. Because following karma is itself the nature, they are not existent; because the nature follows karma, they are not empty. Detached from both "is" and "is-not," and being both "is" and "is-not," truth and falsehood are harmoniously fused, and all conceptual proliferation is utterly severed.

Regarding the cultivation and realization at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there is no longer any secret or essential method. To see this is the seeing of seeing; to hear this is the hearing of hearing. At that very moment, the Ocean Seal (*sāgaramudrā*) emits its radiance.

All phenomena are fully illuminated. The complete title states: "This scripture is named *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-sitātapatra-daśadig-tathāgata-viśuddha-samudra-nayana* (The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Sitātapatra, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions).

Regarding this, those who compose various elaborate explanations in literary prose likely do not grasp the intention of the Supreme Sage in manifesting these signs to secretly benefit those with sharp faculties. It is like the various manifestations of light in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This represents the Dharma-gates of the various stages (*bhūmi*). To provide a brief illustration based on a single sutra, one may understand all others accordingly.

When Mañjuśrī went to protect [Ānanda] with a mantra and the evil spell was extinguished, and Ānanda and Ḍākinī returned to the Buddha’s presence, this signifies that through the practice of correct wisdom, the works of Māra ceased. The introductory section is concluded.

From the following sections down to the middle of the fourth fascicle, the text elucidates the essence of nature to harmonize all phenomena, clarifying the secret cause of the Tathāgata, as described in the *Avataṃsaka* as "first awakening to the Vairocana Dharma-realm. From the fourth fascicle until the end of the sutra, it is entirely cultivation based on nature.

This clarifies the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi*, the foremost of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas; that is to say, it is the subsequent cultivation of the gateway of Samantabhadra’s practices. *Śūraṃgama* means "ultimate firmness.

In this sutra, there is nothing—whether teaching, principle, practice, or fruit—that is not ultimate; thus, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). There are five types of titles, which shall be explained in detail later. As for Ānanda seeing the Buddha, prostrating, and weeping with grief:

he realized that his precept-body had nearly been destroyed by Ḍākinī, and that much learning does not necessarily benefit one's power of the Path. If people were to remain complacent when faced with such a situation, then the wondrous scripture of the *Śūraṃgama* would have no place [to manifest its efficacy].

The arising of the flow of desire within birth and death cannot be obstructed or severed. When Great Expedient Power manifests its traces, how could it not be purposeful? That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*:
"wondrous" (*miao*) refers to the esoteric; *śamatha* and the others are the causes. Although the title is summarized by focusing on the esoteric cause, the request for the Dharma requires detail;

thus, three distinct types are opened up. *Śamatha* is the state of profound stillness and quiescence; *samādhi* is the state of expansive, perfect illumination; *dhyāna* is the non-duality of stillness and illumination. These three arise from their functional applications.

Its essence is eternally one; the three and the one are perfectly interfused, and thus it is called "wondrous. It is the seed-wisdom of all Buddhas, the numinous awareness within each person, and the fundamental essence of the One Vehicle.

The "Principle" (zong) is that which manifests; this is called the "Secret Cause. The "Essence" (ti) is that which is manifested; this is called the "Nature of the Treasury" (zangxing). The Principle and the Essence originally do not differ in their path; how could the fruit and the cause not be of one accord?

Therefore, in the subsequent text, sometimes one is cited to encompass the three, and sometimes the Principle is cited to include the Essence. That which the translators did not translate—its profound and luminous manifestation depends solely upon the person.

As for the "initial skillful means," it is the gateway for entering samādhi. There are distinctions between a general indication and a specific pointing-out. After Ānanda had realized the treasury-mind in the fourth fascicle, [the text continues:]
He requested, saying: "I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; yet I must enter through a gate.

Although the World-Honored One has shown me the two definitive meanings for awakening the initial mind and pointed out the relative superiority of the six sense-faculties so that I might enter deeply through one, he has not yet specifically indicated which gate is essential. Therefore, I request again for instruction on the fundamental faculty of perfect penetration.

The Buddha then had the various sages each describe their own realization, whereby he further explained in general terms the aggregates, bases, elements, as well as the seven great elements, all of which serve as gates for entering the Way.

Mañjuśrī, having received the imperial decree, followed after the various sages and specifically pointed to what Avalokiteśvara had realized. His verse says: "The true essence of the teaching in this land / Is pure within hearing and sound."

To transcend through samādhi, one must truly enter by means of hearing. I pray that you will bestow your grace upon the future, so that they may have no doubts regarding this gateway and be capable of teaching Ānanda and those submerged in the delusions of the final age.

That the Sūtra takes the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty as the primary expedient is beyond doubt. As for being "capable of teaching Ānanda," it is because Ānanda accumulated faults through his habitual use of hearing.

Avalokiteśvara perfected his virtue through the cultivation of hearing; what is called "merit" and "transgression" lies solely within the interval of following sound and entering the stream. Now, this reveals the Great Being’s fundamentally wondrous and perfect faculty as the secret essential for those newly beginning their practice through extensive learning.
This ensures that one does not lose their original footing, so that the great function manifests before them—just as one who has fallen to the ground rises from that very ground once more.

If one abandons this, what will there be to hear regarding the secret causes? If one abandons this, upon what can one rely to discuss the myriad practices? Therefore, Ānanda reproached himself for his failure to fully realize the power of the Way despite his extensive learning, and further recounted the origins of his initial resolve and his vision of the signs.

The World-Honored One, addressing his points of delusion, showed him: "All sentient beings, because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind—the nature that is pure and luminous—employ various false thoughts.

Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence. This nature that is pure and luminous is precisely that which the Buddha represents as being free from all discrimination. To employ [this]...
"Delusive thoughts"—this refers to those who, because of mutual attachment and fondness, wish to cure these thoughts. There is no other method for this; therefore it is said:

"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṃgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate.

Although Ānanda previously requested that all three names be listed, only *samādhi* is mentioned here, because by citing one, the other two are subsumed, and both the essence and the principle are thereby present. As for naming the *samādhi* the "Great Buddha-Crown," this uses words to signify the underlying reality, gathering the esoteric back into the manifest.

Furthermore, "Śūraṃgama" (The King of Heroic Progress) reveals the ultimate, adamantine essence that is to be realized—the one that is supreme among all things. Since there is no function apart from this essence, it is said to be "fully endowed with the myriad practices.

That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions "surpass through a single gate onto the path of wondrous adornment" means that from *samādhi*, they manifest the eternally abiding mind, perfecting Bodhi and returning to the state of non-attainment;

this is the nature of every Buddha. Now, as for why the mind is called "eternally abiding": if it is eternally abiding, then there is nowhere it does not abide. If there is nowhere it does not abide, then it cannot be described by words.

"Abide! Yet, Ānanda, you calculate the internal and calculate the external, even calculating up to non-attachment—is such a thing possible? Observe, for instance, how the Tathāgata emits light from the gate of his face, shaking the realms of all Buddhas;

disparate worlds merge as one, and those dwelling afar hear together. Thus, the seven locations were merely false limitations; they are now suddenly and utterly cleared away. The Nirvana from time immemorial, the originally pure essence, is fully present within yourself and does not reside in the Buddha.

Ānanda, you still take the mind that is capable of deliberation to be the mind; this is no different from mistaking a thief for your own son, thereby losing what is called the tranquil and eternal nature of the mind."
Thus, from the *svastika* once again surged forth precious light, reaching every single Tathāgata as numerous as motes of dust, and leaving no one among Ānanda and the great assembly untouched.

When one realizes that delusory objects cannot obstruct the light of wisdom, how could the wondrous mind differ from the eye of the Way? This leads to entrusting the blind man with the task of distinguishing between the lamp and seeing; the oneness of the mind-eye shines forth clearly.

It causes Dharmapāla (Cenana) to describe the adventitious dust, whereby the wondrous nature of quiescent permanence is revealed. Ānanda’s realization that the hand has opening and closing is like the guest; that seeing has neither expansion nor contraction is like the host.

Furthermore, the movement of the head is like dust; seeing that which is unmoving is like space. Thus, the Tathāgata first used Cunda to awaken Ānanda, and through Ānanda, he rebuked those present in the assembly.

Therefore, he said, "If again... By saying that what moves is called "dust" and what does not abide is called "a guest," he rebuked the assembly for failing to realize the immovability within movement.
Thus he said: "Observe, Ānanda: your head moves of its own accord, yet you see that which is unmoving; your hands open and close, yet you see that which neither expands nor contracts. He spoke thus.

Why is it that you are now deluded regarding the sovereign emptiness of quiescent permanence? By taking movement as your body and movement as your environment, have you not lost the true nature of mind?

By pursuing the turbid adventitious dust of agitation, from beginning to end, you undergo moment-to-moment arising and ceasing; is this not identifying external objects as yourself? The nature of quiescent permanence has been inherently within you, yet you are deluded by it and turn your back upon it;
therefore it is said: "Within this cycle of rebirth, you take for yourself the process of wandering."

*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Two: The Remainder of the Manifestation of the Constant Nature. (Phonetic notes: *qì* [cut by *qǐ* and *nì*];
*pàn* [cut by *pǐ* and *xiàn]*)

At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt their bodies and minds become tranquil. They reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with conditioned objects and engaging in the discrimination of illusory phenomena.
Today they have attained awakening, like a child who has lost his mother suddenly encountering her again.

With palms joined, they prostrated before the Buddha and wished to hear the Tathāgata reveal the true and the false within body and mind, and the nature of illumination in both the manifest arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing. Then King Prasenajit (representing the entire assembly and their desire to inquire) rose and addressed the Buddha: "In the past, before I had received the teachings of the Buddhas..."

The Buddha instructed him, saying: "I have seen Kātyāyana and Vairāṭīputra, both of whom declared that the annihilation of this body after death is called Nirvāṇa. Although I have encountered the Buddha, I still harbor doubts.

How may I manifest and realize this state where the mind is neither born nor extinguished? All those in this great assembly who still possess outflows (āsrava) likewise wish to hear this. The Buddha told the Great King:

"Your body is present now; I ask you again: Is this physical body of yours permanent and indestructible like a diamond, or is it subject to decay and destruction? World-Honored One, this body of mine will ultimately perish and vanish.

The Buddha said, "Great King, you have not yet perished. How do you know that it will perish? "World-Honored One, although this impermanent and decaying body of mine has not yet perished, I observe before me that from moment to moment it undergoes change and passes away.
It is ever-new and never abiding, like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away and dissolving. This process of decay and extinction never ceases; I am certain of this."

"The body must follow toward extinction. The Buddha said, "So it is, Great King. At this stage of your life, you have already grown old and decayed; how does your appearance compare to that of your youth? [The King replied,] "World-Honored One, [it is not like it was]."

"In my former childhood, my skin and flesh were moist and lustrous. As I reached adulthood, my blood and vital energy were full and robust. Now, in my declining years, pressed by senility and decrepitude, my physical form is withered and haggard, my spirit is clouded and dim, my hair is white and my face is wrinkled;
before long I shall pass away. How can this be compared to the time of my full vigor? The Buddha said, "Great King, your physical appearance must not have decayed all at once.

The King replied, "World-Honored One, transformation shifts subtly and secretly; I truly do not perceive it. Through the gradual passage of cold and heat, I have slowly reached this state. Why is this so? When I was twenty..."
Though called young, my appearance is already aged. When I was ten, I thought it was thirty; then at twenty, I felt I had lost another decade.

Now that I am sixty-two, looking back at when I was fifty, I was still quite robust. World-Honored One, I observe this subtle shifting; although this decay occurs, the transition between stages is measured by ten-year intervals.

If I were to contemplate it with minute attention, would the change be limited to a single *ji* (twelve years, though some say ten)? It is surely more than a single *ji*; it is the change of years. But does it stop at the change of years? It also includes the transformation of months. Not only the transformation of months, but also...

Furthermore, it changes daily. Contemplate this deeply and observe with discernment: from moment to moment, from thought to thought, nothing remains stationary. Therefore, know that this body of yours will ultimately undergo transformation and perish.

The Buddha said to the Great King: "You have seen these transformations and shifts occurring without ceasing; you have realized that they perish. At the very moment of their perishing, do you perceive within your own body anything that does not perish?

King Prasenajit joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I truly do not know. The Buddha said: "I shall now show you the nature of non-arising and non-perishing. Great King, at what age did you first see the Ganges River?"
The King said, "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīvaka. As we passed by this stream, I immediately recognized it as the waters of the Ganges.

The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have said. At twenty, one declines from the state of ten; this continues until sixty. Days, months, years, and seasons shift and change from moment to moment; thus, that which was your third year [is now gone]."

"When you saw this river at the age of thirteen, what was its water like? The King replied, "It was exactly as it was when I was three years old; there was no difference at all. Even until now, at the age of sixty-two, there has been no change.
The Buddha said, "Now you lament that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled. Your face must certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your youth.

Therefore, as you observe this Ganges River now, is there any difference between the vision of the river you had in your childhood and the vision you have now in your old age? The King replied, "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face is wrinkled..."

This nature of the essence of vision has never been wrinkled. That which is wrinkled undergoes change; that which is not wrinkled does not change. That which changes is subject to extinction. As for that which does not change, it fundamentally has no arising or ceasing.
How could it therein undergo your birth and death? Yet you still cite those such as Maskarin Gośālīputra, who all claim that after this body dies, there is total annihilation.

Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe that after death one casts off the provisional form of life and proceeds toward the birth of the complete true nature. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy, experiencing a state of wonder never before attained.

[The Vision of the River of Five Contemplations] [Commentary]: Because the body, which is subject to impermanence, arising, and ceasing, reveals the nature that is eternally abiding and indestructible, the vision of the river is cited as a metaphor to clarify the essence that flows yet remains unchanged.

Indeed, among all embodied beings, there is none that does not perish. As for the two types of contemplation on impermanence mentioned in the *Abhidharmakośa*—namely, the destruction of the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) and the destruction of the moment (*kṣaṇa*)—these refer to the nature of the two moments of body and mind.
What is revealed in this text consists briefly of three sections, namely the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). First, from the Buddha...

The question beginning with "Have you never yet extinguished [this]? refers to observing impermanence through the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*); it means that the substance of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*) undergoes transformation and passes away from moment to moment, and its nature of impermanence does not abide even for an instant, like fire turning to ash—this conveys the sense that nothing is renewed.

The second section, beginning with "From the question 'Have you been born into this life...'," refers to observing impermanence through the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*);

it means that the countenance, complexion, and skin are the characteristics of the body. "Infancy" refers to the early years, while "the vigor of blood and qi" refers to the prime of youth; "decline and senility" and "withered exhaustion" collectively refer to the entire span of life.
The description of old age, culminating in the realization that one will not long remain, speaks to the principle of impermanence (*anityatā*).

From "I have followed you in three ways" down to "your physical appearance," this is the contemplation of impermanence through the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), observing the nature of phenomena across the cycles of cold and heat and the passage of years and months. From "I was twenty years old" down to "taking ten years as a limit," this is a broad and coarse observation of the passage of time.

From "in truth, the years change" down to "taking from the broad to the narrow," this is a subtle and detailed observation of the minute characteristics of change. "To pass away" (*cyuti*) signifies the meaning of transition and cessation; it refers to the passing of the years.

The transformation of the moon and its changes all constitute the essence of impermanence; that they ultimately follow through change and extinction points to an inevitable trend. The Buddha’s teaching below reveals the nature of non-transience:
for that which gives birth does not undergo birth, and that which transforms does not undergo transformation. Therefore, although one receives a worldly body, one does not undergo worldly change.

This is why the vision of one looking at a river remains the same whether one is a child or an old man. [Gushan] notes that "the essence of seeing" is the "nature of seeing. That "wrinkles constitute change" reveals that birth and death are impermanent.

If the wrinkles do not change, then the permanence of *nirvāṇa* is revealed. [Commentary: In the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, five kinds of permanence are taught: first, infinite permanence; second, permanence of non-arising; third, permanence of constant presence;
fourth, permanence of profound stillness; and fifth, permanence of immutability. This permanence of immutability is precisely the nature of the river as observed by the Elder.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and knelt on his right knee to address the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if this seeing and hearing are indeed neither produced nor extinguished, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion? We pray that you will arouse your compassion and wash away our defilements.

At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm, turning his palm downward, and pointed it toward Ānanda, saying: "Do you now see my *mudrā* hand (the hand in its seal-position)? Is it upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "Worldly beings consider this to be inverted."
"But I do not know who is upright and who is inverted. The Buddha told Ānanda, "If worldly people consider this to be inverted, then by what standard do worldly people determine what is upright?
Ānanda replied, "When the Tathāgata raises his arm—his hand being as soft as *tūla* cotton (as explained in the previous fascicle)—pointing it upward toward the sky, that is called upright.

The Buddha then raised his arm and said to Ānanda, "If this is inverted, with head and tail exchanged, and all worldly people gaze at it from both sides, then you will understand that your own body is to be compared with the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas to reveal its nature (comparing it to the upright and inverted state of the finger to bring forth this realization)."

“The body of the Tathāgata is called ‘Perfectly All-Knowing’ (samyak-saṃbuddha), while your bodies are termed ‘inverted by nature. As you observe them closely, consider where the designation ‘inverted’ applies to either your own body or the Buddha’s body.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly gazed fixedly at the Buddha; their eyes did not blink, and they were unaware of where the inversion of body and mind lay.

The Buddha, giving rise to compassion and pitying Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered a voice like the tide of the ocean, addressing the entire gathering: “O sons of good family, I have always said...”

He said: "The various conditions of form and mind, as well as all the objects of perception associated with mental factors, are manifested solely by the mind. Your body (the illusory body) and your mind (the deluded mind) are both objects manifested within the wondrously bright, true essence of the wondrous mind.

Why, then, have you lost this fundamentally wondrous, perfectly wonderful, and luminous mind—this precious, brilliant, and wondrous nature—and instead recognized delusion within awakening? You took the obscuring darkness for emptiness; within that emptiness of dark obscuration, you coagulated darkness into form.

Form mixed with false conceptualization, and these conceptual appearances became the body. As it gathered conditions, it wavered within; as it rushed outward, it fled in pursuit. This state of confused turmoil was taken to be [reality]."

The nature of the mind: when it is once deluded, it becomes the "mind," and one becomes firmly deluded into thinking it resides within the physical body. One does not realize that everything outside the physical body—including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is entirely a thing within the wondrously luminous true mind.

It is like discarding a clear ocean hundreds of thousands of miles wide and instead identifying with a single bubble, claiming that this tiny fragment constitutes the entire tide and exhausts the vastness of the sea.

"You all are people who are doubly deluded. It is as if I were hanging down my hand; there is no difference between the two. The Tathāgata says you are to be pitied. [Six: The True Nature Free from Perversions] [Wenling]:

Because of the King’s questions and answers, the dust of doubt was stirred up in reverse, leading him to claim that true nature has arising and ceasing and can be lost. Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, how could it be lost?
The Buddha answered: "The Buddhas and sentient beings share the same single essence; certainly there is no loss. It is only because of inverted views that one speaks of it being lost."

It is like taking what is vertically hanging as "correct" and what is inverted as "reversed," or taking what is upright as "reversed" and what is inverted as "correct"—this is to lose the true essence. [Commentary] From here below, the text gradually clarifies the Mind by means of its objects;

therefore, the Buddha extensively cites the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world to manifest pervasive knowledge. The various conditions of form and mind are the phenomena of the sense organs and their objects;

viewed in terms of their substance, they constitute the wondrous nature of precious luminosity. Those which are employed by the mind are the various phenomena of defilement and purity; viewed in terms of their totality, they are the perfectly wondrous and luminous mind. Indeed, all phenomena are...

Birth is merely what is manifested by the mind; this is the primordial awakening. To abandon this original awakening and grasp at the physical body is to mistake delusion for awakening within that awakening.

It is said that when the luminosity below becomes obscured, one falls into perversion. This means that the true nature is perfectly pervasive, having neither interior nor exterior. Due to a single thought of obscuration, the solid state transforms into space;

subsequently, this obscured state coagulates into form, and various conceptual appearances become the body. The deluded movement of emotion gathers conditions within and flows outward, remaining in a state of restless confusion and agitation, and thus the person grasps at this.

Taking conditioned breath as their own mind, they consequently claim that this mind resides within their insignificant bodies; they do not realize that what extends beyond—the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all the substance of wondrous luminosity.

Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in its dharma-position; the characteristics of the world are eternally present. Because they grasp at the small while neglecting the great, it is like discarding the ocean to recognize only a bubble;
thus, they are "twice as deluded," where "twice" means doubly increased.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate salvation and profound instruction, wept and joined his palms, addressing the Buddha:

“Although I have received from the Buddha such wondrous sounds and awakened to the wondrously luminous mind—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—I have nonetheless used my conditioned mind to perceive the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma. While I have indeed gained this mind (the aforementioned wondrously luminous mind) through my reverent gaze and faith in the Buddha’s words, I do not yet dare to recognize it as my fundamental, original ground of the heart.

I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will proclaim his perfect voice to uproot the source of my doubts and lead me back to the Unsurpassed Way (Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). The Buddha said to Ānanda: “You and the others still...”

To listen to the Dharma with a mind conditioned by it is to have that very Dharma become a condition; this does not constitute attaining the nature of reality (dharmatā). It is like a person pointing out the moon to another with their finger; that person, relying on the finger, should look at the moon.

If one further observes the finger and takes it to be the substance of the moon, this person not only loses the lunar disc, but also loses the finger itself. Why? Because he takes the pointed-at finger to be the bright moon.

Not only does he lose the finger, but he also fails to distinguish between light and darkness. Why? Because he takes the very substance of the finger to be the nature of the moon’s brightness; thus, he confuses the two natures of light and darkness.

Because there is nothing to be comprehended. It is the same with you: if you take this discriminative sound of my preaching the Dharma to be your mind, then this mind should inherently possess the nature of discrimination even apart from the discriminative sound.

For example, it is like a traveler staying overnight at an inn; having rested for a moment, he departs and never remains permanently. Yet the one who manages the inn does not go anywhere and is called the "master of the inn.

It is the same with this: if it were truly your mind, it would have no place to go. How could it then lack the nature of discrimination when separated from sound? This would mean that it is not only the sound that is discriminated.

The mind discriminates its own appearance, yet it is apart from all physical forms and possesses a non-discriminative nature. Thus, it continues until discrimination is entirely absent; it is neither form nor emptiness. Kauśika and others have mistakenly identified this as the "Dark Principle" (Tattva).

When one is apart from the conditions of all phenomena and possesses a non-discriminative nature, then the various objects to which your mind-nature returns must be accounted for. How, then, can it be the master?

Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature has various places to which it returns, then how is it that the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrously luminous original mind as being 'without return'? I pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me. The Buddha told Ānanda:

Difficult. Moreover, you see me; this clarity of seeing is the fundamental source of luminous perception. Although this seeing is not the wondrous, supremely lucid mind—it is like a second moon, not a reflection of the moon—you should listen attentively.
"Now I shall show you the ground where there is no returning. Ānanda, in this great lecture hall, the eastern side is wide open. When the sun rises in the sky, there is brilliant radiance;

at midnight during a dark moon, when clouds and mist obscure the light, it becomes dark and murky again. Through the openings of doors and windows, one sees through; between walls and buildings, one perceives obstruction. In places of distinction, one perceives conditions;

within the vast emptiness, there is everywhere the nature of space. When the appearance of dense and turbid [clouds] arises, it is bound up with murky dust; when the atmosphere clears and the mists subside, one again perceives purity."

[Ananda] replied, “It is difficult. “You have all observed these various manifested forms (namely, the eight kinds of forms mentioned above). I shall now cause each of them to return to its original source. What is the original source? Ānanda, as for these various manifestations: luminosity returns to the sun; why is this?

Because without the sun there would be no light, and since luminosity depends upon the sun, it therefore returns to the sun. Darkness returns to the dark moon; penetration returns to doors and windows; obstruction returns to walls and buildings.”

When the conditions return, discrimination returns; when the stubborn void returns, emptiness returns; when the dense clouds return, dust returns; when the clear and bright sky returns, the weather clears. Thus, all that exists within the various worlds does not transcend these categories.

As for the eight kinds of objects you perceive, within the luminous nature of your seeing, toward which would you wish to return? Why is this? If you were to return to light, then in the absence of light, you would no longer see darkness.

Although there are various distinctions such as light and darkness, the faculty of seeing itself has no distinction. That which can be returned to is naturally not you; that which cannot be returned to—what else could it be but you? Thus, you should know the nature of your own mind.

This fundamental wondrous clarity you have lost through your own delusion and confusion; you have forfeited your original nature and undergo the cycle of birth and death, constantly drifting and drowning within it. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called one who is worthy of compassion.

[The Sevenfold Nature of Non-retrogression and Permanence] [Wenling]: Because he has awakened to the wondrously luminous mind—which is fundamentally perfect and complete without any loss—through hearing the sound of the Dharma, it is called the "ever-abiding ground of the mind.

Yet, his emotional understanding remains crude and his vision is not yet refined; he still takes the "perceiving mind" that hears as the "wondrous nature" that is realized. This is precisely what ordinary people doubt and confuse, taking the sense-faculties for the mind, making them difficult to uproot.

Therefore, he prays that the Buddha will pull him out of this. [Commentary]: Ānanda listens to the Dharma with a perceiving mind, which is none other than the aforementioned discrimination of conditioned objects. Thus, he again...

The guest uses logical inference to challenge the host within the pavilion, using this as a metaphor for the nature of the permanently abiding (śāśvata-dhātu), which is that which "has no place of return" among the eight [objects].

This reveals the culmination of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and serves to clarify the practice of *vipaśyanā* (insight); thus, it demonstrates the nature of non-return. [Wenling] "Discriminating the sound" refers to the mind that takes sound as its object, namely that which discriminates the sounds of the Dharma.

"Discriminating my appearance" refers to the mind that takes form as its object, namely that which complies with what is gazed upon. The phrase "and so forth" includes all six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), none of which possess self-nature.

Because the mind that conditions sensory objects has no substance apart from those objects, Kauśika and others mistook this for the "Dark Principle" (Tattva). [Wuxing] When Ānanda asked about the wondrously luminous primordial mind, the Buddha answered with the "essence of seeing.
One should know that this seeing is also the aforementioned seeing that conditions sensory objects;
