Seventh, it clarifies the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, encompassing all phenomena without exception. If one discusses the arising [of phenomena] from the beginningless past, then consciousness gives rise to seeing; seeing gives rise to space; and because of space, the world first comes into being.

Now, we shall reverse the derivative to return to the fundamental, and move from the limited to the universal. Therefore, we first present the obstructive and conditioned material phenomena of earth, fire, water, and wind, and contrast them with the boundless and immovable void.
We examine each one individually through the seal of its inherent nature (*dharmatā*), collectively designating this as "nature. Furthermore, it is shown that if this void is the nature...

The circumference is all-pervasive and fundamentally without movement. You should know that the present earth, fire, water, and wind are equally called the five great elements; their nature is truly perfect and interfused, all being the *tathāgatagarbha*, fundamentally without birth or extinction.

This section concludes the dialectical discussion between form and emptiness, intending to show through the pervasiveness of space that the preceding four elements are likewise pervasive and eternal. Having clarified the pervasive nature of the dependent [elements], the pervasiveness of the primary [element] has not yet been clarified;

therefore, following the external objects of insentient form and emptiness, it proceeds to cite the internal faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, likewise sealing them with this fundamental nature to demonstrate: [Text continues...]

If one perceives that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are by nature perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unshakable, one should know that the boundless, unmoving void, along with the shifting earth, fire, water, and wind, are likewise so.

All are equally named the six great elements. (And so forth. First, form is fused to return to emptiness; then, both form and emptiness are further fused to return to seeing. This serves as a comprehensive analysis of the union of sense organs and objects.

Furthermore, the organs and their objects are subsumed to return to the consciousness-mind. By means of the pervasiveness of consciousness, it is revealed that every organ and every object is none other than the Dharma-realm, mutually subsuming and mutually pervading one another.

Yet, while having consciousness and having cognition is certainly delusion, when stamped with the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*), there is no separate dharma whatsoever. Therefore, it is said: "The nature-consciousness is luminous knowledge; the awakened luminosity is true consciousness. By this analogy, form is the form of the nature, and emptiness is likewise.

This is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Among the seven great elements, there is none that does not manifest this principle. When one can use this seal of nature to stamp all myriad dharmas, such that the entire nature subsumes form, it is called "the true emptiness within the nature of form" (*prakṛti-rūpa-bhūta-śūnyatā*);

this is *śamatha*. When the entirety of form subsumes emptiness, it is called "the true form within the nature of emptiness" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā-bhūta-rūpa*); this is *samādhi*. When emptiness and form are mutually fused, pure and eternally pervasive, this is *dhyāna*.

Thus, these wondrous forms and wondrous mind are both beyond the reach of conjecture or deliberation; therefore, it is repeatedly concluded that "where there are only words, there is no real meaning. Ānanda’s request for the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna has now reached its conclusion.

What follows consists merely of his realization, expressions of gratitude, and the making of vows. However, while the preceding section clarified that the seven great elements and all phenomena are each universally pervasive, the current realization only clarifies the pervasiveness of the Mind and does not yet address the pervasiveness of form.
This is because, being at the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), the primary task is to clarify fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Thus it is recorded.

It says: "These hosts of devas each know for themselves that their minds pervade the ten directions; with utmost sincerity and refinement, they are pervasive and complete, encompassing the ten directions.

This refers to the pervasiveness of the mind. They see the emptiness of the ten directions as clearly as observing a leaf held in one's hand. When they look back at the body born of their parents, it is like a single bubble floating upon a vast, deep ocean—its arising and ceasing have no source.

This has not yet reached the pervasiveness of form. According to the *Lotus Sūtra*, regarding the mutual functioning of the six sense organs, within this very ordinary body born of parents, it is like pure lapis lazuli, [revealing] the ten realms..."

As for the manifestation of reflections, by comparison with this, one knows that the present statement regarding "attaining the fundamental wondrous mind" and "fundamental awakening abiding eternally" refers specifically to the attainment within the stage of contemplative practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).

It is truly remarkable to observe the old commentators’ claim that the scriptural passage still belongs to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and their further assertion that it merely describes intellectual understanding; they have clearly failed to see the point. As the verse says, "wondrously profound," etc.:

because one awakens to the three kinds of subtle and secret contemplation, one uses the Buddha-dharma itself to praise the Buddha-dharma. Previously, before receiving this instruction, it was merely said, "I see the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks"; this was indeed a state of having [dualistic] vision.

If there are defilements, there is calculation; if there are characteristics, there is birth and cessation. Now, hearing that the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is pure and free from further obstructed views, it is called "wondrously profound" (*miao-zhan*).

This praises the Tathāgata’s virtue of *prajñā*, while the body belongs to the merit of retribution, which arises from *śamatha*. Hearing that the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is perfect illumination and no longer self-limiting, it is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*).

This praises the Tathāgata’s virtue of *vimukti*, while the body belongs to the merit of response, which arises from *samādhi*. Hearing that the essence, nature, and characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna* are of one suchness and no longer subject to birth and cessation, it is called "non-... [the text here is incomplete].

"Movement. This praises the virtue of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. While the body is the myriad dharmas, its efficacy arises from *dhyāna*. The Tathāgata takes virtue as his body and speaks according to realization;

Furthermore, in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, ignorance has eight conditions, and the arising of phenomena also involves this text: first, the mundane dependent origination of experience, meaning that from the eye and form, consciousness arises, which is seeing; from clarity and form, it is manifested."

1. The dependent origination of sustenance (*pratisthāna-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), namely, the three nutriments such as [the consumption of] sheep and so forth. 2. The dependent origination of causal conditions (*hetu-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the causes of killing, greed, and so forth. 3.

The dependent origination of the continuity of the birth-body (*janma-kāya-saṃtati-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the conjunction of perception and craving (*saṃjñā-tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*). 4. The dependent origination of support (*ādhāra-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to all world-systems. 5. The dependent origination of differentiation (*viśeṣa-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the four modes of birth: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. 6.

The dependent origination of purification (*viśuddhi-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to reflection and cultivation based on the teachings. 7. The dependent origination of mastery (*vaśitā-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). These two types of dependent origination are also found in the lower sutras; furthermore, there are eight kinds.
This analysis also appears in this passage from the *Treatise on the Three Non-natures* (*Sanwu xing lun*).

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment—the fundamental wondrously enlightened clarity—is neither increased nor decreased in comparison to the Tathāgata’s mind, then why did the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise without apparent cause?

Now that the Tathāgata has attained the wondrous, empty, and luminous enlightenment, when will the conditioned habits and outflows of mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever arise again? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "It is like this..."
It is like a person who has lost their way in a village and mistakes south for north. Does this delusion arise because of further delusion, or does it emerge through awakening?

Pūrṇa said: "Such a person who is lost neither arises because of delusion nor because of awakening. Why is this? Delusion fundamentally has no root; how could it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not produce delusion;

how could it arise because of awakening? The Buddha said: "When that person who is lost is in the midst of being lost, suddenly there is another person who awakens them by pointing out the way. Pūrṇa, what do you think? Even though this person is lost..."

“Would you become confused again in this village? “No, World-Honored One. “Pūrṇa, it is the same with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. This delusion has no origin; its nature is ultimately empty.

Originally there was no delusion, yet there appeared the perception of delusion. When one awakens from delusion, the delusion is extinguished, and awakening does not give rise to further delusion. It is also like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky; when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish into the sky.
Suppose a foolish person were to wait for those flowers to grow back again in that very spot where they vanished. Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise?”
Pūrṇa said, "In emptiness there were originally no flowers; it was through deluded vision that they arose and ceased. To perceive the cessation of the flowers as emptiness is already an inversion.

To command them to appear again is truly madness. How can such a madman be called either ignorant or wise? The Buddha said, "According to what you understand, why do you ask about the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous emptiness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas?"
When would mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever emerge again? It is like gold ore mixed with refined gold: once that gold is pure, it can never again become alloyed.
It is like wood turned to ash, which cannot become wood again. The Bodhi and Nirvana of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are likewise thus.

[The Four Ultimate Perfect Enlightenments] [Commentary]: The confusion and awakening of sentient beings and Tathāgatas, the presence or absence of habitual outflows before and after, the arising and ceasing of the world’s beginning and end, and the sudden emergence of the opposite state of purity—all these are due to the fetters of false doubt and the arising of delusive causes. Thus, views of extremes such as nihilism and eternalism suddenly emerge.

Since even subtle delusions within this essence of awakening must be questioned, the intent of the objection is that although the principle of the essence of original enlightenment is the same for ordinary beings and Buddhas, the Buddha has already realized the wondrous [state].

If emptiness is luminous awareness, for what reason would phenomena such as mountains and rivers arise again? The Buddha cited this to show that once a deluded person has awakened, awakening does not give rise to delusion;

this serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s ultimate realization of enlightenment, wherein there are no false mountains and rivers. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "Once gold has been formed, it is never again turned into ore; the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is likewise so. What was originally non-delusive refers to the wood, which represents awakening.

When awakening awakens from delusion and delusion is extinguished, this is precisely initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). [Wenling] further explains that the lower eye disease (*timira*) is a metaphor for false seeing, while the flowers are a metaphor for mountains and rivers.
The metaphor of the extinction of flowers in the sky illustrates the wondrous, luminous awareness of emptiness;

furthermore, the subsequent use of gold as a metaphor for the fruit of Bodhi—awareness that never changes—and ash as a metaphor for the fruit-virtue of Nirvana—non-arising—these four metaphors cited in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* serve to show that although delusion and awakening are both illusory, they do not preclude cultivation and realization. [Commentary] This passage clarifies the confusion regarding the two gates of nature and cultivation, which must not be neglected in isolation;
therefore, both meanings are presented together. As Mañjuśrī says in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "The Buddha asked, 'Have you entered the inconceivable samādhi? He replied, 'I have.'"

Regarding the inquiry: "How can it be said that one enters this [state], when it is fundamentally complete and requires no effort of cultivation or realization? Furthermore, it says: "When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I wished to enter this samādhi; it was like a person learning archery—who, through long practice, hits the mark naturally.

These statements suggest that although the nature is fundamentally complete, cultivation and realization are not without purpose. Moreover, it says: "It is like testing gold ore, which must be struck with a hammer and refined. Likewise, the marks of non-retrogressive wisdom require the sphere of practice to be unforgetting and unattached, fully established and immovable; only then is it clearly understood that non-retrogressive wisdom has been attained. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng) states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha: "Son of good family, all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-garbha, yet they do not realize it because they are obscured by afflictions. Son of good family, just as gold ore contains gold within, yet the gold cannot be seen unless it is smelted and refined, so too does the Tathāgata-garbha exist within the bodies of all sentient beings. However, because it is obscured by various afflictions, sentient beings do not perceive it.

Son of good family, just as a skilled smith smelts and refines gold ore until the gold is pure and free from impurities, so too does the Tathāgata teach sentient beings to cultivate the path of wisdom. Through this cultivation, they gradually eliminate the afflictions until they are exhausted, and then they realize the Tathāgata-garbha. Thus, although the nature is fundamentally complete, one must still undergo cultivation and realization to manifest it. This is the meaning of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*.

The Vajra Chapter also employs metaphors such as melting gold to clarify that the characteristics of realized wisdom are non-retrogressive; thus, the incident of Ānanda’s mistaken fall was entirely for the purpose of self-testing.

Pūrṇa, furthermore, you asked: "The natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally round and harmonious, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; yet I doubt that the natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another.

You also questioned how empty space and the great earth, both of which pervade the Dharma-realm, could coexist without conflict. Pūrṇa, it is like this: the substance of empty space is not itself any of the various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those phenomena.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, when the sun shines upon that great empty space, it is bright; when clouds gather, it is dark; when the wind blows, it moves; and when the sky clears, it is serene.
When clear, the air is pure; when the air coagulates, it becomes turbid. When earth accumulates, it forms a haze; when water settles, it forms a reflection. What do you think?

Regarding these various conditioned phenomena in different directions, are they produced because of that [external object], or do they exist within emptiness itself? If they were produced by that [object], Pūrṇa, when the sun shines, since it is the sun’s radiance, the worlds of the ten directions would all share the same solar color.

Why, then, is a round sun still seen in the sky? If it were the luminosity of emptiness, then emptiness should illuminate itself; why then does it not produce such brilliance during the night when there are clouds and mist? You should know this.

This clarity is neither the sun nor space; it is not distinct from space or the sun. Its observed characteristics are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described—like seeking flowers in the sky and binding them into a fruit of the sky.

How can you question the meaning of their mutual suppression and extinction? Observe that the nature is fundamentally true: it is solely the wondrously enlightened clarity. This mind of wondrously enlightened clarity was originally neither water nor fire; how can you further ask why they are mutually incompatible?

The true, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this. When you clarify it through space, then space appears; when you clarify earth, water, fire, or wind individually, then each appears individually;
if you clarify them all together, then they all appear together. How do they appear together? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.

If two people look at it together, the sun in the water seems to move east and west with each of them, so that one goes east and the other goes west. Since there was originally no fixed standard for its location, you should not raise the objection that "this sun is only one."
How can each move separately? Since each day is already a duality, how can they manifest as one? This revolving delusion is beyond the reach of exhaustive inquiry. [5.

The Mutual Interfusion of All Characteristics] In the second part of Pūrṇa’s response concerning the metaphor that empty space has no characteristics yet does not obstruct manifestation, it is said that the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire;

therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "For example, based upon space there exist the great earth, light, water, fire, the sun, and the moon, yet the realm of empty space is not those various characteristics. Furthermore—
The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* states: "The various illusory manifestations of all sentient beings are all produced from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment.

This means that although their essential nature (*tattva*) is empty, it does not obstruct the appearance of illusory forms. Below this, the text distinguishes how delusion lacks reality: If light were produced from the sun, then [the space] would share the same color as the sun, and one should not see the full orb of the sun within the void.

If light were produced from the void, then at midnight when there is no sun, that void should be luminous. Regarding the observation of appearances, it is fundamentally false; thus, they do not mutually suppress or extinguish one another. Regarding the observation of the nature, it is fundamentally true; thus, it does not... [suppress or extinguish].
As for those who claim compatibility, they cite two instances of the sun to demonstrate that all phenomena are illusory and cannot withstand rigorous inquiry.

Pūrṇa, you take form and emptiness to oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgata-garbha; yet the Tathāgata-garbha, following these deluded perceptions, manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, there is the movement of wind and the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun and the darkness of clouds.

Sentient beings become confused and bewildered, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly toil and manifest the appearances of the mundane world. By means of my wondrous...

It is luminous, neither extinguished nor arising, and is conjoined with the *tathāgatagarbha*. This *tathāgatagarbha* is solely wondrous, enlightened luminosity, which perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one; the small manifests the large, and the large manifests the small. Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), it pervades the worlds of the ten directions; its body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions. Within a single hair-tip, it manifests jeweled-king lands (the small manifesting the large);

sitting within a minute speck of dust, it turns the great wheel of the Dharma (the large manifesting the small, being easy to understand, is omitted here). By extinguishing the dust of the senses and merging with enlightenment, it gives rise to the wondrous, enlightened nature of luminosity of *tathatā*. And thus...

The Ālayavijñāna is the fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and complete mind. It is neither mind nor space; it is neither earth, water, wind, nor fire; it is neither eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, nor mind;

it is neither form, nor sound, odor, taste, touch, nor mental objects (*dharma*); it is neither the sphere of visual consciousness. And so on, up to: it is neither the sphere of mental consciousness. It is neither clarity nor ignorance, nor the exhaustion of ignorance (this merely means "no ignorance";

do not be fixated on the two extra characters for "clarity"). And so on, up to: it is neither old age nor death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death; it is neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path; it is neither wisdom nor attainment; it is neither *dāna* (giving), nor *śīla* (precept-keeping), nor *vīrya* (diligence).

It is not kṣānti (patience); it is not vīrya (diligence); it is not dhyāna (meditative concentration); it is not prajñā (wisdom); it is not pāramitā (the perfection [of these six]). Thus, it extends even to being not tathāgata (Tathāgata), and not arhat (Worthy One).

Samyaksaṃbodhi (Perfect Universal Knowledge) is not the Great Nirvāṇa; it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity. Because it is thus "neither this nor that" (concluding the above and initiating what follows), it pertains to both the mundane and the supramundane.

It is the Tathāgatagarbha, the primordial luminosity and the wondrous mind. It is the mind itself, and it is emptiness. It is earth, and it is water; it is wind, and it is fire. It is the eye; it is the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. It is form; it is sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects.

It is the sphere of visual consciousness; and so on, up to the sphere of mental consciousness. It is luminosity and non-luminosity, and the exhaustion of luminosity and non-luminosity. And so on, up to it is old age and...
Death is [identical to] the exhaustion of old age and death; it is suffering, it is its origin, it is cessation, and it is the path; it is wisdom, it is attainment;
it is dāna, śīla, vīrya, kṣānti, dhyāna, and prajñā; it is the pāramitās. Thus, up to and including, it is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Great Nirvāṇa;
it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Because all these are identical—both worldly and supramundane—it is the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind.

It is apart from both being and non-being; it is both being and non-being. How can the beings of the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who transcend the world, use their minds of limited knowledge to fathom the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi, or employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? It is like the lute, the harp, the *konghou*, and the *pipa*:

though they possess exquisite sounds (representing the nature of the treasury), if there are no skillful fingers (representing true wisdom), they can never produce music (representing the arising of function). You and all sentient beings are also like this: the precious, awakened True Mind (corresponding to the aforementioned exquisite sound) is perfectly complete in each and every one. Yet, when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal Samādhi is manifested.

Kāśyapa, as soon as you raise your mind, worldly afflictions arise first; this is because you have not diligently sought the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a small attainment sufficient.

[The Sixfold Threefold Truths of the Wondrous Mind]: "The long-water edition [of the *Sūtra*] states: 'The wondrous, perfect mind is neither mind nor emptiness,' etc., which clarifies the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by way of negating characteristics;

'the primordial luminosity of the mind is wondrous—this very mind is emptiness,' etc., which clarifies the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of affirming characteristics; and 'the primordial wondrous luminosity of the mind is free from both affirmation and negation,' etc., which clarifies the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*) by way of simultaneous negation and illumination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "Ocean Seal" (*sāgaramudrā*), the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "All forms and images existing in Jambudvīpa are manifested as seal-impressions within the great ocean. This means that inconceivable reflections appear and manifest with sovereign spontaneity.
He replied, "The Ocean Seal.

Pūrṇa said, "I and the Tathāgata share the same perfect clarity of precious awakening, the truly wondrous and pure mind, both being equally complete and perfect. Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusive thoughts and have long remained in saṃsāra.

Although I have now attained the Holy Vehicle, I have not yet reached the ultimate end. World-Honored One, when all delusions are completely extinguished, there remains only the wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata about all things—"

“Sentient beings! For what reason do they have delusions? How is it that they obscure their own wondrous luminosity and undergo this drowning in saṃsāra? The Buddha told Pūrṇa: “Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain.

I shall now question you again by means of things present before us in the world. Have you not heard of the one named Yan-liao-da-duo (Śaśaviṣāṇa) in the city of Śrāvastī? One morning, he suddenly looked at his face in a mirror.

He became attached to the head in the mirror, whose eyebrows and eyes were clearly visible, and grew resentful toward his own head for not seeing its features. Thinking it was a goblin, he ran about wildly and uncontrollably. What do you think of this?”

"For what reason does this person run about madly without cause? Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged; there is no other cause. The Buddha said, "The wondrous awakening is perfectly bright, and its fundamental brightness is wondrous.

Since it is called 'delusion,' how can it have a cause? If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion? From these various deluded thoughts, they mutually cause one another; from confusion, confusion accumulates."

Having passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, even though the Buddhas have illuminated the truth for them, they still cannot turn back. Such a cause of delusion exists inherently because of delusion itself. If one recognizes that delusion has no cause, then the false has nothing upon which it can rely;

since there is not even birth, what is there to be extinguished? One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream. Even if the mind were exceptionally sharp and clear, by what causes and conditions could one take hold of objects within a dream?

How much more so when there is no cause and these things are fundamentally non-existent—just like that city of Ayodhyā (in the original, *Yanriaduodu*, translated here as "Cishou"). How could there be any causes or conditions for Śrīghana (translated here as "Yanjueduo") to suddenly become terrified of his own head and run away in madness?
Cease! This head was not obtained from without; even if you had not ceased your madness, what would have been lost? Pūrṇa, such is the nature (essence) of delusion: on what basis does it exist?

You need only refrain from following the threefold continuity of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings. Because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise. Then, within your mind, the madness of *Yajñadatta* will cease of itself.

This cessation is itself Bodhi—the supremely pure and luminous mind—which fundamentally pervades the Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others. What need is there for arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization? It is like this:

A person had tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remained unaware of it; wandering to distant lands, he ran about begging for food. Although he was truly impoverished (as myriad delusions raced across his mind), the jewel had never been lost (the one true reality remained perfectly present).
Suddenly, a wise person points out the pearl to him; his wishes are fulfilled according to his heart, and he attains great wealth and abundance.

Only then does he realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from the outside. [7. Investigating the Root of Delusion] [Wenling]: Since it has been realized that there is no duality, this further clarifies the categories of delusion; therefore, he requests an investigation into its cause.

Below, Pūrṇa refers to how he was formerly beset by false thoughts and addresses the World-Honored One as one for whom all delusions have been completely extinguished. This seems to imply that delusion has a cause and that delusion can be extinguished; therefore, [the Buddha] tells him: "Just as... and so forth.

This restates the analogy to further clarify that delusion is without cause and thus cannot be extinguished. [Supplementary Note] "Not following causes and conditions" refers to the causes and conditions within the three aforementioned types of continuity.
[Commentary] The *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "One first realizes that sentient beings are originally Buddhas; it is said that if the frantic mind ceases, that cessation is itself Bodhi.

It also states: "Birth-and-death and Nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; this is like a person awake recounting the events of their dream. Indeed, mistaking the head for a reflection arises entirely from the nature of this frantic mind.

"If conditions are such that reflections vanish and emotions perish, then the original nature of Bodhi is not obtained from without; therefore it is said: 'What need is there for the toil of refining and realizing through painful effort?

At that moment, Ānanda, amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, rose, and addressed the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, you have just now spoken of the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—though the text stops here, the meaning refers to all sentient beings in the world.

Because these three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; thus, in the mind of Citta-datta, the nature of madness naturally subsides. This subsiding is itself Bodhi, not obtained from another. These causes and conditions are thus clear and evident. Why [is this so]...'"

“Tathāgata, you have suddenly abandoned causes and conditions, whereas I attained awakening of the mind through causes and conditions. World-Honored One, why is it that this principle applies not only to us junior śrāvakas in training, but also to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others in this assembly?
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions from an elderly brahmin, they resolved their minds, attained awakening, and achieved the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Now, if you say that bodhi does not arise from causes and conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svayambhū*) taught by the Kauśīlīs and other non-Buddhists in Rājagṛha would constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). We pray that you will grant us great [compassion].”

How tragic! It awakens one from delusion and confusion. The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just as in the city with the case of Yantradatta; if the causal conditions for his madness are extinguished, then he is no longer mad."

It arises spontaneously; causes and conditions are spontaneous. Reasoning reaches its ultimate limit here, Ānanda. (The following uses causes and conditions to refute spontaneity: If Yajñadatta’s head was originally spontaneous—if it was originally so by itself, such that there is no "so-ness" that is not self-originated—then for what cause and condition did he become terrified of his head and run about madly?

(The following uses spontaneity to refute causes and conditions: If the head is spontaneous, yet he went mad because of causes and conditions, why would it not be spontaneous to lose it because of causes and conditions? His original head has never been lost.

The frantic fear emerges delusively, yet it has never undergone any change; why rely upon causes and conditions? Franticness is fundamentally natural and fundamentally possessed. Before one was frantic, where did this franticness lie hidden?

Being naturally non-frantic, the head was originally without delusion; why then run about in a frenzy? If one awakens to the fundamental head and recognizes the frantic running, then both "causes and conditions" and "nature" are merely frivolous arguments (*prapañca*).

[Eight Causes and Conditions are Spontaneous] [Wenling]: Below, [the text] uses causes and conditions to refute spontaneity. "Spontaneous" means that which is originally natural and does not depend upon causes and conditions.

If it were originally natural, then there would be no going where it is not spontaneous; why then would one need the cause and condition of looking in a mirror, becoming terrified of one's head, and running about in madness?

Thus, the calculation of spontaneity falls away. Furthermore, if madness arises because of causes and conditions, why would it not be spontaneous? If one claims that the terror and madness are also [caused by conditions], then...

If one who is naturally prone to madness were not already mad, where would that madness lie in potential? Nor is it a case of natural madness occurring spontaneously. Therefore, I say that when the three conditions are severed, the Bodhicitta arises;

as the Bodhicitta arises, the mind of birth-and-death ceases. This is merely the cessation of birth-and-death. When both arising and ceasing are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*).

If there were such a thing as "natural" [arising], then it would mean that the naturally arising mind appears and the mind of birth-and-death ceases; yet this too is birth-and-death. That which is without birth-and-death is called [the Unconditioned].

It is spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Just as in the world, when various characteristics blend and harmonize to form a single entity, it is called "the nature of combination" (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*); that which is not combined is termed "the original nature" (*prakṛti-svabhāva*). This original nature is not "original," and this combination (of causes and conditions) is not "combined.

Being free from both combination and originality, and being neither combined nor original—only this phrase is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-dharma*), which is the truly effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*). Even Bodhi and Nirvana remain far distant [from this].

This was not achieved by your diligent cultivation and realization over kalpas. Although you have memorized the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and their pure, wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it has only increased your frivolous arguments.

Though you discourse with certainty and clarity on the nature of causes and conditions, and though people of the world acclaim you as the foremost in erudition, because of this long-term habituation to much learning, you could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman.
Why wait for my Buddha-peak divine mantra? The fire of lust in the Mātanga woman’s heart has suddenly been extinguished, and she has attained the state of *anāgāmin*.
Within my Dharma, he has become a forest of diligence (wherein progress is swift and realization manifold). The river of craving has been dried up, bringing you liberation.

Therefore, Ānanda, though you have spent kalpas memorizing and upholding the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments, it would not equal a single day (or rather, throughout kalpas) of cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) and remaining far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love. Consider, for example, the case of the Mātangī woman: in a former life she was a courtesan, yet by the power of a divine mantra, her lustful desires were dissolved.

Within the Dharma, she is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlā. Together with Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula (who likewise possessed a female body), she realized their past causes and understood the course of their past lives.

In this world, one suffers because of craving and attachment. Yet, through a single moment of cultivation of untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*), one may either transcend the bonds of existence or receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). How can you deceive yourself by failing to recognize this?
You still linger in mere observation and listening, clinging to frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).

[Commentary] To demonstrate the process of returning to cessation (*nivṛtti*) in order to dispel deluded attachments and manifest the true nature (*dharmatā*): the nature of all phenomena is empty; that which arises cannot truly give rise to it, and that which ceases cannot truly extinguish it.

This cessation occurs through the side of meaning related to cultivation and abandonment; within the sphere of deluded effort, various distinctions arise. First, one uses wisdom to dispel attachment, yet one sinks back into the ocean of consciousness. Next, one uses cessation to extinguish cessation, yet one remains stuck in functional capacity.

Even when there is nothing further to be dispelled and the Path merges with non-action, one then realizes the ultimate principle and reaches the limit of returning to the source. Therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* speaks of "gradual detachment."

Regarding the manifestation of the Middle Way through the refutation of attachments within six types of dual extremes, what are these six? First, it refers to the view that all phenomena are ultimately subject to extinction, as well as the attachment to ultimate extinction, and the attachment to the real existence of the grasper and the grasped;
continuing thus up to the sixth, which is the attachment to non-arising and simultaneous arising, and to both the possible extinction and the actual extinction—each of these constitutes an extreme.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Both phenomena and non-phenomena lack intrinsic nature; by awakening to this principle, it is called Bodhi. If this is so, then as for the...
That is to say, for those whose minds are attached to arising and ceasing, all such things are merely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Section Three: The Division on the Arousing of the Mind (Text in two parts).

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions and admonitions, had their doubts and perplexities eliminated; their minds awakened to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and their bodies and minds attained a lightness and ease never before experienced. Once again, they were moved with grief.
Tears flowing as his realization deepened into sorrow, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Unsurpassed Great Compassion, Pure Jewel King!
You have skillfully opened my mind, using such various causes, conditions, and expedient means to uplift and guide us, leading those who are submerged in darkness out of the ocean of suffering.

World-Honored One, although I now receive these Dharma sounds and know that the Tathāgata-garbha—the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind—pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nourishing the pure, jewel-adorned lands of the Tathāgatas, the realms of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings, the Tathāgata further rebukes me.”

"Much learning is of no merit if it does not reach the level of cultivation. I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King (the Son of Heaven, as the Zhou dynasty called him). Although I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through the gate.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion and show me—and all those in this assembly who are still obscured by darkness—how to cast aside the Lesser Vehicle and ultimately attain the path of the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder.

May you cause those in training to know how to subdue their minds, so that they may transcend their former objects of attachment, attain *dhāraṇī* (the nature of wisdom), and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
Having prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, those in the assembly stood with single-minded devotion awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.

[Commentary: This follows from the various teachings in the preceding sutra; since one must possess complete faith and understanding and should accordingly initiate practice to aspire toward the attainment of the holy fruit, the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) follows next.

The text is divided into two parts: first, the arousal of the mind through the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*) to reveal principle, which involves apprehending the contemplation of true emptiness and realizing the virtue of nirvana—this is the practice of *śamatha*; second, the arousal of the mind...

To fully manifest that the merits of the six sense organs proceed from the selection of a faculty into the essential, flowing simultaneously through both the empty and the provisional to advance toward the Middle Way, the third contemplation contains no mention of "arousing the aspiration" (bodhicitta) but possesses the meaning of "cultivating practice.
This section has three parts: the beginning, the middle, and the end.

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those in the assembly—the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas who were not yet masters of the bodhicitta—as well as for sentient beings of the future age of dharma-decline (including those of the Hīnayāna) who shall resolve to attain bodhicitta after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, proclaimed the path of wondrous cultivation of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. He addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:

"You all must resolutely resolve upon bodhicitta and never grow weary in the wondrous samādhi of the Tathāgata (the state of fixed nature). You should first clarify the two definitive meanings regarding the initial mind that awakens. What is the first?"

"Ānanda, the two meanings of the mind are definitive. As for the first meaning: if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas and cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle (the One Vehicle of sudden perfection), entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the fruition.

Ānanda, if at the causal ground you take a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause of your practice, yet seek the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible. For this reason, you should illuminate all the conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world; they all arise from..."
It changes and perishes. Ānanda, observe the phenomena of the world that can be produced: which among them is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space decaying or crumbling.

Why is this? Because space is not something produced; therefore, from beginning to end, it is without destruction or cessation. Thus, within your body, solidity is earth, moisture is water, warmth is fire, and movement is wind.

Bound by these four elements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. From the initial stage (form) to the final stage (consciousness), these five layers become turbid and confused.
"What is meant by turbidity? Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure and pristine by nature. As for things such as dust, soil, ash, and sand, their very substance is obstructive;

this is the natural law of these two entities (their principles ought to be thus). Their natures do not accord with one another. Suppose there is a person in the world who takes that dust and soil and throws it into the pure water. The soil loses its obstructive quality, the water loses its purity, and the appearance becomes turbid."
This is called turbidity. Your fivefold turbidity is also like this. [1. Showing the Fruit and Virtue] [Commentary]:
First, it shows the state of Nirvana, free from arising and ceasing, as the basis for the initial awakening of the mind; "that which is within your own body" refers to the nature of the conditioned.

The clear water is a metaphor for the wondrous, perfectly湛 (zhàn) mind; the dust, soil, ash, and sand are metaphors for the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the phenomena of birth that can cause the eyes to see, the ears to hear, and the faculty of discrimination to discern the *zhàn*.
Because the five layers confound the true, the five aggregates are called turbidity.

Ānanda, you perceive empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions, yet emptiness and seeing are not distinguished. There is emptiness but no substance; there is seeing but no awareness. These interweave to falsely form [this state];

this is the first layer, called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Your body is currently a lump formed from the four great elements as its substance. Seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing (these six faculties of sensation) are congested and made obstructive; water, fire, wind, and earth (these six objective realms) revolve and cause awareness and knowing.

These interweave in delusion to form existence. This is the second layer, called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). Furthermore, within your minds, the recollection of the past, the consciousness of the present, and the study of the teachings give rise to the nature of cognition and vision;

these appear as the six sense objects, yet apart from the objects they have no marks, and apart from perception they have no substance. These interweave in delusion to form existence. This is the third layer, called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*). Moreover, morning and evening, your births and deaths ceaselessly continue;

your cognition and vision always desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma constantly shifts you through lands (also the world). These interweave in delusion to form existence. This is the fourth layer, called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*). You all see [this].

Hearing that there is originally no difference in nature, yet the various sensory objects are separated and distinct, and that they arise differently without apparent cause— wherein their natures mutually recognize one another (for nature is originally without difference), while their functions turn away from one another (as the various objects are separated and arise differently)— this loss of the standard between identity (of nature) and difference (of function),
where these characteristics interweave to form delusion, is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life.

[II. Explaining the Five Turbidities] [Gushan]: The five turbidities depend upon the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Since both the sense faculties and their objects are material (*rūpa*), the meaning of "turbidity" is clearly manifested by the eye-faculty seeing space.

Because the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are all termed *kalpas*, seeing space constitutes the turbidity of the *kalpa* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Since space has no good or bad to be perceived, it is specifically because the seeing of space interweaves with turbid confusion that the true nature is obscured;

thus it is called the turbidity of the *kalpa*. [Commentary]: The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) pertains to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are the six roots of sensation (*vedanendriya*). Water, fire, wind, and earth are the six objects (*viṣaya*).

The objective realm also possesses characteristics because it depends on the sense faculties; it causes obstruction because it triggers cognition through sensory objects, thereby turning toward awareness.

The turbidity of afflictions constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); recollection, consciousness, and the rehearsal of learning all take perception as their essence. Recalling the past, discerning the present, and rehearsing the future—all arise from greed and anger, which are produced by perception.

By the power of conceptual thought, the nature of cognition and vision is activated, and the appearances of the six sense-objects manifest within perception; therefore, perception is the turbidity of afflictions. The turbidity of sentient beings constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), characterized by the incessant arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena.

Because the characteristics of formations (*saṃskāra*) undergo constant flux, they are called the "movement of karma. The deluded perceptions and views of this movement constitute the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); since all formations are impermanent, the realms constantly shift. The turbidity of life constitutes the nature of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Within this nature, there is mutual resonance, which is like having no different surnames; yet, due to the separation by sensory objects (*viṣaya*), they turn away from one another.

"Same" refers to the essence of consciousness, while "different" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects. Because the standards for self and other are lost and names and appearances become entangled, the Sūtra says: "Nirvāṇa is called 'without weaving' (*an-utkṣepa*). Weaving is the interpenetration of two things, the creation and action of warp and woof."

In terms of its meaning, the essence of nirvāṇa is intrinsically pure and does not depend upon various conditions; therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states that "nirvāṇa is so called because it has no destination and because it is free from weaving."

Ānanda, if you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death and rely upon that which is non-arising and non-ceasing, perfected as a perfectly湛 (zhàn) and profound nature.

By means of this profound stillness, you should revolve the false and illusory arising and ceasing, subduing them to restore original enlightenment. Having attained the originally luminous enlightenment and its nature of no-arising and no-ceasing, make this the mind for the ground of practice.

Thereafter, one fully realizes the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition. It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel; when it is deep and motionless, the sand and soil naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one—this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions.

When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance. When the marks of clarity are refined and pure, all transformations and manifestations no longer constitute afflictions;
they all accord with the pure and wondrous virtues of nirvana.

[The Subduing and Severance by the Threefold Knowledge] refers to the karmic functions of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), which are the root of birth and death; it refers to the nature of perfect clarity, the true essence of original wisdom.

First, one subdues adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), meaning that one first eliminates the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and permanently severs the roots, thereby further eradicating the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"Afflictions such as greed are like turbid water and dust, while the dharmas that are the fruit upon non-conceptual wisdom are like the water in a pond, manifesting the Buddha-dharma body and all its merits. Furthermore, there are two ways of entering [the path] to subdue and sever these adventitious defilements. One...

There are two ways of entry: entry by principle and entry by practice. Regarding entry by principle, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "Deeply believe that sentient beings do not differ from true nature;

they are neither identical nor distinct, but are merely obscured by adventitious defilements. One should settle the mind in awakening, contemplate the reality of the Buddha-nature as quiescent, unconditioned, and free from discrimination—this is entry by principle.

Now, the substance of these adventitious defilements refers to the delusions countered by *śamatha*. To illustrate this through analogy: water represents the self-nature which is fundamentally pure, while dust represents the illusory divisions.

Furthermore, regarding the various treatises that adopt the meaning of the sūtras to establish that the nature of the mind is inherently pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), each master has their own positions and refutations. To briefly cite them here:

the Vibhajyavādins quote a sūtra which says, "The mind of sentient beings is originally pure, luminous, and immaculate; it is only because it is covered by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) that it is seen as impure.

When these afflictions are eliminated, one attains liberation. The Vaibhāṣikas refute this, saying: "If the nature of the mind were inherently pure and yet defiled by afflictions such that it is seen as impure, [it would follow that]..."

[Question: Why is it that the nature of the mind, which is fundamentally defiled by afflictions, is seen as pure? [Answer/Explanation: The meaning of the "nature of the mind" (cittaprakṛti) originally appears in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and other scriptures;

it was simply cited by Dignāga. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* sought to refute this by applying logical principles, hence its question: "Why is this not so? In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, Sthiramati’s commentary states:

"That which is called 'adventitious dust' (āgantuka-mala) refers to the fact that because the seeds of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) have not yet been permanently uprooted, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) causes the mind to manifest in two modes of activity (*dvayākāra-vṛtti*). It is not [the case that the mind is inherently pure].

Regarding the statement that "the mind of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-citta*) is [so called] because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is naturally pure," Sthiramati explains that he uses the term "dharma-nature" for the sake of distinction, intending to refute [the opponent's view].

Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the masters of the Sautrāntika school critique this, stating: "The sūtras say that the nature of the mind is originally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) in order to reveal that the essence of the mind is permanent; they speak of 'adventitious defilements' (*āgantuka-mala*) as an explanation.

Sthiramati comments that the Sautrāntikas, wishing to refute others by contradicting their own tenets, resort to such deceptive sophistry to manifest permanence. Moreover, according to the *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra*, this serves to simultaneously refute the attachments to both extremes.

By establishing the meaning of the two sides in tandem, so that the notions of defilement and purity vanish and the distinctions between right and wrong are extinguished, the nature of the mind is revealed. Thus the Treatise says:

"If this were not subject to defilement, all would be liberated spontaneously; if this were not subject to purification, there would be no fruit of effort. It is neither defiled nor non-defiled, neither pure nor non-pure, for the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, and it is only stained by adventitious afflictions."
The Second Arousing of the Mind (Section Four). Regarding the second meaning:
if you truly desire to arouse the bodhicitta and generate great courage within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, you must resolutely abandon all conditioned marks (*saṃskṛta-nimitta*).

You should carefully examine the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*), that is, the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). From beginningless time, these have given rise to karma and moistened rebirth; who is it that acts, and who is it that receives [the results]? Ānanda, if you cultivate bodhi without such careful observation, [you will not succeed].

If one does not know the root of afflictions, one cannot understand the false nature of the sense organs and their objects. If one does not even know where the inversion occurs—the very locus of bondage—how can one subdue it and attain the rank of a Tathāgata?
Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it? You have not heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this?

Because emptiness has no form or appearance, and thus there is neither knotting nor untying. Therefore, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six act as intermediaries for thieves, robbing you of your own family treasure. From this...

Since beginningless time, sentient beings and the world (which is their direct retribution) have been bound by birth; therefore, they are unable to transcend the receptacle world (which is their circumstantial retribution).

[First, clarifying the causal ground: Regarding the "causal ground," it refers to the aforementioned arousal of the bodhicitta and the contemplation of the perfectly湛 (zhan) nature. When this merges with the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*, one takes the nature free from arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation.
Because one relies on this cause to perfect the merits of the resultant ground, the destruction of empty space is used as a metaphor. This is an examination of the cause.

Since the cultivation of the mind through the three contemplations all arises from emptiness and deeply penetrates the far-reaching principle, they must necessarily encompass what precedes them; thus, those cultivating the provisional [contemplation] must rely on emptiness, and those cultivating the middle [contemplation] must take emptiness as their object.

If you wish to understand the meaning of the contemplation of emptiness and the provisional, please examine the first three chapters of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*. [Wuxing] states: "The activation of karma and the moistening of rebirth refer to afflictions; who creates them and who receives them?
This is an investigation into the root."
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation.

You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms. The past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All sentient beings [are contained within these].

The illusory manifestations interweave to form bodies, and these worlds trade with and intersect one another. Although the nature of these realms may be clearly defined by the fixed positions of the ten directions, the world itself is merely designated by east, west, south, and north.

There is no fixed position for above or below, and the center has no fixed direction. Yet, the four numbers (east, west, south, and north) must be made clear; they intersect with the three periods of time (past, present, and future). Three times four (the three periods intersecting the four directions) and four times three (the four directions intersecting the three periods) result in twelve permutations.

These flow and transform through three cycles, totaling one thousand, one hundred, and ten. Encompassing the beginning and the end, within each of the six sense faculties, there are individually twelve hundred merits. Ānanda, you should further examine these within yourself.

To determine their relative quality: as seen with the eye, what is behind is dark while what is before is bright; the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark. When looking to the left and right, only two-thirds are visible. In sum, of its functions, its merit is incomplete;

if one’s merit is reckoned in three parts, it possesses only one part of virtue. One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the ear, it hears all around without omission in the ten directions;

when active, it perceives both near and far (though this is similar rather than real), and when still, it has no boundaries. One should know that the faculty of the ear is complete with twelve hundred merits. As for the nose, it smells by means of the inhalation and exhalation of breath.

There is exiting and entering, yet it lacks the middle intersection. Examining this through the faculty of the nose, one-third is missing; thus, one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.

As for the tongue, which proclaims and fully knows all mundane and supramundane wisdom—its expression has spatial divisions while its principle is inexhaustible—one should know that the faculty of the tongue is complete with twelve hundred merits.

As for the body, which perceives touch and recognizes the disagreeable and the agreeable—it can perceive when in contact, but does not know when separated. Separation constitutes one part, while contact constitutes two. Examining this through the faculty of the body, one-third is missing; thus, one should know that the body...

It possesses only eight hundred merits, yet it silently and spontaneously accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time; whether saintly or ordinary, there is nothing it does not encompass.
To the very limits of its extent, one should know that the faculty of mind (*manas*) is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits.
[2. Revealing the Original Merits] [Wenling]: "World" refers to the shifting flow of the three periods of time; "realm" refers to each abiding in its own position.

Since there are ten realms and three periods of time, and because the principles possessed by a single body naturally interpenetrate one another, it is said that they "exchange and circulate within the body. [Commentary]: Because there are ten directions, they are multiplied tenfold; because the flowing numbers consist of three periods, they are multiplied threefold.

It transforms three times and then ceases; this is why it manifests such transformations. That it possesses the gates of merit is because they all arise according to numerical categories, which is what is being revealed here.

[Supplementary Note] Regarding the statement that there are "one thousand two hundred merits," this means there are two hundred for each of the four cardinal directions and one hundred for each of the four corners.

Because the nasal faculty of olfaction involves both inhalation and exhalation—whereby one smells when inhaling and does not smell when exhaling—and because these two states do not intersect within the process of inhalation and exhalation, one-third is missing from the full count. Thus, all six faculties take their capacity for discernment as their merit.

Furthermore, just as the body has separation and union, so too the sense-object of separation is not known because it lacks a portion of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). The mental faculty’s apprehension of objects extends across the three periods of time and possesses both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Moreover, because the power of habituation within recollection, cognition, chanting, and study is strong, it is able to silently encompass the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Ānanda, if you now wish to turn back the current of the flow of birth and death, you must trace that flow back to its root until you reach the state of neither arising nor ceasing. You should examine these six faculties of sensory reception:

which are conjoined and which are disjoined; which are deep and which are shallow; which serve as the perfect instruments for penetration, and which are incomplete (lacking in function). If you can awaken to the faculty that is perfectly penetrating among these, you will be able to turn back that beginningless flow of delusory karma woven from falsehood.

Those who attain the circular penetration and those with non-circular faculties differ by factors of ten and millions. I have now fully revealed the six profound, circular luminosities; the measure of their original merits is thus.

Choose from among them according to your preference that which you can enter, and I shall clarify it for you so that you may advance. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attained the supreme Bodhi through the cultivation of each of the eighteen realms, and among these there was no superiority or inferiority.
It is only because you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained the circular wisdom of mastery within them that I proclaim this.
I declare: let you simply enter deeply through one gate; once you have entered one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once.

[Commentary: Ānanda’s inferior faculties are in fact that which is wondrously profound and immovable. The eyes and ears perceive objects by being separated from them, while the nose and other organs know their phenomena by being joined with them.

When separated, the object is distant and thus considered "deep"; when joined, the object is near and thus considered "shallow. As the *Xianzong lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the School) states: "The first two of the five faculties function upon distant objects because they do not join with them. The *Abhidharmakośa* says: [End of excerpt]

The function of the eye reaches far and acts with speed; it sees mountains and rivers from afar but does not hear sounds. This is because one first sees the striking of a drum and only afterwards hears the sound. As for the nose and tongue, they have no such capacity to reach distant objects. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, how can one enter deeply through a single gate against the current, thereby causing all six faculties to become pure simultaneously? The Buddha told Ānanda: "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna (entering the stream), no longer entering the six sense-objects.

You have already extinguished the afflictions of the three realms that are abandoned through insight—the eighty-one *śaikṣas*. Yet you still do not know that within the faculties there lies the beginningless accumulation of delusions."

As for these habituations, they must depend upon the factors abandoned through cultivation (namely, the eighty-one volitions) to be attained; how much more so, then, for the specific divisions and enumerations of arising, abiding, change, and cessation within them? Now, you should first observe the six sense faculties present before you.
"Are they one, or are they six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see? Why does the eye not hear? Why does the head not tread? And why do the feet not speak?
If these six faculties are definitively six, then when I now proclaim this subtle and wondrous Dharma-door to you in this assembly, which of your six faculties comes to receive it?

Ānanda said, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "It is your ears that hear; what concern is this for the body or the mouth? It is the mouth that asks about the meaning, and the body that rises to show reverence. Therefore, you should know that they are not one, but ultimately six."
It is not that six become one; it is never the case that your faculties—which are originally one—become six. Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six.

Because since beginningless time they have been submerged in inversion (that is, delusion and karma), the meanings of "one" and "six" arise within the perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound [mind]. You, as a Srotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six, have not yet lost the one. It is like the great empty space, which accommodates and merges with all manner of vessels.

Because the shapes of the vessels differ, the space within them is given different names; yet when one sets aside the vessels to contemplate the space itself, that space is said to be one. How could that great void space be either the same or different for you?
How much less could it be said to be "one" or "not one"? Thus, you should understand that the six faculties of sensory reception are also like this.

[Commentary]: The afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are precisely the eighty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Among these, "habitual traces" (*vāsanā*) refer to the phases of arising, abiding, change, and cessation (*utpāda-sthiti-vyaya-nirodha*).

Regarding the "count of divisions": the ordinary person perceives the phase of cessation; those of the Two Vehicles perceive the phase of change; Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Dharma-body perceive the phase of abiding; and Bodhisattvas at the stage of fulfillment perceive the phase of arising—these are the respective counts of divisions for the abandonment of afflictions.

As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Ārya-brahma-viśeṣa-cinti-paripṛcchā-sūtra*) states: "Those who practice *dhyāna* clearly understand within their minds the count of divisions for arising, abiding, change, and cessation. Furthermore, herein...

The explanation here differs from that [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*] because the meaning of this text intends to sever the arising of those [six], whereas the discourse of that sutra intends to know their number; this is because the observed essence (*dṛśya-tattva*) is different. [Gushan] states:

"Because the Srotāpanna does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas, he attains the extinction of six, yet has not yet forgotten one—this is stagnation in the Nirvana of existence. [Wenling] states: "Space is fundamentally neither identical nor different;

this metaphor illustrates that the perfect stillness is fundamentally neither one nor six. When the vessel is removed from the space, it serves as a metaphor for the arising of the meanings of 'one' and 'six'."

Due to the two aspects of light and darkness, which manifest in mutual contrast, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to, giving rise to seeing. The essence of seeing reflects forms, and by binding with forms, the sense organ is formed. The root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements"; therefore, the substance of the eye is named after its shape, like a cluster of grapes.

This floating root, consisting of the four sensory objects, flows outward and rushes toward forms. Due to the two aspects of movement and stillness, which strike one another, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to, giving rise to hearing.

The essence of hearing reflects sounds, and by rolling up sounds, the sense organ is formed. The root of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements"; therefore, the substance of the ear is named after its shape, like a newly rolled scroll.

The leaf floats upon the four sensory objects; it flows and escapes, rushing toward sounds. Through the conditions of penetration and obstruction, two kinds of characteristics arise. Within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes sticky and gives rise to smelling. The essence of smelling reflects the fragrance.

The gathering of fragrance forms the root. The source of this root is called the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Consequently, the substance of the nose is said to be like a pair of hanging claws. The floating roots [of the senses] pursue the four objects;

they rush toward fragrance through the two types of conditions—tranquility and transformation—which intermingle and blend together. Within the wondrous perfection, the clarity is adhered to, giving rise to tasting. The essence of tasting reflects flavors, and by churning these flavors, the root is formed. The source of this root is called the pure four great elements.

Consequently, the substance of the tongue is said to be like a newly drawn crescent moon. The floating roots pursue the four objects; they rush toward flavor through the two types of conditions—separation and union—which rub against one another within the wondrous perfection.

Within this, the viscous stillness gives rise to awareness; the essence of awareness reflects upon contact, and by seizing upon that contact, the sense-faculty is formed. The fundamental source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements. Consequently, the physical body is named after its shape, resembling the head of a waist-drum.

The four objects of the floating faculties rush forth and flow toward contact. Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing, and so forth—within the wondrous and perfect [state], the clarity of stillness becomes attached and gives rise to cognition. The essence of cognition reflects the phenomena, and by grasping these phenomena, the faculty is formed.

The root of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the mental faculty, like seeing within a dark chamber. The four objects of the floating faculties rush forth and flow toward phenomena.
[3. Refuting the Characteristics to Unite with the True] Externally uprooting the six faculties and internally uniting with the true nature, one causes hearing and seeing to merge into one;

when the perfect clarity opens, it responds universally. Thus, the various faculties function interchangeably, and habitual delusions are entirely eliminated. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If your six faculties do not function interchangeably, then this false thought will never cease, whether they are merged or opened.

One thus knows that the meaning of "uprooting the faculties" lies in severing delusions within the wondrous perfection. This demonstrates that the knots of the faculties arise from the attachment of the visual faculty to the clarity of consciousness, and that the faculties originate from the binding of form.

Because it is that from which [the faculty] is produced, the name and substance of the "eye" are established from this point onward; thus, one knows that the six functions—seeing and so forth—are illusory. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The substance of the grape-like eye is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*); atoms are called 'invisible form' (*anidarśana-rūpa*). Therefore, the source of the seeing-faculty is the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*), while the physical organ (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and its four sensory objects are also able to pursue forms."

Ānanda, it is because of that awakened clarity within these six faculties that there is clarity within clarity and awareness within awareness. Having lost that essential lucidity, they become stuck in delusion and emit light.

Therefore, at this moment, when you are free from darkness and free from light, the substance of seeing does not exist; when you are free from motion and free from stillness, the essence of hearing fundamentally has no reality. When there is neither penetration nor obstruction, the nature of smelling does not arise; when there is neither change nor tranquility, tasting has no outlet.
Neither separated nor united, one awakens to the fact that touch is fundamentally non-existent; there is neither cessation nor arising, and one understands where [the mind] rests in peace.

You need only not follow after movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness—these twelve marks of all conditioned phenomena (all of which are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing). By following and uprooting even a single faculty, you detach from its clinging and settle inwardly. As this settling returns to the original reality, the fundamental radiance is manifested.

When the nature of this radiance shines forth, the remaining five attachments will spontaneously be uprooted and completely liberated. This does not depend on the cognitions and views arising from external objects (externally not depending on objects), nor does clarity follow the sense organs (internally not following the organs); rather, clarity is manifested by relying upon the organs. Thus, the six...

The faculties function as mutual supports. Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees though he has no eyes; the Naga Baddhananta hears though he has no ears; the goddess of the Ganges smells fragrances though she has no nose;

Gavāmpati knows flavors through his extraordinary tongue (his tongue is always like a cow’s whistle); and the Śūnyatā-deva perceives touch though he has no body? They are made to appear momentarily by being reflected in the light of the Tathāgata;

yet since they are of the nature of wind, their substance is fundamentally non-existent. So too are the śrāvakas who have attained the cessation of perception and feeling, such as Mahākāśyapa in this assembly.

The mental faculty (*manas*) has long since ceased, yet there is a perfect, clear understanding that does not depend on mental thought. Ānanda, if your various faculties were now to be completely uprooted, their inner luminosity would radiate forth;

thus, these superficial phenomena and the vessel-world, along with all their changing appearances, would—like ice melting in hot water—be transformed into supreme awareness at the very moment of thought. Ānanda, it is like those people who gather their vision in the eyes:
