These four types of bodhi take compassion and wisdom as their essence. Moreover, the *Dharmadhātu-nirviśeṣa-śāstra* states that the bodhicitta is...

The cause and fruit of the inconceivable are like the first phase of the waxing moon; thus it is also said that the bodhicitta is called the "sentient-being mind" during the impure stage, the "bodhisattva mind" during the stage of both purity and defilement, and the "Tathāgata mind" during the stage of complete purity.
Furthermore, the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* states that there are four types of generating the bodhicitta: namely, through faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

These various forms of bodhi are explained in terms of cause and fruit, as well as understanding and practice. Moreover, the *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* states that regarding all sentient beings, the bodhicitta...

Within the body, there are ten kinds of distinctions: namely, it is "unconditioned" because it is uncreated; it is "without beginning" because it has no arising; it is "without end" because it has no cessation;

it is "unstained" because its intrinsic nature is pure; it is "formless" because it has no sense faculties; and it is "the sphere of activity of the noble ones," for this is the realm of all Buddhas. Furthermore, regarding this bodhicitta, it is explained according to principle.
Moreover, in the *Vajra-kāya-tri-karma-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*, the Tathāgatas of the five directions each have a specific teaching concerning bodhicitta; that of Akṣobhya is as follows:

The Tathāgata teaches through the non-arising and selflessness of all phenomena; Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata teaches through the absence of intrinsic nature and the transcendence of signs of all phenomena;

Amitābha Tathāgata teaches through neither existence nor non-existence; Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata teaches through non-attainment and non-realization; and Vairocana Tathāgata teaches through the equality that is free from the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, and devoid of grasping or rejecting.
Since these various aspects of awakening are explained in terms of the characteristics of *prajñā*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* states that there are four dharmas.
To forget the bodhicitta means to deceive one's ācārya and others; thus the Sūtra says: "Those who give rise to bodhicitta have minds that are upright and free from flattery and deception.
One who wishes to cultivate the perfect penetration of the ear faculty must first give rise to this mind of the Great Way.

That Buddha taught me: "From hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, enter into samādhi. First, within the state of hearing, enter the stream and cause the objects of perception to vanish. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness will clearly cease to arise.

Thus gradually increasing, what is heard and the act of hearing both come to an end. When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell therein; when the awakened subject and the awakened object are both empty, the emptiness of awakening becomes perfectly full. When both the emptiness and that which is emptied have ceased, birth and death are extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before you.

Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, the ten directions become perfectly luminous, and you obtain two kinds of extraordinary excellence: first, you harmonize upward with all the Buddhas of the ten directions..."

The Buddha’s fundamental mind of wondrous enlightenment shares the same power of compassion as that of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. In its second aspect, it descends to harmonize with all sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence in the ten directions, being one with all such beings.

We share the same compassion and yearning, World-Honored One. Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of "Hearing-Pervasion and Hearing-Cultivation," which is like an illusion;
and because I share the same power of compassion as the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, my body has become capable of thirty-two manifestations as I enter all lands.

The following section describes the Dharma-gate of cultivation and realization, referring to the meaning of the three types of wisdom—beginning with hearing—which accord with the faculty of the ear; thus, this sutra constitutes the path of correct practice. From the initial stage "within hearing" up to "hearing itself is not produced" is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Next, from "gradually increasing in this way" up to "the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted" is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). From "realizing the emptiness of that which is perceived" up to "the manifestation of quiescent extinction" is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) are designated as the ground of what is accomplished through hearing, and the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) is designated as the ground of what is accomplished through reflection. The ten [stages]... [are the ground of what is accomplished through cultivation].

The *Dìwén* (Grounds for Cultivation) treats this section as four parts, all of which speak in terms of the cultivation and realization of the ear-gate; thus, there is no contradiction. Regarding the phrase "entering the stream" (*rúlíu*): "stream" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

That is to say, while sounds and objects (*chén*) are in motion, their nature is quiescent. Now, upon first entering the stream, one realizes that the *dharmatā* is fundamentally tranquil and that sounds and objects have likewise ceased to exist.

Therefore, movement and stillness do not arise. The passage beginning with "In this way" uses wisdom to dispel emotional attachments until there is nothing further to dispel. When emotions are extinguished and conceptual understanding is severed, then quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) manifests before one. Suddenly—

However, the subsequent discussion of "transcendence" refers to the function of their identical essence. Thus, one unites with all sentient beings and Buddhas in their shared aspiration and compassion. Regarding the Vajra Samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation:

from the initial stage of perfuming through to the final realization and verification, it consists entirely of the decisive wisdom and severance that is ultimately firm and stable, serving as the true meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).

“World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi and are advancing in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), with their resolute understanding (adhimukti) fully manifest, I appear before them in the body of a Buddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training (śaikṣa) whose tranquil and wondrous clarity is fully manifest in its supreme excellence, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.”

If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the supreme nature manifests in perfection, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training who realize the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, enter cessation through the cultivation of the path, and the supreme nature manifests in perfection, I appear before them in the body of a Śrāvaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.
If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds clearly and do not transgress the dust of desire, wishing their bodies to be pure, I appear before them as a Brahmā King.

I manifest my body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation. If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of the heavens and exercise authority over the celestial realms, I appear before them in the form of Śakra.

I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success. If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to travel throughout the ten directions, I manifest before them in the form of a Śakra Devendra.

I preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment. If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery, flying through the void, I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who love to preside over spirits and deities to protect their lands, I appear before them in the form of a Celestial Great General and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are sentient beings who love to preside over the world and protect its inhabitants, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings...

I appear before them in the body of a king and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve success. If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and to command spirits and deities, I appear before them in the form of a prince of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve success.

[The Thirty-two Manifestations] He teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate by means of the Universal Gate Body (*samantamukhakāya*). Because he has no fixed form from the outset, these are called the thirty-two manifestations. First, regarding the four types of noble beings:

initially, bodhisattvas enter the ocean of universal knowledge through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), yet they have not yet realized it directly. Therefore, [the Buddha] manifests the body of a Buddha to cause them to achieve that supreme, wondrous, and tranquil mind.

The nature of returning to cessation as soon as conditions are severed is what is meant by "supreme nature" (*śreṣṭha-dhātu*); this is said in reference to the superior excellence attained by each respective realm. Next, regarding the six classes of ordinary beings:

these include the Brahma King and Maheśvara, the kings of the two realms of desire and form; the sixth heaven of the desire realm is named the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Īśāna-deva*); those who dwell at the summit of the form realm are named Mahāmaheśvara;

and the General, who serves as the supreme commander of Śakra and is a minister to the Four Heavenly Kings—the crown prince being Nanda and others—capable of commanding ghosts and spirits; all of these are subjects and attendants.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being kings of men, I appear before them in the form of a king of men and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who love to be born into noble clans and are esteemed by the world, I appear before them in the form of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who love to discuss names and terminology and dwell in purity, I appear before them in the form of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal. If there are sentient beings who love to govern a kingdom...

Regarding those who govern provinces and cities: before them, I manifest in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success. As for those sentient beings who are fond of various arts and incantations:

He dwells in self-restraint and vigilance. Before him, I manifest in the form of a brāhmaṇa and preach the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve fulfillment. If there is a man who delights in study and leaves the household life, [I shall likewise act for him].
For those who uphold the various precepts, I appear before them in the form of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are women who delight in learning and renunciation, upholding the various prohibitions and precepts, I appear before them in the form of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are men who take pleasure in upholding the five precepts, I appear before them in the form of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment. If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I appear before them...

I appear before them in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves as pillars of their households and nations, I appear before them in the form of a queen, a state lady, a noble wife, or a matron of great influence, and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings whose male organs remain intact, I appear before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. If there are virgins who cherish their chastity and do not seek sexual assault, I appear before them...

To some, I appear in the form of a young maiden and preach the Dharma to bring them to fulfillment. If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial station, I manifest in a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them.
I cause them to achieve accomplishment. If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga class, I manifest in the form of a nāga and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own class, I appear before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

If there are gandharvas who wish to be liberated from their class, I appear before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment. If there are asuras who wish to be liberated from their class, I appear before them in the form of an asura...

I manifest as an asura body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain accomplishment. If there are kinnaras who wish to escape their kind, I appear before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain accomplishment.
If there are mahoragas who wish to escape their kind, I appear before them in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain accomplishment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans and cultivating themselves as humans, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to attain accomplishment. And if there are non-humans...

Whether with form or without form, with thought or without thought, for those who delight in transcending their own kind, I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

This is called the "Thirty-two Responsive Manifestations of Sublime Purity. These bodies that enter into lands are all accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrous efficacy, cultivated by the permeation of hearing and the practice of hearing via samādhi.

The King of Men governs the people by virtue of his station; the Elder commands his clan by virtue of his merit; the Householder conceals himself while uttering profound words; the Minister presides over the state through administration;

and the Brāhmaṇa sustains his livelihood through arts and sciences—all these belong to the mundane world. The fourfold assembly of Bhikṣus seeks the Dharma and maintains the precepts; the Upāsakas honor the Three Jewels; the Queen of the Heavenly Son is called the "Lady of the State"; the wife of a feudal lord is called the "Lady of the Lord";

a wife who receives her title through her husband’s glory is called a "Lady by Appointment" (Mìngfù); one who assists in governing the inner palace is called a "Great Lady" (Dàjiā)—all these belong to the state. The name of a Yakṣa is... [text ends].

"Light and agile, they are able to fly. *Gandharva* means "fragrance-body" (*gandha-aṅga*); they are the musicians of Śakra. *Asura* means "not handsome"; their women are beautiful while their men are ugly.

*Kiṃnara* means "doubtful deity"; they have human forms with horns on their heads. *Mahoraga* means "belly-crawlers"; in this language [Chinese], they are called pythons. Regarding "non-humans" (*amanuṣya*) and so forth, this includes all others; it should be understood as in the *Ṣaḍakṣarī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
They may manifest as hungry ghosts (*preta*) with hands that emit fragrant-colored milk, or even appear as courtesans to deliver sentient beings who are attached to sensual desire.

World-Honored One, by means of the wondrous power of the unconditioned Vajra Samādhi—perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—I share in the same compassionate longing as all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and three periods of time across the six realms.
Consequently, I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within my body and mind. The first is: because I do not observe [the self] in sound.
First, by observing the observer, one causes all suffering beings throughout the ten directions to observe (and recite) its sound, whereby they immediately attain liberation.

Second, through the reversal of knowledge and vision, even if sentient beings enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them. Third, through the reversal of observation and hearing, even if sentient beings are adrift upon a great flood, the water cannot drown them.

Fourth, by extinguishing deluded thoughts and having no intent to kill, even if sentient beings enter the realms of ghosts, the ghosts cannot harm them. Fifth, by perfuming the faculty of hearing until it becomes true hearing, the six sense faculties are dissolved.

Furthermore, it is identical to hearing sounds; it can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed by weapons that sever them limb from limb to perceive those arms and spears as being like water being sliced or light being blown away.
Sixth, the nature is unshakable. When the clarity of hearing-pervasion permeates the entire dharma-realm, then the nature of all dark obscurities cannot remain intact.

This enables sentient beings such as yakṣas (as previously explained), rākṣasas (including pestilence demons), kumbhāṇḍas (demons of enchantment), piśācas (demons that devour vital energy), and pūtanas (demons of feverish disease)—even when these approach their side, they cannot even look upon them with their eyes. Seventh, the nature of sound is completely dissolved;

as hearing and seeing turn inward (with nothing internal to which they are attached) and one is freed from all sensory dust and delusions (with nothing external to which one is burdened), this enables sentient beings to be unaffected by imprisonment, shackles, or fetters. Eighth, with the cessation of sound and the perfection of hearing (with neither internal nor external dependencies), one universally generates the power of compassion. This can...
It causes sentient beings to pass directly through perilous paths (adverse conditions), so that thieves (afflictions) cannot plunder them.

[The Fourteen Fearlessnesses] Because they are able to liberate others from suffering, they are collectively termed "Fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*). Because their knowledge and vision do not arise following external objects and are not called "self-observation," it causes sentient beings who possess suffering to receive my true observation and all attain liberation.
This is the collective virtue. Below this, because all observations do not follow after sensory objects, they are collectively termed "Revolution" (*āvartana*).

Knowledge and vision belong to fire; seeing and hearing belong to water. When these two revolve back [to their source], they cannot burn or drown. The nature of ghosts arises from delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*); if one cuts off and extinguishes these delusive thoughts, ghosts cannot cause harm.

When the cultivation of hearing becomes one's true nature and the six sense-faculties are all restored, then sound and hearing are of the same substance, and there is no interval between the faculties and their objects.

Therefore, it is said that even when a sword is cut into pieces, or when water is sliced, or light is blown apart, there is no separation. As for "the cultivation of hearing clarifies the brilliant spirit": when the cultivation of hearing has long been refined and made brilliant, one then illuminates the essential nature of both light and darkness, such that they are not two.
Because it is complete, ghosts cannot see it; because the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved, its essential substance has no limitations, so shackles and fetters cannot bind it;

because the cessation of sound is perfectly heard, subject and object do not oppose one another, so thieves cannot plunder it; furthermore, because the hearing of sound is perfectly pervasive, the power of compassion is likewise pervasive, and since compassion has no enemy, there is nothing that can act as a thief.
Ninth, by perfuming the hearing and departing from sensory objects, one is not plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.

Tenth, when pure sound is free from dust, the faculties and their objects become perfectly interfused, such that there is neither subject nor object; this can cause all beings filled with anger and resentment to abandon all hatred.

Eleventh, when dust is dissolved and clarity turns back, the body and mind within the Dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli—luminously penetrating and unobstructed; this can cause all those of dull nature and obstructive ignorance, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of delusion. Twelfth, when [the elements] are fused...

Furthermore, he heard that while remaining unmoved in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he enters into the mundane world without destroying the worlds. He is able to travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust.

At the side of each Buddha, he serves as a prince of the Dharma (*dharmarāja-putra*). He can cause those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no sons, and those who desire a male child, to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.

Thirteenth, his six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are perfectly penetrating; their clarity and illumination are non-dual, encompassing the realms of the ten directions. He establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the empty Tathāgata-garbha, to receive and accord with the secrets of the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.

In this esoteric dharma-gate, there is no loss in receiving and upholding it. It enables those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no offspring—and those who desire a daughter—to give birth to a girl of upright appearance, merit, gentleness, and compliance, one who is loved and revered by all and possesses auspicious marks.
Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm, across ten billion suns and moons, there currently dwell in the world various Dharma-Princes numbering sixty-two billion times the sands of the Ganges River.

They cultivate the Dharma and establish models, teaching and transforming sentient beings; their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the needs of sentient beings, are each distinct. By virtue of...

The fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained is the wondrous gateway of the ear. Thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrously all-encompassing, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

This enables sentient beings who uphold my name to possess a merit equal and no different from those who uphold the names of sixty-two billion *Ganges* sands of Dharma-princes; O World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names.
Because I cultivated this practice and attained true perfect penetration, it is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, wherein blessings are fully perfected.

[The affliction of] birth. Ninth, [the affliction of] desire arises from the habitual engagement with objects; now, by distancing oneself from sensory dust and colors, the sense organs and their objects do not encounter one another, thereby causing sentient beings with much lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.

[Wenling says: Anger arises from that which opposes one’s feelings and is triggered by confronting external objects; since the nature of sound is pure and free from further delusions, it is perfectly integrated, without opposition or conflict.

When subject and object are confronted, one does not give rise to anger. As for delusion (*moha*), its fundamental root is the innate ignorance (*avidyā*) formed by the habituation to darkness; it is an obstruction of the nature.

Now, by dissolving the dust-like delusions and returning to true illumination, the defilements of body and mind are purified, and thus the obstruction of the nature is forever abandoned. *Adinaka* (阿顛迦) means "one without a virtuous mind," which is also an obstruction of the nature.

[Commentary] When the twelve [senses] below are fused with form, the substance is without material obstruction, and thus one traverses the realms without being impaired. Furthermore, because the nature is without proximity or distance when hearing, one is omnipresent without moving. To make offerings to the Buddhas is to fulfill merit.

As a prince of the Dharma, one follows the path of succession and is thus able to respond to requests. [Wenling]: Because it is perfect (*vṛtta*), it is non-dual; because it is pervasive (*vyāpin*), it encompasses all realms.

Its luminous illumination is the substance of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; its encompassing of all realms is the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Thus, it can accord with and follow the Dharma-gates, receiving and accepting them without loss.

"Accordance" refers to the gentle virtue of the earth (*kūn-yī*); "receiving and accepting" refers to the domestic duties of the inner chambers. Because it possesses the way of a woman, it is able to respond to requests. [Sūtra Commentary]: The fourteen lines below merely compare the superiority of merit.

Because the faculties accord with hearing and contemplation, they are called "right practice," and thus the name is said to be superior in merit. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra* states that "superiority in merit" refers to the Dharma-body of Avalokiteśvara;

for the Dharma-body is eternal, whereas the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are impermanent. The aforementioned merits are further characterized by being consummate, dissolving, pervasive, perfect, fused, and penetrating, as one enters deeper and deeper through gradual stages.

World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully obtain four inconceivable and unconditioned wondrous virtues.

The first is that, by virtue of my initial attainment of the wondrous and subtle faculty of hearing, the essence of mind left behind the hearing; thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be separated, becoming one perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.

Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and can preach boundless secret divine mantras. Within these, I may manifest with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, ten heads, or twenty heads...
One head; and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, and eighty-four thousand *lakṣa* heads.

Two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four; and so on, up to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand *mudrā* arms.
Two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes; and so on, up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes.
With eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, concentration or wisdom—they rescue and protect sentient beings and attain great sovereignty.

Second, because I have emerged from the six sense objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am thus able to skillfully manifest every single form and recite every single mantra; as for those forms and mantras, [they are all effective].
I am able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; for this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, all name me the "Bestower of Fearlessness.

Third, because I have cultivated the fundamental, wondrous, and perfect penetration—the pure root of my being—all the worlds I visit cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.

Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized ultimate fruition, I am able to offer various precious treasures to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to the sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm; thus, those who seek a wife obtain one...

If one seeks a wife, one obtains a wife; if one seeks a son, one obtains a son; if one seeks samādhi, one obtains samādhi; if one seeks long life, one obtains long life; and so on, even unto seeking great nirvāṇa, one obtains great nirvāṇa.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "I attained liberation through the faculty of hearing via the Samādhi of Universal Illumination. By bringing the conditioned mind under my own control, I entered the state of 'flowing-in' and thereby attained Samādhi.

This led to the fulfillment of Bodhi; this is the foremost method. World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration, and in the midst of that great assembly, he conferred upon me the title of Avalokiteśvara."
Because I observe and listen to the perfect clarity throughout the ten directions, the name "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanyin) pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

[The Four Inconceivables: First, the inconceivable ability to manifest many names; the wondrous and subtle mind of hearing that flows directly into the center of the Middle Way. [Wenling] states that "initially attaining" refers to the fundamental cause.

The head represents the totality of the six faculties; the arms symbolize the compassion of uplifting and receiving; the eyes represent the wisdom of illumination and understanding. Each follows its original number to reach fulfillment.

This extends up to the eighty-four thousand manifestations (*vyūha*), which represent the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) responding universally to the afflictions of the mundane world. Within this single essence, all phenomena are fully present;

thus, the manifestation of the twenty-four sages illustrates that those partial manifestations are here fully integrated and realized as one. *Śakala* means "vajra," signifying firmness and solidity; *mudrā* means "seal" or "hand-gesture. Through compassion, they gather and transform beings; through majesty, they subdue them;

through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they restore the profound stillness; and through wisdom (*prajñā*), they awaken them. This collectively refers to the many wondrous forms. [Commentary] Esoteric Section.

The Divine Spells were mostly spoken by Avalokiteśvara; they are able to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings and are called "Bestowing Fearlessness. Regarding the relinquishing of the body and precious treasures, the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter) states:
"O Benevolent One, out of compassion for us, please accept these necklaces. This refers to the act of seeking mercy.

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light, which reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Dharma Princes and all the Bodhisattvas.

Those Tathāgatas likewise simultaneously emitted precious light from their five limbs; from those motes of dust in the ten directions, this light came to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head, as well as the crowns of the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats within the assembly.

The forest trees, ponds, and marshes all resounded with the sounds of the Dharma. The interlacing lights meshed together like a net of precious threads. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.

There was. All universally attained the vajra-samādhi. Immediately, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and blended together throughout the voids of the ten directions.

It became the color of the seven treasures. In this Sahā world, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all vanished simultaneously; one saw only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions merged into a single realm, where the chanting of Brahma-songs and hymns was spontaneously performed.
At that time, from the lower realms up to the Brahma heavens, hymns and chants were spontaneously performed, collectively manifesting the auspicious sign of universal penetration.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince: "Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and the Arhats, each of whom has described the initial expedient means by which they attained the Way;
all have declared that they practiced true and universal penetration. In their cultivation, there is truly no superiority or inferiority, nor any distinction of priority or sequence. I—"

"Now I wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening through twenty-five practices. Who is suited to these faculties? Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed Way, by what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and [addressed him].

Receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he spoke these verses in response to the Buddha: "The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; this perfect clarity makes awakening fundamentally wondrous. When primordial luminosity shines forth, an object of perception arises;

once that object is established, the nature of the shining light vanishes. Through delusion and falsehood, empty space comes into being; based upon space, the world is established. As thought becomes still, a land is formed; through cognition and awareness, sentient beings arise. Space is born within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea."

The myriad lands of outflows are all born dependent upon space; when the bubble vanishes, space itself is fundamentally non-existent—how much more so the various realms of the three worlds? The nature that returns to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means have many gates.

The sagely nature has no obstruction; whether following the natural order or acting in reverse, all are expedient means. For those at the initial stage entering samādhi, there are differences in the speed of their progress.

[The Six Selections of Perfect Penetration] The first two lines of the verse praise the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); the following two lines clarify the origin of delusion. The world arises from delusion, and sentient beings exist through delusion;

this refers to what is said: "Know that empty space is born within your own mind. Thus, while the principle of returning to the source is non-dual, the paths of cultivation and realization have many gates.

Although the nature of the sages is such that both the favorable and the adverse can be utilized, there are differences in speed for those at the initial stage of the mind. Therefore, the various sages each attained perfect penetration.

Without discernment, the perceptions of form coalesce into dust; because one cannot penetrate them with clarity, how could one attain unimpeded penetration? Sound is mixed with speech, relying merely upon names, phrases, and meanings;

since one does not contain all others, how can one attain unimpeded penetration? Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain [unimpeded penetration]?

"Perfect Penetration: The nature of taste is not fundamental; it exists only when there is tasting. Since its perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration? Tactile sensation is clarified by what is touched; there is nothing that does not manifest through touch. Yet the natures of union and separation are not fixed;

how can one attain perfect penetration? Phenomena (dharmas) are called internal objects; depending on these objects, there must be a subject. Since the capacity and the object do not pervade all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?

The nature of seeing, though penetratingly clear, sees what is before but not what is behind. It lacks half of the four directions; how can one attain perfect penetration? The breath of the nose passes in and out."

In the present state, there is no mingling of breaths; fragmented and disjointed, they do not interpenetrate. How can one attain perfect penetration through this? The tongue is not an entry point without cause; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavors cease, cognition vanishes.

How can one attain perfect penetration through this? The body and its objects of touch are identical; neither is the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment. Their boundaries do not merge in silent accord. How can one attain perfect penetration through this?

The faculty of cognition is a jumble of discursive thoughts; though it may be clear and lucid, it ultimately has no vision. One cannot escape from these mental conceptions. How can one attain perfect penetration through this?

The perception of form (rūpa-saṃjñā) is first excluded from the six sense objects; the tongue faculty (jihvā-āyatana) is not without cause, for it likewise depends on taste. Since the body possesses both the meanings of "center" and "periphery," it constitutes a boundary or limit.

That which does not reach profound union [with its object] is known as the body through contact (spraṣṭavya). Because distracted thought is characterized by movement, it is not a state of tranquil clarity.

Consciousness and vision are a mixture of the three harmonies; their fundamental nature is called "non-characteristic. Since its own essence has no fixed existence from the start, how can one attain perfect penetration?

The hearing of the mind penetrates the ten directions, arising from the power of great causes. Those with a beginner's mind cannot enter it; how can one attain perfect penetration? The contemplation of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device, intended only to cause the mind to abide. Once abiding is achieved, it becomes that upon which the mind dwells; how can one attain perfect penetration? Explaining the Dharma involves playing with sounds and characters;

this may awaken those who have already attained success. Names and phrases are not themselves untainted; how can one attain perfect penetration? Observing precepts and transgressions merely restrains the body; they do not restrain the mind. How can one attain perfect penetration?

Being unbound, it fundamentally does not pervade all things; how then can one attain perfect penetration? Spiritual powers are rooted in past causes; what connection have they to the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness and its objects are not separate from things (if not separate from things, there is attachment), how then can one attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate the nature of earth, its solidity and obstruction are not pervasive; as a conditioned state, it is not the nature of the sages—how then can one attain perfect penetration?

If you contemplate the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real; suchness is beyond both thought and observation—how then can one attain perfect penetration? If you contemplate the nature of fire, your aversion to existence is not true detachment; this is not the way for a beginner.

[Mañjuśrī] said: "How does one attain perfect penetration? If one contemplates the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without opposition; since opposition is not the supreme awakening, how does one attain perfect penetration? If one contemplates the nature of space, its dullness and obscurity are fundamentally not awakening;

since the absence of awakening differs from Bodhi, how does one attain perfect penetration? If one contemplates the nature of consciousness, observing that consciousness is not permanent, yet maintaining a mind is a delusion;

how does one attain perfect penetration? All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and the nature of thought is originally subject to extinction; cause and effect now yield different results—how does one attain perfect penetration?"

Next, regarding the perception of consciousness, we briefly examine the six consciousnesses; when one interrogates their association with the sense organs and their objects, they are found to have no fundamental basis. As for those of great causal power, it is because these arise from the practice of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); thus, they are not suitable for beginners or those of provisional capacity.

It is for the sake of stopping the distractions of Sunda that the visualization of the white syllable *oṃ* is provisionally taught as a preliminary opening. Furthermore, for those who have already attained accomplishment, the teaching is given accordingly.

Moreover, the meditative visualizations of leveling the earth and filling it—which involve conditioned effort—and the visualizations of moonlight and water are not ultimate realities; likewise, the visualization of Ucchuṣma fire is a method for revulsion toward desire and is not [the final truth].

The true Lapis Lazuli Light Wind contemplates that while the nature possesses movement and stillness, if the nature of emptiness is obscured and darkened, it becomes dull and lacks awareness; if the nature of consciousness engages in discrimination, then that nature is not eternally abiding.
Because Śrī-Ābhāsvara gathers and controls the six sense faculties, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and their fruits are subject to cessation and extinction.

I now address the World-Honored One: When the Buddha appears in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this region lies in pure hearing. If one wishes to attain samādhi, it must truly be entered through hearing.

To leave suffering behind and obtain liberation—how excellent is Avalokiteśvara! (This praises Avalokiteśvara’s voice for delivering beings from suffering and granting them joy. Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as many as motes of dust, attaining the power of great mastery (this praises the thirty-two transformations) and bestowing fearlessness.

Sentient beings (praise the four inconceivables and the fourteen fearlessnesses). "Wondrous Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara" (praise the names according to their virtues). "Brahma-sound" and "Tidal-sound" (praise the reality according to the names). "Saving the world and bringing all peace" (praises the multitude of virtues). "Transcending the world to attain eternal abiding" (is able to save the world from suffering and bestow supramundane bliss). I now address the Tathāgata: as Avalokiteśvara has explained, it is like a person dwelling in stillness;

when drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard at once in all ten places—this is the perfection of true reality. The eyes do not see beyond obstructions; the mouth and nose are likewise so. The body only knows through contact;
the mind’s thoughts are chaotic and disordered. Hearing sounds across a wall, one can hear both the distant and the near; this is something the five sense organs cannot achieve in unison.

This is the universal reality. The nature of sound consists of movement and stillness; within hearing, it exists as both presence and absence. When there is no sound, one is said to have "no-hearing," yet this is not a case of true non-hearing, for hearing has no inherent nature.

Since sound is absent, there is no cessation; since sound is present, there is no birth. Being perfectly free from both birth and cessation, this is the eternal reality. Even when one is in a dream, it does not cease to exist because one is not thinking of it.
It transcends discursive thought and observation; body and mind cannot reach it.

[Wenling: The Sage established his teachings according to different regions; in this region, the substance of the teaching necessarily relies upon sound and hearing, which is also appropriate to the capacities of beings. One who leaves suffering behind is praised as possessing the Fourteen Fearlessnesses;
one who enters lands as numerous as motes of dust is praised for the Thirty-two Marks of Response; one who has attained great sovereign mastery is praised for the Four Inconceivables.

All other titles follow the names of his virtues: he whose preaching of the Dharma is unimpeded is named *Miaoyin* (Wonderful Sound); he who seeks out sounds to rescue those in suffering is named *Guanyin* (Avalokiteśvara); his vocal nature being free from attachment is named *Fanyin* (Brahma Sound); and his responses never missing the proper time is named *Chaoyin* (Tide Sound).

The nature of sound, whether in motion or stillness, belongs entirely to the sense-object of sound; the faculty of hearing is perfectly detached from this and does not follow its arising and ceasing—this is the reality of the true, eternal nature.
"Absence of sound is called absence of hearing" refers to the incident of Ānanda hearing the bell.

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonetics may be proclaimed and made clear. Yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow after sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth. Ānanda, though you possess powerful memory, you cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts. Is this not simply following where one sinks?

If you turn back the flow, you will again be free from delusion. Ānanda, listen attentively! Relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim the Vajra-King, the inconceivable, illusory-like, and true samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas.

Though you have heard all the secret gateways of countless Buddhas, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a source of error. Take up this hearing...

"Hold fast to the Buddha, O Buddha! Why not listen to that which hears? Hearing does not arise spontaneously; it exists because of sound. When you turn back this hearing and detach from sound, who can give it a name once it is detached?

Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts (referring generally to the deluded faculties); the three realms are like flowers in the sky (referring generally to the deluded objects). When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the faculties are removed, the dust of sensory objects vanishes and awareness becomes perfectly pure."

When purity reaches its ultimate limit, there is penetrating illumination; in silent reflection, it encompasses empty space (the liberation of the faculties). Returning to observe the world, it is like events within a dream (the liberation of objects). Mātanga is in a dream— who can detain your form?

Like a skillful magician of the world who conjures various men and women, although one sees the movement of their various faculties, they are all drawn by a single mechanism. When the mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions lose their nature. The six faculties are also like this:

originally they depend on a single brilliant spirit, which divides into the six harmonious combinations. When one point attains rest and restoration, the functions of the six no longer arise. Dust and defilement...

It should be contemplated until it dissolves, becoming perfectly bright, pure, and wondrous. While residual dust remains, one is still among those in training; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Tathāgata. Great Assembly and Ānanda:

Turn back your inverted faculty of hearing and listen inwardly to your own nature. When this nature is perfected, it becomes the Unsurpassed Way. Perfect penetration is truly like this. This is the single path to Nirvāṇa for countless Buddhas; it is the way of all Tathāgatas of the past.

This gate has already been accomplished. All present Bodhisattvas now each enter into perfect clarity. Those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; I, too, have realized it through this, not only Avalokiteśvara.

(These words are spoken with sincere faith, as true as the Buddha, the World-Honored One. When the World-Honored One inquired about my various skillful means for rescuing those in the final age, for those seeking to transcend the world and achieve the mind of Nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is the foremost.

As for all other skillful means, they are entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. They allow one to abandon worldly afflictions through immediate engagement with circumstances; they are not methods for long-term cultivation, whether shallow or deep.

They spoke the Dharma in unison, prostrating to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is untainted and inconceivable. They prayed: "May you bestow grace upon those of the future so that they may have no doubt regarding this gateway;

may it be easily accomplished through skillful means, such that it may be used to teach Ānanda and those sinking in the delusions of the final age. If one cultivates by means of this faculty alone, its perfect penetration will surpass all others (the twenty-four sages). Such is the true mind."

[Commentary]: Those who propound the theory of sound (śabdavādin) take the principles elucidated through sound as their basis, asserting that the three bodies—name (*nāma*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*)—constitute the essence of the teaching.

The common people speak of the fault of following sound because they perceive that names exist in opposition to the sensory object of sound. If one can instead hear one's own nature and transcend the sense organs and their objects externally, then by what could "hearing" even be named?

When seeing and hearing are the roots and the triple world is the dust, if hearing is reversed, the cataracts of the senses are naturally removed; if the dust is eliminated, the mind of awakening is fundamentally pure. To look back at the world is like looking at...
The matter of dreams is thus: while the woman Mātaṅgī was actually within a dream, who could have detained your physical form and prevented you from attaining liberation?

The various sense-faculties (*indriya*) are metaphors for conditioned phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; "a single mechanism" refers to the contrivances of the deluded mind. [Wenling] To achieve the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* and the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, only the faculty of hearing is so capable;

as for the others, they rely on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to bestow empowerment. What is presented here concerns one's own immediate affairs and the relinquishing of worldly toil; it is not a teaching that speaks of a uniform depth or shallowness across the beginning and end of practice.
Section Five: The Part on Cultivation and Realization (Text in three parts).
First, the Fourfold Subduing and Severing. At this, Ānanda and the great assembly were clear in body and mind, receiving a great revelation.

They contemplated the Bodhi of the Buddha and Great Nirvāṇa, just like a person who has traveled far on business and, though not yet returned home, clearly understands their house and the path by which they must return. The entire assembled multitude—the eight classes of devas and dragons, those in training of the Three Vehicles, and all others—[were likewise enlightened].
All those newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands, all attained their original minds, became free from dust and defilement, and achieved the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī became an arhat. Immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is equal to the unequaled.

Ānanda, adjust your robes, join your palms in homage before the great assembly, and with a mind whose traces are perfectly luminous, experience a mixture of sorrow and joy; do this for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings of the future.

I bow my head and address the Buddha: "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, I have now awakened to the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak these words:

'One who seeks to deliver others before they have themselves been delivered is a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind; one who awakens others after having awakened themselves is a Tathāgata appearing in the world.

Although I have not yet been delivered myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final kalpa. World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha, and false teachers preaching the Dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. I desire—

"Having gathered his mind, he enters samādhi. How can he cause him to be established in the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), remain far from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression regarding the bodhicitta?

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda amidst the great assembly: "Excellent, excellent! Regarding your question on how to establish the site of enlightenment to rescue and protect sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly replied, "So be it; we shall respectfully receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "You have often heard within my Vinaya..."

He proclaimed the three principles of definitive practice: namely, to restrain the mind as the precept; from the precept arises concentration; and from concentration issues forth wisdom. These are called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy-avetyaprasādāni*).

[Commentary] First, regarding the subduing and severing [of afflictions]: Now, one who wishes to store pure dharmas must first cleanse the vessel of the body; wishing to cross the torrent of craving, one must first gather the oars of practice.

Therefore, the four grave precepts (*catur-śīla*) are solemnly proclaimed as the skillful means for entering cultivation. Since the meaning of *vinaya* (liberation) is profound and the binding of the passions is urgent, the teachings flow from the person’s own body and speech, and the subtle points are investigated through movement and stillness.

This is why Ānanda later expounded the four *pārājika* offenses and established the site of the path (*mārga-maṇḍala*), in order to clarify the cultivation and realization of the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), and so forth, until—

Rising from his seat, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna; this was a manifestation of having realized the fruit. Although Ānanda had not yet attained liberation, his compassion extended to future generations, and thus he acted as a Bodhisattva who has resolved to attain enlightenment.
However, at the beginning of one's practice, fearing the interference of errors and delusions, he inquired about various skillful means to remain far removed from the works of Māra.

Since the studies of precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are cultivated equally in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, he first elucidated these three trainings here to establish them as the definitive principle for progressive cultivation.

Ānanda, what is meant by "gathering the mind"? That which I call "precept" (śīla) is this: if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death.

You practice samādhi in order to emerge from worldly toil; yet if the lustful heart is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, [you shall not attain liberation].

They will inevitably fall into the path of Māra: those of the highest grade as Māra-kings, those of the middle grade as Māra-subjects, and those of the lowest grade as Māra-maidens. These various Māras also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Final Dharma, many such Māra-subjects will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra).

They cause sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views, causing them to lose the path to Bodhi. Therefore, when you teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, you must first sever sexual desire in the mind; this is called the method of the Tathāgata and the Buddhas of the past.

This is the Honored One’s foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction. Therefore, Ānanda, if one who cultivates meditative concentration does not sever sexual desire, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice.

Even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall still be called merely "hot sand. Why is this? Because this is not the basis for rice; it is composed of sand and gravel. If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous realization, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental nature, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?

You must cause the mechanism of lust to be severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of severance no longer exists. Only then may you hope for Bodhi. What I have spoken thus is called the Buddha’s teaching; if it were not spoken thus, it would not be so.
This was spoken by Pāpīyān.
Because all sentient beings are entangled in birth and death due to lustful desire, he made this the primary precept.

Ānanda, furthermore, in all worlds, if the minds of sentient beings within the six realms do not kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death. As you cultivate samādhi, it fundamentally leads to transcendence from the dust of the world.

Exhausting oneself in this way, the murderous intent will not be eliminated and the defilements cannot be removed. Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, if they do not sever the habit of killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. This applies even to those of the highest grade.
They will become powerful ghosts; those of middle grade will become flying yakṣas and various ghost generals; those of lower grade will become earth-walking rākṣasas.

These ghosts and spirits will also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the final dharma, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat they attain the path to Bodhi.
Ānanda, when I permit bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, these meats are all produced through my supernatural power; they have no original life-force or roots. You...

"Brahmin, the ground there is mostly humid and damp, further compounded by sand and gravel, such that grasses and vegetables do not grow. It is through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power, and by virtue of my great compassion, that these are provisionally called 'meat' so that you may obtain their flavor.

How can it be, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, that you eat the flesh of sentient beings? Though you call yourselves sons of the Śākya, you should know that such meat-eaters, even if they attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, are all great *rākṣasas*.
When their retribution ends, they will surely sink into the bitter sea of birth and death; they are not disciples of the Buddha. Such people as these—"

They kill one another and devour one another; their mutual consumption has not yet ceased. How then can such people escape the three realms? You must teach the people of the world to practice *samādhi* by first ceasing the taking of life.
This is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), it is like a person who blocks his own ears and shouts at the top of his voice, seeking not to be heard by others. Such people are said to seek to hide what is already fully exposed. [This applies to] pure bhikṣus and all bodhisattvas...

Śākyamuni, when walking on a forked path, does not tread upon living grass, much less pluck it with his hand. How could one who possesses such great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food? If [this were the case for] the bhikṣus...

He does not wear silks, cottons, or fine fabrics from the eastern lands, nor does he wear the boots, furs, woolens, curd, or clarified butter of this land. Such a bhikṣu is truly liberated from the world;
he has repaid his karmic debts from past lives and no longer wanders within the three realms. Why is this? Because wearing the products of those lands constitutes a causal connection with them.

Just as a person who eats the various grains grown in the earth cannot lift their feet off the ground, so too, if one’s body and mind, or the products of one’s own body, are not worn or consumed by sentient beings through either the physical or mental paths, I declare that such a person is one who has attained true liberation.
What I have spoken here is called the Buddha’s teaching; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

[Gushan] explains that the Vinaya clarifies the three types of purity—namely, not having seen, heard, or suspected that the animal was killed for one's sake—and now he speaks of five, adding those who die naturally and those left over by birds. [Wenling] states:

"To practice meditation while committing killing is to try to conceal what is increasingly exposed. One does not intentionally tread upon things nor intentionally pluck them; such benevolence extends even to grasses and trees, so how much more so regarding the eating of the flesh of sentient beings?"
The "body" refers to the flesh, blood, and so forth; the "parts of the body" refers to hair, skin, curd, and so forth. To serve these with the mind of greed constitutes two paths.

Ānanda, furthermore, in this world, if the beings of the six realms do not harbor a thieving mind, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death. You practice samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil;

if the thieving mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the thieving mind, you will inevitably fall into deviant paths among the superior-grade spirits.

There will be those of middling quality who are malevolent spirits and those of inferior quality who are heterodox persons, possessed by various demons. These various evil ones will also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such malevolent and heterodox beings will flourish in the world. They will secretly harbor deceit and fraud, calling themselves "Good Knowledge" (kalyāṇamitra), and each will claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person.

They will delude the ignorant and cause them to lose their minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit will suffer depletion and dissipation. I instruct my bhikṣus to wander from place to place for alms, so as to cause them to abandon [such practitioners].

Through greed, one completes the path to Bodhi. O Bhikṣus, do not cook for yourselves; entrust your remaining lives to this journey. Lodging as travelers within the Three Realms, you demonstrate a single coming and going; once departed, there shall be no returning.
What are these "thieving persons"? They falsely wear my robes and trade in the name of the Tathāgata, performing all manner of deeds while claiming them all to be the Buddha-dharma.

Yet they revile those who have left the household life and those bhikṣus endowed with the precepts, asserting that they follow the path of the Hīnayāna. Because of this, they mislead and delude immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell.

After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be bhikṣus who resolve their minds to cultivate samādhi, and who, before an image of the Tathāgata, burn a single lamp on their body, burn a finger joint, or burn a single stick of incense upon their person—I declare this of them: [They shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.]

This person has, at once, repaid their beginningless karmic debts from past lives and takes a long farewell to the world, forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). Although they have not yet clearly realized the path to unsurpassed enlightenment, this person, with respect to the Dharma...

With a mind already resolved, if one does not commit even a minor act of abandoning the body for this purpose, then even if one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one will inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay past debts, just as it was with my own "horse-barley," exactly so and no different.

You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* and only thereafter cease from stealing; this is called the Tathāgata’s third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one who cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) does not cease from stealing, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup, seeking to make it full—even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

For kalpas, there will never be a restoration. If bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, and give the surplus of their begged food to hungry sentient beings at the great assemblies—

With palms joined, he pays homage to the assembly. Whether someone strikes or reviles him, he treats it as if it were praise. He must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished; his flesh, bones, and blood are shared with all sentient beings.
He shall not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into his own interpretations to mislead beginners. The Buddha seals such a person as having attained true samādhi.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the word of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the word of Pāpīyān.

A bhikṣu goes on almsround fundamentally for the purpose of eliminating greed; therefore, he does not cook his own food. For one who travels and lodges, departing is the primary concern. [Wenling]: Among all things difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one’s own body. If one can relinquish even that which is so difficult to relinquish, how much more so other objects of craving?
Should it be that although the body practices relinquishment, the mind still harbors greedy seeking, then one merely increases black karma (evil deeds) without benefit to the Path;

such a person also lacks a resolute mind regarding the Buddha-dharma. [Gushan]: A thief takes another's "dependent retribution" (external possessions) to provide for their own body; now, however, one sacrifices the "primary retribution" (the body itself) to provide for others.
Because they are noble and holy, their karmic debts from beginningless time are repaid all at once.

Ānanda, in such a world, although the beings of the six realms may have perfected the three practices of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust within their bodies and minds, if they commit a great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not be pure;

they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata. This refers to claiming to have attained what one has not attained, or declaring that one has realized what one has not realized, or seeking worldly honor and superiority.

First: This refers to those who say, "I have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhatship, or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha," or who claim to be Bodhisattvas at various stages prior to the ten bhūmis.

Such people seek prostrations and repentance from others, coveting their offerings. These are the icchantikas who extinguish the seeds of the Buddha. It is as if a person were to cut down a tāla tree with a sword;

the Buddha has prophesied that such a person’s roots of goodness are forever destroyed, they will lack further knowledge and vision, and they shall sink into the ocean of the three sufferings, never attaining samādhi. After my parinirvāṇa, I command—
All Bodhisattvas and Arhats should manifest their response-bodies within that age of the final dharma, assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra.

They may appear as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, ministers, officials, boys, or girls; even down to courtesans, widows, thieves, butchers, or merchants. Engaging in the same activities as them, they praise the Buddha Vehicle, causing their bodies and minds to enter samādhi.
Yet they never say of themselves, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat," lest they reveal the Buddha’s secret cause or speak lightly of those who have not yet studied.
Except at the end of life, when the aggregates (skandhas) are left behind as a legacy, how could such a person delude sentient beings and commit a great falsehood?

You must teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, and subsequently eliminate all great falsehoods; this is called the Tathāgata’s fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction from the Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great falsehood, it is like carving the shape of sandalwood out of human excrement and hoping for its fragrance—such a thing is impossible. I teach the bhikṣus to follow the path with a straightforward mind.

"In all activities throughout the four modes of deportment, there is still something false and artificial; how can you claim for yourself the attainment of the dharmas of a superior person? It is like a destitute man falsely styling himself an emperor."

They bring about their own destruction; how much more so for a Dharma King? How could one falsely usurp [this position]? If the ground is not true, the fruit will be crooked. To seek the Bodhi of a Buddha while being like one who tries to bite his own navel—who can achieve success?

If the bhikṣus have minds as straight as a bowstring and are entirely truthful, entering samādhi, they will forever be free from demonic affairs. I certify that such people shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a Bodhisattva.
What I have spoken thus is called the teaching of the Buddha; what is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

[Wenling]: Because one has not attained the four fruits or the ten stages yet claims to have attained them, it is a great falsehood. To crave offerings from others and seek one's own honor and superiority is the demon of craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi-māra*).

Just as the *patala* tree does not grow once it is cut down, so too the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of a person who speaks great falsehoods are forever severed. [Shu]: The four categories mentioned above are called fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). Among those severed by the nine grades [of the path], there are varying degrees of depth;

for example, severing the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) is named *srotāpanna*, and thinning out greed, hatred, and delusion is named the third fruit (*phala*). Therefore, [one should regard] one's own body—its flesh, bones, and blood—as being no different from those of other sentient beings.

Together with this, one severs the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). To demonstrate that once one has gone and returned, there is no further coming back, one severs the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

This person is able to attain a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma; this severs doubt (*vicikitsā*). The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The view of a self-identity of a *srotāpanna* refers to the conceptualization of dependent origination and the conceptualization of the characteristics of the body.

When craving is severed, it does not arise. Why does one not grasp at precepts? Because one clearly perceives the suffering nature of the places where one is born. How is the characteristic of doubt severed? Because one does not perceive other teachers as being [the supreme authority]."
Because they are pure and impure, it is known that all four grave offenses are subdued and severed on the stages above the ground.

Zhen Cheng praised him, saying: "The wondrous contemplation of Avalokiteśvara uniquely uproots the fundamental faculties. Once one faculty returns, the six return to their source. He invited the Buddha to the gate of *nirvāṇa*, where concentration and wisdom were opened anew."
"Forever delivering those submerged in the cycle of existence.

In the *Chuanruliu* (The Transmission of Cutting Off the Stream), it is said: When Avalokiteśvara was about to set forth what he had realized, he recounted events from immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* ago in order to secretly reveal that the nature is fundamentally perfect and penetrating (*yuan-tong*), and that it is truly eternal and constant.

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteśvara; his teacher was the Master of Perfect Penetration (*Yuantong-shi*). The names of teacher and disciple were identical, for the Way is one and the same throughout all time.

"Contemplation" (*guan*) refers to the contemplation of the illusory vajra. "World-Sound" (*shiyin*) refers to the sounds of the ten realms; that which can be contemplated solely through sound is called "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*).

Regarding those who "enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation," they received their teacher’s instruction and carefully examined what was beneficial and what was harmful, thereby attaining realization and entry. Although the practitioner addressed here is indeed called "one of great learning," he had not yet reached this stage;

it was specifically for his sake that [the Buddha] initiated this teaching. As for "first entering the current within hearing so that the object perishes": the ordinary person’s ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness, which constitutes "hearing"; the hearing-consciousness rushing toward objects constitutes the "current. Now, Avalokiteśvara...

"Observing and listening turn back and enter [within]; therefore it is called 'entering the stream' (*praveśa-srotas*). Being able to extinguish sound and perfect hearing, it is called 'the absence of objects. The 'sound-dust' (*śabda-rasa*) mentioned above refers to the external object, while the 'entering the stream' mentioned below refers to the internal flow.

Because the flow is settled within, external dust naturally dissolves; hence it is said: 'Since that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly do not arise. Thus gradually increasing, 'that which hears and that which is heard are both exhausted.'"

By attaining this most wondrous faculty of hearing, the essence of the mind abandons hearing; thus it is called "exhaustion. This is what was previously stated: "When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons.

To perceive the exhaustion of hearing as having an end is itself not exhausted; hence it is said, "dwelling not on the exhaustion of hearing. When that which perceives is realized to be empty, the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, resulting in the liberation of dharmas.

When the emptiness of perception is utterly perfected, that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished—meaning that even the emptiness of the perception of emptiness is emptied, which is what is meant by "the non-arising of the dual emptiness. As for "arising and ceasing," these refer to external objects and internal faculties, and...

By means of the discerning mind, all delusions and karmic actions are termed phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; since they are now entirely empty, it is said that "they have already ceased. Because they have already ceased, they do not cease again.

Therefore, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). The more it is extinguished, the more it is manifested; this is called "manifest presence. The more it transcends, the more it is identical. Thus, above, it accords with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas.

By means of the thirty-two transformations, it enters all lands. Below, it accords with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as those beings.

It bestows the fourteen kinds of fearlessness, providing blessings for all beings, and manifests numerous wondrous forms, able to preach boundless divine mantras. All of these are without a locus of existence.

This is what was heard from the legacy [of the Master]: it is the result of his brilliant penetration and vast illumination. He concludes by saying: "When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I chose the samādhi of perfect illumination.

Because my conditioned mind attained mastery, I entered through the aspect of the 'flow' and realized *samādhi*. This led to the accomplishment of Bodhi; this is the foremost. Some may doubt that the thirty-two manifestations of a Bodhisattva instead appear as the body of a Buddha, or that the fourteen fearlessnesses involve sinking into delusion rather than transcending suffering and affliction.

They may argue that while the body and mind encompass the vast and boundless Dharma-realm, and various hands and eyes manifest in their functions, these are all merely symbolic representations of the Dharma and have never been actualized in reality. Alas!
