Is this not to create an obstacle for oneself by disparaging that Perfect Penetration? One should know that Avalokiteśvara is the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa; why then restrict oneself solely to the traces of his manifestation?

If sentient beings can respond and interact with the Way, how could it be difficult to leave behind the suffering of illusion and delusion? To look up and down once more over the four seas, and yet still act upon the knowledge of conditioned concerns—while body and mind mutually pervade the ten directions—this is only the beginning of the wondrousness that transcends hearing.

When a fish becomes a dragon, its head and horns are no longer the same; when a person ascends to sagehood, their hands and eyes are surely divine. Do not let yourself be like one gazing at the ocean in bewilderment or confined by a narrow well; please apply yourself to entering the stream until there is nowhere to dwell.
Relying further on the radiant light of Great Compassion, you shall be shown once and for all your original face. Only then will you believe in the holy words and holy realization. Not yet...

Or perhaps it was a deception? Yet, since the various sages have already set forth their methods of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), and the World-Honored One emitted light from his five limbs to remotely irrigate the *rajas* (dust-mote) Tathāgatas, while those *rajas* Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs to come and irrigate the Buddha’s crown—this surely signifies that the ultimate purity and luminous penetration are shared by all who attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

That the Bodhisattvas and Arhats of those realms and this land also have their crowns irrigated by light signifies the mutual fusion of cause and effect; what is presented and what is realized is each and every one unsurpassed. Even the forests and ponds all proclaim the sound of the Dharma.

The jewel-lights interlace like a net of precious threads. This signifies that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are none other than the Tathāgatagarbha, and none other than wondrous adornment.

This is a rare and auspicious omen; therefore, it causes all beings to universally attain the Vajra-samādhi. "Vajra" is a metaphor for the swiftness with which delusions are severed. To "attain" this is to reach the stage of the true cause at the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*).

Because one has entered this true position, the heavens likewise respond with various auspicious signs. Within the wisdom of the true cause, the ten realms are perfectly manifested, thereby forming a hundred realms; thus, the heavens rain down a hundred jeweled lotuses.

The flowers—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and blended with powder, signify the gradual and successive entry into the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*bhūmi*), whether by skipping or following the sequence.

That the empty space of the ten directions takes on the color of the seven treasures signifies the attainment of the sevenfold eternal fruits from within the essence of quiescent extinction. Having entered the gate of perfect penetration, habitual outflows are forever eliminated, and the distinction between the primary and secondary realms vanishes.

Therefore, the mountains and rivers of this Sahā world simultaneously disappear, and lands as numerous as motes of dust merge into a single realm. That the sounds of *brahman* chants and hymns are spontaneously performed signifies the realization of entry.
Such people as these have no sounds of dharma to produce; all are like this. This concludes the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

"Observe now these great Bodhisattvas and Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way. In their respective practices, there is truly no superiority or inferiority.

As for the distinctions of before and after, it is because the nature of the sages is such that nothing is not penetrated. Because nothing is not penetrated, such auspicious omens have been manifested. I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening; among these twenty-five [methods], who shall [speak]?"

Regarding its fundamental basis, including myself who have attained parinirvāṇa and the sentient beings of this realm who have entered the Bodhisattva Vehicle—by what gateway of skillful means can they achieve easy accomplishment?

Mañjuśrī, having received the command, selected only the faculty of the ear; this was specifically intended for those whose capacities were suited to it. The verse states: "The nature of the ocean of enlightenment is limpid and perfect; perfect and limpid, the source of enlightenment is primordial and wondrous.

This refers to what was previously called the "wondrous clarity of original enlightenment" and the "primordial wondrous clarity of the nature of enlightenment. In selecting the faculty of perfect penetration, he first indicates the essence of that perfect penetration. By employing the character "ocean," the intention of entering the stream [of the Dharma] is immediately revealed.

The passage below states, "By revolving the flow, one attains non-delusion," which is based on this very principle. Regarding the phrase "the fundamental luminosity gives rise to the object": "fundamental luminosity" refers to the original, wondrous, enlightened clarity. From this fundamental luminosity, delusion arises, and that which is illuminated is established;

hence it is called the "established object. Once the object of illumination is established, the true nature consequently becomes obscured; hence it is said that "the nature of illumination perishes. "The nature of illumination" refers to the true nature that initiates the act of illuminating.

"Delusion gives rise to space; because of space, the world is established" means that the state of obscured darkness becomes space, and within that darkened space, the accumulation of darkness forms matter.

"Thoughts crystallizing into lands; cognition becoming sentient beings" means that matter is intermingled with delusive thoughts, and the characteristics of thought form the body. Thus, due to a single cause of delusion, the environment and its inhabitants are divided;

consequently, the essence of clarity and wondrousness can neither be made perfect nor be made pervasive. This is because, through a single delusion, one takes on a body, and one's confusion is definitively situated within this physical form. Space arises within Great Enlightenment.

It is like a single bubble arising from the ocean; when the bubble vanishes, the emptiness was originally there. How much more so for those within the three realms of existence? This clarifies that the essence of awakening is omnipresent and all-pervasive.

When one does not follow after sensory objects, the essence of perfect penetration is fundamentally without limit or measure. Thus, "when purity reaches its peak, light penetrates everywhere; still illumination contains the void. When a practitioner attains this, all phenomena become wondrous. Therefore, "returning to observe the world, it is like a dream.
Regarding the line, "How can one who hears and upholds the Buddhas not hear the hearer?"—the phrase "Buddha-Buddha" refers to the nature of awakening as expounded by all Buddhas. This...

The essence of awakening is my true hearing. If one cannot hear the hearing, how can one know the Buddhas? Therefore, the *Sūtra* says: "O Great Assembly and Ānanda, turn back your inverted faculty of hearing; by turning back the hearing, you shall hear your own nature.

When Ānanda and the Great Assembly heard this instruction, they contemplated the Bodhi of the Buddhas and Great Nirvāṇa, like travelers who have not yet returned home but clearly understand their house and the path to be followed.

What was previously called "the perfect penetration of wisdom-awakening" and the "discrimination of the fundamental root of perfect penetration" merely clarified the origin of initiating practice; hence it is said, "knowing the path."
...and that is all. If you wish to return home, you must first prepare your provisions; therefore, I request that you gather your mind according to the rules and establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*.

From the instruction on the fifty-five stages of the true path of Bodhi, this section precisely clarifies the cultivation and realization of the myriad practices. As for why the precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are collectively termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*): it is because the ocean of awakening within sentient beings is fundamentally perfect and limpid.

However, by clinging to stillness, consciousness arises; as it flows outward and rushes toward objects, it is called "outflow. Now, by relying on pure discipline (*vinaya*) to restrain body and mind, there is inner clarity and the radiance of light, which is the wondrous penetration of *samādhi*, the correct concentration.

Wisdom is fully possessed within all of these. The Buddha has proclaimed the grave transgressions of sexual misconduct, killing, theft, and falsehood one by one; he has repeatedly and emphatically declared them to be definitive and clear instructions. Furthermore, he stated that it is not otherwise than what has been said.

As for what Pāpīyān says: this characteristic of the precepts is originally a dharma that is easy to know and easy to understand, yet it constitutes a practice that is difficult to accept and difficult to maintain.

That saṃsāra is rooted in suffering, while blissful, wondrous, and eternal [liberation] does not arise apart from this—when one contemplates the Buddha’s earnest and urgent exhortations, how can one not feel shame unto death and dread of death?

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Mystical Causes and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Seven:
Binding the Altar to Attain Realization.

Ānanda, regarding your question on "binding the mind," I shall first explain the wondrous gateway for entering *samādhi* and practicing its cultivation. Those who seek the path of a bodhisattva must first maintain these four kinds of precepts.

Their demeanor is as bright and pure as ice and frost; they cannot give rise to any thoughts of the second or third [unwholesome] paths, nor to those of the fourth. Since such thoughts would arise without cause, they simply do not occur.
Ānanda, if these four matters are not neglected, the mind will not even take as its objects form, sound, smell, taste, or touch. How then could any demonic activities arise?

If there are residual habits that cannot be extinguished, you should instruct this person to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra, the *Mahā-sattva-jaṭāmāṇava-pattra*, from the Radiance of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa. This is the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown.
The Unconditioned Mind-Buddha radiates light from the crown of his head and sits upon a precious lotus flower. Regarding the heart-mantra he has proclaimed:

furthermore, the karmic causes and conditions between you and Mātanga over successive kalpas, as well as your habitual tendencies of affection, have not been limited to a single lifetime or a single kalpa. Once I have proclaimed this, your love-attachment will be forever severed and you shall become Arhats.

Even she, a courtesan who had no intention of practicing, was secretly aided by my spiritual power and swiftly realized the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). How much more so for you, the Śrāvakas gathered here, who seek the Supreme Vehicle and are certain to attain Buddhahood? It is, for example, like using...

Dust blown by a favorable wind—what difficulty or danger could there be? If there is one in the末法 (final age) who wishes to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they must first uphold the pure prohibitive precepts of a bhikṣu.

They must specifically select a person of pure precepts as their teacher, the foremost śramaṇa. If they do not encounter a truly pure monk, their ritual observance of the precepts will certainly not be accomplished.

Once the precepts are fulfilled, they should don new, clean robes, burn incense, dwell in seclusion, and recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, they should perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandhana*) and establish [the altar].

At the site of enlightenment, throughout the ten directions, the unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in their respective lands will emit rays of great compassion and descend to anoint the crowns of their heads.

Ānanda, when such pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or lay donors (*dānapati*) of the末法 (final dharma) age extinguish greed and lust in their hearts and uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts, they shall, within the site of enlightenment, give rise to the bodhisattva vows.

Bathing and entering and exiting [the hall], they shall practice the Way during the six periods of the day and night without sleep. After three weeks have passed, I myself will manifest my body before that person, touch their crown to comfort them, and cause them to awaken.

[Commentary by Wēnlíng: Awakening consists in internal containment as the essential; therefore, the sublime gate is proclaimed: first, uphold the four precepts. When the four precepts are pure, the branches and leaves do not sprout;

one does not encounter the objects of sensory dust, and demonic affairs are subtly eliminated, so that one may enter right concentration. [Sub-commentary: Next, those who cannot sever their fetters do so because their chronic afflictions are deep and heavy; thus, they require the secret assistance of divine mantras to enable them.
When karmic obstacles are slight, the roots of delusion gradually subside. *Mahā-satvara-patara*—translated as "Great White Parasol"—refers to the Unseen Summit (the *uṣṇīṣa*).

In the *Mahā-śvetā-parasolā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the Sanskrit is translated as "The Mother of Buddhas, the White Parasol, emerging from the *uṣṇīṣa* of all Tathāgatas; none other can uphold it; this alone upholds.
Regarding the "afflictions of attachment and habitual tendencies" resulting from the past-life causes and conditions of Mātaṅga: according to the *Mātaṅga-sūtra*, once Ānanda had returned...

The girl wept without ceasing, her thoughts fixed on Ānanda, as she followed him to the gate of the monastery. The Buddha sent someone to summon her and asked, "Why do you follow Ānanda? What do you seek?

The girl replied, "I have heard that Ānanda has no wife, and I myself have no husband. The Buddha said, "Ānanda is a śramaṇa who has no hair; would you be willing to shave your head? After the girl returned and informed her mother, her mother gave permission for her to shave her head.
The Buddha asked, "What is it about Ānanda that you love? She answered, "I love Ānanda’s eyes; I love Ānanda’s ears; I love Ānanda’s mouth; I love Ānanda’s nose. The Buddha—
"Ānanda, in the eye there is only tears; in the ear, only wax; in the mouth, only saliva; in the nose, only mucus; in the body, only excrement and urine.

Where there is a husband and wife, there is impurity; from impurity, a child is born; with a child, there is death; with death, there is weeping. What benefit is there in this body? What is there for you to love?
When the daughter heard these words, she immediately rectified her own mind and attained the path of Arhatship. The Buddha said, "This woman Mātaṅgī, in a previous life, [was... (The text ends here).

For a hundred generations she was Ānanda’s wife; they always respected one another and were constantly filled with mutual affection. Even now, when husband and wife see each other, it is as between brothers. Thus, through our sūtras and precepts, they have attained the Way.
What is said here regarding the divine mantra is due to the merit of its dark assistance. With pure precepts as one's teacher, the essence becomes truly refined and the subtle body swift;
thus, it moves the Buddha to emit light and come to anoint the crown of the head. Reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times signifies the subduing of the one hundred and eight afflictions.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, having received the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction, my mind has already been awakened. I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path, and the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) is accomplished.

For those practicing during the Final Dharma, how should one establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) so as to accord with the pure rules of the Buddha, the World-Honored One? The Buddha told Ānanda, “If people of the final age wish to establish a site of practice, first construct a platform.

Prior to this, they should take a powerful white bull from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fragrant grasses of those mountains. This bull drinks only the clear water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle.”
One may take its dung and mix it with sandalwood to plaster the ground. If it is not a cow from the Snowy Mountains, that cow is foul-smelling and unfit for smearing the ground.

Instead, one should select a plain and dig five feet below the surface to take the yellow earth from beneath; this should then be mixed with sandalwood, aloeswood (*agaru*), *suhak*, *kunduruka*, saffron, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *devadāru*, and *jintong*.

Take sweet flag (*gandhatṛṇa*) and clove (*kakkolaka*). Grind these ten ingredients into a fine powder and mix it with earth to form a mud plaster. Spread this over a square area of sixteen feet (one *zhang* and six *chi*) to construct an eight-cornered altar (*maṇḍala*).

At the center of the altar, place a lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood. Upon the flower, set a bowl (*pātra*). First fill the bowl with dew collected during the eighth month; within the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available.

Take eight round mirrors and place them one at each of the cardinal and intermediate directions surrounding the flower and bowl. Outside the mirrors, erect sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners, interspersed as offerings.
Spread out lotus flowers and arrange incense burners, burning only aloeswood so that the flames are not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels.

Prepare milk pancakes, along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, milk porridge, storax, honey, ginger, pure clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and pure honey—sixteen of each, arranged outside the lotuses, surrounding them to offer to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
At every mealtime, or at midnight, take half a *śeṣa* of honey and three *liǎng* of clarified butter; separately install a small brazier before the altar.

Having prepared scented water by boiling *turuṣka* incense, he bathed the charcoal with it and then ignited it until it blazed fiercely. He then cast the ghee and honey into the flaming furnace, burning them until no smoke remained.

When making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if the practitioner’s cultivation does not yield results due to obstructions from beginningless time, it is necessary to construct a maṇḍala. If the Buddha responds by appearing, one may then realize entry [into the path].

The maṇḍala serves as the foundation for establishment, while faith is the root of entering the Way. The white ox of the Snowy Mountains symbolizes pure power; its consumption of only what remains after mastication represents the two aspects of internal reality and true purity.

Harmony and principle are the union with the profound; incense is used to communicate this faith. It must consist of ten types, which is the mark of perfect penetration. Excluding the ground as the site, the earth is piled up to form the altar (*maṇḍala*).

Principle is circular while phenomena are square; the altar has eight corners. Its square and round dimensions of sixteen *zhang* represent the four fruits and four stages of progress, realized through the sixteen moments of mind upon seeing the Path.

This altar’s numerical proportions are derived from the methods of the Ācārya; as the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (Great Teaching King Sūtra) states: "The four dharmas, sixteen dharmas, eight dharmas, and the twelve activities of the Ācārya—these together constitute it."

Regarding the Dharma, that which is called the "manifestation of the Dharma" (*vyakti-dharma*) is described in the Sūtra as follows: "Taking the mind of faith and understanding as the thread, one measures according to the prescribed proportions.

Using wisdom as the measuring line, one establishes the three karmas and performs the visualization for twelve *hasta* (cubits). One constructs the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate corners, the four gates, and the four pavilions.

This refers to the construction of the maṇḍala, wherein there are various rites for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as rites for the *Hāṭaka* [deities], each having its own specific number of *hasta* measurements. That same Sūtra states: "The Ācārya must strictly follow these instructions without deviation; he is none other than the previously mentioned monk of pure precepts."

The Master is represented by the flower, which opens the awakening-water to manifest the True Principle; this flower being in the center symbolizes the fundamental wondrous contemplation. The four patiences and four wisdoms constitute the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
Next, the sixteen lotus-flower food vessels represent the sixteen mental states of principle and wisdom. The power of faith being truly pure is called "burning aloeswood";
true wisdom being inwardly merged is called "smokeless incense."

One should cause banners and flowers to be hung everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the chamber of the maṇḍala, upon the four walls, one should arrange the images of all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and their various Bodhisattvas.
One should display the images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and the great emanations of Avalokiteśvara facing forward;

furthermore, Vajragarbha should be placed at his left and right. [Also to be placed are] Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, as well as the Cūḍāmaṇis, the Piṅgalas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Vināyaka.

Kāśyapa, hang [the mirrors] at the sides of the entrance, placing them to the left and right. Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the air, so that they face directly toward the square mirrors installed within the mandala site.

During the first seven days, let their forms and shadows interpenetrate one another in successive layers. With utmost sincerity, prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those bearing the title of Arhat.

Constantly, throughout the six periods of the day, recite mantras around the altar and practice the Way with a sincere heart, performing one hundred and eight recitations at each session. During the second seven days, focus the mind single-mindedly on making Bodhisattva vows without interruption;

in my Vinaya, there are previously established instructions for such vows. During the third seven days, throughout the twelve periods, focus single-mindedly on upholding the Buddha’s *Pāṇḍaravāsinī* (Bhadrakarātrī) mantra.

Reciting the mantra until the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear. At the place where the mirrors reflect one another’s light, he shall receive the Buddhas’ empowerment by the stroking of their crowns. Thereupon, within the site of practice, he shall cultivate samādhi.
This enables those who practice and study in such a manner during the final age to have bodies and minds as clear and pure as lapis lazuli.

Ānanda, if among this bhikṣu’s original preceptor or the ten bhikṣus within the assembly there is even one who is not pure, then such a site of enlightenment will for the most part not be accomplished. After three weeks have passed, he should sit upright and dwell in retreat.

After one hundred days, those of sharp faculties attained the stage of Srotāpanna without rising from their seats. Even if their physical and mental bodies had not yet fully realized the holy fruit, they knew with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood was unerring (having seen the truth and firmly maintained it).
Thus, the Dharma-assembly you asked about is established in this manner.

When the central position facing east is established, Vairocana is the presiding lord of the Buddha Family; Avalokiteśvara and others are the presiding lords of the Holy Assembly; Ucchuṣma and others are the presiding lords of the Vajra Family;
and Vināyaka is the presiding lord of the Deva Family—as explained extensively in the *Guhyatantra*. This is the method of the *ācārya* for managing the ritual mandala:

to perfect its precision and to harmonize its universal application by positioning the deities of the eight assemblies. Therefore, for twenty-one days, one should pay homage to the Buddhas, recite their names, chant the *Vinaya*, and make great vows to clarify the three karmas.
Through diligent mutual interaction, they secretly provide assistance and subtly effect their purpose. As the Sūtra says: "The three types—body, speech, and mind—are called 'the secret.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and so forth are called 'the assembly. One should know that the dharmas employed are secret in number as well. When mirrors reflect one another's light, the Buddha-wisdom arises; during the sequence of the empowerment of touching the crown of the head, there is a subtle resonance and meeting.
Within this very state, one cultivates *samādhi* and attains the clarity and purity of body and mind, like lapis lazuli. Thus, one’s virtue accords with *nirvāṇa*, which is the essence of *śamatha*.

The essence was revealed; having remained in retreat for one hundred days, he realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Thus, the appearance of the Buddha Radiant Convergence (*Prabhāsa*) previously was precisely the precursor to attaining this fruit within this [present] stage.

After the mantra had been recited three times and the invisible power had been bestowed, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since I left the household life, relying on the Buddha’s affectionate love and seeking much learning, I have not yet realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). I encountered that Brahmā..."

I was constrained by the malevolent arts of celestial beings; though my mind was clear, my power was not free. Fortunately, I encountered Mañjuśrī, who caused me to attain liberation. Although I have received the Tathāgata’s divine *uṣṇīṣa* mantra, [it has not yet been fully effective].

We have secretly obtained its power, yet we have not yet heard it directly from you in person. We pray only that, out of great compassion, you will proclaim it once more, to piteously rescue all those practicing in this assembly, as well as those in the future who remain within saṃsāra.

By receiving the Buddha’s secret voice, may their bodies and minds attain liberation. At that time, the entire great assembly in the gathering prostrated themselves and waited expectantly to hear the Tathāgata’s secret verses.

Then, from the uṣṇīṣa on his crown, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewel-lights; from within these lights, thousand-petaled jeweled lotuses emerged, upon which emanation Tathāgatas sat amidst the precious blossoms.

From the crown of his head, ten rays of light composed of a hundred jewels were emitted. Each ray of light universally manifested ten *gaṅgānadīvāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Vajrapāṇis, who held mountains aloft and grasped vajra-clubs.

Pervading the entire realm of empty space, the great assembly looked up in awe, their hearts filled with both fear and love, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate protection. With single-minded devotion, they listened to the Tathāgata Emitting Light from the Unseen Crown of His Head as he proclaimed this divine mantra.
