Ānanda, this is the Secret Gāthā of subtle and wondrous phrases from the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-Sitātapatrā*, which gives birth to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.

By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By holding this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions subdue all demons and restrain all non-Buddhists.

By mounting this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are born from precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust. Containing this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.

Holding this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to bestow the prophecy of Buddhahood by touching their heads throughout the ten directions; even when their own fruition is not yet complete, they likewise [act] throughout the ten...

Now, having received the Buddha’s prophecy, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon this mantra-heart to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the manifold sufferings throughout the ten directions—namely, those of the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.

The sufferings of blindness, deafness, muteness, and dumbness; the suffering of encountering those one hates; the suffering of separation from those one loves; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; the blazing intensity of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); and all manner of great and small calamities—these shall all be simultaneously liberated.

Perils from bandits, perils from armies, perils from kings, perils from prisons, perils from wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty—these shall dissolve away upon mere recollection.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, in accordance with this mantra-heart, enable one to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions; within the four modes of deportment, offerings are made according to one's wishes. Within the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one is promoted to the rank of a Great Dharma Prince. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions...

Come! Practice this mantra-heart. It can gather and sustain karmic affinities throughout the ten directions, causing those of the Lesser Vehicle who hear the Secret Treasury not to give rise to alarm or fear. Thus do the Tathāgatas of the ten directions [speak].
By reciting this mantra-heart, one attains supreme enlightenment, sits beneath the Bodhi tree, and enters Great Nirvana. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart;
after their parinirvāṇa, they entrust it with the affairs of the Buddha-dharma so that it may be maintained to the ultimate end, and the precepts are strictly purified, all becoming perfectly pure.

If I were to speak of this Buddha-Usnīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya Pañcara-mantra from dawn until dusk, with its sounds linked together and its syllables and phrases never overlapping, even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I could never finish. Furthermore, this mantra is also called the Tathāgata.

I exhort you disciples in training who have not yet exhausted saṃsāra: if you resolve with utmost sincerity to attain arhatship, do not sit in the place of enlightenment without upholding this mantra, thereby causing your body and mind—
It is impossible—indeed, it is absolutely impossible—that one could distance oneself from the works of Māra.
Ānanda, the power of this divine mantra is revealed below: the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the Way through this mind; therefore, this mantra-mind can give birth to all Buddhas.

Thus, there are thirteen successive phrases that manifest the efficacy of this fundamental mantra-mind: it serves as the cause for the Tathāgatas’ attainment of Buddhahood, it serves as the function for subduing Māra, and it serves as the response [to sentient beings].

The mind that manifests is the mind that expounds the Dharma; the mind is the mind that bestows prophecy; the mind is the mind that uproots suffering; the mind is the mind that serves spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*);

the mind is the mind that embraces and gathers [disciples] as close causes; the mind is the mind that attains enlightenment and enters parinirvāṇa; and the mind is the mind that entrusts the great matter.
Because these phrases are ultimately firm and grounded in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), their benefit and purpose are thus.

Ānanda, if in any world, in whatever land, among all sentient beings born in that country, one were to write this dhāraṇī on birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk, or white woolen cloth, and store it in a fragrant pouch;

and if that person’s mind is dull such that they are unable to recite or memorize it, yet they either wear it upon their body or keep it written within their home—then you should know that for as long as that person lives, [they shall be protected].

No poisons whatsoever can cause them harm. Ānanda, I shall now further recite this mantra for you, which protects and saves the world, grants great fearlessness, and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite it themselves or teach others to recite it, you should know that such beings who uphold and recite it—

Fire cannot burn them; water cannot drown them. Neither great poisons nor minor poisons can harm them. Thus, even the evil spells of dragons, devas, ghosts, and spirits, as well as *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, and *mārās*, cannot take hold.

Their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*). All curses, hexes, sorcery, and toxic drugs—whether from gold, silver, plants, trees, insects, snakes, or the poisonous vapors of the myriad things—when they enter their mouths, turn into the flavor of nectar (*amṛta*).
No malevolent stars, nor any ghosts or spirits, nor those with cruel hearts and poisoned minds, can cause harm to such a person.
The malevolent Piṇāyakas, the various evil kingly ghosts, and their retinues shall all receive this profound kindness and constantly provide protection.

Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* koṭis of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas; each one has a host of vajra-beings as their retinue, who attend upon them day and night.

Should there be sentient beings who, even with a distracted mind or not in a state of samādhi, remember this in their hearts and maintain it with their mouths, these Vajra Kings will constantly follow them.

If this is so for those good sons, how much more so for one who possesses the resolute bodhicitta? These Vajra Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, will secretly and swiftly stimulate their divine consciousness with refined intent.
At that moment, the person’s mind will be able to remember eighty-four thousand *Ganges-sand* eons, comprehending them all-pervasively and attaining freedom from doubt, beginning from the first eon.
Even unto their final bodies, throughout successive births they shall not be born [in such states].

Yakṣas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and all other hungry ghosts—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—in such evil realms, these sons of good family, whether reading or reciting, copying or transcribing, wearing or concealing [this], or making various kinds of offerings, will not be born in poverty, lowliness, or unpleasant places for kalpa after kalpa. Even though these sentient beings may, of their own accord, fail to perform meritorious deeds...

The karma [is such that] all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon this person. By virtue of this, for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), unspeakable, and beyond description, they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.
Their immeasurable merits shall be like a cluster of akṣa fruits, cultivated together in one place, never to be dispersed. Therefore, it is able to cause—

For those who have broken the precepts, their roots of virtue shall become pure; for those who have not yet attained the precepts, they shall cause them to attain them; for those who are not diligent, they shall cause them to be diligent;

for those who lack wisdom, they shall cause them to possess wisdom; for those who are impure, they shall quickly attain purity; and for those who do not observe the fasts and precepts, they shall naturally come to observe them. Ānanda, when these good sons and daughters hold this mantra, [these benefits shall arise].

Even if one has committed violations of the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them, after holding this mantra, all offenses of breaking the precepts—regardless of whether they are light or heavy—are extinguished at once.

Even if one subsequently drinks alcohol or eats the five pungent roots and various kinds of impurities, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not regard these as transgressions.

Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, one is entirely pure. Even if one does not construct an altar, enter a *maṇḍala*, or practice the Way, by reciting and upholding this mantra, it is the same as having entered [the sacred precinct].

The merit of performing the ritual path at the altar is no different. If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution or various offenses against bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—such as the four pārājika or eight saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses—and recites this mantra, such grave karma will be entirely eradicated, just as a fierce wind blows apart a heap of sand until not even a hair’s breadth remains. Ānanda, if there are sentient beings...

From immeasurable and incalculable kalpas past, all karmic obstructions of light and heavy offenses committed since previous lives that have not yet been repented— if one can read, recite, copy, or wear this mantra upon one's person,

or place it within one’s dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then such accumulated karma will be dissolved like snow melting in hot water; before long, one shall all attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Next, the exhortation to uphold [this mantra] is explained through seven kinds of merit: 1. "If in all worlds... and so forth explains the merit of copying [the text]. 2. "If after my parinirvāṇa... and so forth explains the merit of reciting and chanting.

Regarding "birch bark, palm leaves, and so on," this means that one may write it down whenever such materials are encountered, without making any particular selection. Among the worldly substances such as gold, silver, grass, and wood, all possess poisonous vapors;

only the recitation of this mantra can eliminate them. 3. "One should know that this mantra... and so forth explains the merit of protection. "With a refined mind, secretly and swiftly" refers to the Vajra who upholds the mantra.

"By means of wondrous, refined, and brilliant clarity, the spiritual consciousness is secretly awakened. "The first kalpa" refers to the initial moment of generating the bodhicitta; "until the final body" refers to the time of attaining Buddhahood. From "These four good sons...
onwards, it clarifies the merit of making offerings. From "Ānanda... onwards, it clarifies the merit of eradicating transgressions.

A bhikṣu who commits the four pārājika offenses is termed a "four-abandoner," and a bhikṣuṇī who violates the eight rules of non-respect is termed an "eight-abandoner"; since this dhāraṇī alone can eliminate them, he exhorts [the assembly] to receive and uphold it.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet borne children and desires to conceive, if she can recollect this dhāraṇī with a sincere heart, or wear this *Śītavana-tārā* on her person, she will give birth to a son or daughter endowed with merit and wisdom.
Those who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who seek the swift fulfillment of karmic rewards shall swiftly attain fulfillment.
It is likewise so for their physical vitality and strength. After the end of their lives, they will surely be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows.

One shall not be born in the borderlands, among the low-born, or even in mixed forms. Ānanda, if in various kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages there be famine, pestilence, or the calamities of weapons, bandits, strife, and all other such lands of misfortune, one should transcribe this divine mantra and place it at the four gates of the city, as well as at various caityas, or upon the tops of towers.

One should cause all sentient beings within that kingdom to welcome this mantra, prostrate to it with reverence, and offer single-minded worship. Furthermore, one should cause the people to each wear it upon their person, or each [to carry it]...
Wherever one dwells, all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished. Ānanda, in every place, throughout all lands, wherever this dhāraṇī exists, the devas and nāgas will rejoice;

wind and rain will fall in their proper seasons; the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will be peaceful and happy. Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars; according to the direction, no strange portents or obstructive disasters shall arise.

No one shall suffer untimely death; they shall not be bound by cangues, fetters, stocks, or shackles. They shall sleep peacefully day and night, never having evil dreams. Ānanda, in this Sahā world, there are eight...
There are fourteen thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and furthermore eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns.

Appearing in various forms when they manifest in the world, they are able to produce all manner of calamities and anomalies among sentient beings. Wherever this mantra exists on earth, they shall all be completely extinguished for a distance of twelve *yojanas*, becoming a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*).
No evil omens or portents shall be able to enter. For this reason, the Tathāgata has proclaimed this mantra to protect beginners and all practitioners in future ages.

Entering samādhi, body and mind become tranquil and one attains great peace and security. Furthermore, no demons, ghosts, or spirits, nor any karmic calamities from beginningless time, nor old debts of past karma, shall come to cause harm or affliction.

You, as well as all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, by relying upon my maṇḍala and maintaining the precepts according to the Dharma, and receiving the precepts from a pure monk, shall harbor no doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart. Such a son of good family, regarding these [limbs] born of his parents—

If one cannot attain mastery over the mind within this very body, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods—how could they possibly offer such exhortation and how could they be so earnest?

Sixth, "If there is a woman... and below explains the merit of *Pratisara* (Seeking Aid). Seventh, "If in various lands... and below explains the merit of pacifying calamities (*śānti*). A *caitya* is a Buddha-land; "disasters" refers to eight types:
famine, pestilence, warfare, financial hardship, strife, wind and snow, legal punishment, and portents such as malignant stars.

When the sun and moon lose their proper course, eclipses become portents; when wind and rain do not occur at their proper times, they cause destruction as disasters; when the five planets lose their proper course, they afflict the entire nation.

To suffer calamity for such perverse and rebellious reasons is brought about by human conduct, to which Heaven responds with transformations. Thus, when tyranny is punished, there are many whirlwinds; when laws are perverted, there are many locusts and moths;

when the innocent are killed, the land turns crimson and crops fail; when orders are not collected, there is much excessive rain. As for the mention of eighty-four thousand, these refer to the stellar mansions (nakṣatras) that encircle the heavens.

The twenty-eight stars constitute the longitudinal threads of the celestial sphere, while the eight great ones—the planets Rāhu, Ketu, and Bhauma, along with the five other planets—constitute the latitudinal warp following those meridians. This is the principle of harmonious response.

When merit is obstructed, it becomes calamity; therefore, these are called "calamitous transformations" caused by malevolent stars. Now, because they are dispelled and averted through the power of incantations, the adverse forces instead follow along with auspiciousness, and all existing misfortunes and difficulties are entirely extinguished.
For this reason, the Tathāgata next clarifies the merit of responsive resonance, stating that those born of parents who attain mental penetration are manifestations of the signs of response.

When these words had been spoken, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *vajrapāṇis* in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall with sincere hearts protect those who thus cultivate bodhicitta. At that time, the Brahmā King, together with Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four Great Kings, also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:

"If there truly are such virtuous persons practicing and studying [the Dharma], we shall exhaust our hearts and with utmost sincerity protect them, so that all they do throughout their lives may be as [intended]."

Furthermore, there were immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, vināyaka great ghost kings, and various ghost commanders who also joined their palms and prostrated before the Buddha.
"I too vow to protect and sustain these people, causing their bodhicitta to be swiftly brought to full perfection.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable sun and moon devas, as well as the masters of wind, rain, clouds, and thunder, along with the lord of lightning and the annual circuit officials, and all the stars.

The retinues also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying: “We, too, shall protect these practitioners of the path, establishing them in the *bodhimaṇḍa* so that they may attain fearlessness.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable mountain deities, ocean deities, and all the spirits of the earth, water, land, and air; the vital essences of the myriad things; the Wind Deity Kings; and the gods of the Formless Realm.

Before the Tathāgata, they simultaneously prostrated themselves and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, rose from their seats within the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we have long since attained Bodhi; yet we do not enter Nirvāṇa, but constantly follow this mantra to provide salvation."

To protect those who cultivate samādhi in the final age, O World-Honored One, for such practitioners who cultivate the mind seeking right concentration—whether they are in the place of practice or otherwise walking in meditation—

"Even when they wander through villages with distracted minds for recreation, we and our retinues shall always follow and attend upon this person. Even if Māra or Maheśvara should seek an opportunity, they will ultimately find none.
As for the minor spirits, they shall remain ten *yojanas* away from these virtuous people, except for those who have resolved their minds and delight in practicing dhyāna. World-Honored One!"
If such an evil Māra, or a member of Māra’s retinue, should come to harass this virtuous person, I shall shatter their head with my precious vajra until it is like fine dust,
and I shall ensure that this person always accomplishes whatever they wish.

The above has generally revealed the power of protection and sustenance; since all these various spirits have attained their own fundamental wondrous mind and are able to establish great benefit, they employ two skillful means—either through contrariety or through conformity—to bring about such benefit.

The commentary states: According to the sutras, it is frequently said that the benefits of the mantra’s efficacy are meager for those who merely recite and uphold it. This is because the transmission has lost its authenticity and they do not understand its meaning.

Within the Secret Division (*Guhyatantra*), there are specific ritual procedures for recitation; if one does not perform these rites, even if the practice is profound, it will be of no benefit. Now, regarding the reading of the *Bhagavati Ratnadhvaja* (or *Cundā*) Bodhisattva...
Regarding the great mantras recited in the *Sādhanas*, although the root mantra is unique, there are differences according to the specific application for each rite.

For instance, when reciting "Oṃ Jvale Jvāle Dīpye," if it is for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one says "Svāhā"; for the rite of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one says "Mocaṭa"; for the rite of magnetizing (*vaśya*), one says "Namo";

for the rite of subjugation (*abhicāruka*), one says "Jahi Hūṃ Phaṭ"; for the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), one says "Hrīḥ"; and for the rite of dispatching (*visarjana*), one says "Hūṃ. This is the retention.

First, the recitations differ; second, the sacred images worshipped are also diverse. For instance, when painting images of the deity Pinanaye-ka (Pāñcika), they may have two arms, six arms, or even up to sixteen arms, each representing a specific symbolic meaning.

Furthermore, whether one employs Caṇḍālas, Mātangas, or even human flesh and the five pungent spices, these methods are all applied according to what is appropriate for the occasion and should not be disparaged.
Moreover, the practitioners of Vidyādhara (Holders of Wisdom) vary between being compassionate or wrathful in various ways, just as with the single matter of the prayer beads. If...

For the rite of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), use crystal for the beads; for the rite of faith and acceptance (*anugraha*), use red sandalwood for the beads; and for the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), use *kṣaumaka* (wooden nut) seeds for the beads.

One must certainly select the day, time, lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), and planetary position (*tārā*) for each according to their respective differences, as prescribed in the methods of empowerment (*adhitiṣṭhanavidhi*). Alternatively, one may use sweet flag (*vaca*), sandalwood, white mustard seeds, and so forth;

furthermore, the mantras of the various families (*kula*) also differ, such as those in the Lotus Initiation Family (*padmābhiṣekakula*), which vary in their phonemes and syllables, as well as in the distinctions of clarity and turbidity, or the inhalation and exhalation of breath. If even slightly...
To preserve errors while omitting essentials makes the invocation inconsistent; thus, what is called a *mantra* is the original speech of the sages of the five families.

This cannot be clarified through oral transmission alone, for its principles cannot be understood through mere profound mystery. Therefore, those who claim that their doctrine of the "perfect penetration of the manifest and the secret" has thoroughly mastered the threshold of the esoteric—if they hope for spiritual resonance and efficacy, it is unlikely such a principle exists.
The Second Part of the Section on Cultivation and Realization (Textual Division Three): First, the Twelve Classes of Beings.

Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We who are foolish and simple have been fond of much hearing, yet regarding our minds subject to outflows, we had not sought liberation.

Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation; our bodies and minds are refreshed, and we have gained great benefit. World-Honored One, such cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s samādhi has not yet reached—"

"Nirvana! What is meant by the stage of 'dry wisdom'? Through what sequence of the forty-four mental states does one obtain the eye of cultivation? By reaching what destination is one said to have entered the stages? And what is meant by an 'Equal Enlightenment' Bodhisattva?

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The great assembly, with one mind, waited expectantly for the Buddha’s compassionate voice, gazing up at him with wide-eyed devotion.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have been able to universally provide for the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna—showing from the stage of an ordinary person up to the ultimate Great Nirvāṇa the unsurpassed path of correct cultivation. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.

Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed their hearts, and silently received the teaching. The Buddha said: "Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, free from all names and marks. Fundamentally..."

In reality, there are no worlds or sentient beings; they arise because of delusion, and because of arising, there is cessation. Arising and cessation are termed "delusion," while the cessation of delusion is termed "truth.
This is called the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and great nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

[Commentary] Herein, the second [section on] cultivation and realization also relies on the passage concerning the second arousal of the bodhicitta in the preceding sutra; by showing how the characteristics of worlds interpenetrate, it reveals the fundamental merit.

Therefore, this question clarifies the stages of cultivation and practice, and furthermore, it proclaims the causes for the twelve classes of sentient beings, as well as the accomplishment of the fifty levels of Bodhi through the three gradual stages, thereby answering the second meaning of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
In the initial stage of "Dry Wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) within the question, one realizes the nature of reality as it is, which is manifested through the severing of delusions.

The stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration, along with the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), are called the forty-four minds. From these, one attains the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is termed "cultivation. That which begins from the stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) is called the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Following the ten stages is what is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). The Buddha spoke this as an answer to explain the basis for cultivation and realization: that which is called arising and ceasing, truth and falsehood, bodhi and nirvāṇa, are all merely names and signs.

Within the wondrous nature, these have never existed from the beginning. It is only because of the mutual causality of delusion and awakening that there is cultivation and realization. Thereupon, one turns away from non-awakening.

Because one relies on bodhi to transform birth and death and thereby relies upon nirvana, there are two bases for names. Desiring to correctly receive [the teachings], one must first recognize the causes of delusion;

therefore, the two kinds of inversion regarding the world of sentient beings are discussed. This clarifies the root of transmigration and demonstrates the conditions for the various classes of beings.

Ānanda, if you now wish to cultivate the true *samādhi* and go directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you must first recognize these two causes of delusion regarding sentient beings and the world.

When delusion does not arise, this is the true *samādhi* of the Tathāgata. Ānanda, what is meant by the delusion of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the mind is luminous and the nature of the mind is perfectly full, one takes that luminosity as a cause and gives rise to a [false] nature;
from this, false seeing arises. From absolute non-existence, it becomes ultimate existence. This existence and its objects do not have a cause that serves as their cause; they abide [in themselves].
The characteristics of that which abides are fundamentally without root. Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established. [Commentary:

Ānanda, the following explains the nature of the various marks of conditioned phenomena. The "clarity of the mind" refers to the mind-nature that is wondrously luminous and inherently awakened. This "clarity and perfection of the mind-nature" means that its nature is universally pervasive and luminous without exception.

"Arising from clarity to manifest the nature" refers to the nature of illumination and discernment. From false clarity, false awakening arises; because of the false nature, there are false appearances. Thus it is.

From the absence of marks, the true, there arises the presence of marks, the false; this is the origin of the world of sentient beings. All that exists is characterized by arising and ceasing, yet these characteristics of arising and ceasing are fundamentally without cause.
Because they take what is not a cause as their cause, and because abiding in these characteristics is fundamentally nothing but delusion, one realizes they have no root at all.

This is what is called the characteristic of the world of sentient beings—the substance of conditioned arising and ceasing. Now, the conditioned is explained based on three types of distinctions: namely, cause, fruit, and consciousness. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The characteristic of mental consciousness..."

Greed, hatred, and pride that are capable of functioning throughout the three periods of time are associated with the five consciousnesses; however, these instances of greed, hatred, and pride bind only their own respective period because they are specific-characteristic delusions (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-kleśa*).

For this reason, the conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) of the three periods are established. [Commentary] First, regarding the explanation of the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-svabhāva*): The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that conditioned phenomena have arising, abiding, change, and cessation as their essence.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are three conditioned characteristics, namely: arising, abiding, change, and cessation. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the conditioned is established by way of four meanings.

The characteristics of the world are established in four ways: first, by way of category; second, by way of characteristic; third, by way of temporal stage (*avasthā*); and fourth, by way of mutual dependence.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of distinctions: first, the distinction based on investigation by cognitive wisdom (*buddhi*); second, the distinction based on investigation of material form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); third, the distinction based on the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa-santati*); and fourth, the distinction based on temporal stages. [Commentary:

Based on the aforementioned meanings, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* establishes its thesis here that the three time periods (*trikāla*) exist as real entities. Thus it says: "If a person asserts that all..."

There is a school that must certainly admit the existence of the past and future, because they maintain that all three time periods are definitively and substantially real; this is the Sarvāstivāda school.

If someone asserts only the present and the future—claiming the future does not exist because it has not yet yielded its fruit, and the past does not exist because its karma has already yielded its fruit—that person may be accepted as belonging to the Vibhajyavāda school.

[Commentary] Next, regarding the explanation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as momentary: the *Vibhāṣā* states that within a single moment of a conditioned phenomenon, there are simultaneously three characteristics.

Because their functions differ, there is no contradiction. However, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* refutes this, stating: "If one maintains that the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) exist externally to the characterized entity (lakṣya), and that each moment possesses four characteristics because the entities are distinct and their functions are different, such a fault is incurable.

[Commentary: The *Vibhāṣā* masters, fearing that [the opponent] would cling to the characteristics as being temporal, established the four characteristics as having different functions while existing simultaneously.

The *Abhidharmakośa*, fearing that it would refute the temporal nature of the characteristics, established the differences of the three times based on their essential natures (svabhāva). Thus, they are both present together.

There are three meanings that establish the differences between the three time periods and the identity of the four characteristics, such that they exist simultaneously without any contradiction. Thus, the treatise states: "Because there is a distinct meaning, arising is itself cessation.

This means that the arising of form and the cessation of form have a distinct meaning. "Distinct arising and distinct cessation" means that future arising and present cessation have a distinct meaning.

"Arising in a time" refers to being subsumed within the time of actual arising; because it arises from the present world, it is not of the same moment as the future world. [Commentary] Third, the analysis of existence and non-existence refers to conditioned phenomena.

The two schools—the Dharma-nature school (Faxing) and the Characteristics school (Xiang)—each have their own established positions. The Dārṣṭāntika masters say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not possess a real intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*).

To refute this attachment, the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that [the dharmas] exist throughout the three periods of time. [Commentary: When the Dārṣṭāntikas say they "do not exist," they speak in terms of *nature* (*xing*). When the Vaibhāṣikas say they "exist together" (*sahabhū*), they speak in terms of *characteristics* (*xiang*).

As the Sūtra says: "Nature gives rise to false views; arising is precisely characteristic. Furthermore, it says: "From ultimate non-existence, one achieves ultimate existence"—this is the meaning of nature and characteristics.

Therefore, each of the two treatises relies on [these points] as the basis for their refutation and establishment. However, the intent of the Sūtra is to reveal that this essence is neither existent nor non-existent;

thus, it generally employs the critique of false views to refute the dualistic views of nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa). The *Vibhāṣā* states: "To say 'neither arising nor ceasing' reveals that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are fundamentally nothing but delusion."

Delusion of the originally perfect luminosity gives rise to false imagination. This false nature has no substance and is not based upon anything. When one intends to return to the truth, that which is intended as "true" is already not true; the nature of true suchness does not seek to be restored through what is not true.

Thus, there are established characteristics that are neither non-existent nor produced, neither abiding nor mind, nor phenomena. From these, they arise successively; the power of production manifests, and through perfuming, karma is formed.

Like karmas attract one another; because of this, there is karmic response. Through mutual extinction and mutual production, there thus come to be the inverted states of sentient beings. Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world? It is this...

There is that which exists; through the false arising of fragmented divisions, the realm (*dhātu*) is established. It is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abode; it flows on without staying still, and thus the world (*loka*) is formed.

The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and interact, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form;

touch arises from fragrance; taste arises from touch; and phenomena (*dharma*) are known through taste. Because these six disordered delusions constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions revolve through this cycle.

Therefore, in this world, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles undergo twelve transformations, forming a single cycle. Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there exist in this world beings born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, and born by transformation;

those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; those who are neither with form nor without form; and those who are neither with perception nor without perception.

[Commentary] This clarifies the characteristics of returning to cessation. To say "about to restore the truth" means that, apart from True Suchness (tathatā), all cultivation and realization belong to the delusory; therefore, it is said:

"Already not 'neither-arising-nor-abiding'" (*na-ajāti-na-sthiti*), which restates the seeing of nature as delusory arising and abiding, which is the characteristic of what is dwelt upon. "Neither mind nor dharma" restates the seeking to restore what is not true, which clearly constitutes the characteristic of non-existence.
"The power of arising manifests the matter of karmic response": "arising" is the fruit, "power" is karma, and "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) is the delusion of distant karma, just like the present life.

The body is manifested by the power of past karma and is further drawn toward future results by the heavy delusions arising in the present; thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that conditioned phenomena belong to causes and conditions.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing, taking and giving results, and falling within the three periods of time.

Having both prior and subsequent limits, and being characterized by superior, middling, and inferior qualities, they are not the true nature of permanence; therefore, there is the flux of the three periods of time. Because these three periods combine, they transform sentient beings into the twelve categories. However...

The essence of "beings of similar birth" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) briefly comprises seven meanings: first, name; second, meaning; third, sentient being (*sattva*); fourth, aggregation; fifth, karma; sixth, conditions; and seventh, fruit. First, regarding "name": According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the Chinese term *zhòngshēng* (衆生) is used; the Tang translation uses *yǒuqíng* (有情).

"Sentient being" (*yǒuqíng*) is precisely what is meant by "beings of similar birth. Second, regarding "meaning": The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that the term "beings of similar birth" carries the meaning of "sentient beings" (*sattva*). Third, regarding "sentient being":

This means that the name for sentient beings is established based on their sentience (*citta*), not based on their realm of rebirth (*gati*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "Although the realms of rebirth consist of sentient beings, they do not encompass all [of them]; therefore, this [term] refers exclusively to sentience."

1. "Arising from the combination of four" refers to sentient beings being born through the convergence of karma and conditions. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun) states: "Because they arise from the conjunction of karmic conditions, they are said to be 'born' (*jāti*);

yet there is no arising that occurs without conditions. 2. "The five types" refers to those born solely by the power of karma. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Because their karmic force is so strong, they do not depend on [external] conditions. 3. "The six conditions" refers to establishing names based on the conditions from which one arises.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "There are those with conditions, such as those from eggs; because they are designated by the name 'egg,' they are called 'egg-born' (*aṇḍaja*), and so forth. 4. "The seven fruits" refers to that which depends upon... [text ends].

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that those who experience the fruits of the desire realm are called "sentient beings of the desire realm" and so forth; therefore, the concluding summary clarifies that the three causes—karma, afflictions, and fruits—set the existence in motion.

The "movement of sound" refers to the power of karma; the "six types of deluded conceptualization" refer to the category of afflictions; and the phrase "the world of egg-born, womb-born, and so forth" refers to the category of fruits.

Ānanda, because the world is subject to false, deluded saṃsāra and the inversion of movement, the combination of vital energies (*vāyu*) gives rise to eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.

Thus there exist the egg-born *kalala* beings, who circulate through various lands as fish, birds, turtles, and snakes, their species filling every place. Furthermore, because the world is subject to defiled saṃsāra and the inversion of desire...

Through the combination and nourishment of eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts, there arise the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages of fetal development. Thus, beings transmigrate through various lands—humans, animals, dragons, and immortals—filling all categories.

This is due to the world’s causes, their attachment to saṃsāra, and their pursuit of inverted views. Through the combination and heating of eighty-four thousand overturned disordered thoughts, there arise moisture-born *peśī* forms.

Thus, beings transmigrate through various lands as wriggling insects and crawling creatures, filling all categories. This is due to the world’s causes, the cycle of transformation, and false inverted views.

Therefore, through the conjunction of conditions, eighty-four thousand new and old disordered thoughts are formed. Because of this, there arise transformed forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages), which circulate through various lands, undergoing metamorphosis and flying about.
Their species fill [the world]. [Commentary]:

The egg-born are named "reversal of movement" because they are moved by the false activity of karma through the conjunction of thought and conditions; their flying or sinking consists solely of the power of the karma of movement.

Thus, they induce the egg-born as their condition. Fish and birds are born from conditions; the womb-born arise from emotion, which is defiled desire-emotion. Because it spreads horizontally and vertically, they take the womb-born as their condition to become humans and animals. The moisture-born take only conditions [as their cause].
Because the convergence of attachment and the destination toward which one proceeds are not fixed, moisture serves as the condition for birth as wriggling and crawling creatures.

Because they are illusory and do not depend on [external] conditions, yet undergo transformation and metamorphosis due to the power of karma being predominant, these four modes of birth are categorized into four types based on the convergence of the superior characteristics of both karma and conditions.
Due to the world of causes, because of the obstruction of inverted delusions within the cycle of saṃsāra, they combine and adhere to form eighty-four thousand confused thoughts of radiant brilliance.

Consequently, there are *kalala* (embryonic stages) with physical forms that circulate through the lands; those who are brilliant in their prognostications of fortune and misfortune fill these realms.

Due to the world of causes, because of the confusion of inverted delusions within the cycle of saṃsāra, they combine and adhere to darkness to form eighty-four thousand confused thoughts of hidden obscurity. Consequently, there are *kalala* without physical forms that circulate through the lands; those who are dispersed and submerged in emptiness fill these realms.
They are obstructed. Because the world is filled with the delusive cycle of rebirth and inverted reflections, the combination of memories forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thought.
Thus there exist *kalala* (embryonic stages) with mental characteristics; they circulate through various lands, and their species—gods, ghosts, and spirits—are everywhere abundant.

Because the world is filled with the cycle of ignorance and the inversion of folly, the combination of dullness forms eighty-four thousand parched thoughts of chaos. Thus there exist *kalala* without mental characteristics; their spirits transform into earth and wood as they circulate through the lands.
Metals and stones are of such a kind that they fill the world.

Those with color arise from the predominance of specific conditions; they are established as "arising from results" because they possess brilliance and resistance, and are thus the form of karmic fruit.

Therefore, they exhibit distinctions of auspiciousness and calamity, fortune and misfortune—such as the firefly’s glow or the pearl in an oyster. Those without color are dissipated and hidden, like the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*); because the power of karma is so strong, they do not depend on external conditions.

Those with perception arise solely from karma; being formless and void, they become ghosts through the coagulation of perceptions, manifesting clarity and spirit without depending on the convergence of external conditions.

Those without perception, because their emotional karma is inferior, are dull, stubborn, and ignorant; these exist merely due to conditions, such as metal, stone, wood, or earth. These four types of birth are divided into four categories because the respective conditions and karma are predominant, and their characteristics are distinct from one another.
Due to the world of causes, through mutual dependence and cyclic wandering, because of false inversion, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causes.

Thus there exist non-material forms that take on material characteristics as *kalala* (embryonic stages), flowing through the lands such as the various jellyfish, which use shrimp as their eyes; these species fill the world.

Due to the world of causes, through mutual attraction and cyclic wandering, because of the inversion of nature, they combine with incantations to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of summoning. From this, there exist non-non-material forms as non-material *kalala*.

South: In the lands of transmigration, there are those born through curses and incantations; their kind fills the world. This arises because, due to the world, they combine with delusion and revolve in saṃsāra, and because of their inverted nature, they harmonize disparate elements to form eighty-four thousand confused and alternating thoughts.

Thus, there are the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages, which are formed from the perception of what is not-existent as existent. In these lands of transmigration, creatures such as the *pulu* (parasitic insects) are formed by the transformation of different substances;

their kind fills the world. This arises because, due to the world, they revolve in saṃsāra through mutual resentment and harm, and because of their inverted nature of killing, they harmonize strange elements to form eighty-four thousand [beings] who eat their own fathers.

The perception of a mother. Because of this, there exist those with non-perception who, despite lacking the characteristics of perception, undergo the *kalala* stage and transmigrate through various lands, such as the earth-owl (*bhūmy-olārika*) which uses clods of earth for its offspring, and the mirror-cracking bird (*ādarśa-bhedin*) which takes the fruit of a poisonous tree and embraces it as its young;
once the young have matured, both parents meet their destruction at the hands of their own progeny. Such species abound, and these are called the twelve types of sentient beings.

Next, as for those who are not of form yet manifest form: because they lack dependence on existence and rely on falsehood as their cause, their karmic power is subtle; thus they must depend on external conditions, just as the *siphonophora* (water-jelly) requires the shrimp as its eyes.
As for those who are not of non-form yet manifest non-form: because existence induces non-existence and summons it to constitute their body, both the conditions and the karma are subtle;

therefore, at the time of taking birth, they must rely on incantations and curses. As for those who are not of perception yet manifest perception: because their karma is subtle, they falsely grasp at other conditions, just as the *gallopeda* (wood-worm) lacks the perception of being a bee due to the karma and conditions [of its transformation].

Because they are subtle, they are attached to what is different; thus bees are not those who possess perception because they were previously non-perceptive. This is because the deluded mind attaches to and detaches from other conditions, just as a *kṣetrapa* (earth-owl) clings to a clod of earth, or as a poisonous fruit from a shattered mirror brings harm to its mother.
These four modes of birth (*yoni*) involve the subtle attachment to and detachment from conditions and karma, and are therefore divided into four types.

Regarding the aforementioned categories of beings, they depend solely on the thickness or thinness of their conditions and karma, which results in the superiority or inferiority of the fruits they experience. Thus, there are three, four, twelve, and so forth, differentiated by this principle; only a Buddha [can fully know them].

The World-Honored One is able to exhaustively fathom the nature of the light and heavy karma of sentient beings and clarify the causes of their transmigration; therefore, it is called the "nature of perversion. Zhen Cheng praised him, saying:

"Upholding the pure precepts, he established the ritual arena; the divine mantra of the 'Crown Light' was widely propagated. Having completed the meritorious work of cultivating the Way, he pays homage to the Compassionate King."
He further expounded the subsequent excellent verses.

As transmitted by Cejliu, he said: "To extensively clarify the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s practice and cause one to maintain the fourfold ethical discipline as pure as ice and frost—such that not even a single branch or leaf can grow—is because, although the myriad practices are numerous, this is their very root.

If people today can truly refrain from being conditioned by form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, demonic activities will naturally dissolve. Alas, how difficult it is due to past habitual tendencies!"

When led by external influences, the mind becomes equal to that of the Buddhas; yet at dusk, its conduct falls short of even that of ordinary beings. The more one hears and sees, the more one's delusions and karmic afflictions blaze forth; this cannot be remedied except through the power of divine mantras.

Ultimately, there would be no way to attain liberation. Now it is clarified that by constructing a ritual altar and reciting mantras, one can realize the sacred fruit. The transformation Buddha becomes the inconceivable Buddha, and the mantra becomes the inconceivable Dharma.

The altar constitutes the inconceivable realm; the assembly of those with pure precepts constitutes the inconceivable persons. Together with such people, generating such a mind, entering such a realm, practicing such dharmas, and attaining such fruits—this is certain and beyond doubt.

Because the mantra possesses supreme benefit, the eight classes of devas and dragons, as well as all ghosts and spirits, vow to provide protection. Those who uphold it shall encounter no demonic obstacles.

In this degenerate age, those who abandon the mantra and the mind [of its practice] while discussing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* merely increase their erudition in vain. May practitioners exert themselves. Thus concludes the section on Principle and Practice.

Now that [the stages] are complete, if the "sacred positions" (*ārya-bhūmi*) were not opened up, by what means could the characteristics of the realization of the fruit be manifested? The first fascicle states:

"Because the mind and speech are direct, from the beginning thus even unto the final stage, there is forever no trace of deviousness in between. This must now be explained in detail; therefore, he requests: "What is meant by the 'ground of dry wisdom' (*śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi*) and the forty-four minds?"

To what gradual sequence does one arrive to reach the culmination of practice? To which place must one go to be said to have entered the stages (*bhūmi*)? What is meant by the name "Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva" (*Samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva*)?

Now, although the questions list the gradual sequences among the various stages, this is primarily to first cause [the practitioner] to know the three gradual sequences so as to encompass all the stages. When the Buddha was about to reveal the positions of the various sages, he first revealed the two causes of delusion regarding sentient beings and the world;
for when their nature is inverted, they transform Bodhi into afflictions and thus become the twelve classes of beings, whereas when their nature is not inverted, [they attain liberation].

To transform birth-and-death into nirvāṇa constitutes the sixty stages of the sages; this is the source of both delusion and awakening, and must be discerned. To state the essential point: the nature is the luminous primordial mind.

When a fleeting false luminosity arises, both the subject that covers and the object that is covered are both non-abiding. Based upon this non-abiding, the world and all sentient beings are established. If one realizes this non-abiding...

Thus one knows that the delusion has no basis, and that the truth likewise does not exist. To desire to return to the truth is itself the root of perversion, from which the twelve classes of beings first arise.

Therefore, the world exists because of movement and sound; up to the sixfold chaotic delusions, they constitute the nature of karma. That the twelve divisions revolve through this cycle clarifies how the delusions of the primary and secondary worlds interweave to serve as the fundamental source for the arising of the twelve classes of beings.
Thus, when the worldly sounds, smells, tastes, and touches exhaust their twelve transformations and become a single revolving return, it is [repeated].

Within the formation of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the retributive environment), the three periods of time and the four directions interpenetrate one another. This causes sentient beings who undergo transformation to constitute the number twelve.

Form, sound, odor, taste, and touch serve as the agents of transformation; these are the very basis of the world. The world’s revolving and mutual interpenetration constitutes the number twelve. "Revolving" (*xuanfu*) carries the sense of turning back upon itself, as stated below:

"Because they ride this wheel of inverted transmigration. Thus, there are the egg-born and other modes of birth within the mundane world. In this way, one cannot exhaustively distinguish the twelve transformations such that the agent of transformation (*nengbian*) becomes the object of transformation (*suobian*). Twelve.

Regarding the statement that each and every category of sentient beings possesses twelve inversions: because they share the same principle-nature (*li-xing*), each and every one mutually possesses them. What Tiantai clarifies as "actualization" refers to the "phenomenal creation" (*shi-zao*); that which remains latent and dormant is "principle-possession" (*li-ju*).

This possession has nothing to be possessed; it is entirely the single essence of awakening (*jue-ti*). If one were to subsume this within the framework of the "six identities" (*liu-ji*), it is what is called "identity in principle" (*li-ji*).

Because one’s birth-nature is itself the Buddha, one may advance in cultivation. Upon hearing the principle once, it immediately becomes the "name-and-word" [stage]. Now, within these three gradual stages, one first eliminates its auxiliary causes and hollows out its primary nature;

this belongs to the two stages of "contemplative practice" (*guanxing*) and "semblance" (*xiangsi*). As the text says: "From one's own parents' fleshly body, without needing the divine eye, one naturally perceives the ten directions, up to the purity of past lives, attaining freedom from hardship and peril"—this belongs to the stage of semblance.
The third stage, "contradicting present karma," further builds upon the preceding two stages of contemplative practice and semblance to clarify the subsequent progress.

This refers to partial realization. The text states: "When the flow is reversed and the six functions cease entirely," this means that the five abodes [of ignorance] are completely suppressed, which is identical to the preceding stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing wei*).

"The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, and all the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of the Tathāgatas appear therein"—this indicates that view-delusions and thought-delusions have already been severed, which is identical to the preceding stage of semblance realization (*xiangsi wei*).

That this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) means that they have transcended the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and entered the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

This is the stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), wherein ignorance is first broken. From this point, one gradually cultivates and establishes the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*). What is indicated here is the aspect of ascending within that very stage of partial realization; it does not refer directly to the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

When the text concerning dry wisdom is combined with what precedes it, it shares the same meaning as before: the craving for desire is dried up, the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, the flow is completely reversed and unified, and the six functions cease to operate. The grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of...

"Wisdom" (*prajñā*). The nature of this wisdom is perfectly luminous and bright, illuminating the ten directions of the world-system. This is identical to the meaning previously explained regarding the ten directions of the lands being "resplendently pure.

If it refers to a state where the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* (afflictions of views) and *bhava-kleśa* (afflictions of existence) have not yet been destroyed, it belongs to the phase of the "practice of contemplation" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) on the verge of completion. If it refers to a state where the *dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa* have already been destroyed, it is identical to the "conformable" (*pratirūpa*) signs within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Since the "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) currently under discussion precedes the ten faiths, it should be directly explained as belonging to the stage of the practice of contemplation. However, the ten-fascicle version states: "From within the mutual functioning [of the six senses], one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine Dry Wisdom," and so forth.

The text says: "Thus, those who transcend the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the ten abodes (*vihāra*), etc. This is a cross-referencing of the sūtra’s passages; it does not mean that the six sense faculties are used interchangeably from the very beginning of entering faith, but rather refers to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

From this point onward—through the stages of faith, abode, practice, and dedication, up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)—there is no level that does not belong to this contemplation of adamantine observation. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:

"Having reached Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Adamantine Mind. It does not say that it is attained within Wondrous Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*), because perfect Bodhi returns to the state of non-abiding.

This is because they have been attained. Now, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*) up to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one further defines these by means of the "six identities" (*ṣaḍ-yoga*).

That which is inherently possessed by ordinary beings prior to Dry Wisdom is the Identity in Principle (*li-ji*). From this point on, hearing [the teaching] constitutes the Identity in Name (*ming-tzu-ji*). Dry Wisdom is the Identity in Contemplative Practice (*kuan-hsing-ji*). The Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the Identity of Similarity (*xiang-si-ji*).

From the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) through Equal Enlightenment (*samyaṅ-bodhi*) is the Identity of Partial Realization (*fen-zheng-ji*). Wondrous Enlightenment is the Ultimate Identity (*jù-jìng-ji*). Regarding the fact that the sutra begins with Dry Wisdom and ends with Wondrous Enlightenment, forming twelve stages—both single and combined—the individual opening of each position constitutes the "single" [stages].

Each stage possesses ten aspects; thus, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages constitute five cycles. Furthermore, there are the stages of dry wisdom, warmth, summits, patience, and the supreme worldly dharma.
"Miao" (Wondrous) constitutes the seven single [units]. By taking the seven singles and the five doubles, the number becomes twelve; the explanation is as in Changshui’s [commentary]. The Sūtra says:

"These various stages are all, within śamatha through the observation of the ten profound metaphors by means of the diamond-like [wisdom], purified and realized through the application of various vipaśyanās, gradually entering deeply. "Observation" (*guan*) is another name for the mind.

Furthermore, examining the two characters "jie yi" (all by means of), it should also be said: "Having reached up to Equal Enlightenment," because it is only upon attaining the diamond-like mind that one first gains [the stages of] the first faith, second faith, and so on up to the tenth.

Regarding the Grounds (*bhūmi*): when it is now said that "this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) within the Vajra-mind," it means that the initial aspiration and the ultimate realization are not distinct;

it does not mean that there is a separate stage of Dry Wisdom within the mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samayakīti*). This principle is no different from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which clarifies that Sudhana’s journey begins with his first audience with Mañjuśrī and concludes with his final reunion with Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, the statement that one "gradually enters deeper" indicates that this gradual progression permeates all the stages; one must not assume that the three gradual steps directly lead to the stage of Dry Wisdom. Thus, these are all increased by three.

Because of this progress, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi. Within these stages, there is successive advancement through the similarity of contemplative practice.

This is proven by the similarity of the stages and by the culmination of those stages. Furthermore, it does not exclude the three gradual steps that precede the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana). Counting the single sevens and the double fives, there are fifty-seven stages in total.

When it is now said that "fifty stages constitute the true path of Bodhi," this is because Dry Wisdom is not the "true" [stage] and Sublime Enlightenment (miao-jue) is not the "path"; thus, there are only fifty-five. The interpretation is as explained by Wu-xing.

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Myriad Practices Cultivated and Realized by All Bodhisattvas, Volume Eight:
The Three Gradual Stages.

Ānanda, within each and every class of such sentient beings, there are likewise each possessed of twelve inversions. It is like pressing upon the eyes, causing a chaotic profusion of flowers to appear; these inversions [obscure] the wondrous [nature].

Perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind is fully endowed with such [qualities]. As for these false and deluded thoughts (in one edition, the word "Ānanda" follows "deluded thoughts"), as you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, they are the very deluded thoughts that originally served as the cause.

Only by establishing three gradual stages can [the afflictions] be eliminated. It is like a vessel that has held poisonous honey: one must remove the poison, wash the vessel with various hot waters mixed with ash and incense, and only then store ambrosia within it.
What are these three gradual stages? First, through cultivation, one eliminates their auxiliary causes. Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out their primary nature.

Third, through advancement, one opposes their manifest karma. What are the auxiliary causes? Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves independently; they rely on the four kinds of nutriment for their existence.

These are the food of morsels (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), the food of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*), the food of volition (*manasikāra-āhāra*), and the food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Therefore, the Buddha said that all sentient beings subsist upon food.

Ānanda, all sentient beings live by consuming what is sweet (where "sweet" means non-toxic) and die by consuming what is poisonous. Those sentient beings who seek *samādhi* must sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world (scallions, garlic, leeks, and *hingukhāra*).

These five pungent substances, when eaten cooked, arouse lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger. In such a world, those who eat pungent things—even if they can proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures—the celestial beings and sages of the ten directions will loathe their foul stench.

They all remain far removed from them. As for the various hungry ghosts, because of that person's eating, they lick their lips and mouths; constantly dwelling with such a ghost, their merit and virtue daily diminish, and they find no long-term benefit.
When such a consumer of pungent roots practices *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and virtuous deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them.

A powerful Mara King will seize this opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to preach the Dharma to them, reviling the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance. At the end of their lives, they will naturally become members of the Mara King’s retinue; once their demonic blessings are exhausted, they will fall into the Avīci Hell.
[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, one who cultivates bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots. This is called the first stage of progressive cultivation. [Commentary]:
Because the principle of ultimate realization is difficult to ascend to suddenly, three kinds of gradual stages are established as skillful means for entering the position.

Since it was previously explained that sentient beings already know the characteristics of the perversions of karma and afflictions, these three gradual stages are established to subdue and eliminate them. Regarding the afflictions of lust and killing, this is the first gradual stage."

Since the fundamental root remains entirely intact, one merely eliminates the auxiliary causes. These "auxiliary causes" refer to the five kinds of pungent vegetables: when eaten cooked, they incite lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger.
Because desire is thin, greed and hatred are first subdued and eliminated. Furthermore, in Yoga, one maintains moderation in eating by observing the causes of food and the faults inherent in food.

This means that because one has not yet permanently subdued the signs of the grasped object and the grasping subject within the objective sphere, one seeks to dispel and eradicate them; thus, within the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*), one guards against and observes the spheres of activity.

"One does not grasp at their characteristics within [the middle way]. [Commentary: According to the *Ghanavyūha*, the ālayavijñāna possesses two kinds of characteristics: the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka). It is like a two-headed snake that moves toward its desired destination together.

However, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* identifies the six sense-objects (*viṣaya*) as the seeds of the grasped, the six sense-faculties (*indriya*) as the seeds of the grasper, and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) as the seeds of that grasping.

Thus, one knows that the "guarding of the sense-faculties" (*indriyasaṃvara*) in the *Yogācāra* tradition is precisely the subduing of the seed-nature within the ālayavijñāna; for the sense-faculties and sense-objects are themselves the ālayavijñāna.
Because it is the direct object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), the seed belongs to the object-part; because it serves as the direct condition for the eight consciousnesses.

What is the "correct nature" (*samyaktva*)? Ānanda, such sentient beings who enter *samādhi* must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever sever the mind of lust, abstain from wine and meat, consume food purified by fire, and never eat raw, living energy. Ānanda, if these practitioners do not sever lust and killing, there is no way they can transcend the three realms.

In this regard, one should contemplate sensual desire as being like a venomous snake or like encountering a hostile thief. First, by upholding the four parājikas and eight parājikas of the śrāvaka, one maintains physical stillness;

subsequently, by practicing the pure discipline of a bodhisattva, one maintains mental non-arising. When the prohibitive precepts are thus perfected, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing within the world, and acts of theft and robbery will not occur.

Free from the burden of karmic debt, one shall no longer have to repay past obligations within the world; such a person is pure. Cultivating samādhi, they need not rely on the divine eye, for they naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions with their physical bodies.
They behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy instructions. Attaining great supernormal powers, they travel through the worlds of the ten directions.
With their past lives purified, they encounter no hardships or perils. This is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.

[Commentary]: Pure precepts refer to the four *pārājika* offenses and so forth. Since [the practitioner] has already suppressed and prevented their arising through the gradual stages of the four afflictions such as lust, they are now permanently severed;

therefore, it is said that one has "excised their very nature. Lust and killing are the roots of transgression, yet because violations still arise within the conditions [of daily life], they must all be abandoned through the precepts.

Not consuming living breath is the ultimate form of compassion for the prevention of killing. The continuity of rebirth and mutual retribution all stem from lust, killing, theft, and falsehood; once these are purified, there is no need for the physical bodies of one's parents to rely on the heavens.
This is the power of the eye to sever delusions. The three types of gradual stages take precepts as their essence. Precepts belong to *śamatha*; as the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* states:

"By means of precepts, one conforms to the portion of *śamatha*, because precepts are the cause of samādhi. By means of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), one conforms to the portion of *vipaśyanā*, because it enables the attainment of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). This is what is meant.
"What is manifest karma? Ānanda, when a person thus purely maintains the prohibitive precepts, their mind is free from greedy lust and does not flow excessively toward the six external sense objects.

Because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to the source and return to themselves. Since the sense objects no longer serve as conditions, the faculties have nothing with which to pair. The flow is reversed and the six functions cease; the lands of the ten directions become brilliantly pure."

It is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli; body and mind are blissful, wondrous, perfect, and impartial, attaining great peace and stability. Within it, the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas are fully manifested.

This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). From this point, they gradually practice, establishing themselves in the stages of sagehood according to their initial resolve.
This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.

Third, by gradually building upon the merit of prior subduing and severing, the manifest outflows are forever stilled and one returns to the source; thus, the world becomes pure and as clear as lapis lazuli, whereby the substance of true emptiness is revealed.

The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "Pure *śamatha* is like a mirror reflecting all forms. Therefore, the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of all Tathāgatas are all manifested therein.

As for the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this refers to the stage of Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* states that it serves as the antidote to all...

Because the fruit is designated as "non-arising," the subsequent statement that the remaining substrate no longer continues to arise is precisely due to the power of this patience (*kṣānti*). [Commentary: According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, patience is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of wisdom;

thus, this statement regarding the attainment of "dharma-patience" is followed by the clarification of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), from which we know that the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the stage of dry wisdom.

Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Because it takes non-arising as its object, it is called 'knowledge of non-arising' (*anutpāda-jñāna*); because it takes knowledge as its object, it is called 'knowledge-knowledge' (*jñāna-jñāna*). Here, "knowledge-knowledge" is an *upapada-samāsa* (dependent compound). However—
Although wisdom (*jñāna*) is what realizes [the truth], it is the function of patience (*kṣānti*) that is able to sever the afflictions; therefore, in all stages, wisdom is preceded by patience.

Ānanda, when this son of good family’s craving for existence has dried up, and the faculties and their objects no longer meet, his remaining physical form before him will not continue to be reborn. His grasping mind becomes empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, polishing the ten directions. Possessing this wisdom alone, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).
Through these three gradual stages, the craving of desire dries up; since desire is the root of continued rebirth, once it is permanently severed, one does not continue to be born.

Because the sense organs and their objects do not encounter one another, the grasping mind becomes empty and luminous, and thus consists purely of wisdom. When the realm of desire flickers, wisdom is perfected; when desire dries up, insight arises.

Because it relies on wisdom for its sustenance, it is called "earth. In the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm, compassion and wisdom flow as a dual stream; because this state possesses only wisdom, it has not yet interfaced with [compassion]. [Commentary: According to the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), this corresponds to the stage of Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*).

Having completed the cultivation of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one next gives rise to "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*); this is the same as the present text. However, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that one enters the "stream of Dharma" (*dharma-srotas*) at the seventh stage, which differs from this text.

This discrepancy arises because their methods of teaching and contemplation differ. That which is called "dry wisdom" refers to contemplating the true reality (*tattva*) alone, whereas "entering the stream of Dharma" refers to the simultaneous application of both tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Thus, while this sutra speaks of entering the stream at the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks of entering it at the seventh stage—is this not indeed a difference in their respective teachings and contemplations? Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "The seventh..."
Because it is for this reason that a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage, within a single thought-moment, practices both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in tandem and enters the flow of the Dharma;

yet, while the habits of desire are beginning to dry up, they have not yet connected with the flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. By means of this very mind, one flows into the center of the center, where it blossoms perfectly and wondrously. From the truly wondrous perfection, the truly wondrous is manifested again.

Wondrous faith is eternally abiding, and all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder. This state of pure truth on the Middle Way is called the Abode of Faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*). When true faith is clear and lucid, all...

The three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements cannot obstruct this perfect penetration. Thus, even throughout countless eons of the past and future, as he discards one body and receives another, all habitual tendencies manifest before him.

This son of good family is able to recollect them all without any loss; this is called the dwelling of the mind in mindfulness. It is wondrous, perfect, and purely true; from this true essence, transformation and manifestation arise.

The habitual tendencies from beginningless time pervade a single brilliant lucidity. To advance toward true purity solely through this brilliant lucidity is called the "mind of diligence. When the essence of the mind manifests before one, consisting purely of wisdom, it is called the "abiding of the mind in wisdom";
