it maintains and upholds the clarity of knowledge, which is all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound, with wondrous stillness constantly coalescing—this is called the "abiding of the mind in concentration. As the light of concentration illuminates and the nature of clarity penetrates deeply, advancing only without retreating, it is called the "non-retrogressive mind.

When the mind advances with serenity, maintaining this state without loss, the vital energies of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interpenetrate and support one another—this is called the "mind that protects the Dharma. Through the preservation of awakened clarity...

He is able, through his wondrous power, to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha as he dwells in peace. It is like two mirrors facing each other; their radiant light reflects one another, so that within them, wondrous images are layered and mutually interpenetrated.

It is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). Through the secret dedication of the light of the mind, one attains the Buddha’s eternal constancy, supreme wondrous purity, and abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), thereby achieving non-forgetfulness; this is called the dwelling of the mind in ethical discipline (*śīla-citta-vihāra*).

Abiding in the sovereignty of ethical discipline, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions, proceeding wherever one’s vows lead; this is called the dwelling of the mind in aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

First, the abiding of the mind in faith: entering the stream for the first time while contemplating both the ultimate and conventional truths is called the "wondrously perfect unfolding of the initial entry into the stream.

Repeatedly giving rise to the true wondrousness and deeply entering the stream is the second stage. This "double unfolding of the wondrous" constitutes the middle [stage]. This means that whereas previously one was parched by desire and craving and possessed only wisdom, now, having entered the flow of the Dharma, one turns wisdom toward compassion;

thus, Bodhi grows, which is why it is called the "wondrously perfect unfolding. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "The samādhi like an illusion is like a sprout gradually growing. This is the perfection.

The wondrous mind enters the stream and abides therein; this is called the constant abiding of wondrous faith. Because the Bodhisattva has already dried up the flow of desire and attained the nature of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), his mind easily abides.

Thus, the second is the mind that abides in mindfulness, which is able to recollect habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); these three—aggregates, bases, and elements—are the worldly places of birth and their habitual tendencies.

Third is the mind of vigor: although one previously recollected the habitual tendencies, they had not yet been integrated; now that this [mind] is refined and bright, one is able to initiate transformation. Fourth is the mind that abides in wisdom. [Wenling]: Since delusive habits have been exhausted, the mind is refined.

The present progression toward what is called "Pure Wisdom Without Practice" is termed the "Abiding Mind of Wisdom. [Commentary: Fifth, regarding the Abiding Mind of Samādhi: if there is wisdom without samādhi, then the attained virtue will not coalesce;

therefore, one next uses samādhi to consolidate wisdom, which is the characteristic of pervasive, tranquil, and perfect concentration. Sixth, the Non-regressing Mind: because samādhi has long produced radiance and its profound stillness reaches a state of movement, it is able to advance.

Seventh, the Protecting Dharma Mind: because long-term advancement involves movement that risks losing composure, one maintains this without loss by means of protecting the Dharma. Eighth, the Dedication Mind: since...

Because one’s own spiritual essence (*dhātu*) intersects with that of the Tathāgata, one is able to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light toward oneself, and likewise turn one’s own body and mind toward the Buddha.

By thus mutually redirecting one’s own body and the Buddha’s body, they become like two mirrors facing each other. When the ninth stage, the dwelling of the mind of precepts (*śīla-citta-vihāra*), is attained, one can turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back upon himself; therefore, he receives protection from the Buddha and remains eternally concentrated.

"Concentration" (*niṅ*) refers to the wondrously pure and unconditioned essence (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). Abiding therein without contradiction is called the "mind of precepts. In the tenth stage, the dwelling of the mind of vows (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*), one dwells in the sovereignty of the precepts, such that the precepts no longer act as a constraint.
Therefore, they are able to travel through the ten directions, unhindered wherever they go.

Ānanda, these good sons, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds. The essence of their minds radiates brilliance; the ten functions interpenetrate one another, perfectly forming a single mind.

This is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Within this mind, illumination occurs like pure lapis lazuli, within which pure gold appears. Taking that former wondrous mind as the path, they tread upon it to form the ground. This is called the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman-vihāra*). The mind-ground extends its cognitive reach.

Attaining clarity in all things, they travel through the ten directions without obstruction; this is called the Dwelling of Cultivation. Their practice becomes identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual influence, like an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) seeking parents;

their subtle faith communicates with the unseen as they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata; this is called the Dwelling of Noble Birth. Having entered the womb of the Way, they personally serve the heirs of Enlightenment; like a fetus already formed, their human characteristics are complete; this is called the Dwelling of Fulfillment of Skillful Means.

Their appearance resembles that of a Buddha, and their mental characteristics are likewise the same; this is called the Dwelling of the Right Mind. Body and mind become unified, and they grow daily; this is called...

The stage of non-retrogression is the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi), wherein the ten bodies and spiritual marks are simultaneously perfected, like a child emerging from the womb. The stage of the Dharma Prince (Dharmarājaputra) signifies becoming a full adult;

just as a great king of a nation delegates all state affairs to his crown prince, so too does that Kṣatriya king, once his eldest son has reached maturity, perform the ceremonial consecration, which is called the stage of Consecration (Abhiṣekabhūmi).

1. The Dwelling of the Initial Resolve (*Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*): This refers to the aforementioned ten kinds of wondrous minds attaining perfection and abiding as one; thus it is named the Dwelling of the Initial Resolve. 2. The Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*Caryāpratipatti-vihāra*):

By traversing the principle of the aforementioned wondrous minds and thereby establishing the ground, one abides therein; thus it is named the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground. "Traversing" (*li*) has the meaning of "cultivating" (*zhi*), while "ground" (*di*) refers to the true gold manifested within the wondrous mind, signifying that it is clearly revealed and visible.

3. The Dwelling of Practice (*Caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*): Abiding the mind within the object is termed "traversing" (*li*) to establish the ground; abiding the object within the mind is termed "mind-ground" (*xin-di*). These two involve mutual penetration.

Because one knows that the mind and its objects cannot be displaced, one attains clarity and is able to travel throughout the ten directions; this is called the practice of the "Noble Abode of Birth" (*janma-ārya-vihāra*). [Wenling] states:

When the wondrous mind enters into secret resonance, the wondrous principle responds in profound stillness, and one is about to be born into the Buddha-family as a Dharma Prince; this is named the "Abode of Noble Birth. The metaphor of the "shadows" (*skandhas*) illustrates the principle of profound resonance. This is the "Abode of Fulfillment of the Five Expedient Means."

[Gushan] "This [stage], while still within the causal phase, possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others identical to those of a Buddha without deficiency; thus it resembles the embryo of the Path and is named the 'Abiding in the Fulfillment of Expedient Means' (upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra).

The sixth is the 'Abiding in the Right Mind' (samyak-citta-vihāra). [Shu] Since their outward appearance is already identical, their minds also correspond accordingly; hence it is called 'Right Mind. The seventh is the 'Abiding in Non-retrogression' (avaivartika-vihāra). Because internal and external are unified and one is able to increase [virtue], it is called 'Non-retrogression.

The eighth is the 'Abiding of the Youthful Truth' (kumāra-bhūta-vihāra). [Wenling] It is called 'youthful' because it embodies the form yet remains minute [in its development]. The ninth is the 'Abiding of the Dharma Prince' (dharma-rāja-putra-vihāra). [Shu] From the time of first generating the aspiration..."

Reaching the stage of "Birth in Nobility" is called entering the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*); from there, through the stage of "Perfected Youth," it is called the nurturing of the noble embryo; reaching this point, the work of nurturing is completed, and emerging from the womb, one becomes a Dharma Prince.
The tenth stage, "Abiding in Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), signifies the achievement of the perfection of the noble path; therefore, it is metaphorically termed "consecration."

Ānanda, when these sons of good family have become children of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas; this is called the Practice of Joyful Compliance. They are skillfully able to benefit all sentient beings; this is called the Practice of Beneficiality.
Having awakened themselves and awakening others, they attain freedom from opposition and resistance; this is called the Practice of Freedom from Anger and Resentment.

Their manifestations arise in succession, reaching to the end of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions; this is called the Practice of Exhaustlessness. All things are unified within their various dharma-gates, attaining freedom from error; this is called the Practice of Freedom from Delusion and Confusion.

As they practice, within the midst of sameness, a multitude of differences manifests; yet within each distinct characteristic, one perceives sameness. This is called the "skillful manifestation of practice. Thus it continues, even throughout the emptiness of the ten directions.

Fulfilling as many atoms as there are, within each and every atom, one manifests the realms of the ten directions; these manifestations of atoms and realms do not obstruct or hinder one another—this is called the Practice of Non-attachment.

These various manifestations appearing before one are all the foremost *pāramitā*—this is called the Practice of Reverence. Such perfect interfusion can accomplish the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions—this is called the Practice of Wholesome Dharmas.
Each and every one of these is pure and without outflows, the single true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because their nature is inherently so—this is called the Practice of Reality.

The practitioner abides in these and advances by taking the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) as their essence: 1. The Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*) is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); because one accords with the ten directions and acts in accordance with one's own practice, it is called "joy.

2. The Practice of Benefiting Others (*artha-caryā*) is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); because ethical discipline is free from affliction and harm, it is able to benefit others. 3. The Practice of Freedom from Resentment (*an-āghāta-caryā*)—the *Avataṃsaka* names this "freedom from opposition" (*a-virodha*)—is so called because, being without opposition, there is no resentment.

4. The Practice of Exhaustlessness (*akṣaya-caryā*) is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); the *Avataṃsaka* names this "freedom from cowering or yielding. "Freedom from cowering or yielding" is the meaning of diligence.

The birth of all classes of ordinary and holy beings is inexhaustible; this meaning has two aspects, namely the horizontal and the vertical dimensions. That is to say, the three periods of time are equal, and the ten directions are inexhaustible.

Fifth, the practice free from delusion and confusion is the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*); because dhyāna can arrest distraction, one is free from delusion and confusion. Through the absence of delusion and confusion, various dharma-gates are attained without error.

Sixth, the practice of skillful manifestation is the perfection of prajñā (*prajñāpāramitā*). Principle can manifest phenomena, such that within the same name, difference appears; phenomena can manifest principle, such that within different characteristics, sameness appears. This is accomplished through the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).

Therefore, the seven practices of non-attachment, in which principle and phenomena are perfectly manifested, are the practice of skillful means (*upāya*), for skillful means takes provisional expediency as its objective; the manifestation of the realms within the dust of sensory objects is what is revealed by expedient wisdom.

Eighth is the practice of reverence, which is the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*); in the *Avataṃsaka*, this is called the "difficult-to-attain practice," for there is nothing more difficult to attain than reverence. Ninth is the practice of wholesome dharmas, which is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), because the rules of circular integration are themselves wholesome dharmas.
Tenth is the practice of reality, which is the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*), because that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is all truly real wisdom.

Ānanda, when these good sons have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of Buddhahood, they will be pure, clean, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions. They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing all marks of deliverance; turning their minds toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they proceed upon the path to *nirvāṇa*.

This is called the "Dedication to Protecting and Saving All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Mark of Sentient Beings. Destroying that which can be destroyed, yet remaining far removed from all forms of detachment, it is called the "Indestructible Dedication.

Their fundamental awakening is serene and still, its realization equal to the awakening of the Buddhas; this is called the "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas. Through the brilliant manifestation of essential purity, their ground becomes like the ground of the Buddhas.
It is called the dedication reaching all places. When the worlds and Tathāgatas mutually interpenetrate without obstruction, it is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

Within the same Buddha-ground, pure causes arise within each stage; by relying on these causes, one manifests and takes up the path to Nirvāṇa—this is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accord with equality.

Once the true root is established, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature; as this nature is perfectly fulfilled, one does not abandon sentient beings—this is called the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.

That all phenomena are free from all marks; that in both "being thus" and "being free," there is no attachment to either—this is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Truly attaining what is such, being unimpeded throughout the ten directions, is called the dedication of liberation without bondage.
When the virtues of one's nature are perfectly accomplished and the measure of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is extinguished, it is called the dedication of the immeasurable dharma-realm.

[Wenling says: In the previous ten abodes and ten practices, the mind for transcending the mundane was great while the practice of great compassion was inferior. Therefore, by means of these vows, one rescues compassion and dwells within the mundane to benefit living beings;

one turns toward the mundane from the ultimate, and turns toward compassion from wisdom, so that the ultimate and the mundane are perfectly integrated and compassion and wisdom are non-dual. This is called the Ten Dedications, and they are also called the Ten Vows. [Commentary:

Because the sublime practices of the preceding stages were fulfilled, and because spiritual powers were pure, refined, and authentic, the spirit reached far beyond all obstructions. Thus, "spiritual penetration" (shentong) generally refers to the fact that the ten abodes consist mostly of self-cultivation that transcends the mundane.

The essence of the ten practices consists largely of entering the mundane world to benefit others as their function. Now, within the contemplation of the Middle Way, the true and the conventional revolve around one another, and principle and phenomena face each other;

therefore, it is called the "First Dedication. Because the meaning of dedication lies in the identity of appearance and the transcendence of appearance: by virtue of this identity, one should deliver sentient beings; by virtue of this transcendence, one eliminates the very notion of "delivering.

Second is the "Dedication of Non-Destruction," which takes *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra* as its meaning of dedication. That which can be destroyed is the realm of *saṃsāra*; that which transcends destruction is the mind of *nirvāṇa*. Because of this destruction... [the text continues].

Because it is devoid [of self], one does not abide in saṃsāra; because one is free from all forms of detachment, one does not abide in nirvāṇa. The *Abhidharmakośa* defines nirvāṇa as "detachment" (virāga).

The dedication of all Buddhas refers to the meaning of both original and initial awakening (*mūla-bodhi* and *ādi-bodhi*), which is the profound stillness of original awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*). One who is equal to the Buddha’s awakening is thus at the stage of Equal Awakening (*samyak-sambodhi*).

Regarding the fourth point, "reaching all places": this refers to the meaning of dedication as the pervasive nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). True essence is True Suchness, and the ground is that which is pervaded. Since there is no place where the Buddha-ground is not pervasive, True Suchness is pervasive everywhere.

Regarding the fifth, the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit": 1. The dedication based on the mutual interpenetration of the "supported" (the environment) and the "supporter" (the beings)—dedicating toward the Tathāgata—is called "correct," as the world is the support;

because these two aspects interpenetrate, one attains non-obstruction. 2. The dedication that accords with equality through the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)—dedicating toward the single Buddha-ground—is "one," while the various arising of pure causes is "many.

Because these two aspects interpenetrate, one attains equality. Furthermore, "equality" refers to the root of goodness of pure *nirvāṇa*, while "roots of goodness" refer to the causes for all births. 7. Equanimously contemplating all sentient beings...

Because the dedication for oneself and others arises based on causes, it is called the "True Root. All are my own fundamental nature; I dedicate sentient beings as myself. Without losing sight of sentient beings, I dissolve myself to become identical with others.
(8) The dedication to the characteristics of True Suchness: because True Suchness follows conditions, it is all phenomena; because it follows conditions without changing, it is free from all marks.

This is the meaning of dedication as the unity of nature and characteristics. (9) The dedication of neither bondage nor liberation: because True Suchness is like its objects, and the objects are likewise like True Suchness, there is no obstruction throughout the ten directions.

Throughout the ten directions, there is nothing that is not unimpeded, for it is suchness (*tathatā*); because it is true suchness, it is neither bound, as there is no object to be bound, nor is it liberated. This very state of being both subject and object of bondage and liberation constitutes the meaning of dedication.

The immeasurable nature-virtue of dedication throughout the ten dharma-realms is perfectly fulfilled, thereby concluding and synthesizing the preceding meanings. When the measure of the dharma-realm is extinguished, traces are swept away and marks are obliterated, clarifying the severance of conceptual understanding.

Ānanda, these sons of good family have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds. Next, they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*). They take the Buddha’s awakening as their own mind (this taking of the Buddha’s wisdom as the causal mind).

Whether [the fire] has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling for fire; desiring to ignite the wood, this is called the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*). Furthermore, they take their own mind to become what the Buddha treads upon (this making the causal mind identical to the Buddha’s realm). Whether [they] rely [on it] or do not rely [on it],...

It is like ascending a high mountain: when the body enters the void yet there remains a subtle obstruction below, it is called the Ground of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). When the mind and the Buddha are identical, skillfully attaining the Middle Way, it is like a person enduring an ordeal—neither harboring resentment nor venting it—and is called the Ground of Patience (*kṣānti*).
When numerical conceptions are extinguished and both delusion and awakening are the Middle Way, such that neither has a referent, it is called the World-Highest Ground (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Because one is about to enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one gives rise to the preparatory application (*prayoga*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The preparatory application of the first stage (*bhūmi*) refers to that which precedes the Path of Seeing.

Regarding the explanation of "preparatory application" (*prayoga*), there are briefly three meanings: (1) essence (*svabhāva*), (2) nature (*dharmatā*), and (3) differentiation (*prabheda*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Preparatory application has 'investigation' (*vitarka*) as its essence and 'sealing and maintaining' (*avasthāpana*) as its nature;

based on the four investigations, there are four applications. Regarding the first [application], the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*): the explanation of its name has three aspects. First, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on the Samādhi of Attaining Radiance (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*), it is named 'Heat. It is so called because one first acquires the precursor aspect of the sun of wisdom."

Therefore, this "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is explained in terms of wisdom; the *Abhidharmakośa* states that it is called "heat" because it can burn the fuel of afflictions, acting as the precursor to the fire of the Four Noble Paths.
This "Heat" is also explained in terms of abandonment; the *Vibhāṣā* states that the movement of wisdom toward its object is called "heat.

Since this "Heat" is spoken of by combining the correspondence between the object and wisdom, the phrase "taking the Buddha’s awakening-function as one's own mind" refers to the fact that, from the perspective of analytical observation, the duality of subject and object has not yet been extinguished through realization.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "If one places even a small object before oneself, one is not abiding in *vijñaptimātra*, because there is still the mind observing with mental images (*sanimitta-darśana-citta*). Regarding this, the stage of the Peak (*mūrdhan*) has two aspects of *vijñaptimātra*:

first, in terms of preparatory application (*prayoga*), and second, in terms of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "The culmination of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) gives rise to the highest grade of superior roots of goodness;

this is called the Peak. In the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are also two aspects: first, in terms of being most excellent (*agra*), and second, in terms of being subject to regression (*parihāṇi*). The *Abhidharmakośa* says: "Among the fluctuating roots of goodness (*cala-kuśalamūla*), this dharma is the most excellent; or, it is so called because from this point one progresses."

"Retreating from both extremes is like standing on a mountain peak. To say that one's own mind is what the Buddha treads upon means that observing the mind is itself the objective realm (*ālambana*), because the dependent follows the basis upon which it relies;

this is metaphorically likened to ascending a height and entering the void. Regarding the "Dharma of Patience" (*kṣānti-dharma*), the *Abhidharmakośa* provides two meanings: first, patience toward the principle is called "patience"; second, being free from falling back is called "patience. The *Kośa* states:

"Because it is the ultimate ability to endure the principles of the Four Truths, and because there is no falling back. Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are two meanings: first, sealing and conforming is "patience"; second, firm maintenance is "patience."

Regarding the stage of *kṣānti* (patience), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it is established as the stage of patience because one definitively seals and maintains [the truth] by relying on the meditative concentration of sealing (*mudrā-samādhi*). Previously, the mind and the object were mutually exclusive, each remaining on its own side;

now, because the mind and the Buddha are identical, one attains the Middle Way. Although the function has been actualized, there is still something to be attained; therefore, it is neither "retaining" nor "emerging," similar to a person who endures a situation.

The Venerable Dharmatrāta says that the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has volition (*cetanā*) as its nature, and all minds and mental factors are specific manifestations of volition. However, the explanations in the sūtras and śāstras regarding the Supreme Worldly Dharma are brief.

There are six kinds, namely: first, separation; second, conjunction; third, identity; fourth, difference; fifth, the middle; and sixth, the extremes. One should now briefly recognize these six types of discourse regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). First, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This dharma is mundane because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*);

it is called 'supreme' because it is the most excellent. Thus, being the most excellent among the contaminated, it is named the 'Supreme Mundane'. This refers to its separation from the contaminated and its status as the most supreme. Second, a sutra states:

"When quantity and measure are extinguished, and both delusion and awakening are absent within the Middle Way, this is named the 'Ground of the Supreme Mundane' (*laukikāgradharabhūmi*). This refers to the two [extremes] having no objective referent.

1. This refers to the synthesis of the two dharmas of delusion and awakening, which is named "the Supreme Worldly" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). As for its numerical definition, it consists of delusion and awakening; because it is "supreme," it cannot be called delusion, and because it belongs to the "world," it cannot be called awakening.

Thus, these two are not what is being designated. 2. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Among the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this dharma is the most excellent, and is thus named 'Supreme Worldly.

This means that within the state of an ordinary being, that which manifests as the most excellent is named "Supreme Worldly. 3. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Based on the immediate concentration (*anantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the seal of wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna-mudrā*)."

Second, regarding the emptiness of the two apprehensions (*dvaya-grāha-śūnyatā*), it is called "the world" (*loka*) because the wisdom of the distinct patience (*viśeṣa-kṣānti*) is named "the supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

Fifth, Dharmatrāta says that the supreme mundane dharma resides between the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), being without partiality toward either; thus, as it manifests the middle between the two paths of the ordinary and the noble, it is named "the supreme mundane dharma.

Sixth, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the supreme mundane dharma marks the beginning of the noble path and the end of the state of an ordinary being; thus, as it signifies both the beginning and the end of these two extremes, it is named "the supreme mundane dharma. Thus it has been said.
The four aforementioned stages of application are all termed "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). As the Sūtra says:

"If one accomplishes roots of goodness such as 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they are called 'pseudo-saints' (*ārya-pratirūpaka*). Ānanda, these sons of good family attain excellent penetration regarding Great Bodhi; their awakening penetrates the realm of the Tathāgatas and the entirety of the Buddha's domain—this is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

When distinct natures enter into sameness and that same nature is also extinguished, it is called the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*). When purity reaches its limit and luminosity arises, it is called the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*). When luminosity reaches its limit and awakening becomes full, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). Regarding all things, whether identical or different...

That which cannot be reached is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Unconditioned True Suchness (*asaṃskṛta-tathatā*), its nature pure and luminously manifest, is called the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Reaching the limit of True Suchness is called the Ground of Far-Going (*Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*). The single mind of True Suchness is called the Ground of Immovability (*Acalā-bhūmi*). The activation of the function of True Suchness is called the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Ānanda, from this point onward, these Bodhisattvas have completed their cultivation and practice.

The perfection of merit is also designated as this stage; it is called the Stage of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*). When the wondrous clouds of the shade of loving-kindness cover the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, it is called the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Buddha-dharma is boundless and that the first stage is its foundation. The "stages" (*bhūmi*) herein comprise six names in total: first, the stage; second, the Joyful; third, the Penetrating; fourth, the Path of Seeing; fifth, the Clear Realization;
and sixth, the Departure from Birth. Why is it called a "stage"? The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "It is so named because it comprehensively gathers all merits to serve as a supreme support."

It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it causes [virtuous qualities] to grow and flourish. Why is it called "joy"? Because upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness);

having attained mastery over many hundreds of gates, one knows for oneself that great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) will soon be realized, and thus gives rise to joy. Why is it called "penetration of consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātratā-prativedha*)?

Because when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) takes *tathatā* as its object, the arising of this wisdom is termed "penetration. Why is it called the "path of seeing"? Because it is the first illumination of the true principle. Why is it called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*)? Because from—

Because this has already been named "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), why is it said that one is "separated from birth"? The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Once the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has arisen, the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is crushed so that they no longer increase.

Second, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*): having already abandoned the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is called "entering the same as others. Since there is no commonality with those who possess common characteristics, even that "common characteristic" is extinguished.

Consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) holds that because the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being is severed in the first ground, one attains communion with the awakening of the Tathāgata. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* considers this ground to be the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), which remedies subtle transgressions of the precepts.

The third is the Ground of Luminous Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*): because it is free from defilement as previously mentioned, the light of this ground arises; through the realization of *vijñapti-mātra*, the obstacles of dullness and ignorance are severed, and a pure, extreme luminosity arises, whereby one achieves supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and great dhāraṇīs, capable of emitting the infinite light of wondrous wisdom.

As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states, this is due to the "superior training in concentration" (*adhipati-samādhi-śikṣā*). The fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*): because the light produced in the preceding ground has now reached full awakening, the flames of wisdom surge forth.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that on this ground, one dwells in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and thus the flames of wisdom increase. The fifth is the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

The Ground of the Nature of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātratā-bhūmi*) is so called because, by means of this ground, the ignorance regarding birth and death is severed; it unites the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional, causing them to correspond, and because it is difficult to surpass as it transcends the phenomena of the ultimate and conventional that are either identical or different.

The Sixth Ground, the Ground of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), is so called because once identity and difference have been distanced, the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is clearly revealed and manifests before one. Consciousness-only is so named because in this dwelling, the wisdom of dependent origination and non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) manifest before one.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the three upper grounds are designated as the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). The Seventh Ground, the Ground of Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), is so called because the wondrous nature of *tathatā* has reached far.

Because it reaches the limit of the infinite, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains that this stage is called "Distant" (*dūra*) because it dwells at the final limit of effortlessness and transcends the paths of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The commentary states that this is because the first six stages are those realized in common by the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Both the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* agree with this explanation. From the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Radiant Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), one gradually distances oneself from defilements;

from the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*) up to the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), one gradually manifests [purity]. Thus, this stage is purely and solely True Suchness (*tathatā*), and is therefore named the Immovable Stage. The nature of True Suchness is fundamentally...
Because it is subject to movement, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that by attaining the spontaneous continuity of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one achieves immovability.

Because the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), gives rise to and proclaims excellent wisdom based upon suchness (*tathatā*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* notes that this stage accomplishes the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and excels in preaching the Dharma; thus, this stage is also designated as "one who has completed the task.

On the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*), both knowledge and practice are already perfected and are characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Regarding the tenth stage, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "It covers all [realms] and fills the body of reality (*dharmakāya*). Thus, the merit of the ten stages is complete.
The categories of virtue and meaning are boundless; now, to further clarify them, there are briefly ten kinds of distinctions:

namely, the cultivation of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) for the sake of attaining the ten kinds of bodies, for the sake of counteracting the ten kinds of hindrances, for the sake of realizing the ten kinds of *dharmadhātu*, for the sake of obtaining the ten kinds of *tathatā*, for the sake of cultivating the various *dharmamukha*, for the sake of the distinct meanings of the various stages, for the sake of the mutual counteraction of opposites, for the sake of the naming of the various stages, for the sake of realizing the titles of the four fruits, and for the sake of the gateway to the names of realization through the cultivation common to the three vehicles. First, the attainment of the ten kinds of bodies.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: In the first bhūmi, one attains the body of equality because one penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and perceives equality;

in the second bhūmi, one attains the pure body because of the purity of precepts; in the third bhūmi, one attains the inexhaustible body because of being free from anger; in the fourth bhūmi, one attains the well-cultivated body because one constantly exerts effort in practicing and cultivating the Buddha-dharma;

in the fifth bhūmi, one attains the dharma-body because one perceives the principles of all truths (*satya*); in the sixth bhūmi, one attains the body free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), because the principle of dependent origination is not known through applied and sustained thought; in the seventh bhūmi...

Because they attain the inconceivable body and are fully endowed with skillful means, in the eighth stage they attain the body of tranquility, being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and devoid of afflictions.

In the ninth stage, they attain the body equal to space, because its physical characteristics are immeasurable and pervade all places. In the tenth stage, they attain the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*), because they have accomplished the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Regarding the second point, the antidotes for the ten obstacles, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The ten stages are taught because they serve as antidotes to the ten obstacles: first, the obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of self (*ātman*); second, the obstacle of wrong conduct; third..."

The ten obstacles to hearing, reflecting, and meditating are: first, the obstacle of the four dharmas; second, the obstacle of pride; third, the obstacle of the conceit of "I"; fourth, the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of subtle afflictions; fifth, the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of subtle marks; sixth, the obstacle of having marks despite being without activity;

seventh, the obstacle of being unable to skillfully benefit sentient beings; eighth, the obstacle of not attaining mastery over all dharmas. Regarding the realization of the ten kinds of dharma-spheres (*dharmadhātu*), the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:

"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the all-pervading dharma-sphere, because one attains the dharma-nature of equality between self and others; in the second stage, one realizes the most excellent dharma-sphere."

Because they are able to cultivate practices identical to those of renunciation, on the third stage they realize the *dharmadhātu* of the superior outflow; knowing that the teachings they have heard are the most excellent outflow, they would enter a great pit of fire for the sake of seeking this Dharma without regarding even a trichiliocosm as difficult.
Because they realize the *dharmadhātu* of non-appropriation on the fourth stage, such that even their attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is entirely transformed.

Because they realize the *dharmadhātu* of non-differentiation in continuity on the fifth stage, they attain the pure mind of equality through the ten types of resolute intention (*āśaya*). On the sixth stage, they realize the *dharmadhātu* that is neither defiled nor purified.
Because one knows that the phenomena of dependent origination within the *dharmadhātu* are neither defiled nor pure, on the seventh stage one realizes the various non-differentiated *dharmadhātus*.

Because one knows that phenomena are signless (*animitta*) and do not proceed toward the various characteristics of the Dharma such as the *sūtras*, on the eighth stage one realizes the *dharmadhātu* of neither increase nor decrease. One perfectly attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), for among defiled and pure phenomena, one does not perceive even a single phenomenon as increasing or decreasing.
For this reason, it is said there are four kinds of mastery: first, mastery over non-conceptuality; second, mastery over the pure land; third... [the text continues].

Regarding mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) and mastery over karma (*karma-vaśitā*): the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) can only penetrate the former two; the ninth stage penetrates mastery over wisdom because one attains the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);

and the tenth stage further penetrates the basis of mastery over karma, as it can manifest transformations at will to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings. Regarding the realization of the ten kinds of suchness (*tathatā*), this is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the cultivation of various dharma-gates, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In the second stage, one contemplates afflictions; in the third stage, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

Contemplating impermanence is practiced on the four stages; the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) on the four [stages]; the noble truths (*āryasatya*) on the fifth stage; contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) on the sixth stage;

cultivating both tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) together on the seventh stage; and the perfection of tranquility and insight on the eighth stage. Regarding the distinctions in cultivation and realization across these stages, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "On the first stage, one attains the pervasive true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and courses in the Mahāyāna Dharma. On the second stage, one cultivates the threefold aggregate of ethical discipline (*tri-śīla-skandha*).

On the third stage, one attains superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and gives rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), benefiting and bringing happiness to others with equanimity. On the fourth stage, one realizes the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and is free from..."

On the various levels of discernment, the fifth stage abandons the delusions of views through non-discriminative observation; by contemplating the Four Noble Truths as the nature of equality, one subdues the enmity of Māra.

On the sixth stage, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination and remains far removed from the discriminative thoughts and attachments of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. On the seventh stage, one realizes the principle of signlessness and is sustained by the joy and bliss of the vast flavor of the Dharma.
On the eighth stage, all afflictions no longer manifest, and one transcends the five fears. On the ninth stage, one enters with certainty and is termed "non-retrogressive."
On the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the Great Dharma-body and raises clouds of great compassion to rain down the great Dharma-rain, thereby eliminating the suffering of sentient beings.

Regarding the various characteristics of the stages and the antidotes practiced therein, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: The first stage involves attaining several hundred concentrations and seeing several hundred Buddhas; these are its resultant characteristics.

Abandoning all evil and refraining from negligence are the characteristics of the second stage. Because one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and contemplates the sevenfold right path on the second stage, one remains free from deviant conduct, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—namely, the ten unwholesome actions.

Regarding practice, the ten inexhaustible phrases of the first stage (*bhūmi*) constitute the cultivation of ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*) within the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), and so forth. Eighth, as for the explanation of the names of the stages, the *Mahāyāna-praveśa-śāstra* states:
"The first stage is called the Joyful Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) because one transcends the state of ordinary beings and attains the inconceivable supramundane path, thereby giving rise to joy.

The second stage is called the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*) because one is free from the defilement of breaking the precepts. The third stage is called the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) because one relies on the twelve gates of dhyāna to attain luminous wisdom. The fourth stage..."

The fifth stage is called the *Arciṣmatī* (Flaming) because one attains superior awakening and discerns the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa*), thereby burning the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*). The sixth stage is called the *Sudurjayā* (Difficult to Conquer) because, although one cultivates the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) and subdues the afflictions, one has not yet fully mastered them.

The seventh stage is called the *Abhimukhī* (Manifest) because one is able to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) both in direct and reverse order, causing the Dharma to manifest before one.

The eighth stage is called the *Dūraṃgamā* (Far-Reaching) because, while loving the Buddha’s virtues, one successively ceases to hear other [mundane] thoughts and enters deeply into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). It is also difficult to overcome because it is firm and free from the marks of form and so forth.

The movement is named the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*); because one enters the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), understands all sounds, and is able to engage in question and answer, it is named the Good Wisdom Ground (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
On the tenth ground, because one is able to receive all Buddha-dharma like a great cloud that can pour down the rain of Dharma, it is named the Dharma Cloud Ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the names of the nine proofs of the four fruits, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* states: "Bodhisattvas have four fruits: first, at the time of entering the first ground, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata, which is the fruit of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); second, within the eighth ground..."

1. Receiving the prediction of attaining the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* occurs within the tenth stage (*bhūmi*). 2. Receiving the appointment [to the rank of Buddha] within the tenth stage is the fruit of *anāgāmin*. 3. The stage of Buddhahood is the fruit of *arhat*.
Regarding the "Gates of Names for the Cultivation and Realization of the Three Vehicles in the Ten Assemblies," the *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-mūla-karma-sūtra* states:

In the Sanskrit language, *kumārabhūta*; in the language of Qin (Chinese), it means "逆流" (*niúlìu*, flowing against the current). *Sukhāvatī-bhūmi*—in the language of Qin, it means "逆流離垢地" (*niúlìu lígòu dì*, the Ground of Flowing Against the Current and Freedom from Defilement). *Sudṛśā-bhūmi*—in the language of Qin, it means "逆流" (*niúlìu*, flowing against the current).

*Prabhākari-bhūmi* (Ground of Illumination), *Srotāpanna* (in the language of Qin: "One who Enters the Stream"); *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi* (Ground of Blazing Radiance), *Sakṛdāgāmin* (in the language of Qin: "One who Returns Once"); *Sudurjayā-bhūmi* (Ground Difficult to Conquer), *Anāgāmin* (in the language of Qin:

"One who Does Not Return"); *Abhimukhī-bhūmi* (Ground of Manifestation), *Arhat* (in the language of Qin: "One who has Transcended the Three Existences"); *Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi* (Ground of Far-reaching Progress), *Anarhat* (in the language of Qin: "One of Transformational Birth");

*Acalā-bhūmi* (Ground of the Immovable), *Arhanta* (in the language of Qin: "One of Wisdom-Light"); *Sādhumatī-bhūmi* (Ground of Excellent Wisdom), *Dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Ground of the Dharma-Cloud), *Mahāikaṣa* (in the language of Qin: "Great Harmony").

The *Animitta-vimalā-bhūmi* (Stage of the Stainless, Signless) is the stage of the *Bhagavān Buddha*, which in the language of Qin means "Sublime Enlightenment. It is the unsurpassed stage of the Son of the Buddha; therefore, it is called a "Gate of Names" (*nāma-dvāra*) because it encompasses all meritorious practices.

Neither Buddhas nor Bodhisattvas fail to enter this Gate of Names. Furthermore, the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The bodies of Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas are without distinction;

however, there is a difference in that their merits are either fulfilled or not yet fulfilled, and their defiled obstructions are either remaining or non-remaining. This is like the moon from its first day to the fifteenth day: although the waxing and waning differ, they are both the moon."
The essence is without differentiation; thus, the merits possessed from the first bhūmi through to the tenth bhūmi are likewise so. Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"From the sixth bhūmi onward, a bodhisattva is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) yet does not realize [nirvana].

Although one may possess the *dhāraṇī* of hearing in the fifth bhūmi, they do not attain the *dhāraṇī* of meaning, because a mind of equal purity is extremely difficult to obtain. Moreover, it is most difficult for supramundane wisdom to delight in and manifest mundane wisdom," and so forth.

The Tathāgata flows against the current; the Bodhisattva likewise proceeds in accordance with it until they reach the point where awakening and the limit intersect, which is called Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Ānanda, from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) up to Equal Enlightenment, this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind (*vajra-citta*).

[Commentary] "Equal Enlightenment" (Samatā-bodhi) refers to the Bodhisattva Dharmamegha and the Tathāgata of Reverse Flow meeting at this stage; because their two modes of awakening are equal in essence, it is called Equal Enlightenment. There are three meanings to this term:

first, the meaning of immediate succession (*anantara*), as it belongs to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); second, the meaning of perfect equality, as the *Ekottarika-āgama* speaks of eight paths of equality;

and third, the meaning of pervasiveness, as the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states that "equal" means to be all-pervading. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* says: "Equal Enlightenment illuminates stillness, while Sublime Enlightenment is stillness-illumination. It further states: "As for Equal Enlightenment..."

Regarding the name "Gradually Awakened" (*anupūrva-bodhi*), if explained by way of subsuming the categories of phenomena (*vastu*), there are eight further meanings: 1. **In terms of the number of persons:** It refers to the *Avalokita-sūtra* (瓔珞), because in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) there is only one person. 2.

**In terms of the fixed [stages]:** It refers to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Rājan-pāramitā-śrī-sūtra*), which states that the Bodhisattva of Consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the King of the Fourth Dhyāna, first enters the Vajra [samādhi]; since all is immediately realized, this is the Vajra-samādhi. 3. **In terms of the stages (*bhūmi*):** It refers to the *Avalokita-sūtra*, which designates Equal Enlightenment as the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*). 4.

**In terms of abandonment:** It refers to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, which states that the three grades of consecrated beings of Equal Wisdom eliminate the remaining residual habits (*vāsanā*) from what preceded. There is no further text provided for translation.

1. Regarding the illumination of conditions (*pratyaya*): because it severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). 2. Regarding the [Four] Truths (*satya*): as the *Renwang jing* says, "because of the remaining habits of ignorance," and because when the principle of the two truths is fully exhausted, all is ended;

thus, it subsumes both truths. 3. Regarding the eons (*kalpa*): as the *Yingluo jing* says, "The Bodhisattva Vajrajñānadhvaja dwells in the Samādhi of the Summit (*mūrdhan-samādhi*), dwelling for a hundred eons and cultivating one thousand three hundred samādhis.

4. Regarding the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*): this refers to the aforementioned Bodhisattvas manifesting as ancient Buddhas; they possess only the name of a "response" (*nirmāṇa*). 5. Regarding the mind: as the *Yingluo jing* says, "Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*) is called the Fourth."

The eleventh stage is named "Entering the Dharma-realm Mind" because one enters the Gate of the Double Mystery (*chongxuan*). Thus, the *Renwang jing* states that at the end of thirty births, one becomes equal to the Great Enlightened One.
In this manner, through these successive layers—twelve stages in total, both single and double—one finally exhausts the state of Wondrous Enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.

[Commentary] "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue) refers to the stage of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), meaning that the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), through the power of severing delusions, departs from [the final stages of] patience and realizes wisdom, thereby attaining the Great Dharma-body;

this is termed Sublime Enlightenment. Regarding the phrase "exhaustive sublime enlightenment," there are two meanings of "exhaustive": first, it signifies the ultimate limit, as the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "He has attained supreme perfect enlightenment"; second, it signifies pervasiveness, where "enlightenment" means wondrous realization.

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "Right Universal Knowledge and Wondrous Realization are both fully perfected. Furthermore, according to the interpretation based on the inclusion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*), there are seven further meanings, the first of which concerns the severance of the jeweled necklace (*hāra*).

First, regarding the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), the ignorance severed therein is called "non-comprehension of all dharmas" because it deludes one regarding the *dharmadhātu* and gives rise to the karmic fruits of the three realms. Second, regarding the person, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:

"The stage of Equal Enlightenment (*deng-jue*) is the third ground, and Wondrous Enlightenment is the three bodies; within the nine consciousnesses, they are fundamentally luminous and pure. Third, regarding the grounds, the *Sutra on the Necklace of the Grounds* states:

"Wondrous Enlightenment is named the Ground of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). It is neither existent nor non-existent, as all marks are exhausted; it suddenly realizes Great Enlightenment and exhaustively penetrates the spiritual essence of transformation. Fourth, regarding... [text truncated]

1. Regarding the transformation of patience (*kṣānti*): The *Renwang jing* states that within the stage of the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), one contemplates the lower grade; by transforming this patience into wisdom, the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is eternally serene. This is because patience is transformed into wisdom. 2. Regarding the transformation of birth:

The *Renwang jing* states that the formless perfect wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) rules the three realms; when the thirty births are exhausted, one is equal to the Great Enlightened One. This is because the characteristics of birth are completely extinguished. 3. Regarding the transformation of the truths (*satya*):

The *Renwang jing* states that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is eternally peaceful and secure; when the source is exhausted and nature is fully realized, wondrous wisdom abides. This is because one realizes the ultimate truth. 4. Regarding the transformation of retribution (*vipāka*): The *Renwang jing* states that the three... [text truncated]

The fruition of the ten abodes of the noble ones is exclusively for the Buddha alone, as he dwells in the Pure Land where both karma and its fruits are exhausted; thus it is said that the twelve are "single" and "multiple. "Single" and "multiple" refer to the substance of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while "twelve" refers to the number of stages.

Regarding contemplation: the three preceding types of faith are gradual and constitute single cultivation of *śamatha*. Once one has entered faith and thereafter cultivates both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the conventional (*prajñapti*) in equal measure, this is termed "multiple.

This corresponds to the meaning of "single" and "multiple" in the *Samantabhadra-vyūha* (the *Niyata-cakra* of the *Awakening of Faith*). The commentary states: "Now, to further briefly explain the meaning of 'single' and 'multiple,' there is yet another [point]."
Having completed the Sūtra and the Śāstra, we shall now first explain the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and subsequently explain its single and combined forms.

This is because *śamatha* and so forth take cessation and contemplation as their essence. The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra-śāstra* states: "To settle the mind in right concentration is what is called cessation (*śamatha*); to correctly abide in the discernment of phenomena is what is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Such is the nature of this consciousness. Furthermore, it says: "One who universally desires all merits should cultivate both; one who does not [desire them] fully should cultivate only one part. Because there are both single and dual [cultivations], the commentary explains: "One part constitutes the single; that which is not one part constitutes the dual."
"Paired" (*śaṃśa*) means "repeated" (*āvṛtta*); this is the meaning of "single" and "repeated. Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "There are four kinds of paths:

those who have already attained *śamatha* proceed to cultivate *vipaśyanā*; those who have already attained *vipaśyanā* proceed to cultivate *śamatha*. The commentary explains: "These two dharmas are both cultivated singly. It further states:

"If one has not attained either of the two, one should suppress dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) by cultivating the two paths together. If one has already attained the two paths, then one should cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in equal union."

The *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "These two dharmas are both to be cultivated again. This refers to the meaning of the single and the multiple. Regarding the enumeration of stages (*bhūmi*), the scriptures and treatises differ in their delineation of these stages; only the twelve abodes (*vāsa*) of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* accord with this text.

That treatise designates the stage prior to the [ten] grounds as the Abode of Practice through Resolute Belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*); the first ground as the Abode of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*); the second ground as the Abode of Higher Ethics (*adhiśīla-vihāra*);

the third ground as the Abode of Higher Mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*); the fourth ground as the Abode Corresponding to the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-pratisaṃyukta-vihāra*); the fifth ground as the Abode Corresponding to the Truths (*satya-pratisaṃyukta-vihāra*); the sixth ground as the Abode Corresponding to Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-pratisaṃyukta-vihāra*); and the seventh...

The first stage is abiding in signlessness with effort; the eighth stage is abiding in signlessness without effort; the ninth stage is abiding in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); and the tenth stage is the supreme Bodhisattva stage.

Adding the subsequent stage of the Tathāgata makes twelve stages. Since the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* also explains it in this way, the state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) is the ground where the source is exhausted and nature is fully realized;
thus, through these twelve stages—both single and combined—one exhausts the essence of wondrous enlightenment and accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way.
These various stages are all [examined] with the diamond-like [samādhi]. One observes them through the ten kinds of profound metaphors regarding their being like an illusion.

[Commentary]: "All are examined with the diamond" explains the method of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This means that the wisdom and the abandonment (*prahāṇa*) of each stage are all termed the "diamond-like samādhi" (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is called "diamond-like observation.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the diamond-like samādhi generally relies upon the nine stages; briefly speaking, according to the nine grades of what is abandoned, there would be eighty-one such concentrations. This is not the ultimate [state].

This refers to the subsequent Vajra-samādhi. The *Vajrasamādhi-prakṛti-viśuddhi-sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, they cultivate one hundred samādhis and subsequently enter the Vajra-samādhi.
These one hundred samādhis arise from the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the ten pāramitās;

while dwelling in the stage of *Jvalanā*, they naturally and constantly attain eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi without cultivation or effort. Among all phenomena, they perceive no signs of coming, going, abiding, or ceasing. Its...

When the mind is tranquil, one immediately attains entry into the Vajra Samādhi. This Vajra Samādhi does not diminish the fetters (*saṃyojana*); rather, the fetters are extinguished of their own accord.

This Vajra Samādhi emerges from *vipaśyanā* and enters into *śamatha*. This Vajra Samādhi does not abide, does not arise, does not cease, is not destroyed, is not interrupted, is not different, and is not detached;

it is immutable. It enters the nature of luminous wisdom, giving rise to the profound knowledge of the single integrated mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Having seen neither body, nor mind, nor dharmas, one subsequently achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The meaning of the vajra-phrase of *samyaksambodhi* is briefly of several kinds; as stated in the *Śuddhamudrā-sūtra*, there are fourteen phrases, one of which is the "vajra-concentration" (*vajrasamādhi*). This refers to the vajra-phrase that "all phenomena are Buddha-dharmas," because it enters into and understands all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, it is said: "This vajra-phrase can, through successive understanding, realize the vajra-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). Thus, one knows that the vajra-concentration is that which is manifested within all phenomena. As for what are called the fourteen phrases, the sūtra states: [The fourteen phrases follow: 1. All phenomena are Buddha-dharmas; this is the vajra-phrase. 2. All phenomena are non-Buddha-dharmas; this is the vajra-phrase. 3. All phenomena are neither Buddha-dharmas nor non-Buddha-dharmas; this is the vajra-phrase. 4. All phenomena are the realm of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 5. All phenomena are not the realm of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 6. All phenomena are neither the realm of the Buddhas nor not the realm of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 7. All phenomena are the nature of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 8. All phenomena are not the nature of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 9.

All phenomena are neither the nature of the Buddhas nor not the nature of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 10. All phenomena are the body of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 11. All phenomena are not the body of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 12. All phenomena are neither the body of the Buddhas nor not the body of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 13. All phenomena are the speech of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. 14. All phenomena are not the speech of the Buddhas; this is the vajra-phrase. Thus, the sūtra sets forth these fourteen phrases.]

"One's own body is a vajra phrase, because its intrinsic nature is non-conceptual; ignorance is a vajra phrase, because it enters into all luminosities; the five deeds of immediate retribution are a vajra phrase, because they are equal in their lack of volitional application;
the limit of aversion is a vajra phrase, because it is equal to the limit of loving-kindness; the limit of delusion is a vajra phrase, because it is equal to the light of wisdom;

all sentient beings and a single sentient being are a vajra phrase, because one universally enters into the equality of all sentient beings; the minds of all sentient beings and the mind of a single sentient being [are likewise a vajra phrase]."
The mind is a vajra phrase, because it enters into the state of no-mind. All Buddhas are one Buddha, a vajra phrase, because they universally enter the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*).

All lands are one land, a vajra phrase, because they universally enter inexhaustible lands. All phenomena are Buddha-dharmas, a vajra phrase, because wisdom enters into and understands them in all places.
The activities of all Māras are the activities of the Buddha-dharma, a vajra phrase, because by entering the activities of Māras, one is able to awaken others. All speech...

The statement that the Tathāgata’s speech is a vajra-word is because it universally enters all sounds and understands them accordingly; that all phenomena are unborn is a vajra-word because they are without cessation;

and that all phenomena are unarisen is a vajra-word because they enter into the state of non-resting. The commentary explains that the meaning of these phrases is as follows: first, non-conceptuality, which is the universal essence;

second, entering into all light and darkness; third, the absence of volitional application; fourth, the equality of aversion and compassion; fifth, the equality of ignorance and wisdom; and sixth, the unity and multiplicity of the assembly.
1. The equality of arising; 2. The equality of the seven minds and the mindless; 3. The equality of one and many Buddha-natures; 4. The equality of exhaustion and non-exhaustion; 5.

The equality of all according to their understanding; 6. The equality of the false and the correct; 7. The equality of all speech; 8. The equality of arising and ceasing; 9. The equality of rising and subsiding. Such is the meaning of the Vajra-body nature.
Furthermore, according to the *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, the meaning of the "Vajra phrase" is explained in summary as seven points. The treatise says:
That which is "vajra" is difficult to obstruct or destroy; the meaning realized is likewise so. Furthermore, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*) because it can serve as a fundamental basis.

Regarding the "seven phrases," they refer to the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, sentient beings, bodhi, merit, and karma. Even the mind's objects of perception cannot know them, let alone names, chapters, or phrases.

Since this contemplation is employed throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that these various stages are all observed by means of the vajra. As for the ten kinds of profound metaphors such as "like an illusion," they are for the purpose of...

Because they involve the cultivation of prevention and restraint, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* uses the analogy of a phantom; for if dharmas such as form were non-existent in reality, the cultivation of various practices would be in vain. To guard against this fault, the analogy of a painter is taught.
Furthermore, to prevent the failure of initiating the practice, the analogy of a magician is taught.
Within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas to purify, cultivate, and realize [the path], gradually entering deeper.

Ānanda, it is by means of these three progressive advancements that one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi. One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly; any other contemplation is said to be a false contemplation.

[Commentary] This concludes the formation of the essence of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It is said that because the practices of the three contemplations all possess a sequential order, they are termed "gradual. Now, to briefly explain the essence of these three contemplations: what is the essence of the practice of contemplation?
Regarding *śamatha*, its essence is the illumination and realization of one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding *samādhi* (here *samāpatti*), its condition is the discernment of objective realms.

As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Śrī-mahā-samaya-sarva-tathāgata-tattva-saṃgraha*) states: "Śamatha is quiescence; samādhi is correct mindfulness and retention. These are thus one essence with three names, designated as "correct concentration," "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), and "totality" (*samantabhadra*).
"Holding" (*dhāraṇā*) is also called *vipaśyanā*, which has the meaning of "observation. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that *śamatha* has nine modes:

causing [the mind] to abide, causing it to abide closely, causing it to abide firmly, causing it to abide near [the object], disciplining it, pacifying it, thoroughly pacifying it, focusing it on a single point, and maintaining it with equanimity.
As for *vipaśyanā*, there are four general categories: first, the discernment of all phenomena as they exist; second, the most thorough discernment of all that exists...

Therefore, there are three types of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*): that is, because one establishes the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) by means of wisdom accompanied by conceptual attention (*vikalpa-manasikāra*).

There are four types of detailed examination (*parīkṣā*): that is, because one investigates them exhaustively and completely. The treatise further explains: "In this context, these phrases are spoken either with reference to the objects of pure conduct (*caritaviśuddhi-ālambana*), or with reference to the objects of skillfulness (*kauśalya-ālambana*), or with reference to the objects of afflictions within pure conduct.

Regarding *dhyāna*, the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Mahābodhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*) says: "Dhyāna is solely quiescent extinction (*śamatha-nirodha*); it is like the resonance of a bell within its vessel."
"Extinction" (*nirodha*) means the cessation of the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes. "The gong-rim within the vessel" means neither identical nor separate, being without obstruction.

This has two names: one is *upavicāra* (or *upacaya*), translated as "equanimity" (*upekṣā*). Furthermore, there are four names: first, "equality," and so forth, including "neither defiled nor pure. These three are the essential characteristics of the contemplations.

Moreover, the sutra says, "These various stages and their gradual deepening penetration," which summarizes the contemplative methods of the various stages (*bhūmi*), from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to [the final stage].

The wondrous enlightenment is entirely attained through the three contemplations in their gradual sequence, as explained in various treatises. First, the *Vyūha-śāstra* states that regarding the two dharmas of śamatha and vipaśyanā, if they are practiced on the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), it is called "cultivation based on reliance";

from the first bhūmi upward, there are four types of cultivation: the first bhūmi is "universal cultivation" (*sāmānya-bhāvanā*); from the second to the sixth bhūmis is "cultivation of the expedient means with signs" (*nimitta-upāya-bhāvanā*);

the seventh bhūmi is "signless cultivation" (*animitta-bhāvanā*); and the final three bhūmis are "unconditioned cultivation" (*asaṃskṛta-bhāvanā*). Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of dharmas at the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) as explained in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, the treatise says: "Heat..."

"Dharma" refers to that which is individually realized within; its essential characteristic consists of the śamatha and vipaśyanā arising from the mental engagement with the objects revealed by the sūtras and other teachings—based upon the truths as the predominant influence—by means of a mind purified through meditative concentration.
Furthermore, as it is explained regarding the contemplation of dharmas in the stage of the path of seeing:
"The path of seeing refers to the samādhi and its associated dharmas obtained immediately after the 'supreme mundane dharma,' having as their essence non-conceptual śamatha and vipaśyanā."

Regarding the characteristics, as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning the seventh stage (*saptamī bhūmi*), it says: "In the seventh stage, one practices the two modes of śamatha and vipaśyanā simultaneously within a single thought-moment.
It further states: "One should know that the wisdom of the eighth stage consists solely of the path of practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā, for they are perfected there. The commentary explains:
these passages refer to the application of various contemplative methods (*vipaśyanā-dharma*) within these stages.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "What shall this sutra be named?

How should I and all sentient beings uphold it? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is named 'The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa,' 'Sitatapatrā,' 'The Unsurpassed Jewel Seal,' and 'The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.
It is also named 'The Savior and Protector of Kinsmen and Causes,' for it delivers Ānanda and the bhikṣuṇī of this assembly, enabling them to attain [liberation]."

The Bodhicitta enters the ocean of universal knowledge; it is also called the Secret Cause of the Tathāgatas and the Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization. It is also called the Great Vaipulya, the King of the Wondrous Lotus, the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, and the Dhāraṇī Mantra.
It is also called the Consecration Verses, the Myriad Practices of all Bodhisattvas, and the Śūraṅgama. You should uphold it!

[Gushan said: "The purpose of initiating this sutra is to save Ānanda; therefore, it first opens up the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), next reveals the perfect practice, and through the completion of practice, one enters the stages culminating in the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-jñāna*).
To provide a model for future generations, it has both a beginning and an end; thus, Mañjuśrī asks about the name of the sutra and the method of its upholding. [Commentary:

At the beginning of this sutra, the *Uṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī* is used to save Ānanda while simultaneously delivering Mādrī; hence it is called the *Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa*. It is also called "Saving One's Kinsmen" because it subsequently investigates Ānanda’s initial resolve and thereby opens the Buddha’s wisdom.

Because it is seen, it is called the "Pure Ocean-Eye. To speak of "entering the ocean of universal knowledge" means to attain the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It is named "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) to manifest the essence of the three greatnesses.

"Great and Square" refers to its essence and characteristics; "Broad" refers to its function. Being pure amidst defilement, it is named the "Wondrous Lotus King. Because it gives birth to the Great Enlightenment, it is called the "Buddha-Mother Dhāraṇī.

According to Wu-xing, this sutra flows forth from the Secret Section (*guhyatantra*), and is therefore titled the "Consecration Phrases. All sutras explain their titles in order to summarize the complex and bring it into concise grasp.
It is easy to receive and uphold.
