Textual Passage Eight) Having spoken these words (concluding summary), Ānanda and the great assembly immediately received the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the Pañcarakṣā, and further heard this sutra (referring generally to the profound mysteries of the preceding sutras). Thus they attained complete understanding.

The Enumeration of Terms: The Sudden Enlightenment of *Dhyāna*, the Cultivation and Progression through the Holy Stages, and the Sublime Principle of Exalted Increase. When the mind becomes empty and still, one severs the three realms and eliminates the six grades of subtle afflictions that perturb the mind.

Thereupon, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, your compassionate voice is all-encompassing and skillfully opens up the subtle, deep-seated delusions of sentient beings.
Today my body and mind are filled with joy, and I have attained great benefit. World-Honored One, if this wondrously luminous, truly pure, and sublime mind is fundamentally..."

It comes forth as all-pervading and perfect. Thus, even down to the great earth, grasses, trees, and all wriggling, sentient beings, their original source is True Suchness (Tathatā). This very essence is the true body of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood; the Buddha-body is truly real.

How is it that there are further realms such as those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas? World-Honored One, do these paths exist inherently from the beginning, or are they produced by the deluded habitual tendencies of sentient beings?

World-Honored One, for example, there was the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā, who upheld the Bodhisattva precepts yet secretly engaged in sexual misconduct, falsely claiming that practicing lust was not [an offense].

"Killing is not stealing; there is no karmic retribution. Having spoken these words, a great, fierce fire first arose from his female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires burned through every joint of his body.

He fell into the Avīci Hell. So it was with King Virūḍhaka and the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra. Because Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Śākya clan, and because Sunakṣatra falsely claimed that all phenomena are empty, they were cast alive into the Avīci Hell.

Are these various hells fixed locations, or do they arise spontaneously? Each person, having given rise to their own karma, experiences its results individually and privately. We pray that you will bestow upon us your great compassion.

To enlighten the ignorant and cause all sentient beings who uphold the precepts to hear this definitive meaning, they shall receive it with joy and veneration, remaining pure and free from transgression.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "Speaking of these" refers to the attainment of benefit through understanding and the afflictions to be abandoned by means of the path of cultivation—namely, the afflictions such as greed—which are divided into nine grades across the nine stages of the three realms.

By abandoning six grades of the desire realm, one realizes the second fruit; by abandoning the final three grades, one realizes the third fruit; and by abandoning each of the nine grades of the higher realms, one realizes the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). Ānanda has already attained this.

Because one has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one further severs six grades [of afflictions] within this state to realize the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*). The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "The afflictions of all sentient beings do not transcend the triple world;

the retributions of all sentient beings also do not transcend the triple world; and the transformation bodies and dharma bodies of all Buddhas likewise do not transcend the triple world. Therefore, it is said:

"If one believes that the fundamental karma of sentient beings is precisely what the Bodhisattvas originally practiced and what is cultivated throughout the ten stages—that is the fundamental karma of the Buddhas. When the World-Honored One asks below about the causes of karma, he is addressing both [the afflictions and the retributions].

Because it upholds the Vinaya, the fragrant lotus of the precepts jewel [removes] lustful greed; because of King Vaidūryarāja’s execution, [it removes] the false speech of Sunakṣatra. Regarding the "fixed location," this refers to the place where hell resides.

Regarding "natural," this means appearing according to the retribution of one's karma. "Private experience" means that the agent alone experiences the result, which others cannot see together with them. If it were seen together by all, then its location would be fixed; if it is natural, then it is merely a private experience.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Excellent indeed is this question! It shall cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure. Because of that deluded vision, deluded habits arise. Due to this, they distinguish between the internal and the external.

Ānanda, the 'internal' refers to the internal realm of sentient beings. Because of various attachments and defilements, deluded emotions are stirred up. As these emotions accumulate without ceasing, they can produce the water of craving. Therefore, when sentient beings think of delicacies in their minds, water flows from their mouths."

Emerging, he recalls the previous person, feeling either pity or resentment; his eyes fill with tears, and as he greedily seeks wealth and treasures, a stream of lustful saliva flows from his heart, his entire body becomes lustrous and moist, and with his mind attached, he engages in sexual intercourse.

The male and female organs naturally discharge fluids. Ānanda, although various cravings differ, their outflowing fetters are the same. Moistening and unable to rise, they naturally fall downward; this is called the "internal portion.

Ānanda, the "external portion" refers to that which is external to sentient beings. Because of various thirsts and yearnings, they give rise to empty imaginings. When these imaginings accumulate without ceasing, they can produce a superior vital energy (*vāyu*).

Therefore, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure; when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their gaze becomes heroic and resolute; when their minds desire to be born in heaven, they dream of flying upward; and when their minds dwell upon the Buddha...

In this realm, the sacred visions manifest in the darkness. One serves a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), even at the cost of one’s own body and life. Ānanda, although various thoughts may differ, the quality of lightness and elevation is the same; one soars and moves without sinking. This is naturally transcendent and is called the "external division.
Ānanda, throughout all the worlds, birth and death continue in succession. Birth follows from habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and death follows from the flow of transformation.

At the moment of death, before warmth and tactile sensation have been abandoned, the good and evil of one’s entire life appear simultaneously and instantaneously. When the two habits of death (the inverse) and birth (the conforming) intersect, if there is pure thought, one will immediately fly upward and be born in the heavens. If one flies...

If one possesses both merit and wisdom within the mind, along with pure vows, the heart will naturally open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands, attaining rebirth therein according to one's wishes.

If one’s emotions are slight but thoughts are many, one will be lightly lifted up without traveling far, becoming an immortal who flies, a powerful ghost-king, a flying yakṣa, or a land-walking rākṣasa, roaming through the four heavens without hindrance wherever one goes.

Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma, or who observe the prohibitive precepts following those who maintain the precepts; or who protect divine mantras following those who recite them;

or who protect meditative concentration and preserve the patience of the Dharma—such beings (like the eight classes of devas and nāgas) dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata. Their mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*) and emotions (*cetanā*) are balanced, so they neither fly upward nor fall downward, but are born among humans.

If their conceptions are clear, they are intelligent; if their emotions are deep, they are dull-witted. If emotions predominate and conceptions are few, they flow into the realm of horizontal birth, becoming heavy as fur-bearing beasts or light as winged fowl. If emotions are sevenfold and conceptions threefold, they sink down into the waters.

Born at the edge of fire, they receive the breath of fierce flames; their bodies are those of hungry ghosts, constantly being burned. Water harms them; for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they have neither food nor drink.

With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of principle, they descend through the wheel of fire; their bodies enter the confluence of wind and fire, passing through the ground of the two [realms]. Those with light offenses are born in the *Avīci* (Intermittent) Hells, while those with heavy offenses are born in the *Avīci* (Uninterrupted) Hells.

These two types of hells are for those of pure passion; they sink directly into the *Abhirati* (A-wei) Hell. If within their sinking hearts they have slandered the Mahāyāna, violated the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, spoken deceptive and false teachings, vainly coveted offerings of faith, unworthily received respect, or committed the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses, they will further be born in the *Abhirati* Hells throughout the ten directions.
Following the creation of evil karma, though they invite this upon themselves, within the commonality of all such beings there is also the primordial [karmic cause].

"Ānanda, all these are the results of the karma produced by those sentient beings themselves. They create ten causes of habitual practice and undergo six types of intersecting retributions. [First, the internal division of cause and effect:

Because sentient beings continue their births through emotional attachment, they are called 'sentient beings' (sattva). Since craving is the root of emotional delusion, it is termed the 'internal division.

As for designating 'conception' as the external, this refers to gradually transcending the enclosure of emotion so as not to sink downward; this indicates the conceptual mind of humans and devas, not the wisdom-conception of the Three Vehicles. One should serve virtuous spiritual friends."

If one disregards one’s own body and life, then one will likewise disregard those of similar kind. Next, we shall distinguish between the various states of feeling and perception. Sentient beings naturally love life and hate death; this is the delusion of emotional and perceptual views.
The thought of merit and wisdom enables one to see the Buddha, while the thought associated with emotional attachment enables one to ascend by flight.

Furthermore, through upholding the precepts and protecting the Dharma, one forms pure supramundane thoughts, thereby being able to personally dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata. Regarding "sinking down to the water wheel," the *Abhidharmakośa* states that at the very bottom of the great earth lies...

Within the wheels of gold, water, and wind, there are eight cold and hot hells. Because those in the cold hells take fire as their bodies, they are consumed by fierce flames upon encountering water; thus, even water harms them.

The eighth hot hell is also called the Five Uninterrupted (Pañcānantarya) Hells, so named because the five factors—the instruments of punishment, the size of the body, the duration of the kalpa, and the lifespan—are all without interruption.

Those who slander the Mahāyāna sūtras and sever the seed of the Buddha commit the gravest offenses and therefore enter these hells. The mention of "original grounds" (*mūlabhūmi*) therein refers to each individual according to their original causes.

What are the ten causes? Ānanda, first is the habit of lustful practice through sexual union. It arises from mutual friction; when this grinding continues without ceasing, a great and fierce fire is thereby ignited within.

It is like two people rubbing their hands together until the sensation of warmth appears before them. Because these two habits ignite one another, there arise such things as iron beds and copper pillars.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate the act of lust by the same name: "the fire of desire. When Bodhisattvas see desire, they avoid it as they would a pit of fire. Second is the habit of greed through mutual scheming. It arises from...

They inhale one another; they draw in and grasp without ceasing. Because of this, there is accumulated cold and solid ice within which they freeze. It is like a person drawing in air through the mouth, whereby a sensation of cold arises.
As these two habits contend with one another, there arise the *ṭha-ṭha*, *pa-pa*, and *ra-ra* hells, as well as the Blue, Red, and White Lotus Hells, and other such icy phenomena.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking by the common name "the water of greed. When Bodhisattvas see greed, they avoid it as they would a miasmic sea. Third, the habit of pride involves mutual rivalry, arising from mutual reliance and flowing on in haste.

It does not cease. Because it is thus, there is surging and rushing; the accumulation of waves forms water. It is like the human mouth and tongue mutually moistening each other with flavor, whereby water is produced. As these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the pouring and swallowing of molten copper. For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize *māna* (conceit) as follows: [The text continues: "The mind is like a monkey, leaping and bounding about; it is like a wild horse, galloping and racing forward. It is like a flowing stream, never ceasing for a moment.

Thus, there is surging and rushing; the accumulation of waves forms water. It is like the human mouth and tongue mutually moistening each other with flavor, whereby water is produced. As these two habits strike against one another, there arise such phenomena as rivers of blood, rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the pouring and swallowing of molten copper. Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions identify *māna* (self-conceit) as the root of these afflictions.

This is called "drinking the water of delusion. When Bodhisattvas see arrogance, they avoid it as if fleeing from a great drowning. Fourth, the habit of anger clashes and collides; arising from mutual opposition, this opposition knots together without ceasing.

The mind becomes feverish and ignites fire, forging the vital energy (*prāṇa*) into metal. For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron enclosures, sword-trees, and sword-wheels, axes, halberds, spears, and saws. Like a person harboring a grievance, the murderous energy flies and stirs.
Because these two habits strike one another, there are punishments such as castration, dismemberment, beheading, hacking, mincing, piercing, and beating with clubs.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate hatred as the "sharp sword. When Bodhisattvas see hatred, they avoid it as they would an execution. Fifth, the habit of deceitful enticement arises from mutual seduction and incites an unceasing cycle.

Because of this, there are punishments involving ropes, wooden stocks, strangulation, and shackles—like water soaking a field so that weeds and grass grow. Because these two habits extend and perpetuate one another, there are punishments such as cangues, fetters, stocks, manacles, whips, staves, clubs, and maces. This is...

Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize deceit and hypocrisy with the same name: "the slanderous thief. When Bodhisattvas encounter fraud, they regard it as they would fear a jackal or a wolf.

[Wenling] Regarding the first of the ten habitual practices, it first describes the objective realm experienced as a result, and subsequently clarifies the specific retribution received. Sensual desire evokes the karma of fire; because the causal factors grind against one another, the subject and object blaze together.

This is called "the two habits burning each other," and thus there is retribution such as the iron bed. Because the Tathāgatas act as guides, they characterize these states to serve as warnings; because Bodhisattvas are practitioners, they [regard them with such dread].

Therefore, one should deeply fear and avoid them. The habit of greed induces water; it arises from absorption and accumulation, and the wind of inhalation and storage becomes cold wind, which congeals the water into ice.

As the *Abhidharmakośa* says, "Ṭaṭa, paṭa" refers to the sound of enduring the cold, while blue, red, and white lotuses refer to the colors of the cold ice. The habit of pride induces arrogance and contempt, arising from relying on oneself; because of this haughty and dissolute rushing flow, one experiences a realm of surging and turbulent waves.

Because it accumulates and brings about foul venom, there is the retribution of being drenched and swallowed by rivers of blood. The mind belongs to the element of fire, while the breath belongs to the element of metal; this is the nature of hatred.

This arises because the mind produces qi, which in turn moves the mind; when this qi strikes back and opposes it, the fire of the mind becomes even more blazing and the metal of the qi becomes even more rigid.

Thus, the heat of the mind ignites fire, forging the qi into metal. Deceptive habits rely on villainy to give rise to evil, which gradually spreads like weeds. Just as water poured onto a field causes grass and wood to grow, because they are drawn along and extended by one another, they evoke incidents of entanglement and dragging, such as those involving ropes and wood.
Slanderers, thieves, and deceivers are those who ruin what is correct. [Commentary] All matters concerning prisons involve seeing two aspects in a single thing, arising from the past.

It clarifies the implements possessed by one who possesses subsequent illumination, and the retributions bestowed upon them. For example, if one has the habit of anger, there will be the implements of the mountain of knives, the iron millstones, the sword-tree, and the wheel of swords;

there will be the retribution of being struck, beaten, and hacked to pieces. If one has the physical form of axes, halberds, spears, and saws, there will be the function of being cut, chopped, pierced, and minced. The *Tattvasiddhi* states: "To give rise to names based on what does not exist is called deceitful crookedness;

to feign goodness with a crooked mind is called flattery (*śāṭhya*); for the affairs of a flattering mind to be accomplished is called deception (*māyā*). Regarding the distinctions among types of pride (*māna*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Being stained by attachment to one's own qualities and being haughty and self-indulgent is called arrogance (*mada*); [to be so] toward others is [pride]."

The sixth is the habit of deceit, which involves mutual deception arising from the intent to mislead. When such falsehoods do not cease, the mind soars to commit villainy. Consequently, there arise dust, soil, excrement, and urine—filth and impurities as pervasive as dust carried by the wind, where each person can see nothing at all.

Because these two habits reinforce one another, there occur various events such as drowning, being submerged, leaping, tossing upward, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking. Therefore, throughout the ten directions...
All Tathāgatas designate deception by the same name: "killing by robbery" (*kāla-haraṇa*). When a Bodhisattva sees deception, they view it as treading upon a venomous snake.

Seventh is the habit-pattern of enmity and mutual resentment, which arises from harboring hatred. Because of this, there are flying stones, thrown rocks, being confined in chests or carriage-cages, or being trapped in jars and sacks.

Like a person of hidden malice who harbors evil within, because these two habits swallow one another, there occur various acts such as throwing, seizing, striking, shooting, tossing, and grasping. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate an enemy by the name "harmful ghost" (*vighna-rākṣasa*). The Bodhisattva...

The sentient being perceives the enemy as if drinking poisoned wine. Eighth, the habitual tendencies perceive mutual illumination, like the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), the grasping at precepts and prohibitions (śīlavrataparāmarśa), false awakenings, and various karmas, which give rise to opposition and rejection.

Birth is the opposite of this. It is for these reasons that there are royal messengers and chief clerks who strictly hold the registers. Like travelers on a road meeting one another as they come and go, their two practices intersect;

thus there arise interrogation, guile, examination, cross-examination, investigation, and inquiry. There are boys who scrutinize and illuminate [the records], and good and evil youths who hold ledgers in their hands to explain various matters. For this reason:

All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate false views with the same name: "The Pit of Views. When Bodhisattvas encounter various delusions and biased attachments, they regard them as if facing a precipice of poison.

Ninth, when the habit-energy of injustice and malice intermingle, giving rise to slander, there consequently arise mountains and stones that crush, grind, plow, and rub. This is like malicious slanderers who oppress and wrong the virtuous.

Because these two habits clash, there are matters such as pressing down, hammering, squeezing, straining, and measuring. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate resentment and slander with the same name: "Slander."
The tiger. When the Bodhisattva sees his own deceptions, it is as if he has been struck by a bolt of lightning. Tenth, the habit of litigation arises from concealment and mutual clamor.

For this reason, there is the mirror of discernment that illuminates and shines forth, like being in the midst of the sun where one cannot hide one's shadow. Because these two habits present themselves together, there is the "karmic mirror" of evil friends and the "fire-pearl" that reveals all;

past karma is verified through various matters. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate concealment with the same name: the "hidden thief. The Bodhisattva contemplates concealment as if wearing a high mountain upon his head while treading upon a vast ocean.

[Wenling]: Deceivers are those whose wills are fraudulent and whose minds are as flighty as wind blowing dust so that others cannot see; hence they experience the retribution of being submerged in or tossed about by filthy and evil environments.
Because they harbor resentment and malice in secret, intending harm, they experience the retribution of being struck by flying stones, crushed in sacks, or pelted and seized by projectiles.

[Commentary]: "Flying stones" refers to throwing them, as when Zhang Liang struck the Qin [army] by hurling stones. "Throwing stones" refers to tossing them, as when the *fēngrén* (guardian of the border) threw pebbles and gravel.

"Storing in a casket" means to capture; it is like the saying "storing in a casket" or "using a carriage cage to seize. "Filling a jar" means to strike or shoot, which is the same as the incident of overturning a bronze bell filled with fire.

"Sacking and striking" means to pounce and seize, as when the Qin [emperor] "sacked his two younger brothers," all of which were done secretly and covertly so that no one would see the injury. Seeing these familiar proofs, [one realizes] they arise from self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).

*Kāya* (body) refers to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "Adherence to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the attachment to what is not the fruit as being the fruit; "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the attachment to what is not the cause as being the cause. Because these involve opposition and contradiction, they induce such objective realms.

The "interrogation of the king’s envoys" refers to the chief officials who employ guile and deception. The "examination of documents" refers to the interrogation and investigation based on written records.

The fact that passersby on the road must inevitably be questioned and scrutinized, and that matters at the prison gates and watchtowers are investigated, examined, and verified—all these are induced by evil views. [Wenling] notes: "This is inappropriate."
To bend what is crooked is called "deviousness" (*wǎng*); deviousness is not true feeling, but arises from slander and calumny. To oppress others, the retribution is such as this.

[Commentary] "Squeezing and filtering" refers to the matter of crushing mountains and grinding stones; "measuring across" refers to the matter of being crushed by rollers and plowed by the soil. [Wēn-líng] "Lawsuit" does not mean a lawsuit before an official; it refers to publicly exposing what has been covered up.

When one exposes the other's secrets, it is called "mutual clamor. Secret malice and concealment lead to self-harm when exposed; the very crime of concealing guilt is sufficient to cause one's own downfall.

Because one falls, it is like wearing a mountain on one's head or treading upon the sea. [Commentary] To "mirror" means to perceive evil companions; to "illuminate" refers to the karmic mirror and the fire-jewel, for they reveal everything with clarity, such that one cannot conceal one's shadow even in broad daylight.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, for all sentient beings, the evil retributions summoned by the karma created through the six consciousnesses emerge from the six sense organs.

How do these evil retributions emerge from the six sense organs? First is the retribution of sight, which draws forth evil fruits. When this visual karma intersects with other factors, at the time of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions.

The deceased’s spirit and consciousness fly downward, riding upon the smoke, and enter the Avīci Hell. Two phenomena manifest therein: first, the phenomenon of clear vision, whereby one can see all manner of evil things everywhere, giving rise to immeasurable fear. Second—
This is dark seeing. Seeing nothing at all in the silence, immeasurable fear arises. Thus one sees fire that burns the hearing, becoming cauldrons of boiling brine and molten copper;
it burns the breath, becoming black smoke and purple flames; it burns the taste, becoming scorched pellets and iron gruel; it burns the touch, becoming hot ashes, furnaces, and charcoal;

and it burns the mind, producing sparks that scatter and fly, fanning and filling the void. Second is hearing as retribution, which summons evil fruits. When this karmic hearing intersects with death, at the moment of passing, one first sees waves submerging heaven and earth; the deceased’s consciousness—

Descending and flowing along the current, it enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two aspects: first, "opening the hearing," wherein one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes muddled and disordered;

second, "closing the hearing," wherein there is silence and nothing is heard, and the dark soul sinks into oblivion. Thus, when the waves of hearing pour down, they can become accusations and interrogations; when the waves of seeing pour down, they can become thunder and roars, and the breath of evil poison.

When the waves of smelling pour down, they can become rain and mist that drenches all venomous insects, which completely cover the body. When the waves of tasting pour down, they can become pus and blood, and various other impurities.

Filth. When focused on touch, it can become livestock or ghosts, or become excrement and urine. When focused on the mind, it can become lightning and hail, crushing the heart and soul. These three are retributions for smelling.
This draws forth evil fruits. When this karmic inhalation intersects with [the senses], at the moment of death, one first perceives poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings.

The deceased’s consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs: First is "obstructed hearing": being permeated by various foul vapors, the mind becomes extremely disturbed. Second is "blocked hearing":

the vapors overwhelm and block the senses, causing one to fall unconscious upon the ground. When such vapors strike the breath, they can become the physical body and its path; when they strike the sight, they can become fire and torches; when they strike the hearing, they can become drowning and...

If it encounters flavor, it can turn one into hunger or distaste; if it encounters contact, it can cause one to burst or rot. It becomes a great mountain of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes that insatiably devour.
If it encounters thought, it can turn one into ash, miasma, or flying sand and gravel, shattering the body.

[Sixfold Interchange]: Because the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) perform karma through mutual conditioning and assistance during the causal stage, when the fruit is experienced, they likewise receive retribution interchangeably among the six organs.

[Warming and Freezing]: Since seeing and cognition belong to fire, one experiences fierce flames and feels terror; upon encountering objects, one fears them and hides them within the mind. Hearing and listening belong to water, thus one encounters boiling cauldrons and molten copper.

The nose governs scent, thus one encounters black smoke and purple flames. The tongue governs taste, thus one encounters balls of gruel and various flavors. The body governs touch, thus one encounters ash, charcoal, and similar textures. [Second: Receiving Retribution] Note.

Because sounds are heard and produced, they become objects of reprimand and interrogation; when the mind is focused on them, they manifest as the roar of thunder and the surging of water, while fire produces sound.

When the breath ceases, it becomes rain and dew; water transforms according to the vital energy (*prāṇa*). Even up to the manifestation of lightning, all respond according to the conditions of perception. [3. The Retribution of Smell] That which is obstructive and that which traverses the unobstructed are both supported by the karma of smelling.

Starvation and sensory discordance cause the categories of flavor to fray and break, and the categories of form to rot and decay; when the mind is filled with chaotic thoughts, these perceptions result in ash and sand.

The fourth is the retribution of taste, which draws forth evil fruits. When this karmic action of taste intersects with death, at the moment of passing, one first sees an iron net with fierce, blazing flames that completely covers the world.

The deceased’s consciousness passes downward through the net, its head hanging upside down as it enters the Avīci Hell. Two manifestations appear: first, the inhaled breath solidifies into freezing ice, which cracks and tears the flesh of the body;

second, the exhaled breath flies up as a raging fire, which sears and rots the marrow and bones. Thus, when such tastes are experienced repeatedly, they become the basis for endurance and suffering; when such sights are experienced repeatedly, [the same occurs].

When it manifests through burning, it can become molten gold and stone. When experienced through hearing, it can become sharp weapons. When experienced through breathing, it can become a massive iron cage that covers the entire land.

When experienced through touch, it can become bows and arrows, crossbows and projectiles. When experienced through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky. These five types of tactile retribution attract and draw forth evil fruits.

When this karma of touch intersects with death, at the moment of passing, one first sees a great mountain approaching from all four sides, closing in until there is no way out. The deceased’s consciousness then sees a great iron city filled with fire-snakes.
Fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions; ox-headed jailers and horse-headed rākṣasas, wielding spears and lances, drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell.

Two kinds of contact manifest: first, contact by conjunction, where mountains press against their bodies, crushing their bones, flesh, and blood; second, contact by separation, where swords and blades strike their bodies, slicing and tearing their hearts and livers. Such is the contact by conjunction.

When encountering [objects] through touch, they can act as a path, an observation, a hammer, or a press. When encountering them through sight, they can act as burning, or incineration. When encountering them through hearing, they can act as a collision, a strike, an impalement, or an arrow-shot.

When encountering them through respiration, they can act as a snare, a bag, an interrogation, or a binding. When encountering them through taste, they can act as plowing, a pincer, a severing, or a cutting. When encountering them through thought...

Thus, they may cause things to fall or fly; they may cause them to be boiled or roasted. Sixth is the retribution of thought: it summons and draws forth evil fruits. When these thoughts and karmic actions intersect, at the moment of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land.

The deceased’s spirit-consciousness is blown upward into the void, then whirled down with the wind and falls into the Avīci Hell. This gives rise to two manifested appearances: the first is lack of awareness.

When delusion reaches its extreme, one wanders aimlessly and runs on without rest. When the two states of non-delusion and awakening are present, suffering is immeasurably scorching and its pain so deep it is difficult to endure.

Thus, when false thoughts are bound, they act as the directions and locations; when views are bound, they act as the mirror and the witness; when hearing is bound, it acts as the great congealing stone, as ice and frost, and as earth and mist;

when breath is bound, it acts as the great fire-cart, the fire-boat, and the fire-cage; when tasting is bound, it acts as the great wailing, as regret, and as weeping; and when touch is bound, it acts as...

They can become large or small; within a single day, they undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths; they are cast face down or face up. Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six effects of hell.
All are created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings. If sentient beings collectively commit evil karma, they enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.

If the six sense organs each commit [evil], and the actions performed by those organs, together with their respective objects and faculties, are combined, such a person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells (Aṣṭāvīcika). If one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three gates of body, speech, and mind, such a person enters...

Regarding the eighteen hells, if one does not commit all three types of karma together, but instead commits even a single instance of killing or a single instance of stealing, such a person will enter thirty-six hells; this is seen by observing each individual faculty.

If a person commits even a single karmic act, they will enter one hundred and eight hells. Because sentient beings individually perform and individually create [the aforementioned five evil karmas], they enter the corresponding realms within the world-system.
Deluded conceptualization arises; it does not exist from the beginning. [The Retribution of the Four Flavors] (Wenling):

Because the tongue devours living beings, causing them to endure suffering, one experiences various tastes that give rise to pain, thereby compelling oneself to accept endurance. Because of attachment to flavors based on visual perception, one smelts gold and stone;

because of malicious intent arising from auditory perception, one wields sharp blades; because of the desire for fragrance based on olfactory perception, one encounters great iron cages; because of the sensation of harming objects through tactile perception, one receives the bow.

Because one relishes objects through the conditions of self-inflicted injury, one experiences flying iron to satisfy that craving. [The five retributions of touch] include the coming together of great mountains, which is the experience of various harsh touches;

these are the bases for tactile karma, characterized by the states of being joined, torn apart, or separated. The "path" refers to the road leading to hell, while the "gate-tower of the King of Hell" refers to the hall and desk where punishments are administered—the locus upon which the body depends.

The "enveloping sack" is that which collects the vital breaths; because the mind is tossed about by karmic actions, one experiences flying and falling, and is impaled with blades—this refers to the torture of being pierced and shot.

"Binding" refers to mutual dependence and lateral elevation. [The six types of retribution for volition (*ṣaḍ-cetanā-vipāka*): Volition belongs to the earth element, yet it is tossed about; thus, the evil wind destroys the nation, and the mind wanders in confusion.

To know suffering is to awaken to volition. Because one relies on volition, there is that which exists; therefore, it becomes the locus where one incurs retribution. [Commentary: "Seeing" is able to verify and reflect;

"hearing" acts as ice and frost, being bound by the waves of what is heard. It is like a carriage or a cage; it is like a fire or a boat, the place through which one enters and exits. It is the speech uttered by the tongue in cries, lamentations, and weeping. It is the body’s various postures—large and small, reclining and stretching.
"Karma," Ānanda—this concludes the intent of the sutra. When all ten causes arise together, it constitutes a "perfect" (complete) creation; when arising through another, it is a "concurrent" object;

and when arising from the body, it is a "concurrent" faculty. The *Niraya Sūtra* states that there are eight hot hells and eight cold hells, as well as eighteen "grid-iron" hells (*kalasutra*), which are the intermittent hells, along with thirty-six hells and one hundred and eight hells, all of which are subordinate hells.

Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings—having violated the codes of discipline (*vinaya*), transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, and subverted the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, as well as having committed various other miscellaneous karmas—are scorched by suffering through successive kalpas.

When their retribution is eventually exhausted, they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts (*preta*). If, in their original cause, they committed the sin of greed for material things, when their retribution is exhausted, they encounter matter and take form; these are called *guǎiguǐ* (strange ghosts).

If they committed the sin of greed for sensual beauty, when their retribution is exhausted, they encounter wind and take form; these are called *bóguǐ* (drought ghosts). If they committed the sin of greed for delusive confusion, when their retribution is exhausted, they encounter animals and take form; these are called *mèiguǐ* (infatuating ghosts).

The *gui* (demon). Through greed and resentment they commit offenses. When this person’s offenses are exhausted, they encounter insects and take form; they are called *gu-du* (poisonous) demons. Through greedy recollection they commit offenses. When this person’s offenses are exhausted, they encounter decay and take form.

They are called *ghora* ghosts; their sin was greed and arrogance. When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter *vāyu* (wind/air) and take form, being called hungry ghosts (*preta*). Their sin was greed and deception.

When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter the obscure and take form, being called *yāma* ghosts. Their sin was greed for light. When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter *tejas* (essence/spirit) and take form, being called *vaṃśa* ghosts. Their sin was greed for accomplishment.

When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter brightness and take form, being called *karmadāsa* ghosts. Their sin was greed for factionalism. When these people’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter humans and take form, being called *dūta* ghosts. Ānanda, these...
All people fall due to their pure passions; scorched by the fires of karma, they emerge above as ghosts. All such states are summoned and drawn forth by the karma of one's own deluded thoughts.
If one awakens to Bodhi, then it is wondrous, perfect, and luminous—fundamentally nothing at all exists.

[The Four Ghost Realms]: Regarding the primary causes, these refer to the places where one commits transgressions; regarding the timing of the encounter with objects, this refers to the moment the fruit is experienced. If one is driven by greed for form (*rūpa-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a withered drought-demon (*parṇa-sarpa*).

If one is driven by greed for delusion (*moha-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a *chi-mei* (goblin). If one is driven by greed for resentment (*vaira-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a *gu-du* (poisonous insect). If one is driven by greed for recollection (*smṛti-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a decaying pestilence.

If one is driven by greed for arrogance (*māna-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a hungry ghost (*preta*). If one is driven by greed for obscurity (*tamas-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a *yan-ghost*. If one is driven by greed for brilliance (*jyotis-rāga*), one experiences the fruit of a *wang-ghost*.

The *liǎng* ghosts who formed attachments through greed are moved by their past obligations to serve those who share their greed; the ghosts who formed attachments through seeking advantage are moved by their past obligations to convey those who seek advantage.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of these ghosts is exhausted, both their emotions and their perceptions become empty. Only then, within the world, do they encounter those with whom they were originally in debt as karmic adversaries. Taking birth as animals, they repay their past debts.

As for the ghosts of material anomalies, once the objects have perished and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as owls and similar creatures. As for the ghosts of wind and drought, once the winds have subsided...

When their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world; as such, they mostly manifest as omens of calamity. Ghosts that possess animals, when the animal dies and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the human world; they mostly become species of foxes.

Ghosts of insect-pestilence, when the pestilence is extinguished and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the human world; they mostly become species of venomous creatures. Ghosts of decay and miasma, when their decline and poverty reach their end and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the human world.

Those who were mostly *āvilas* (parasites) are ghosts that receive their existence through vital energy (*vāyu*). When this energy dissipates and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as species that eat. Those who were ghosts of lingering obscurity are ghosts whose obscurity has dissolved and whose retribution is exhausted;

when born into the human world, they mostly become clothing. Those who were ghosts of harmonious emotion are ghosts whose harmony has dissolved and whose retribution is exhausted; when born into the human world, they mostly become responsive phenomena.

Those who were ghosts of luminous spirits are ghosts whose light has been extinguished and whose retribution is exhausted; when born into the human world, they mostly become auspicious omens. As for all these various classes of ghosts that depend upon humans, when the person dies and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as those who follow along.
Ānanda, these beings have all been withered by the fire of karma and are now repaying their past debts as animals. These states, too, are all summoned by one’s own deluded karma.

If one awakens to Bodhi, then these illusory conditions will be seen to have never existed at all. As you have said regarding Jewel-Lotus Fragrance and others, King Vairōcana, and the Bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—such evil karmas originally manifest from within oneself;
they do not descend from heaven, nor do they emerge from the earth, nor are they bestowed by humans. They are summoned by one’s own delusions and must be received by oneself in return.
Within the mind of bodhi, all things are merely floating and empty. Through the solidification of deluded thoughts, [the five classes of animals] arise.

When the physical substance has dissolved and the retribution for past karma is exhausted, one transforms into an animal form to repay residual karmic debt. The owl’s attachment to clods of earth is the residual retribution for greed;

its greedy nature is a portent of calamity and a premonition of misfortune. The drought-demon’s craving for snow is its residual retribution. Foxes and wolves possess much delusion; snakes and vipers possess much venom. Worms and maggots are of an evil class; pigs and sheep are of a class that consumes fodder; silkworms are insects.
The *fú* (birds of prey) class corresponds to the *yàn* and *zǔn* (hawks and falcons); the *yīng* (owls) class corresponds to auspicious omens;

the *línpín* (qilin and cats/dogs) class follows its own remaining categories. Furthermore, Ānanda, when these animals repay their prior debts, if the debtor repays more than what is owed, these sentient beings will again become human and demand the repayment of that surplus.
If the debtor was powerful and possessed merit, they will not lose their human form among men while repaying that power; if they lack merit, they will again become...
As animals, they must repay the remaining balance to that person. Ānanda, you should know this: whether by using money and goods or by employing their labor, the debt is repaid and the cycle stops.

However, if in the interim they take the life of that being or eat its flesh, then for as many eons as there are atoms, they will continue to devour one another and slaughter one another, revolving like a wheel, alternating between being the victim and the predator without ever finding rest.

Except for those who have attained *śamatha* or for when a Buddha appears in the world, one cannot rest or sleep. You should now know this: those of the owl class, once their retribution is fulfilled and they restore their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the dull-witted class.

Those of the omen-of-fault class, once their retribution is fulfilled and they restore their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the eccentric class. I, of the fox class, once my retribution is fulfilled and I restore my physical form, will be born among human beings as a member of the mediocre class.

Those of the venomous class, once their retribution is fulfilled and they restore their physical form, will be born among human beings as members of the cruel class. Those of the worm class, once their retribution is fulfilled...

Regarding form: those born among humans who have merged with subtle classes, if they were of the "eating" class, receive retribution sufficient to restore their form and are born among humans, merging with gentle classes; those of the "serving" class [receive similar retribution].

Having fully repaid their debts, they regain their forms and are born among the human realm; those who correspond to the category of laborers join the class of toil. Those who correspond to the category of refinement regain their forms, are born among the human realm, and join the class of letters.

Those who possess auspicious signs regain their forms, are born among the human realm, and join the class of clarity. Those who follow the various categories of order regain their forms, are born among the human realm, and join the class of the accomplished.

Ānanda, all these have fully repaid their past debts and regained human form; yet from beginningless time, their karmic calculations have been inverted, leading them to give birth to one another and kill one another. Not...
Having encountered a Tathāgata yet not hearing the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).

Such individuals are called "those worthy of compassion. [The Six Paths of Humanity] [Wenling]: To serve as livestock is the proper recompense; if one exceeds this portion, it becomes a perverse retribution. Exceeding the portion refers to irrational forced labor, excessive consumption of food, and so forth. [Commentary]:

Those of the *xiāo* (owls/crows) lineage who have returned to human form are mixed with the dull-witted class; this is also due to residual habits (*vāsanā*). Like stubborn wood, they make no distinction between kin and stranger. They are different [from others].

Those who are deceitful, eccentric, mediocre, or dull; those who are fierce, predatory, lowly, or weak; and those who are diligent or even refined and erudite—these differences arise because their habitual tendencies differ, and thus their karmic retributions are likewise different.

Ānanda, there are furthermore those who follow others and do not rely on the Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts to preserve their forms and solidify their bodies, wandering in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary men.
Ānanda, there are ten kinds of such immortals (*ṛṣi*). Those beings who steadfastly consume medicinal elixirs without ceasing, until the path of food is perfected, are called earth-walking immortals.

Those who steadfastly ingest herbs and plants without ceasing, until the path of medicine is perfected, are called flying immortals. Those who steadfastly refine gold, stone, and cinnabar (*dhātuka*) without ceasing, until the path of transformation is perfected, are called roaming immortals.

The *khecarī-ṛṣi*: Firmly stabilizing movement and stillness (regulating the body through the vital energies) without ceasing, one achieves the perfection of the *vāyu* and *śukra*; this is called the *khecarī-ṛṣi*. Firmly stabilizing the *rasa* (saliva/essence) (expelling the old and inhaling the new) without ceasing, one achieves the perfection of the virtue of moisture (*snigdha-guṇa*).

One who is firm in refined essence and color (clad in rainbows and drinking dew), practicing without rest until the absorption of the pure is perfected, is called a *devacara-ṛṣi*. One who is firm in incantations and prohibitions, practicing without rest until the mastery of ritual arts is perfected, is called a *vihāyacara-ṛṣi*.
One who is firm in contemplation (serenely concentrated and refined reflection), practicing without rest until the perfection of recollection, is called a *pratibhānacara-ṛṣi*.

One who is firm in sexual union, practicing without rest until the perfection of responsive resonance, is called a *sūkṣmacara-ṛṣi*. One who is firm in transformations, practicing without rest until the perfection of awakening, is called an *atyantacara-ṛṣi*. Ānanda, these are...

All such as these refine their minds among human beings but do not cultivate true awakening; they instead attain a mode of existence with a lifespan of ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far from the haunts of men.

Yet this too is saṃsāra, a wandering through deluded thoughts; failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

[The Seven Paths of the Immortals: The "Immortal" (xian) is one who dwells among the mountains, severs ties with the world, and distances themselves from secular life; by maintaining focused visualization, they solidify their physical form—this constitutes a distinct practice.

Nevertheless, because they must take harmony, benevolence, and sincerity as their foundation, they are ranked inferior to the Celestial Beings (tian) yet superior to ordinary humans. Those who use medicinal herbs to arrest the span of life but have not yet attained the ability to levitate are called "Earth-Walking" (dixing) practitioners. Those who use elixirs (*huandan*) for transmutation and travel through the human realm at will are called "Wandering" (youxing) practitioners; these are those who achieve practice by relying on external objects.

Those who practice prostration, stillness, and guided breathing (*daoyin*), moving and acting according to their own natural impulses, are named "Space-Walking" (kuxing) practitioners. Their internal fluids and essences are moistened within, and they move with graceful elegance.

Purity and clarity is called Celestial Practice (*devacara*); absorbing the refined essence to produce radiance and color is called Penetrating Practice (*vyomacara*); employing incantations and secret arts to transform all things is called Path Practice (*mārgacara*), for this is that which can achieve supernatural powers.

Refining the mind through pure contemplation so that it shines alone is called Illuminating Practice (*ābhāsacara*); the mutual interaction of the *kan* and *li* trigrams, representing water and fire, is called Essential Practice (*sāracara*);
profoundly investigating the principles of transformation and awakening to the spontaneity of things is called Ultimate Practice (*atyantacara*), for this is the most transcendent of all.

Ānanda, there are those among the people of the world who do not seek permanence and have not yet been able to relinquish their affection for wives and concubines; yet, amidst sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander, and through clarity and purity, they give rise to illumination.

After the end of their lives, they dwell near the sun and moon—this class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). There are others whose lustful attachment toward their own wives is thin and slight; while they enjoy the purity of their abodes, they cannot fully savor its flavor.

After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm—this class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When encountering desire, they unite briefly.

They are free from discursive thought and recollection. In the human world, their movement is slight while their stillness is abundant. After the end of their lives, they dwell serenely and radiantly in the void of space;

even the light of the sun and moon cannot reach them from above. These beings possess their own natural radiance. This class of beings is called the Suyāma Heaven. At all times they are tranquil; though there may be contact that arises, they are unable to be disturbed by it.

After the end of their lives, they ascend to a state of sublime refinement, no longer reaching the realms of humans or devas in the lower worlds, and remain so until the kalpa is destroyed, beyond the reach of the three calamities. Thus it is.

One class is named the Tuṣita Heaven. They have no desire-thoughts; they engage in worldly affairs as you do, yet at the time of union, their experience is like chewing wax. After their lives end, they are born in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
One such class is named the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. They have no worldly thoughts, yet they perform worldly affairs together with others; in the midst of sexual intercourse, they clearly transcend it.

After their lives end, they are able to universally surpass the realms of both emanated and non-emanated existence. One such class is named the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Ānanda, these six heavens, though their forms are beyond [the human realm]...
Movement: When the traces of the mind and its objects still intersect, the realm from this point downward is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

[The Eight Celestial Paths: 1. The Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*): Because one’s conduct does not match the celestial standard, it is termed "sexual misconduct" (*kāmamithyācāra*). By being able to obstruct such misconduct, the depths of the mind become clear and translucent, and one is thus reborn in the first heaven. 2. The Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three):

Because one previously ceased sexual misconduct but had not yet regulated what is proper, and even that was now slight, one attains birth there. 3. The Yāma (Yama Heaven): Although one previously... [text fragment] ...though previously...

The clouds are thin, yet the mind remains subtle and faint; it has not yet attained purity in the flavor of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. Since this [state] briefly intersects with the former [realm], there is an interval, and thus movement is slight while stillness is abundant, resulting in retribution here in these four Tuṣita heavens.

[Wenling]: Although the quieted mind increases further, one cannot yet avoid responding to contact; though this [state] involves few desires, one has not yet reached the state of no-mind in the five Nirmāṇarati heavens.

[Commentary]: "I am originally without mind, merely responding to you. The phrase "chewing wax" means it is tasteless. "Transcending the Nirmāṇarati stage" means to surpass them. Sixth, before the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.
Although he is without mind, he still responds to circumstances; though he has transcended them, he temporarily conforms to the world. Chen Cheng praised him, saying:

"In his cultivation, progress increases until the realization of the fruit is perfected. The *Śūraṅgama* and myriad practices are expounded in a single word. His resolve for the auxiliary path is diligent and earnest; though the various realms of existence are chaotic, his preparation through the precepts dwells within the field of his mind."
The Transmission says, as if cutting through a torrent: "To clarify the titles of the five kinds of sūtras, they are called the 'Concluding Sections' (*jié jīng fēn*).

Because the preceding sections on opening the understanding, interpreting the principles, and explaining the practice and realization are vast and extensive in their textual meaning, it is necessary to summarize and condense the essential points so that they may be easily memorized. Therefore, Mañjuśrī asked: 'What should this sūtra be named? How should I and all sentient beings receive and uphold it?
The name of this sūtra is *Mahābuddhōṣṇīṣa-sitātapatra-anuttara-ratnamudrā-daśadig-tathāgata-viśuddha-samudra-nayana*. This [title] is derived entirely from the divine mantra."

The name encompasses both essence, doctrine, and function. *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā* is the general designation for this divine mantra. Because it was spoken from the crown of the Great Awakened One’s head, it is called "Unsurpassed.

Because it can distinguish between demons and outsiders, it is called the "Jewel Seal. Since all Buddhas of the three periods of time have, without exception, relied upon this to shatter the dust of delusion and penetrate the illumination of the myriad phenomena, it is called the "Pure Sea-Eye.

A single drop of the sea contains the essence of all rivers; thus, by mentioning only the "eye," the entire body [of the teaching] is present therein. It is also named "Protecting and Delivering Kinsmen and Causes, Saving Ānanda."

Furthermore, regarding the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmitra in this assembly who attained the bodhicitta and entered the ocean of universal knowledge, the text is found within the fourth fascicle; she is so named because she employs the essence of the school (*zongti*) to receive her title.

She is also called "The Definitive Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata"; although the text belongs specifically to the stage of seeing the path (*darśanamārga*), its essence is fundamentally pervasive from beginning to end.

This name is derived by combining the essence and power of the school with its functional application and the characteristics of the teaching. It is also called "The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," as seen in the fifth fascicle.
Previously, this [title] was named by combining both essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*). It is also called "The Mantra-Phrases of Consecration for All Bodhisattvas’ Myriad Practices of Śūraṅgama.

Although these are divided between the two categories of cultivation (*xiū*) and realization (*zhèng*), they also penetrate the former [essence], because the function encompasses both the essence and the primary doctrine (*zōng*). Regarding the term "consecration" (*guǎndǐng*): generally in India, all profound Vaipulya sūtras containing esoteric language are subsumed under the Consecration Section.

According to this specific sūtra, it refers to the Buddhas emitting light that mutually consecrates their crowns, as well as the bodhisattvas receiving their offices through the consecration of the water of wisdom.

It is for this reason that it is said so. In general, Tiantai’s method of explaining a title consists of five aspects: namely, Name (míng), Essence (tǐ), Principle (zōng), Function (yòng), and the Characteristics of the Teaching (jiàoxiàng). Within the aspect of Name, there are further seven types: the three single [terms], the three compound [terms], and the one complete [title].

The title at the beginning of this sutra comprises the three categories of Person, Dharma, and Parable, all of which are fully present. "The Great Buddha-Crown" together with the Emanated Buddha constitutes the Person; the "Dhāraṇī Heart" is the Dharma.

Ānanda, there are those among all people in the world who cultivate their minds without relying on *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) and lacking wisdom, yet are able to restrain their bodies from practicing sexual desire.

Whether walking or sitting, they are free from such thoughts, and because no defilement of craving arises, they do not remain bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Once the habitual tendencies of desire are eliminated, the mind free from desire manifests. One takes joy in and accords with all forms of discipline (*vinaya*). Such a person is able, at the appropriate time, to practice the virtues of Brahma—namely, ethical conduct and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*).

This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*), having transcended the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmakāyika*). Their bodies and minds are wondrously perfected, their deportment is flawless, and they possess pure prohibitions and precepts, further augmented by clear awakening.

Such a person is able, at the appropriate time, to preside over the assembly of Brahmās as the Great Brahmā King (*Mahābrahmā*), possessing ethical conduct, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*). This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Great Brahmā, having transcended the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā. Therefore, among the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), first is Avṛha (No Affliction): where suffering and pleasure were previously in conflict, with the mind daily at war, now both have ceased; thus it is called "Non-intercourse. Second is Atapa (No Heat):
