Believing oneself to be already sufficient, one suddenly gives rise to groundless and great *māna* (conceit). Thus, even *māna*, *atimāna*, *mānātimāna*, *abhimāna*, or *ūnamāna* may all arise at once.

Within the mind, one still holds the Tathāgatas of the ten directions in contempt, let alone those of lower status, such as the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*. This is called "viewing oneself as superior.

Lacking wisdom to save oneself, there is no fault if one awakens to this; it is not a sign of saintly realization. If one takes it to be a sign of sainthood, then a portion of the demon of great *māna* will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to fail to pay homage to the stupas.

They destroyed the temples, smashing the scriptures and images, and said to the donors: "These [images] are made of gold or copper, or perhaps of earth and wood; these scriptures are made of tree leaves, or perhaps of layered flowers; only the physical body is truly eternal."
They do not respect themselves, yet they venerate earth and wood; this is truly a perversion. Those who have deep faith should smash [such objects], burying them in the ground.

To mislead sentient beings is to enter the Avīci Hell and lose right concentration, leading inevitably to a downward fall. Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, those good men see the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha) become clear.

Within their brilliant clarity, they perfectly realize the subtle principle and attain great conformity. Suddenly, a sense of immeasurable lightness and ease arises in their hearts, and they claim to have become sages, attaining great mastery. This is called the cause...

Wisdom. One attains various states of lightness and purity; upon awakening to them, there is no fault. Yet these do not constitute holy realization (*ārya-siddhi*). If one mistakes them for such realization, then a portion of the "demon of fondness for lightness and purity" will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to believe oneself satisfied and no longer seeking further progress.
Most of these become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings and fall into the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), they shall surely sink into ruin.

Furthermore, within that meditative absorption, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright. Within this clarity and awakening, they attain a nature of empty luminosity. Within it—

Suddenly turning toward eternal extinction, they deny cause and effect and enter exclusively into emptiness; with the mind of emptiness manifest before them, they even give rise to the view of perpetual annihilation.

To realize this [as it is] is without fault, yet it does not constitute a holy realization. If one takes it as a holy realization, then the demon of emptiness will enter their heart and viscera, leading them to slander those who uphold the precepts and label them as followers of the Hīnayāna. Such a person merely claims to have realized emptiness like a Bodhisattva.

What constitutes upholding or violating the precepts? Such a person constantly drinks alcohol and eats meat, and widely practices lewdness with faithful donors. Due to the power of demonic influence, they cause those people to be captivated and not give rise to doubt or slander.

When the ghost’s mind has long entered them, they may consume excrement and urine; these are of one kind with wine and meat—both are empty. They violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, mistakenly incur the sins of others, lose right concentration (*samādhi*), and shall surely fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative absorption, good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear. They savor its empty luminosity, penetrating deeply into the mind.

Regarding the bone: suddenly, infinite love arises within his mind. When this love reaches its peak, he becomes insane; this is then termed "greed. This is called the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

It settles smoothly and enters the mind, but lacking wisdom to sustain himself, he mistakenly falls into various desires. If he awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy. If he takes it to be a holy realization, then the demon of desire will enter his heart and viscera, and he will unilaterally preach that desire is the path to Bodhi.

He will convert laypeople, practicing desire with equality. Those who engage in sexual misconduct will be called "sons who uphold the Dharma. By the power of spirits and ghosts, in the final age, they will gather in [beings].
Ordinary fools, numbering up to a hundred, or even one hundred, two hundred, five or six hundred, or as many as ten million, will cause the demons to feel weary and leave their bodies.
Deprived of their majestic power, they will fall into royal calamities; they will mislead sentient beings and enter the Avīci Hell. Having lost right concentration, they shall surely sink into ruin.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner within the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation); thus these phenomena appear. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves when they encounter such causes.

Due to this condition, they are deluded and fail to recognize themselves, yet claim to have attained the state of a sage. Having committed a great lie, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You all should likewise take up the words of the Tathāgata after my parinirvāṇa.

Transmit this teaching to the age of the Dharma’s decay, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity; maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

[Commentary] Sixth, lacking wisdom while maintaining self-possession, one gives rise to limitless joy; seventh, through the view of superiority, one lacking wisdom gives rise to great conceit (*māna*);

eighth, through the cause of wisdom, one feels light and pure, giving rise to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); ninth, with the realization of emptiness manifest before one, one repudiates cause and effect; tenth, because the perception of the exhaustion of craving manifests, there are matters of covetous desire.

Regarding the three aspects of sensation (*vedanā*), that which arises among various objects as sorrow, decline, and anxious distress is the sensation of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) arising from disagreeable objects; that which arises as valor is... [the sensation of pleasure].

For those with great joy, pride, and greed, it arises in response to pleasant objects as physical pliancy and mental emptiness; for those with doubt and hesitation, it arises in response to neutral objects. Ānanda, regarding the ten demons of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):

when that good son cultivates *samādhi* and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet ended, his mind detaches from its form like a bird escaping from a cage, and he is already able to achieve [this state].

Thus, proceeding from this ordinary body, one ascends through the sixty stages of the bodhisattvas to attain the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), moving everywhere without obstruction. It is like a person who, while in deep sleep, utters words in a dream.

Although this person has no distinct object of cognition, their speech already possesses rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing even those who do not sleep to fully comprehend their words. This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, it is like removing dust and grime from the awakened, luminous mind. When one cycle of birth and death is perfectly illuminated from beginning to end, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception.

Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), observing that its origin lies in pervasive delusive conceptualization (*yǒngtōng wàngxiǎng*), which serves as its fundamental basis.

[Commentary] This general summary describes the manifestation of the perception of emptiness (*śūnyatā-saṃjñā*) to clarify the profundity of entering the stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, one attains the traversal through the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva;

that is, from the three gradual sequences (*tri-krama*) up to the two stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), which constitute the sixty positions. Regarding the "body born of mind" (*manomaya-kāya*): it is also called the *dharma-kāya* born of mind.

It is so named because its movement is as swift as the faculty of mind (*manas*), and because it transcends the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) by being free from grasping (*upādāna*). There are three types of this, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: because from the third stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one attains the body born of mind through the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi-sukha*).

"Sleep-talking" refers to the characteristics of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception). It means that when the five faculties, such as the eyes, are clear and not asleep, perceptions arise from the mind and permeate the five consciousnesses, causing them all to awaken to those words.

Because these are subtle characteristics of deluded thought, it is said that one is "unaware of them oneself. Thus, the ten māras take transformation as their characteristic and lustful desire as their object;

because perception (*saṃjñā*) belongs to the category of integration, there is much transformation, and because it belongs to the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), there is much lustful desire. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "All afflictions reside within the sixth consciousness."

Because the sixth consciousness is activated by mental conceptions and because the eyes and other faculties serve as its pathways, Ānanda, when that son of good family’s aggregate of feeling is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration becomes luminous within samādhi. At that time, his mind comes to cherish this perfect clarity;

he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful methods. Then, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatches a spirit to possess a person, and speaks the teachings of the sūtras. That person does not realize they have been possessed by a Māra.
Claiming for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, they come to the dwellings of those sons of good family who seek skillful means. They arrange seats and preach the Dharma;

in an instant, their forms may appear as bhikṣus so that others may see them, or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a bhikṣuṇī, or remain in a dark room while their bodies emit radiance. Such people are deluded and confused, mistaking them for Bodhisattvas and placing faith in their teachings.

Their minds are shaken and agitated, and they violate the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly indulging in lust. In their speech, they delight in talking of calamities, auspicious omens, and supernatural transformations, or they say: "As if..."

They will come to such-and-such a place to manifest in the world, sometimes speaking of the kalpa-ending fires or the calamity of war to terrify people, causing their family wealth to dissipate for no reason.

This is called the "strange ghost" who, having grown old, becomes a demon; it harasses and disturbs these people until its desires are satisfied, at which point it leaves the person's body. Both the disciples and the master will then fall into royal peril.
You must be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary]: "Single-mindedly loving perfect clarity" means desiring to perfectly clarify all phenomena in order to universally know them all. Because this arises from a mental attachment, one sharpens one's refined contemplation and greedily seeks skillful means.
Such a person does not realize they are possessed by a demon; it is what is called the "master being deluded. Thus, all ten demons arise from mental attachment.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has become empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes luminous. Within this state of samādhi, his mind may come to love wandering and roaming;

it casts its refined thoughts abroad, greedily seeking out experiences. At that time, a celestial Māra watches for such an opportunity and sends forth his essence to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth. That person, moreover, does not realize they have been possessed by a Māra.

He also claimed to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and came to the dwelling of that good man who sought his teachings. He spread out a seat and preached the Dharma, yet his own physical form underwent no change.

Those listening to the Dharma suddenly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into masses of purple-gold light. Every member of the assembly experienced this, attaining what they had never known before.

This man was deluded and confused; he led them to believe he was a Bodhisattva, while his mind was licentious and dissolute. He violated the Buddha’s Vinaya, secretly indulging in lustful desires. He was fond of saying that various Buddhas had appeared in the world, pointing to such-and-such a place...

That person must be an emanation of a certain Buddha who has come here; that other person must be a certain Bodhisattva or the like who has come to transform those among humanity. Because people see them, their hearts give rise to a yearning of devotion.

When false views arise secretly, the wisdom of all-knowledge is extinguished; this is called the *pātra* ghost. Having grown old, it becomes a demon that harasses and disturbs the person. Once its desires are satisfied, it departs from the person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary]: "The two minds wandering in attachment" refers to the actual events experienced; "the physical form remains unchanged" points to the person possessed by a māra. Furthermore, these ten māras are identical to the aforementioned ten ghosts, such as those who commit sins through greed for objects or those who manifest as monsters.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (samādhi) becomes luminous. Within this samādhi, the mind develops a subtle attachment; it clarifies its refined contemplation and greedily seeks a point of accord.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatching a spirit to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person is truly unaware they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks such accord, spread their seat, and preach the Dharma. Their physical form and those people listening to the Dharma remain externally unchanged.

Transformation: it causes those who hear it to attain spontaneous awakening before they have even heard the Dharma; their thoughts shift and change moment by moment, such that they may gain knowledge of past lives, possess the power of knowing others' minds, or see the hells.
Some may come to know the various matters of human likes and dislikes; some may speak verses aloud, while others recite sutras themselves. Each finds such joy as they have never experienced before.
Such people are deluded and confused, mistaking this for a bodhisattva. Their hearts become deeply attached to it, and they violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in lustful desires.

They take pleasure in saying that there are "great" and "small" Buddhas—that a certain Buddha is a former Buddha and another is a later Buddha—and that among them there are both true and false Buddhas, as well as male and female Buddhas; the same applies to bodhisattvas. Because they see these things, they wash away their original resolve and easily fall into heterodoxy.

"Awakened One! This is called a *māyā-ghost*. Having grown old, it becomes a demon (*māra*) that harasses and disturbs this person. Once its desire is satisfied, it leaves the person's body; then both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity."
"You should awaken first; do not enter saṃsāra. If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. [Commentary:

The three minds of love and attachment are matters of "mysterious union" (*minghe*). That which is hidden and mysterious yet in accord with reality is entirely false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Before hearing the Dharma, the mind was already capable of awakening;
that one can also perceive the likes and dislikes of the human world is itself a matter of mysterious resonance.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous. Within this *samādhi*, the mind cherishes its fundamental source and exhaustively examines the transformations of things, tracing the beginning and end of their nature.

The mind becomes refined and alert, greedily seeking analytical discernment. At that time, a celestial Māra, waiting for such an opportunity, dispatches his essence to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma.

That person does not initially realize they are possessed by a Māra, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. He comes to the place of the son of good family who seeks the ultimate source, spreads out a seat, and preaches the Dharma; his body possesses majestic authority.
The deity subdues those who seek [refuge], causing them to submit naturally even before hearing the Dharma beneath his seat. These people regard the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, bodhi, and dharma-body as...
This very physical body of mine, wherein fathers and sons are born in succession from generation to generation, is itself the Dharma-body, eternally abiding and uninterrupted.

Pointing directly to the present, this is the Buddha-land; there is no separate Pure Abode, nor the golden-hued marks of a Buddha. Such people accepted this with faith, losing their former resolve, and surrendered their bodies and lives, attaining what they had never experienced before.

These deluded and confused ones mistook themselves for Bodhisattvas; yet upon examining their hearts, they were found to have violated the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practiced lustful desires. They were fond of saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure.

The earth and the two organs of male and female are the true locus of bodhi and nirvana. Those who do not know this believe them to be foul words; these are called the evil spirits of *gudu* and *yan-sheng*.

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people. Once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary: Fourth, to exhaustively survey the transformation of things is to clarify the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative. Yet, while things have a fundamental and a derivative aspect, and affairs have a beginning and an end, those who enter into meditative absorption do not perceive this as their current realm;

they are merely disturbed by demons. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "What is not heard from them can never be grasped. Father and son, father and son, succeeding one another in mutual generation—this is the principle of the transformation of things.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the light of perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes manifest. Within this *samādhi*, the mind craves a distant response;

it circulates and investigates exhaustively, greedily seeking a hidden resonance. At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity to dispatch his essence to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth. That person has no prior awareness of being possessed by a Māra, and they even claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks such a response, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma, causing the listeners to momentarily see their bodies as if they were hundreds of thousands [of Buddhas].

Year after year, their hearts gave rise to attachment and they were unable to relinquish it. They served as slaves, providing the four types of offerings without feeling weary, each causing those in their retinue to do the same.

Know that this former teacher was originally a *kalyāṇamitra*, yet he has separately given rise to attachment to dharmas, becoming as sticky as glue or lacquer; such a person has attained what was never before experienced. This man is deluded and confused, falsely claiming to be a Bodhisattva.

Those who draw near his mind violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires. Such people are fond of saying: "In a previous life, during a certain birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person;

at that time they were my wife, concubine, or brother, and now I have come to deliver them. They claim they shall accompany you back to a certain world to make offerings to a certain Buddha, or they say there is another great radiance.

"O Deva, the Buddhas dwell therein; it is the ground where all Tathāgatas rest. Those who do not know this, who believe it to be false and deceptive, and who lose their original mind—these are called fierce ghosts."

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people. Once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will enter the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "five minds of longing and anticipation," one should immediately know through remote cognition that the manifestation of a thousand-year lifespan was due to his former master being a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); this is what is meant by "longing and anticipating through remote cognition."

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become void and subtle, and one is no longer beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration manifests its brilliance within *samādhi*. At that time, the mind desires to penetrate deeply;

one exerts oneself with diligent effort, delighting in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and craving a state of tranquil silence. Then, the celestial Māra seizes his opportunity, dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma.

That person originally does not realize they are possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks the aggregate [of sensation], spread out their seat, and preach the Dharma, causing those who listen to each recognize their own original nature.

Karma. Or, at that place, he says to one person: "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal. He then commands another person to step on the tail from behind, instantly causing that person—

He could not be overcome. Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in reverent submission. If someone gave rise to a thought, he already knew its very inception. Beyond the Buddha’s disciplinary code, he redoubled his ascetic rigor;

he slandered bhikṣus, reviled the disciples, and exposed private affairs without avoiding censure or suspicion. He delighted in speaking of future calamities and blessings, and when the time arrived, there was not even a hair’s breadth of error.

This powerful ghost had grown old and become a demon; having exhausted his appetite for tormenting this person, he left the individual's body. Both the disciple and the master fell together into the king’s prison.
Difficult! You should awaken first; do not enter saṃsāra. If you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell. [Commentary:

When the six consciousnesses deeply enter, this refers to the matter of deep knowledge. Because one delights in the tranquility of the aggregates (*skandha*) and greedily seeks stillness and secrecy, one achieves the merit of deep entry.
Each knows its own fundamental karma; even before death, one acts as a beast—this is the proof of deep entry.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become void and subtle, and one is no longer beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination. Within this *samādhi*, the mind comes to cherish knowledge and vision, diligently and painfully investigating and seeking after past lives.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity; his essence flies forth and attaches itself to a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their own mouth. That person is entirely unaware they have been possessed by a Māra, and they claim for themselves the attainment of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks such knowledge, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma. Without any apparent cause, at the place where the Dharma is being preached, that person obtains great treasures.

The Māra may at times transform himself into an animal, with its mouth holding a pearl, as well as various precious jewels, bamboo slips, tablets, and other extraordinary objects; he first bestows these upon that person.

Later, he would manifest his physical form, or entice listeners by concealing himself underground where a bright moon-jewel (candrakānta-maṇi) shone, illuminating that spot; thus, those listeners experienced what they had never known before.

He consumed many medicinal herbs instead of fine delicacies, sometimes eating for a day only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat, yet his body remained plump and full due to the power of Māra’s sustenance.

He slandered bhikṣus and reviled their followers without avoiding public censure. He was fond of speaking of hidden treasures in other regions—all such extraordinary matters—and of the places where holy sages of the ten directions were in concealment; those who followed after him often saw [these things].

There are extraordinary beings known as the spirits of mountains, forests, lands, city walls, rivers, peaks, and marshes. As they grow old, they become demons; some may even indulge in licentiousness and violate the Buddha’s precepts.

Together with their attendants, they secretly indulge in the five desires. Or, while some may be diligent, subsisting solely on grasses and trees, there are those who perform no fixed practices to disturb and confuse these people. Once the practitioners become weary and satisfied, the demons leave the bodies of those individuals;

both the disciples and the masters then fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary]: The seven mental states of craving, knowledge, and views clarify the matter of vision; one knows the precious jewels and knows the noble ones—this vision is free from doubt. "To proclaim licentiousness" means to speak of it openly.
In the *Zuozhuan*, it is recorded that Lord Ling of Chen practiced licentiousness in the court, where ruler and ministers engaged in lewd jesting.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is void and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination. Within this *samādhi*, the mind comes to crave supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and various transformations.

One investigates the source of these transformations and greedily seeks spiritual power. At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity; he hurls his essence to possess a person, who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma.

That person truly does not realize they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks such powers, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma. This person may even hold fire in their hand.

The light. He grasped that light with his hand and distributed it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who were listening. On the crowns of the heads of all those listeners, flames of fire each several feet long appeared, yet they possessed no quality of heat.

He was never burned by fire. Sometimes he walked upon water as if treading on level ground; sometimes he sat motionless in mid-air. He entered into jars or stayed within bags, passing through windows and piercing walls without any hindrance.
Only before weapons did he lack mastery. Claiming himself to be a Buddha, he wore white robes and accepted the prostrations of bhikṣus.

He slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, reviled his followers, and exposed the private affairs of others without avoiding ridicule or suspicion. His mouth constantly spoke of his mastery over supernatural powers, or he would cause people to see a Buddha from the side.

The spirits of the earth delude people with demonic power; they possess no reality. They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior, taking all manner of lewdness to be the transmission of the Dharma.

These are known as the great-power mountain spirits of heaven and earth, the spirits of the sea, the spirits of the wind, the spirits of the rivers, and the spirits of the soil—all of whom are the accumulated essences and phantoms of plants and trees over many kalpas. Or they may be dragon spirits, or immortals who, at the end of their lives, return to life as demons.

Or they may be those whose time as immortals has ended and who, though their years dictate they should die, remain in physical form and become possessed by other monsters. As they grow old, they become māras, tormenting and confusing these people until they are satiated.

When the mind arises to depart from that person's body, both the disciple and the teacher are often entangled in royal calamities. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

[Commentary]: "The eight minds of loving supernatural powers" refers to the study of the source of transformation—that is, investigating the origin of transformative change. "Dividing fire, walking through space, leaping over walls, and penetrating barriers" serves to illustrate supernatural powers and transformations.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become void and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts, within the *samādhi* of the "perfect concentration that illuminates," the mind may long for entry into cessation and investigate the nature of transformation, greedily seeking profound emptiness.

At that time, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity; his essence flies forth and attaches itself to a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a Māra, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks emptiness, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. In the midst of the great assembly, their form suddenly becomes empty, and the assembly has nothing [to perceive].

He was seen returning from the void, emerging suddenly; his appearance and disappearance were at his own will. At times he manifested his body, transparent as lapis lazuli; at other times he extended his hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of sandalwood.

Some, like thick stones or dense clouds, defile the precepts and hold the ordained in contempt; they constantly speak of non-causality and the absence of karmic fruit, asserting that death is eternal extinction with no further rebirths for either ordinary beings or sages.

Though they attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly practice lustful desires, claiming that those who indulge in such desire also attain the "empty mind. Thus they deny cause and effect. These are known as the vital energies of solar and lunar eclipses;

or as gold, jade, *zhicao* fungi, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes, which do not die for thousands of myriad years and become spirits. They are born into this land, and as they grow old, they become...

Māra will harass and disturb this person; once he has become weary and satisfied, he will depart from that person's body. Both the disciple and the teacher will often fall into royal calamities. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of saṃsāra.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell. [Commentary:

The ninth mind involves the entry into cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which concerns the matter of existence and disappearance. By investigating the nature of transformation and craving for profound emptiness, one attains the principle by which existence is maintained;

Ānanda, when that son of good family cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies vanish. Whether awake or asleep, he remains constant in one state.

His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, free from further coarse and heavy shadows of external objects. When observing the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers, they are like reflections in a clear mirror; as they come, there is nothing to which they adhere.
Transgressions leave no trace; they respond to illumination only in emptiness. Having completely understood that habitual tendencies are non-existent, there remains only the singular, refined truth.

From this point, the fundamental source of birth and death is revealed. One perceives all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category. Although one has not yet penetrated the individual origins of their respective destinies, one sees their common basis of birth, which is like a mirage—vibrant, clear, and turbulent.

This serves as the ultimate pivot for the floating sense-faculties and their objects. This is what is called the domain of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). If this vibrant, clear, and turbulent essential nature enters into its original clarity, and once clarified, returns to its original state...

As for the habit-energies (*vāsanā*): when they are like great waves that have subsided and transformed into clear water, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāluṣya*). When one examines their origin, it is found to be subtle and hidden delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

[He] takes this as its basis. [Commentary: The dreaming and sleeping of the night are the same as the mental imagining of the day. When the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, waking and sleeping become one. Since the shadows of sensory objects have already vanished, mountains and rivers are like reflections in a mirror, without any differentiation;

they are merely empty responses. What is called "long-standing habituation" refers to the root-source of the arising and ceasing of past habitual perceptions and conditions; it is the essence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). All sentient beings throughout the ten directions share this.

The basis of this life flickers in a state of daze and confusion. When these thoughts cease, this mind becomes like a clear void; as its activity manifests, the drifting dust of defilements stirs within it. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitutes the thread by which one establishes one's destiny.

Its nature is originally clear, and when its activity is broken to return to the source, the flowing habits are suddenly extinguished; thus, it serves as the cause for the water to become clear. Regarding what is reckoned by the mind, there are also ten demons (*māra*).

However, among the two demons of activity and thought, the demon of thought takes "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "delusion" (*saṃjñā*) as its essence. Within the various views of activity, there are sixty-two, namely the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭayaḥ*). [Commentary: Six...

Regarding the twelve views (*dvādaśa-dṛṣṭi*), ancient masters have not clarified their meaning; consequently, for ten centuries, people have remained equally deluded. Although the names of these views appear in the sūtras and śāstras, their essential nature has not been set forth.
Only the account in the *Dīrgha Āgama* accords with this present sūtra; however, while its categories are numerous, the specific explanations are inconsistent.

Since the meanings within the sūtra all rely on calculations of world-systems and kalpas, the sixteen views—from the four types of "eternalism" to the four types of "erroneous theorizing"—constitute the fundamental views regarding the primary eon (*pūrvakalpa*). From the sixteen views of the self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) up to the five [views regarding] nirvāṇa...

The forty-four views in the *Pāṭha* [of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*] are designated as "views of the final eon" (*antakālika-dṛṣṭi*); therefore, in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the two theories of non-causality (*ahetu-vāda*) are placed between the fundamental and the derivative views, making sixty-two in total.
This is why the sequence of these sūtras and śāstras each follows its own original source.

Ānanda, you should know that among those sons of good family who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*, their minds are concentrated and upright; thus, the ten classes of celestial Māras find no opportunity to harm them.

Only then are they able to investigate with refinement and exhaust the root of all living beings. When the source of the life-element is revealed within its fundamental class, they contemplate that profound, pure, and perfectly turbulent source of movement.

If, within that perfect source, they give rise to speculative calculations, such a person falls into two theories of causelessness. First, this person perceives that the origin is causeless. Why is this? Because this person has already completely shattered the mechanism of birth.

Riding upon the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty, one sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas. One perceives the winding currents of karma as they die here and are born there, seeing only the cycle of these beings revolving in those places.

Beyond eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing can be observed; thus, one forms this interpretation: "These worldly beings of the ten directions have existed spontaneously for eighty thousand kalpas without cause.

By such conceptualization, one loses right and universal knowledge, falls into the ways of external paths, and becomes deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. Second, this person sees that the end has no cause. Why is this?

Regarding birth, this person has already observed its roots: they know that humans give birth to humans, and realize that birds give birth to birds. Crows have been black from the beginning; cranes have been white from the beginning.

Humans and devas are fundamentally upright; animals are fundamentally horizontal. White is not produced by washing; black is not created by dyeing. From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change or alteration. Now, at the end of this present form, it is likewise so.

Since I originally did not perceive bodhi, how could there be any further matter of attaining bodhi? You should know that today all phenomena are fundamentally without cause. Based on this calculation—

The "Deliverance of the Deceased" and the "Perfectly All-Knowing" [schools] fall into the ranks of the external paths and delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the first external path, which establishes the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).

[1. *Yuan-yuan-ji-du* (The Universal Calculation of the Origin): There are two types of causeless doctrines. The first is the universal calculation of the primary origin as the cause. By means of the merit of the eye-faculty, one perceives back through eighty thousand *kalpas*.

This is because one calculates based on the numbers of the mundane world and relies upon the perceptions of the primary *kalpa*; thus, beyond those eighty thousand *kalpas*, there is nothing dark or obscure.

The observer then calculates that those who have flowed through the winding currents of karma from time immemorial are such that humans are reborn as humans and birds are reborn as birds. These two views regarding the absence of causes in the past are identical in meaning to the preceding doctrine;

however, this observation concerns the future self, based on the final eon and arising from the view of the end. The commentary states: According to the *Āgama*, these two theories of causelessness are situated after the four types of perverse views and before the sixteen types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, they are established based on the contemplation of one's own past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and the arising of speculative views. Regarding the first theory of causelessness: there are those who [claim] that existence arises from nothingness.

Regarding the second [type of] causelessness, which arises from recollecting past events within conceptualization—wherein those events were originally non-existent—one observes with mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*) and forms such a calculation. The commentary states:

All views possess both the characteristics of a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) and mundane wisdom, because they rely upon the two objects of the fundamental [wisdom] (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Ānanda, within this samādhi, these good sons concentrate their luminous and upright minds so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

If, within this perfect and eternal reality, they give rise to speculative calculations, such people fall into the four theories of universal permanence. The first is when these people exhaustively investigate the nature of mind and objects, concluding that both have no cause.

First, this person practices until they can know that within twenty thousand kalpas, all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions circulate in a cycle, never being lost or scattered; they reckon this to be permanent.

Second, this person exhausts the source of the four great elements and finds that their four natures are eternally abiding. They practice until they can know that within forty thousand kalpas, all births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions are essentially constant, never being lost or scattered;

they reckon this to be permanent. Third, this person exhaustively investigates the six sense faculties, the manas, and the grasping of the mind, intellect, and consciousness, reaching the original source from which they arise.

Because its nature is eternally constant, through cultivation one is able to know that throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings circulate without losing [this nature]; it is primordially and permanently abiding, and even in their ultimate exhaustion, they do not lose their nature.

They reckon this to be permanent. Fourth, these people, having exhausted the source of perception (*saṃjñā*), find that the principle of their physical existence no longer functions; the movement and circulation of the mind of birth-and-extinction have now been eternally extinguished.

Within this principle, they naturally conclude that there is neither birth nor extinction. Based on what their minds have measured, they reckon this to be permanent. Because of this reckoning of permanence, they lose right and universal knowledge and fall into the ranks of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the second external path: the doctrine of establishing a perfect permanence.

[The second category, the views of permanence and eternity,] constitutes the four theories of universal permanence (*sarvatraga-śāśvata-vāda*). These four theories of universal permanence are: first, contemplation of the mind and its objects; second, contemplation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); third, contemplation of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*);

and fourth, contemplation of the principles of the aggregates (*skandha*). Calculating these collectively as permanent, they are called the four theories of universal permanence. Furthermore, the four theories of universal permanence in the *Āgamas* arise from contemplating the duration of kalpas:

first, those who can remember twenty kalpas of formation and destruction; second, those who can remember forty kalpas of formation and destruction; third, those who can remember eighty kalpas of formation and destruction; and fourth, those who observe by means of their own wisdom.
The world collectively reckons that both self and others are eternal; this is called the fourth view of universal permanence.

Furthermore, within samādhi, O sons of good family, when one’s mind is firm, concentrated, and upright, Māra finds no opportunity. One exhaustively investigates the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

If, amidst the consideration of self and others, one gives rise to speculative calculations, such a person falls into the four inverted views, specifically the doctrine that "one part is impermanent and one part is eternal. The first of these is when this person contemplates the wondrous...

They clarify their minds and, pervading the worlds of the ten directions, take this profound stillness to be the ultimate *ātman*. From this, they reckon that their self pervades the ten directions, remaining concentrated, luminous, and unmoving.

They hold that all sentient beings are born and die within the center of their own mind; thus, they name their own mind-nature "constant," while regarding those who undergo birth and death as truly impermanent in nature. This is the second type of person.

They do not observe their own minds, but observe throughout the ten directions all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Where they see kalpas being destroyed, they call this the "ultimate nature of impermanence. Where kalpas are not destroyed, they call this "ultimate permanence.

Third, these people separately observe their own minds as subtle, refined, and minute, like fine dust, circulating through the ten directions. They hold that its nature is unchanging, yet it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant.
That which is indestructible in nature they call the "permanence of the self-nature," while all death and birth flowing forth from it they call the "nature of impermanence. Fourth, these are...

When a person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they reckon this constant flow of the aggregate of formations to be a permanent nature. They regard the fact that form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth have now been extinguished as being impermanent (*anitya*).

Based on this calculation, because they hold that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the third non-Buddhist doctrine:

[The three types of self-and-other conceptualization] constitute four inverted doctrines: first, regarding the object of observation, taking the principle of profound stillness as permanent while regarding the nature of arising and ceasing as impermanent;

third, observing the mind as subtle and flowing, wherein even these subtle characteristics arise and cease; and fourth, taking the flowing nature of the aggregates and formations as permanent.

Form, sensation, and perception are impermanent. Furthermore, the *Āgama* discusses the "Treatise on Perversions" (*viparyāsa-śāstra*) concerning the views held by gods and humans, which are categorized into four: first, regarding Brahmā as eternal while sentient beings are impermanent;

second, regarding those who die while engaged in play as impermanent while others are eternal; third, regarding those whose minds have lost their composure and undergone transformation and extinction as impermanent;
and fourth, regarding the contemplation of the world through one's own wisdom to conceive of it as either eternal or impermanent—these are called the Four Perversions.
Furthermore, within samādhi, all you sons of good family who maintain a firm and concentrated right mind will not be given an opportunity by Māra.

When you exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if you engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states, such a person falls into the four theories of finitude. He clarifies that everything existing in the world is half-finite and half-infinite. From such deliberations, he posits finitude and infinitude.

Falling into the ranks of external paths, they delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fourth type of external path, which establishes the doctrine of finitude (*antavāda*).

Within this knowledge and vision, those who give rise to speculative calculations fall into four kinds of perverted, non-dying, evasive, and universally conceptualized false theories. The first is the person who contemplates change...

The source of transformation: where one perceives shifting flux, it is called "change"; where one perceives continuity, it is called "permanence. Where one perceives that which is seen, it is called "arising"; where one does not perceive the locus of seeing, it is called "cessation.

The person replies: "I am now both arising and ceasing; both existent and non-existent; both increasing and decreasing. At all times, they confuse their speech, causing the questioner to lose the essential points of the teaching.

The nature of the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), the indecisive equivocation regarding immortality (*amarā-vikṣepa*), and the pervasive conceptualization of false doctrines—these constitute the four kinds of deceptive discourse (*vitaṇḍā*). First, because one understands by contemplating the eight objects in their totality, knowledge and views are manifold and the responses are indeterminate.
