Regarding these four types of evasive and confused responses (*vāg-vibhramśa*), the first represents complete knowledge, the second and third represent pervasive perversion, and the fourth represents a middle position.

Furthermore, according to the *Āgamas*, there are four kinds of evasive discourse arising from calculating views concerning cause and effect, wherein one gives different answers to different questions: (1) giving different answers to different questions regarding the retribution for good and evil; (2) giving different answers to different questions regarding the existence or non-existence of future lives;

(3) giving different answers to different questions regarding what constitutes good and evil; and (4) giving different answers to different questions based on ignorance, delusion, and dullness. Each of these comprises sixteen views.

Regarding the first three [stages], all are realized through the samādhi of concentrated intent; regarding the last one, it is observed through the wisdom of swift characteristics (*kṣipra-lakṣaṇa-jñāna*), which is the principle of establishing the conventional from the ultimate.

Furthermore, within this *samādhi*, O sons of good family: with a mind firm, stable, and upright, Māra finds no opportunity. One exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source within the inexhaustible flow.

Those who give rise to conceptual calculations will fall into the view that there is a sign after death; their resolve becomes inverted, such that they may either cling to their own bodies, saying "form is the self," or perceive...

"I am round," encompassing the entire realm; "I have form," or following previous conditions, as they revolve with me, "form belongs to me"; or again, "I depend upon it," continuing through the formations, "I am within form"—these are all conceptual reckonings.
After death, there is a sign, and thus one cycles through sixteen such signs. From this, one may further reckon in terms of ultimate affliction.

Ultimate Bodhi consists of two natures that proceed side by side, each without touching the other. Based on this speculative calculation, they assert that there is existence after death; thus they fall into the ranks of the externalists, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the sixth externalist school’s doctrine of the five aggregates, which maintains that there is a sign of existence after death—a theory of inverted mind.

[The Six Inexhaustible Speculations] There are sixteen aspects; the Sūtra indicates four speculations while also presenting their causes: first, because one speculates that form is the self, one clings to one's own body;

second, because one perceives the nature of the self as all-pervasive, one speculates that the self possesses form; third, because one perceives preceding conditions as following the self, one speculates that form belongs to the self;

fourth, because one perceives the continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one speculates that the self exists within form—and the same applies to sensation, perception, and formations, making sixteen views in total. These are reckoned as the "Jewel of Views."

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Self" refers to the nature of a sovereign; "what belongs to the self" refers to the nature of the five aggregates. Furthermore, in the *Āgamas*, sixteen types of views of self are enumerated based on contemplating one's future place of rebirth and giving rise to conceptualizations.

These are the views of the final aeon (*antakalpa*), specifically the views of the end (*antadṛṣṭi*). First: [the view that] after my death, I will be born with form and with perception. Second: [the view that] I will be born without form but with perception. Third:

[the view that] I will be born with both form and no form, yet with perception. Fourth: [the view that] I will be born with neither form nor no form, yet with perception. Fifth: [the view that] I will be born with a finite limit.

1. Those with perception who are born in the realm of infinite space; 2. Those with perception who are born in the realm of infinite consciousness; 3. Those with perception who are born in the realm of nothingness; 4. Those with perception who are born in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; 5. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of the first dhyāna; 6. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of the second dhyāna;

7. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of the third dhyāna; 8. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of the fourth dhyāna; 9. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of joy; 10. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of rapture; 11.

Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of equanimity; 12. Those with perception who are born in the realm of the gods of form; 13. Those with perception who are born as beings possessing only a single perception; 14. Those with perception who are born as beings possessing manifold perceptions.
Fifteenth is the perception of limited existence; sixteenth is the perception of immeasurable existence.

Furthermore, when those sons of good family within *samādhi* maintain a firm, concentrated, and upright mind, Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings, contemplating that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

Among those who, having previously eliminated form, sensation, and perception, give rise to speculative calculations, such persons fall into the view that after death there is no appearance. Their resolve becomes inverted; seeing that form has ceased, they perceive that the physical shape no longer exists.

One observes the cessation of perception; the mind has no attachments. One knows the cessation of sensation, such that there is no further connection. The nature of the aggregates dissolves and disperses;

even if the processes of life persist, they are devoid of sensation and perception, being the same as grass and trees. When this physical substance is present before one, it cannot even be grasped; how could any signs remain after death? Through such investigation, one finds that after death, all signs are absent.

Thus it revolves in cycles. There are eight signless states. From this, some may reckon that the causes and effects of *nirvāṇa* are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to annihilation.

Based on such speculative reckoning, because they hold that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ranks of the external paths (*tīrthika*) and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the seventh external path: the perverse doctrine of the signless mind after death, established within the five aggregates.

[The seventh: the calculation of prior extinction. "There are eight aspects. [Wenling says: The dissolution of the nature of the aggregates refers to the cessation of form, sensation, and perception; the underlying principle is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because these four aggregates are discussed in terms of the present cause being extinguished and the future fruit being extinguished, they constitute eight aspects when cause and effect are treated together. [Commentary: The *Āgama* states:

"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the view of the end, give rise to the doctrine of non-perception (*asaṃjñika-vāda*), asserting: 'After my death, there is birth with form but without perception; there is birth without form but without perception; there is birth..."
There is the view that there is both form and no-form in the rebirth of non-perception; the view that there is neither form nor no-form in the rebirth of non-perception;

the view that the rebirth of non-perception is finite; the view that the rebirth of non-perception is infinite; the view that the rebirth of non-perception is both finite and infinite; and the view that the rebirth of non-perception is neither finite nor infinite—these are the eight views.

Furthermore, among the sons of good family within *samādhi*, those who have stabilized their minds in right concentration and for whom Māra finds no opening, investigate the fundamental source of all living beings—that which is profoundly pure yet constantly agitated.

While abiding in the sphere of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). They dualistically calculate existence and non-existence, causing their own essential nature and characteristics to conflict. These individuals fall into the "neither-exist-nor-not-exist" state after death and give rise to inverted theories.

Within form, sensation, and perception, they perceive both existence and non-existence; within the flux of mental formations, they contemplate both non-existence and not-non-existence. Thus they cycle through and exhaustively analyze the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*), eventually grasping one of the eight aspects of "neither-exist-nor-not-exist."

Regarding these conditions, all say that after death there are both the possessed of marks and the markless. Furthermore, because they calculate that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, the mind gives rise to a penetrating realization that both existence and non-existence are neither, and one loses the distinction between the real and the unreal.

Based on this speculative reckoning, they conclude that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence; because the future limit is obscure and beyond description, they fall into the ranks of the externalists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the eighth externalist school:
the theory of the inverted mind which posits that within the five aggregates there is neither existence nor non-existence after death.

[The Eightfold Calculation of Existence and Cessation] There are eight aspects: because the first three have already ceased, one perceives within form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) that they both exist and do not exist; because the last one still remains, one perceives the flux of formations (*saṃskāra*);

by internally contemplating that there is neither existence nor non-existence, and by simultaneously contemplating both existence and non-existence as being neither, these constitute the eight aspects—namely, it is not that form, feeling, perception, and formations exist, yet it is also not that form, feeling, perception, and formations do not exist.

Regarding the *Āgama*’s "Treatise on the Eightfold Neither-Existence-nor-Non-existence," it refers to certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, during the final eon and holding views regarding the end, give rise to the notion of the "Neither-perception-nor-non-perception" realm (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

The doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññīvāda) asserts that after this life ends, there is rebirth as one who possesses form yet has neither perception nor non-perception;

or rebirth as one who is formless yet has neither perception nor non-perception; or rebirth as one who possesses both form and formlessness yet has neither perception nor non-perception; or rebirth as one who possesses neither form nor formlessness yet has neither perception nor non-perception;

or rebirth as one who has a finite existence yet has neither perception nor non-perception; or rebirth as one who has an infinite existence yet has neither perception nor non-perception; or rebirth as one who has both a finite and an infinite existence yet has neither perception nor non-perception.
"Neither-perception-nor-non-perception," "existence," "neither finite nor infinite," and "neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—these constitute eight views.

Furthermore, O sons of good family, within *samādhi*, when one stabilizes and concentrates the upright mind so that Māra finds no opportunity, and one exhaustively investigates the root of all living beings, observing that source which is profound, pure, yet constantly agitated, if one subsequently engages in speculative calculations regarding its non-existence, such a person falls into the seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
These include calculating the annihilation of the body, the annihilation of desire, the annihilation of suffering, or the annihilation of the extreme..."

Pleasure ceases, or there is the cessation of ultimate equanimity; thus they cycle through these states until the seven limits are exhausted, whereupon they manifest and then dissolve, and once dissolved, they no longer exist. Based on this calculation, they conclude that after death there is annihilation.

Having fallen into the ranks of the external paths, they delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the ninth external path: the inverted doctrine of the mind that asserts the annihilation of the five aggregates after death.

[The ninth is the absence of discursive calculation. Regarding the seven proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), the *Āgama* states: "There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the future limit and the view of the end, give rise to theories of annihilationism;

there are seven such views in total. Some calculate that my body, having arisen from causes and conditions, must inevitably return to destruction; some calculate that I shall be annihilated among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); some calculate that I shall be annihilated among the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

some calculate that I shall be annihilated in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); some calculate that I shall be annihilated in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); or some calculate that I..."

To conceive that extinction occurs within the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), or to reckon that the self is extinguished within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—these constitute seven views.

Furthermore, O sons of good family, when one’s mind is firm, concentrated, and upright within *samādhi*, Māra finds no opportunity. One exhausts the root of all living beings and contemplates that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

Yet, if one subsequently gives rise to speculative calculations regarding future existence, such a person falls into the five theories of *nirvāṇa*. Some take the Desire Realm as the true basis for transformation; observing the perfect luminosity therein, they give rise to attachment.

They may aspire to the first dhyāna because its nature is free from sorrow; or to the second dhyāna because the mind is free from suffering; or to the third dhyāna because it follows upon extreme bliss;

or to the fourth dhyāna because both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and one does not undergo the cycle of birth and death, as that is its inherent nature. Thus, they become deluded regarding the tainted heavens, taking them to be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding these five abodes as secure, they regard them as the supreme, pure refuge.

Thus, by cycling through these five states to their ultimate limit, they calculate and conceptualize these five as being "present nirvana. Consequently, they fall into the ranks of the heterodox and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the tenth heterodox school:

establishing "five present nirvanas" within the five aggregates (*skandhas*), a doctrine of inverted mind. Ānanda, these ten kinds of wild interpretations of *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) in a state of mutual interaction;

thus, these realizations appear. Beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not examine themselves, and when these states manifest before them, they mistake delusion for understanding and claim to have attained the rank of a Sage. Great!
Lying leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell. You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma.

Cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning, so that the demons of the mind do not give rise to deep calamities within themselves. Maintain and protect them, causing false views to subside; instruct their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning.

On the Unsurpassed Way, let them not encounter divergent paths, and do not allow their hearts to seek the small and consider it sufficient. Become Great Enlightened Kings, providing pure pointers for others.

[The Ten Speculations on Future Existence: Regarding those who propound five theories of *nirvāṇa*, because they seek the return to the source through the exhaustion of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), they grasp at five kinds of fruits.

Since only the desire realm possesses the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they perceive its clarity and perfection and thus give rise to attachment and delight. As the *Āgama* states: "One gives rise to the theory of *nirvāṇa* within present phenomena. This is entirely included within the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*).

That is to say, some say: "I am self-indulgent in the five desires of the present; this is present *nirvāṇa*. Or, they take the first dhyāna as present *nirvāṇa*, or they take the second dhyāna as present [nirvāṇa].
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, some take the third dhyāna as the present *nirvāṇa*, while others take the fourth dhyāna as the present *nirvāṇa*; these constitute five views.
Furthermore, it is said that if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas hold views concerning the future eon (*aparantika*) or views of the future limit (*aparantadṛṣṭi*), they all fall within these forty-four views;

or those who hold views concerning the past eon (*pūrvāntika*) or views of the past limit (*pūrvāntadṛṣṭi*) fall entirely within the eighty-six views; or those who hold views concerning both the past and future eons fall entirely within the sixty-two views. Only the Tathāgata knows these views.
Abiding thus and maintaining thus, that which is known likewise transcends this; though knowing it, one does not cling to it—this is the subtle and great Dharma-light of the Tathāgata. Commentary:

These sixty-two views, the World-Honored One likewise knows and likewise sees them, yet he merely does not cling to them. This is because non-Buddhists establish their knowledge through their views, thereby forming a web of views;

whereas the Tathāgata, through his knowledge and vision being devoid of [subjective] seeing, achieves Bodhi. Therefore, the conclusion states: "They fall into the ways of non-Buddhists and delude the nature of Bodhi."

Furthermore, regarding the general discussion of the origin of various views, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* explains the sixty-two views as having the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root, because it speaks in terms of their basis and origination.

The *Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states that various divergent views all rely on existence and non-existence, speaking in terms of speculative investigation (*vitarka*). The commentary says: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states, "Whether there is existence or non-existence," etc.;

these rely upon these various views, which fully comprise the sixty-two, and this is precisely the meaning of speculative investigation. Moreover, if one summarizes the origin of all views, they do not go beyond [these categories].

The five利使 (sharply active afflictions) are precisely the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only); therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the views of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are the masters of the five views and the sixty-two views.

Ānanda, regarding the ten demons of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): when that good son practices *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the various natures of the world—those subtle, pure, and turbulent movements of the commonality of life-force—suddenly shatter.

The deep-seated cords and knots, the *pudgala*, and the profound channels through which karma is requited are all suspended and severed. In the realm of Nirvāṇa, he is about to attain great awakening, like the crowing of a rooster at dawn.

Gazing toward the east, there is already a refined radiance. The six sense faculties are empty and still, no longer wandering or dissipated. Internally and externally, they are profoundly clear and bright; one enters that which has nowhere to enter.

One deeply penetrates the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions and the fundamental source from which their lives originate. Observing this source, one realizes it is rooted in grasping; thus, the various classes of beings cannot summon one back. Within the realms of the ten directions, one has already attained their commonality.

This refined radiance does not sink away but manifests what was hidden and secret. This is called the domain of the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*). If, within this state of having attained the commonality of all summoned beings, one grinds away the six gates until their opening and closing are perfected, then seeing and hearing become interpenetrating.

The neighboring realms mutually employ the pure worlds of the ten directions, as well as their own bodies and minds, so that they are transparent and luminous inside and out like vaidūrya; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life-force. Observing its origin, one finds it to be based on a phantom-like voidness and inverted false conceptualization.

[Wenling] states: This passage generally describes how activity (*saṃskāra*) ceases and consciousness (*vijñāna*) manifests. Activity is the essential nature of the world’s flux and the pivotal cord that stirs the mechanism of life; it is the profound pulse through which sentient beings repay their karma.

Therefore, when the aggregate of activity is exhausted, the pivotal cord of the life-mechanism suddenly snaps, the deep pulse for repaying karma is severed from its resonance, and the nature-heaven of *nirvāṇa* is about to shine forth in great clarity as awakening occurs.

[Shu] states: Consciousness is the source of receiving one’s life-destiny. Since activity reaches its limit and consciousness manifests, one penetrates deeply into the source of life. Thus, the six sense-faculties become empty and exhausted, and there is no longer... [text ends].

Furthermore, when the galloping and fleeing [of the mind] ceases, the mechanism of arising is no longer disturbed. As the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) flows on, it does not transcend the phenomena of sense organs and objects;

because the resonance between them has become suspended, both the internal and external are profoundly clear. Since the various categories do not summon one another, one enters that which is nowhere to be entered. Having attained this sameness throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one transcends the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).

Because the six gates have been worn away, the opening and closing [of perception] are perfected. Through the mutual penetration of seeing and hearing, the six dusts (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are no longer obstructed, and the various faculties function interchangeably. Yet, consciousness remains as that which must be returned to its source.
Because this is the ground [of all], the various vehicles falsely establish causes and dependencies here to grasp at the realization of the fruit; these collectively constitute the ten māras.

Ānanda, you should know that this good man has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and returned to the source within consciousness (*vijñāna*). He has already extinguished birth and death, yet regarding this state of quiescent extinction, his subtle sentiment is not yet perfected.

This enables him to cause his own physical faculties to interpenetrate, merge, and open; he also communicates with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions, and through this pervasive awakening, he is able to enter the perfect source. If, however, regarding that to which he returns, he establishes it as "True" [and clings to it]...

Regarding those who constantly give rise to a superior resolve based on causes: such persons fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons, becoming companions of Śivika who takes refuge in the obscure principle (tattva). They become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.

This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that seeks attainment, thereby forming a fruit to which one returns; it violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the seeds of external paths.

[The Adherence to a Cause of Causes] [Wenling]: Because consciousness flows from formative forces (*saṃskāra*), when formative forces are empty, one returns to the source. Yet, taking this very state as the true ground of return and establishing it as the true cause, one falls into the adherence to a "cause of causes.
[Commentary]: The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The ālayavijñāna is the object of the samādhi of 'dwelling in happiness in the present life' for all noble ones;
it is the cause for all realms of existence, such as those of humans and devas, and for all Buddha-lands; it constantly serves as the seed-nature for all vehicles. This is precisely that meaning.

Ānanda, furthermore, there is a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death. Yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), his subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected.

If he regards that to which he has returned as his own self-nature, and perceives that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space are but a single class flowing forth from within his own body—should he form such a superior conviction (*adhimukti*), this person falls into the attachment to "the agent" and "the non-agent.

Maheśvara will manifest an infinite body to become his companion; thus he becomes deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and loses his true knowledge and vision. This is called the second [type of] establishment.

It can act as the mind to accomplish the fruit of its functional activities. This is contrary to and far removed from perfect penetration; it turns its back on the city of Nirvana and gives rise to the gods of Great Pride (*mahāmāna*).

It is the seed of the pervasive and perfect "I. [The second is the attachment to both the capable and the incapable: one grasps the source of consciousness as one's own self and claims that all sentient beings flow forth from this. Consequently, one clings to the notion that "I" can produce them, yet in reality, I cannot.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected—such a person may, regarding that which is to be returned to, take it as a place of refuge.

They then suspect that their own body and mind flow forth from that [refuge], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it. Thus, regarding the very ground from which everything flows forth, they conceive the notion of a true, eternal body free from birth and death.

While still within the midst of birth and death, they prematurely claim it to be eternally abiding. Being deluded about non-arising and likewise confused about birth and death, they dwell securely in this deep-seated confusion. One who forms such a superior resolve is a person who...

They fall into the attachments of permanence and impermanence, reckoning Īśvara as their companion; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the third: establishing a cause based on the mind.
This constitutes the fruit of false conceptualization, which is far removed from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

[3. Grasping at the Permanent as Impermanent] Because one takes the source of consciousness as a refuge, one doubts its capacity to give rise to both the self and all phenomena; consequently, one reckons that the ground from which they arise and flow forth is the essence of true permanence.

Since this is a false conceptualization of permanence within the midst of arising and ceasing, it both deludes one regarding the truly non-arising nature and confuses one regarding presently manifesting phenomena of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, the *Ghanavyūha* states: "The supreme principle (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), the Lord (*īśvara*), time (*kāla*), and so forth, which are clung to by outsiders, are all in fact the pure *ālayavijñāna*.

Furthermore, son of good family: one may exhaustively realize the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding this state of quiescent extinction, the subtle and wondrous [realization] is not yet perfected.

If, regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), one's cognition is not universally pervasive, and based on that cognition one establishes a view such that the grasses and trees of the ten directions are all called sentient beings and are no different from humans—such that grasses and trees become humans, and upon human death they return to becoming the grasses and trees of the ten directions without distinction—[this is an error].

"Vatsa, those who give rise to such resolute conviction regarding 'universal knowledge' fall into the attachment of knowing non-knowing. They become companions to Pāṭha and Sainika, who cling to the notion of universal awakening; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit true knowledge and vision.

This is called the fourth calculation: the mind that reckons itself as universally cognizant. It results in empty error, strays far from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives birth to the seeds of inverted knowledge."

[The attachment to the knowledge of the four objects as being non-knowing: That which is known is the very source of consciousness. This means that consciousness possesses knowing, and all phenomena arise through transformation based on this knowing.
Based on the calculation that the essence of knowing is perfectly pervasive throughout all phenomena, one then claims that insentient things possess knowing and are devoid of any discrimination.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize their emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose clarity and vigor regarding that cessation have not yet reached full perfection—such a person, within the state where the sense faculties are interfused and mutually functional, attains a degree of adaptability.

Consequently, they give rise to various manifestations through total transformation: seeking the radiance of fire, delighting in the purity of water, craving the circulation of wind, or contemplating the perfection of sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

Taking each of these sensory objects as the primary cause for their development, they establish a view of permanence. Such a person falls into the attachment to "birth" while clinging to the notion of "non-birth. This applies to all the Kāśyapas and the Brahmins...

This is the gate of diligent application of mind and labor of body, serving fire and venerating water to seek escape from birth and death. They become companions in this delusion, losing sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeiting true knowledge and vision.

This is called the fifth attachment: the veneration of external objects. Their minds are deluded as they follow external things, establishing false causes for their seeking and falsely hoping for results. Thus they remain far removed from perfect penetration and turn their backs on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.

[The Grasping at Birth and Non-birth in the Five Modes of Birth] [Commentary]: Because one attains the nature of perfect interfusion through the mutual functioning of the sense organs, one then calculates that all phenomena are capable of being produced and transformed.
Consequently, one venerates fire, serves water, and clings to wind; one contemplates sensory objects as the causes of perfect transformation, seeking superior fruits distinct from ordinary beings.

Furthermore, son of good family, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena to realize emptiness and has already extinguished the cycle of birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected—should such a person, regarding the perfect luminosity, reckon that the voidness within that luminosity is not the extinction of the manifold transformations, and thus takes this eternal extinction as a basis for their refuge, giving rise to a resolute conviction therein, this person falls into the attachment of "taking refuge in that which is no refuge. They become companions among the *śūnyatā* (void) beings in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

Having lost sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeited their true knowledge and vision, this is called the sixth fruit: the mind of "perfect voidness" resulting in the loss of existence, which is far removed from the Perfect [Middle Way].
They turn their backs on the city of Nirvana and give rise to the seeds of annihilationism.

[The sixth: clinging to that which has no refuge as having a refuge. (Wenling): Because they do not contemplate the principle with clarity, they mistakenly fall into falsehood; thus, within the perfectly luminous nature, they reckon all things to be empty and non-existent.
Consequently, they sever all manifestations of transformation and return to eternal extinction, taking emptiness as their refuge.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena to realize their emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose clarity and vigor regarding this state of cessation have not yet reached perfection—such a person may develop a resolute conviction that by fortifying the body to remain permanent, they will become identical with that perfected clarity and never again decline or pass away.
This person falls into the attachment of "clinging to life" (or "clinging to non-clinging"). They become companions to those *asiddhas* who seek long life;

they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh attachment: clinging to the source of life. It establishes a cause of solid delusion and leads to the fruit of prolonged toil, remaining far removed from the Perfect [Enlightenment].
Turning one's back on the city of Nirvana, one gives rise to the seeds that prolong delusion.

[Regarding the seven types of attachment and non-attachment: The essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous and remains profoundly still without wavering; this is called "the permanent. Now, seeing what appears to be permanent, you cling to the physical body as being identical to that fundamental essence.
Yet the body is inherently impermanent and truly not to be craved; it is but empty toil to labor in vain.

Furthermore, good son, when one has exhausted all conditioned phenomena to the point of emptiness and already extinguished birth and death, yet within that state of quiescent extinction, his subtle and wondrous realization is not yet perfected; he perceives that life-force is interpenetrating and, fearing its total dissolution, deliberately retains the defilements of worldly toil.

At this juncture, he sits within a Lotus Palace, extensively transforming the seven treasures and increasing his retinue of precious women, indulging his own mind until it gives rise to a superior resolve.

Such a person falls into the attachment to "the real as unreal" and becomes a companion to the *Ṭakkirāja* demons. He is deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and loses his true insight and vision. This is called the eighth instance of giving rise to deviant thoughts.

Consequently, they establish the fruit of "blazing dust," which is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of celestial and demonic beings.

[The eighth: clinging to what is not real as real] They take the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the essence of their life, for it interpenetrates the three periods of time; since they believe that if the consciousness-aggregate were exhausted, their lives would also end, they transform various objects of desire to maintain their defilements and prevent them from being extinguished, regarding this as true.

Furthermore, good son, one who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to realize their emptiness and has already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state within cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected, distinguishes between the refined and the coarse within the clarity of life, and discriminates between the true and the false.

Believing that cause and effect must reciprocate, he seeks only for spiritual response; thus he turns his back on the path of purity. This is what is called "seeing suffering and abandoning the origin, realizing cessation and cultivating the path," wherein one rests once cessation has been attained.

They no longer advance. Those who give rise to such superior resolve fall into the category of śrāvakas of fixed nature. They become companions to those unlearned monks of overweening pride; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.

This is called the ninth stage: the perfectly refined mind responding to the objective. It results in the fruit of quiescent seclusion; it violates and distances itself from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of being entangled in emptiness.

[The Śrāvaka of Fixed Nature] [Commentary]: To clarify the principle based on consciousness is called "illumination of life" (*jīva-prakāśa*). This means that arising and ceasing depend on consciousness; the coarseness or subtlety of existence depends on karma.

One distinguishes and discerns according to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: taking suffering and its origin as coarse and false, and cessation and the path as subtle and true. One exclusively cultivates the cause of the Path to seek the realization of the fruit of cessation.

Once abiding in cessation, one rests and does not proceed further; this is termed the "Śrāvaka of Fixed Nature. The *Sūryaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Fearing suffering and loathing the body, one sets one's will upon Nirvāṇa and falls into the state of an Arhat."

Furthermore, good son, having exhausted all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) into emptiness and already extinguished birth-and-death, one may yet find that within this state of quiescent extinction, the subtle and wondrous has not reached full perfection.

If, regarding the perfectly integrated, pure, awakened clarity, one investigates its profound subtlety and establishes it as *nirvāṇa*, failing to advance further toward the development of superior resolve, such a person falls into the category of a *pratyekabuddha* of fixed nature.

They become companions to those solitary practitioners who do not turn their minds back toward enlightenment; they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth stage: the mind of perfect awakening stagnates and forms a fruit of limpid clarity, thereby remaining far removed from the Perfect [Awakening].
[The Ten Determinate Pratyekabuddhas] turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa, giving rise to a perfected clarity of awakening (*bodhi*) rather than the seeds of transformation.

Because their wondrous, perfect true essence has exhausted both delusion and habit-energy, it is called "pure, clear, and enlightened awareness. Within profound stillness and wondrousness, they reach the ultimate fundamental truth and develop a deep investigation of the subtle and wondrous;

taking this as their fruit, they are named "Determinate-nature Pratyekabuddhas. Thus, the *Riju-ming jing* says: "They cling to the physical marks of the Buddha and do not penetrate the skillful means of the Middle Way, and so they stop there."

One may fall into the path of the pratyekabuddhas; however, this aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) presides over the eight consciousnesses, and since these eight consciousnesses are the root of all vehicles, it is within this that the methods of cultivation and realization for both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are universally explained.

Thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The Buddhas and all bodhisattvas are all the ālayavijñāna. It is named the Buddha, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—those who have seen the principle and are free from cowardice;
what they perceive is all this very consciousness.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through their practice because they rely on delusion; within what is not yet attained, one gives rise to the realization of fulfillment.

All of this arises from the interaction of the mind with the *vijñāna-skandha*, and thus one arrives at this stage. Beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves; when these states manifest before them, each rests according to their own attachments and previously practiced deluded minds, taking them to be the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.
They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *bodhi*. Thus, the great false speech is established, and the karma produced by such externalists and malevolent spirits is incurred.

In the end, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas shall not achieve further progress. You all should maintain this intention and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, and propagate this Dharma-gate after my parinirvāṇa.

I transmit this to the final age so that all sentient beings may universally awaken to and understand this meaning. Do not allow them to encounter demons or create their own deep-seated calamities; protect, console, and rescue them, causing evil conditions to subside, so that their bodies and minds may enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

From the very beginning they shall achieve success and never encounter divergent paths. Such a Dharma-gate, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in past ages, has enabled countless Tathāgatas to open their minds by relying upon it and attain the Unsurpassed Way.

When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably. From within this mutual functioning, you will be able to enter Bodhi.

The vajra-dhāraṇī of adamantine dry wisdom and the perfectly luminous, refined mind issue forth from within it, like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon. In this way, one transcends the ten stages of faith and the ten abodes.

The ten practices, the ten dedications, the four preparatory minds—these are the conducts of the bodhisattvas. The ten vajra stages, the perfectly luminous equal enlightenment, they enter directly (without gradual progression) into the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornments.

"Perfecting Bodhi, one returns to the state of non-attainment. This is what the World-Honored Buddhas of the past realized through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: the subtle demonic affairs arising from the analytical discernment of enlightened clarity.

When such demonic realms manifest before you, if you can recognize them, the defilements of the mind will be washed away; you will not fall into false views, the *skandha-māras* will be extinguished, and the *deva-māras* will be shattered.

Greatly powerful spirits and ghosts will lose heart and flee, while *chis-mei* and *wang-liang* demons will never arise again. Until you reach Bodhi, you shall lack nothing; even those of inferior capacity will advance toward Great Nirvāṇa."

Bāna, your mind shall not be confused or distressed. If, in the final age, there are foolish and dull-witted sentient beings who do not yet recognize *dhyāna*, who do not know how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing *samādhi*, you may fear that they will fall into heterodoxy.

I wholeheartedly exhort you to uphold this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī mantra. If you are unable to recite it, write it down in your meditation hall or carry it upon your person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to disturb you.
You should reverently honor the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, cultivate and advance toward the ultimate goal, and follow these final instructions.
Ānanda, the concluding summary of the preceding sutra—referring to the "Vajra-dry-wisdom" and so forth—summarizes cultivation and realization.

Because what is cultivated in this *dhyāna* does not pass through the various stages, it transcends faith and other levels to enter directly into the ocean of wondrous adornment, thereby accomplishing the practices of Samantabhadra.

In the *Eightfold Discourse on the Bonds*, Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance and memorized it without error. Within the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more:

"Regarding the five kinds of delusion within the characteristics of the five aggregates that the Buddha has described as being the fundamental mind, we have hitherto not received such subtle and detailed elucidation from the Tathāgata. Furthermore, as for these five aggregates..."
"Is it for simultaneous eradication? Or is it for gradual exhaustion? Thus, across these five stages, what constitutes their boundary?

I only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion, to clarify the minds and eyes of this great assembly, and to serve as the future eye for all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age. The Buddha told Ānanda: "The essence of purity, wondrously luminous, is the fundamentally awakened, perfectly pure state.

It does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements; even empty space arises solely from the production of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This is originally the wondrously luminous, true essence of fundamental awakening, yet through delusion, it gives rise to [phenomena]."

The various receptacle worlds arise like Yajñadatta, who, deluded, mistook his own head for its reflection; thus, within a state of false conceptualization that is fundamentally without cause, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions—

It is called "spontaneous. That nature of space is itself like a real illusion produced by causes and conditions. Ānanda, all that is spontaneous is merely the conceptual construction of the deluded mind of sentient beings.

Knowing where delusion arises, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion; yet if delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then the causes and conditions of delusion would fundamentally not exist at all. How much more so for those who, lacking such knowledge, speculate about spontaneity?
Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false imagination.

[Commentary] From "The true essence, wondrously bright" (*zhēn jīng miào míng*) onwards, the text further clarifies the elimination of delusion, which is a continuation of the *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) section. By simultaneously discarding both "causes and conditions" (*yīnyuán*) and "spontaneity" (*zìrán*), it causes emotional attachments to become empty and the underlying principle to become tranquil.

This summarizes the general purport of the entire sutra. Because [the path] does not end in extinction, the way back [to enlightenment] flourishes; thus, the five delusions are identified as the root, and their dissolution is directed toward the ultimate refuge.

Below, Ānanda asks about the causes and conditions for the arising of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which he considers to be the original mind. Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates, are they to be eliminated all at once, or are they exhausted sequentially?

Regarding this question concerning the causes and conditions for cessation, the Buddha spoke as follows to refute the sentiments of [belief in] causes and conditions and spontaneity (*svabhāva*). The commentary states: According to the sūtras and śāstras, there are several ways of explaining the meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (or *Xianzong lun*) says: "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to that which can produce; "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to that which can nourish. Through the assistance provided by the cause, the cause is then able to produce;

once produced, the power of the condition nourishes its continuity. Alternatively, the cause may be singular while the conditions are numerous. Furthermore, that which is not shared is the cause, whereas that which is shared is the condition—such as the eye and visible form. Moreover, that which performs its own specific function is called a cause; that which performs a general function is called a condition.

Other matters are termed "conditions" (*pratyaya*); furthermore, that which can induce [an effect] is called a "condition," while that which sustains it is called a "cause" (*hetu*). That which is proximate is termed a "cause," and that which is remote is termed a "condition.

A cause is that which can produce, whereas a condition is that which can bring about [the manifestation]. Furthermore, that which possesses the sense of primary existence is called a "cause," while that which assists in making the meaning manifest is called a "condition. Because causes are intimate and conditions are remote, one should contemplate their remoteness and frequency within the context of causes and conditions.

Moreover, "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*) may be termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), "intrinsic characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*), "intrinsic entity" (*svātman*), "intrinsic dharma" (*svadharma*), or "self-awakening" (*svasaṃbodha*), and so forth.

The substance of your body was originally produced from the thoughts of your parents. If your mind were not characterized by thought, it would be unable to enter into the realm of thought to transmit life.

As I have previously said: when the mind thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva arises in the mouth; when the mind thinks of climbing a high place, a tingling pain arises in the soles of the feet. Though the precipice does not exist and the vinegar has not arrived, the substance of your body is certainly not a false phenomenon like common things.

For what reason would saliva emerge upon speaking of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that this present physical form of yours is called the first solid delusion. This is precisely what is meant by "the thought of being on a height."

The mind can cause your physical form to truly experience bitterness and astringency; arising from causes and conditions, it can move the substance of the body. Now before you, both that which is favorable and beneficial and that which is adverse and harmful manifest and drive you about.

This is called the second false imagination, "empty clarity. It arises from your thoughts and deliberations, which drive your physical body. Your body is not of the same category as thought; for what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?

It assumes various forms and appearances, with the mind generating shapes that correspond to thought. When awake, it is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams. Thus, your thoughts and perceptions cause the deluded emotions to fluctuate; this is called the third false imagination, "interfusion.

Its transformative principle never ceases, moving on in secret and subtle shifts: nails grow, hair lengthens, vital energy wanes, and the face wrinkles. Day and night they replace one another, yet you are never aware of it.

"Awakened! Ānanda, if this [mind] were not you, how could its essence undergo change? If it must be truly yours, why do you have no awareness of it? Thus, your various mental formations (*saṃskāra*) ceaselessly stop at every moment;

this is called the fourth subtle and hidden false imagination. Furthermore, that which is your brilliant clarity, profoundly still and unshakable, and which you name 'the eternal,' does not depart from the body in its seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

If it were truly brilliant and real, it would not tolerate the cultivation of delusion. For what reason, then, did you once in years past behold a wondrous object, yet after the passage of years, there was neither memory nor forgetting of it, until later, suddenly—"

Upon looking back at what was previously different, the memory remains vivid and clear, without the slightest loss. Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness, there is a continuous perfuming moment by moment;

how could there be any calculation [of its duration]? Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the ultimate reality. It is like a rapid current of water that appears tranquil from a distance; because the flow is so swift it is not seen, yet it is not that there is no flow.

If this were not the source of perception, how could it receive the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of perception? This deluded thought—which is not the mutual functioning, opening, or closing of your six sense organs—never ceases. Therefore, within your present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, these habits are deeply ingrained.
To what extent? It is a profound clarity wherein internally there is the formless and the void; this is the fifth inversion, a subtle and refined conceptualization.

A single solidified false imagination serves as the causal condition for receiving a body. [Wenling’s Commentary: Conceptualization is a false image. Due to the deep-seated channels of desire and love, the residual body naturally flows forth from within self-conceptualizing love, producing the *ālayavijñāna* (the shadow-mind).

This mind rides upon the dark pursuit of conceptualizing love, as illustrated by such accounts as seeking sour plums. This serves to verify that because the substance arises from the bonds of delusion, it accords with the principle of delusion. Second, the Void.

The delusion of clarity (*vidyā-vikalpa*) acts as the cause and condition for opposition and compliance; it is like the empty space of a hollow vessel where the sensations of astringency and bitterness arise. Since both opposition and compliance are illusory, the resulting harm or benefit is merely a manifestation of mental agitation.

The delusion of fusion (*saṃsarga-vikalpa*) acts as the cause and condition for grasping at forms; those who harbor such thoughts and deliberations possess a void mind, while the physical body possesses substantiality. That these two—void and substance—are so disparate yet can influence one another is due to the fusion of thought.

The delusion of the obscure and hidden (*gūḍha-vikalpa*) acts as the cause and condition for the shifting of the essence. This subtle shifting occurs without your awareness; how could it be that your essence itself undergoes this shifting? If it were indeed your own essence, you should naturally perceive it.

Subtle delusive thoughts serve as the causal conditions for habitual cultivation. [Wuxing’s Commentary: "Seeing and hearing" constitute the essence of clarity and vigor (*jingming*), while their functioning constitutes the constant substance.

Since consciousness has no fixed location, it pervades all the sense organs. When the organs encounter objects, their functioning remains in a state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*). Prior to the arising of good or evil, this is the very substance of clarity and vigor. Fearing that sentient beings might reckon this to be permanent, the Buddha uses the notion of "habitual delusion" to refute it.

[The Sub-commentary (*Shu*): "Clarity and vigor" refers to the essence of the consciousness-nature’s limpid stillness. To abide in clarity and vigor is to stagnate in a clear emptiness and a stagnant silence, thereby abandoning the establishment of wholesome practice.

The gate of transformation refers to those who have not yet broken through the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), namely, those who sit upon the tip of the staff; therefore, the Buddha taught that this is not the true state, intending for them to break the aggregates to manifest wisdom, escape the entanglements of views regarding emptiness, and enter the gate of initiating practice.

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of deluded conceptualization. If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form;

only contact and separation constitute the limit of sensation; only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception; only cessation and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into the merging with the profound constitutes the limit of consciousness. These five aggregates originally arise in successive layers.

Their arising is due to the existence of consciousness, and their cessation proceeds from the elimination of form. In principle, they are suddenly awakened to, and through awakening, they are simultaneously dissolved; yet in practice, they are not suddenly eliminated, for...

The knots have been untied one by one until they are exhausted. I have already shown you this knotting of the *kārpāsa* cloth; what is it that you do not understand that you must ask again? You should take this root-source of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain penetration.

Transmit this to future practitioners during the age of the Dharma’s decay, so that they may recognize the nature of falsehood, develop a deep weariness with their own [deluded] births, realize the existence of Nirvana, and no longer cling to the three realms.

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are also called the five aggregates of existence (*pañcaskandha*), yet there is a distinction between them. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "These are called 'aggregates with clinging' (*sopādāna*); they are simply aggregates (*skandha*) but not clinging (*upādāna*).

This refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena. The commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains: "In the Buddha’s fruition-body (*vipākakāya*), there are conditioned untainted phenomena; because these are not produced by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, they are untainted. The *Abhidharmakośa* further states:

"In this context, the aggregates that have afflictions as their clinging are called 'aggregates of clinging' (*upādānaskandha*) because they arise from clinging, like fire from grass or chaff. Alternatively, when an aggregate belongs to clinging, it is called an 'aggregate of clinging,' just as one speaks of a king’s minister. (From the *Jianru*).

"Uniting the profound stillness" means that the upper "profound stillness" is the refined essence of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), while the lower "profound stillness" is the essential substance of the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). These six aspects of profound clarity and brilliance are originally derived from the eighth consciousness;
now that they have entered into union, these two forms of profound stillness merge into one another—this is their ultimate limit.

“Ānanda, suppose there were another person who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures and offered them as a gift to as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never failed.
What do you think? Would this person, by virtue of these causes and conditions of giving to the Buddhas, obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, “The empty space is inexhaustible.”
Precious jewels are boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to a Buddha; by relinquishing his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

How much more so for one who, before our very eyes, offers precious jewels throughout the entirety of empty space and all Buddha-lands—such merit, even if one were to contemplate it for an entire kalpa, could not be fully grasped. How then could this merit have any limit? The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never false. Furthermore, if there were a person whose body committed the four grave offenses and the ten pārājikas, yet in a mere instant passed through this world and other worlds to the Avīci Hell..."

In hells, and so on, until they exhaustively pass through every single Avīci hell throughout the ten directions, they will be able, with a single thought-moment, to take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied it during the final kalpa.

The karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished at the mere thought [of this teaching]. Their cause for suffering in hell will be transformed into the Land of Peace and Bliss, and they shall obtain blessings that surpass those of the aforementioned donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousand millionfold, and even to the point where calculation or analogy cannot reach. Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra...

One who can uphold this mantra will, as I have extensively explained, reach the end of it even if an eon were exhausted; by following my instructions and practicing according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi and no longer encounter demonic activities.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world, as well as the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, holy seers, and youths from other regions, along with the powerful spirits and deities who had first resolved their minds, were all greatly rejoiced. They paid homage and departed.

Furthermore, if one were to compare the merit of these two, the excellence of the latter would surpass that of filling the world with precious jewels and offering them as a gift; this refers to the benefit of the circulation [of the teaching]. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The various classifications of dharmas are all for the purpose of propagation and preservation. If they are correctly expounded, the Buddha’s true teaching will abide in the world.

Why is this so? [The verse says: "The Great Teacher, the Eye of the World, has long since closed; those capable of serving as witnesses have mostly perished. Without seeing the True Reality, people lack restraint due to their base deliberations."

Regarding the "Disorderly Explanation of the Holy Teachings," the commentary states that those capable of serving as evidence refer to the Buddha’s true Dharma; however, because it has largely been dispersed and extinguished, it cannot be cited as proof.

For instance, Master Weizze cited Tiantai’s explanation of *siddhānta*, stating: "*Si*" means "pervasive" (*biàn*) and "*tan*" means "bestowal" (*shī*). Yet even Tiantai had no basis for this, having merely adopted the words of Zhiyi (Siming Daoshi), whose own words were not intended as a formal citation.

These are all instances of failing to cite what is available in the literary record—a fault of one's own negligence. Furthermore, Qingliang [Xuanzang] categorized the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)... [text truncated].

In the *Śāstra on the Three Times*, the sixty-two views were explained; however, because [the author] did not cite scriptural authority and instead relied solely on his own speculative reasoning (*vitarka*) to effect their abandonment, such errors consequently arose. Therefore, in composing this commentary, I have followed the principle of citing the words of the Noble Ones as authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for every illustration.

Zhen Cheng praised him, saying: "In the ocean-like assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Ānanda encountered the causal conditions of the Mātanga girl whose mind was entangled in passion; by the light [of the Buddha] he was gathered before the World-Honored One, where his true nature was revealed and he was rescued."
Chanting and recitation benefit humans and devas.
The Verse of True Reflection states: I prostrate to the Original Teacher, the Lord of Dharma, And to all the World-Honored Ones who speak with one voice.

The Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Exoteric and Esoteric Śūraṅgama, The Tathāgatagarbha of the ten realms which is neither-identical-nor-different, The Perfectly Penetrating Honored One, Avalokiteśvara, And the assembly of sages and worthies who each enter perfect clarity. May the majestic power of these Three Honored Ones silently sustain us; This is the secret purport and subtle word.

May this cause [the Dharma] to be developed and flourish. May these commentaries not contradict the original intent, and may the thematic continuity from beginning to end be harmoniously integrated. May they accord with the capacities of beings, accord with the truth, and accord with the Buddha’s mind, so that we may together consume a single drop from the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.

If, by means of a mere glimpse through a tube, we happen to coincide with the Sage’s intention, may the conditions for its circulation be fulfilled and it be swiftly transmitted and upheld. May those who see or hear it, in the present and the future, plant excellent causes and together realize the inconceivable power of hearing and cultivation.

The Transmission says, as if cutting through a torrent: "Such a Dharma-gate—in past worlds throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—has enabled Tathāgatas as many as motes of dust to open their minds by riding upon this [mind] and attain the Unsurpassed Way.

If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is exhausted, then your present sense-faculties will function interchangeably. From within this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).

Your perfectly luminous and refined essence will manifest transformation therein, like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within. In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the four stages of preparatory application."

The Bodhisattva’s practice of the mind is the Vajra Ten Grounds. With equal enlightenment perfectly luminous, one enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments; fulfilling bodhi, one returns to non-attainment.

Knowing that even Bodhi is ultimately unattainable, how much more so other things? One who can penetrate this principle will find that all māras naturally cease. The statement that "through mutual functioning, one enters the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *kandha-vidyā*" (dry wisdom) refers generally to adamantine wisdom; it does not exclusively refer to the stage of dry wisdom prior to the ten faiths (*śraddhā*). Therefore, it is said that such a person transcends the stages of the ten faiths and so forth. As for the summary: following this account of the demonic realms, he again requested instruction on the cultivation and severance of the various marks of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The essential point of the reply states: "In principle, one must attain sudden enlightenment; riding upon that enlightenment, all things are simultaneously eliminated."

Matters are not eliminated instantaneously but are exhausted through successive stages. Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "I have already shown you the *kārpāsa* cloth; what is it that you do not understand, that you must inquire about this again?

You should take this root of deluded thought and allow your mind to attain penetration"—this clarifies self-benefit. To transmit this to the future so that those in the age of the Dharma’s decay may recognize the nature of false appearances—this clarifies benefiting others.

This clarifies the benefit for others. To deeply loathe one’s own birth, to know that there is *nirvāṇa*, and not to cling to the three realms—this clarifies the application of effort. The main body of the teaching concludes here;

what follows is solely an extensive explanation of the supreme benefits, concluding with an exhortation to uphold and propagate it, serving as the section on circulation. This sutra originally began with Ānanda’s failure to understand that the Buddha’s body is neither form nor that his voice is neither sound;

this led to Daṅga’s lustful person being transformed by illusory spells. The Buddha then, based on her arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment, examined her mind; based on her perceptions and appearances, he analyzed her vision, proceeding through the four categories and the seven...

Extending even to the exhaustion of the sūtras, the repeated inquiries regarding the characteristics of the exhaustion of the five aggregates have never gone beyond this. Therefore, one can understand that the transformed Buddha atop the crown-light and form and sound are fundamentally illusions.

If this is so, then who is it that undergoes transformation while Mādrī is in a dream? Alas! The teaching of the Great Buddha-Crown is indeed ultimate. It should be realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and its unity may be understood through both formal teachings and written words.
Furthermore, to awaken to the image and forget the words is the intent of "cutting off the stream" (*cèliú*).

Generally speaking, those who are exceedingly clever are most prone to causing errors. Why is this? It is because intelligence alone gives rise to conceptual thought.

He saw this. Because his attachment arose so suddenly, he could not bear to let go or sever it. Those who are deeply submerged in the river of craving and the ocean of desire are all people of extreme intelligence.

Ānanda, being the pinnacle of such intelligence, could not bear to let go or sever it. It was not until the time of Kāśyapa that he finally attained liberation as the Second Patriarch. Yet, he had to wait for Kāśyapa to exert his power to exclude him and refuse to speak with him;

he also had to wait for the great assembly to disperse and view him as an enemy. Thus, Ānanda was frantic and at a loss. Only when there was nothing more to be done and he reached the ultimate point of helplessness did he finally relinquish it.

Only by overturning his former understanding can one truly certify Kāśyapa’s transmission of the Dharma as that of the Second Patriarch; even if Ānanda were to possess a single hair’s breadth of cleverness upon which to rely.
How can one awaken to this delusory body, which is as minute as a speck of dust and as illusory as a bubble? Those who do not drown in the river of craving and the sea of desire are few indeed.

Therefore, when the Buddha preached the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it was entirely for the sake of Ānanda, whose cleverness made it difficult for him to relinquish [his attachments]; he opened various gates of expedient means and provided manifold exhortations, aiming directly to restore his original face.

This was truly to guide and rescue him from within the river of craving and the sea of desire. Lu Xiangshan had a saying: "This principle is easy for those drowning in profit and desire to enter, but for those drowning in..."

The words of those who hold biased opinions are difficult to accept. People say that the learning of Mount Xiang approaches Chan Buddhism; could this possibly be true? They do not realize that there is neither Chan nor Confucianism in true learning, yet they recklessly make such distinctions.

These various scholars of the Song dynasty were not only dominated by their own opinions; they were also largely clouded in mind by greed and desire. If one examines the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with care, one will certainly not give rise to false discriminations, thereby shattering all notions of difference and identity.
